Tuesday, 19th December, 1939.
The Third Session of the Fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed
to meet on 19th December, 1939, in the
Fourth year of the Reign of King
George VI, was opened by the Governor
(His Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
THE
VOLUME XXIII.
The House met at Five Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland) in
the Chair.
as

Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Acting
Gentleman Usher said:
IN THE
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Two
of the Clock, and then resumed.

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such
or other corrupt
practices.
bribery
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of this evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime
or misdemeanour; and this House will
proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.

with the utmost severity against such

ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do
take care that, during the Session of
Parliament the passages through the
streets leading to this House be kept free
and open, and that no obstruction be
permitted to hinder the passage of Members to and from this House, and that
no disorder be allowed in the precincts of
or in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts, and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no persons but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.

his attention has been drawn to the

in Kilmood Street, Belfast, when one

of the length of time that elapsed before.
the Fire Brigade responded to the call
for assistance in extinguishing the fire,

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware of the
facts as set out in the hon. Member's
informed that
question. I am
Sunday, 3rd instant, at 7-40 a.m., a call
of fire to No. 33 Kilmood Street, Belfast,
was received at Fire Brigade Headquarters from the police by telephone.
The section of men on duty at Headquarters immediately responded to the
call and arrived at Kilmood Street
within five minutes, the distance being
approximately one mile. Another section
of the Fire Brigade, withdrawn from the
Alhambra fire in North Street, also proceeded to Kilmood Street, a distance of
1 miles, and arrived at 8-2 a.m.
It is deeply regretted that a life was
lost as a result of the outbreak, but I am
satisfied that this was not in any way
due to delay on the part of the Fire
Brigade in answering the call. I do not,
therefore, consider that the circumstances
call for investigation.

KING'S SPEECH,
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech on
behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech
is as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
When I last addressed you our Country
was at peace. Since then the United
Kingdom has been forced into what may
prove to be a prolonged campaign in
defence of universal liberty and justice.
From the day war was declared
Northern Ireland has given proof of her
willingness to play her full part in this
great struggle.
To me it is a source of deep satisfaction
that the young men of the Province have
offered themselves in such large numbers
as volunteers for service in His Majesty's
Forces. Their rally to the colours has
been fully up to the high standard
expected, and the women of the country,
too, are loyally carrying out their duties
in many spheres of activity, both on
Service and in their homes.
My Ministers have devoted constant
attention to Civil Defence and I am
gratified to learn that the Act passed last
Session has enabled precautions to be
taken for the protection of our people
from the worst effects of attack by hostile
aircraft. These arrangements are being
improved and developed day by day with
the cordial co-operation of local authorities, and, in fact, all sections of the
community. The training of volunteers
been
continues, and those who have
King's Speech
King's Speech
HOUSE OF COMMONS
enrolled are discharging with diligence
their allotted tasks.
Food production is one of the most
essential national services at this time. My
Government has, therefore, laid plans for
the ploughing of a quarter of a million
additional acres of grassland in 1940, and
every effort is being made to meet the
needs of farmers by the provision of
tractors, ploughs, and other implements.
No less important than the production
of food supplies is the provision of
essentials required for the successful
prosecution of the war, and I am glad
to know that in this sphere, as in all
others, our industrialists are making an
important and growing contribution to
the national effort.
I am further pleased to observe that
the importance to the nation of maintaining overseas trade is fully realised,
and that my Ministers are working in the
closest co-operation with United Kingdom
Ministers in order to facilitate the
development of Northern Ireland export
trade, compatible with the requirements
of the home country. My Government is
also actively engaged in assisting industry
to surmount the many difficulties with
which it is faced, while, at the same time,
ensuring that the interests of employees
are duly safeguarded.
a
The necessity for borrowing large sums
of money for the purpose of prosecuting
the war has been the subject of legislation at Westminster, and an intensive
campaign covering the United Kingdom
as a whole has been launched with the
object of
of obtaining the maximum
response from small investors. I am
gratified that my Government has created

The PRIME MINISTER: Very well.
My war aims are very simple. I only
wish that I could do as I did beforetake a greater part in the war than I am
at my age fit to take. My war aims are to
stress every nerve and to ask all my
fellow-countrymen to support in every
way they can the war aims of Mr.
Chamberlain and his Cabinet and crush
the evil of Hitlerism and all it stands for
so that we may live in a free country.
Does anyone doubt what are the aims
of my colleagues and myself with regard
to the war? It is an insult to ask such
a question. I take it as a personal insult flung at myself, because the hon.
Member must know that at my age I am
precluded from doing more than I am
doing. The hon. Member went on to say
I am sitting on a seat of dynamite. Did
you ever hear anything so ridiculous in
all your life. We have sat here now for
almost twenty years and not a man has
placed dynamite under our seats. The
hon. Member knows that perfectly well.
It is ridiculous to talk in terms of that
sort. We have no fear whatever. I am
glad to say that after all these years and
with the war upon us at the moment our
position in the United Kingdom and
Empire is based on stronger and firmer
foundations than in the whole history of
Ireland. Not only are we appreciated
by Ministers of the Crown on the other
side, not only are all the Dominions looking to us to lend a hand as they are
doing in this vast struggle for humanity,
not only are our Ministers continually
consulted by opposite Members on the
other side, but we have the fullest assurance of their generous co-operation with
us in some of our special difficulties.
All these signs prove definitely that we
stand high in the estimation of people
who realise what real loyalty means to
the Crown,

Ülster officers and men passing through

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Henderson]
My Ministers are fully alive to the
need, in the national interest, for the
most rigid economy, and it will be
their policy not to sanction any new
services or extensions of existing services, which are not essential for purposes connected with the war or for
the supply of very urgent needs, and
I am also gratified that our local
authorities are taking measures to
ensure that a like rigid economy is
observed in the administration of local
government . . .
That has brought about a state of
affairs which I am sure the Government
of this country never anticipated. It is
quite true to say that the unemployment
figures have decreased to a considerable
extent. What has caused that? It has
been caused and we are justly proud of
this fact by our young men and young
women volunteering to fight for their
King and Country. It cannot be said
that the reduction in the number of unemployed has been brought about by
increased production in our industries. I
should like to point out that this rigid
economy can be wrongly applied. For
instance, many schemes essential to local
taxpayers have been suspended. The
result has been that hundreds of men
have been thrown out of employment for
the duration of the war, and the worst
part of it is that many of them are at
an age when they cannot volunteer for
service in the Army or Navy. This
economy has gone too far. Why should
roads which have been in a bad state for
30, 40, 50 or even 60 years be allowed to
continue in that condition? I think that
is monstrous. The taxpayers are paying
for these roads to be kept in a proper
condition, but the Government have
gone out of their way to introduce rigid
economy
and many men have been
thrown out of work.
In many parts of the country this is
going to be a very bleak Christmas for
the unemployed notwithstanding the fact
that an increase of 1s has been allowed.
I contend that is wrong. Take the
Ministry of Home Affairs and the rigid
economy they impose. What is happening with regard to the hospitals? There
is not a solitary hospital being constructed
with the exception that the basements are
being improved. There are 7.000 persons
in Belfast diagnosed as suffering from
some sort of tuberculosis. Of this number
1,800 ex-servicemen were stated to be
suffering from the disease, and on the
ground of economy the building of a new
sanatorium is being prevented. If such
is economy it is not Christianlike that
men and women must live in little houses
with only two or three rooms. In many
cases the father and mother with two or
three children have to sleep in the front
room. The Ministry of Home Affairs has
decided that we must effect rigid economy
at the expense of these patients. It
means that if that view is right thousands
of children who come in contact with
tubercular parents will contract the
disease. I cannot understand the
mentality of a Government that allows
such a state of affairs to exist. There are
a thousand and one things that could be
complained of.
Is any economy being effected on the
administrative side of the Government of
this country? If there is one place in the
world where rigid economy should be
brought in it should be in this Government. Nearly all the people, rich and
poor alike, with one voice say that the
administration as carried on here is one
of the most costly in any part of the
world. It would be a good thing if the
Minister of Labour, who I am sure will
reply, could induce the Prime Minister
to see that economy could be effected in
regard to the administration of affairs in
the Province. The Minister of Labour
will, I am certain, admit that we have
more civil servants here than in Czecho-
Slovakia or Poland or Finland. I
believe we have even more than they have
in Germany. The Prime Minister in face
of all this would be justified in going into
the question in order to see if rigid
economy could be effected in running the
affairs of this area.
I know this is not an opportune time
to criticise as far as the Government is
concerned. May I take the opportunity
of saying that I am proud and pleased

Minister of Commerce looking so hale and
hearty. On behalf of my colleagues I
wish him a very happy Christmas and
prosperous new year. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) That expression applies to
every other Member. At the same time

fire broke out when the owner of the

We can at any rate

necessary lest I might be misunderstood

to do to win this war. There never was
a war as necessary as this war.
I agree

It is no use anyone telling the public
that we are not at war with the German

every time, and perhaps no one has as
bad an opinion of them as I have.
know they are an ingenious people, but I

I almost think they would go the length

I saw this thing coming since the end.
of 1935, and I did my best in my own

could not do anything. How could I
when the greatest man in Ulster, the

Ribbentrop here for five or six weeks
showing him all that could be shown. It
is no laughing matter. It has turned out

Having said that, I have some
criticisms to make, I believe there is a
reckless waste of money going on. Some
of it the Northern Ireland Government is
responsible for, and some of it they are
not. I cannot discuss what they are not
responsible for, but in the end money will
be more scarce than men. Every war is
won on money, and this war is going to
be won on money. Sometimes a man tells
you of money being spent as proof that
we must be doing well and doing the
right thing. Not at all. It is not what
is spent, but how it is spent. I know,
for instance, that public petrol is being
wasted, but it would not be fair to go
into that, because I am not sure that the
Government of Northern Ireland is the.
guilty party. Therefore I will not touch
on that.

The League of Nations is one thing

When Finland was attacked they passed

If Great Britain had been as strong in
1937 as she is now we would not have
been at war. The Member for Queen's
University, to whom I have referred, tells
us that after the war we want a federation of nations with an army at their
command to keep the peace. He stated
that in this House, not yesterday, but
on another occasion. Suppose we had an
army of half a million Russians, half a
million Germans, half a million French,
half a million British, and half a million
Italians. Whom would the soldiers of
that army obey if there was a dispute?
Of course they would obey their own
Government. It is necessary to say that,
because these gentlemen who make these
suggestions are doing a lot of harm.
About a month ago I was in the
Donegall Place branch of the Belfast
Bank, and I got into casual conversation
with a clergyman. He did not know me
and I suppose that, judging from the
exterior, he thought I was soft. He said,
"What about the war? Do you think we.
are right?" I replied, "We never were
as right before,' " and I believe that.
Great Britain never was as right before, as
she is now in connection with this war.
What was Hitler going to do. I know
well what he was going to do. If he had
got off with Poland and had got another
12 months to prepare, some morning
at five o'clock every arsenal and
aerodrome and defence work in
Great Britain would be bombed, and
that would be the first intimation you
would get that you were at war. That
was what he intended to do, and when
he had Britain finished the rest would
be easy.
Now we must win this war or
go down for ever. But we will win it.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

I am not a thread. If he wore hmself

a
The Government have been wisely
guided in concentrating on war measures
and the efforts necessary to bring it to
a speedy and successful conclusion.
Every hon. Member in the House must
be gratified at the news we have received
during the past two or three days. Our
gallant Navy has covered itself with
glory, and we are proud of the fact that
we can produce such men as Rear-
Admiral Harwood. I recognise it is
necessary, if we are to win the war, to
have on the Statute Book many war-time
measures, and we must get accustomed
to war-time restrictions. When we feel
them somewhat irksome we must remember that we, too, have a part to play
in the war, and we should remember that
it is a very small part compared with
what our soldiers, sailors and airmen are
bearing in order to bring the war to a
successful termination.
I should like these war-time measures
and restrictions carried out in a friendly
spirit rather than in a vindictive one.
A great deal more might be done in
getting the Ulster people to co-operate
with the authorities in carrying out all
the necessary restrictions, and we should
always remember that Ulster people will
be led, but they will not be driven.
When I mention the control of food
and feeding stuffs I know I am treading

to which hon. Members have referred.

Northern Ireland, but in the distribution of food more use should be made
of the channels through which food
flows. If people who are accustomed to
dealing with foodstuffs were brought in

deal of butter was stored up in the

accept the Prime Minister's statement

matter.

be

Now I have a very pathetic letter from
one of my constituents which I received
yesterday morning. It is only typical of
many cases I could cite.
Dear Mr. Elliott, I wish to ask your
kind advice as to my position as a pig
breeder. I have six sows farrowing in
a little less than two weeks starting
about the 26th inst. Meal I can
scarcely procure for love or money. I
have used every turnip, potato and
nearly four sacks of corn to eke out the
scanty allowance of emergency ration
meal which I got. I held on to my
sows, and now I am worried to death
for the way things are. I am keeping
my young stock of pigs alive, nothing
more. I know you will give me good
counsel, and I shall sincerely appreciate it. Yours faithfully.
That is only a typical case of many of
the farmers of Northern Ireland. It is
very difficult for me to give that man any
advice. The only advice I can give is
the advice I am taking myself that is,
to reduce very considerably my stock
until the prices of food stuffs are more
reasonable. I do think that if we had a
producer or consumer on the Committee
of Control with Sir Roland Nugent we
should have perhaps a better and more
equitable distribution. I find that in
some districts there is a fair quantity of
feeding stuffs available. In other districts
like Aughnacloy and South Tyrone, very
far away from the port of Belfast, they
are specially hard hit. That letter is
from
a constituent who lives near
Aughnacloy. There it is impossible to

In Eire they seem to have maize meal.
Some of my neighbours have been able
to get smuggled across some maize meal.
While I have no sympathy with
smuggling, when a man's stock is squeal-

Debate on the Address
[Mr. Agnew]
of bombs, bullets, mines and other
weapons of destruction. If we look at
science and scientific discoveries we find
them used to-day by Governments for the
destruction instead of the betterment of
the human race. It shows beyond question or doubt that the stupidity of statesmen has launched us where we are to-day.
There were 21 years in which to settle all
the disputes of Europe and statesmen
could not find any way out because as
long as we have imperialistic expansion
taking place, so long as the tentacles of
imperialism spread throughout the world.
you will always have war. Imperialism
and exploitation are the main principles
which cause war, but the working classes
are never consulted. Their lives are
demanded and they must fill the gaps
to bolster up the decay of capitalism
throughout Europe and the world.
I remember that last year we had the
Munich Agreement signed and the British
Prime Minister came away with a document "Peace with honour." Let us ask
ourselves the question to-day where is
that peace with honour? Where was the
gentlemen's agreement? We find Europe
in a state to-day which no man could give
any explanation for. They have not even
yet declared war. We are told it was to
free Poland. It was to free the
capitalists' investments in Danzig. That
is why Poland became the scapegoat
of Europe at the behest of British
Imperialists. It was Belgium in the last
war. It was then the Kaiser; now it is
Hitler. They must find something to
fight about. If the real facts were considered deeply enough by the working
classes who pay the price there would be
a different atmosphere created. There
would be a demand for peace, which is
only right. There would be a demand
that they would no longer be dupes or
fools at the behest of statesmen. Their
duty is to themselves.
Let us take into consideration the cost
in money, not considering the cost in life.
It is six million pounds per day. When
this Government-and even the British
Government-was asked to grant even a
small concession to old-age pensioners and
those in need we were told there is no
money. In order to carry on the war we,
who belong to the working classes, are
bearing our burden and share, and we
feel that that burden is becoming too
heavy. When we asked for a concession
for the unemployed we find a grateful
Government granting ls each to man and
wife and 6d for each child. What a
glorious heritage and a glorious ideal to
fight for. That is the system which we
are asked to bolster up; that is the
system we are asked to defend. Yet in
peace time if we only asked for one-third
or even one-tenth of the amount to bring
about a better system of society and a
decent standard of life we were told there
was no money. Still that large sum of
six millions per day is spent without the
least thought. That is one price we pay.
Let us consider the terrible hardships
at sea and on land, and visualise the
number of human lives swept away by
the progress of science for destruction.
These things are just glossed over and
mentioned casually as if they were a mere

this a distressed area, yet it is obvious
that it is really distressed. As regards
schools, this is a matter which I have
studied very closely because the education
of the children is something to be.
admired. I do not, however, see any
provision by the Government of free
meals or free books. That is a burden
on the people, and when we put the
question forward to the committees they
say it is a State responsibility. We
would ask the Government to look into
this matter very seriously.
The postponement of the school-leaving
age is another matter of serious concern,
simply because it will add to the scourge
of unemployment. The additional year
at school would have meant that those
who are out of employment would have
had some chance of getting work, but
each year there will now be the usual
number of children leaving school at
fourteen years of age.
Of course, education committees stand for keeping the
school leaving age at 14, but I do not
see why the Government should any
longer postpone raising the age.
Taking the King's Speech in detail, I
perused it very carefully and I came to
the one conclusion that to those who are
looking for help and guidance and for
relief it contains no hope. I omitted to
mention the question of relief, but I am
not too late. Our poor-law authorities
should at least have sufficient sympathy
to deal with old-age pensioners on the
same basis as they do in England, where
they give them a supplemental grant.
To-day in Northern Ireland there is not
one I know of who is receiving a supplemental grant. If there are any they
are few and far between.

gallant Members who proposed and
As regards the war, I pledge my faith
that peace is best. It would be much
better to talk over terms of peace, even if
the discussions lasted for two years, than
to have six months of this war. There
are ample supplies in the world for all,
and when greed and plunder are stopped,
and when the extension of Imperialism

hope for peace. So long as I have breath
to breathe I will always advocate that
message which was given to us on that
first Christmas morning-peace on earth
and good will to men.
seconded the Motion for the Address. I
felt that yesterday was a unique day for
Ulster. It was the first time we had
opened our Parliament while we were
engaged in a gigantic war. The heart of
every loyalist rejoiced when we found
that the heroism of our Navy had compelled the Graf Spee to commit suicide.
I was surprised to hear the way the
Member for South Armagh talked about
peace. He talked about discussing peace
for two years.
While we were discussing
peace Hitler and his satellites were
marching into Poland, and if the hon.
Member upholds that I am sorry to call
him an Ulsterman. I am afraid there is
not a single man in the Christian world
to-day who can say one single syllable
that is good about Hitler or his satellites.
I am one of those who hold that we
are at war not only with Hitler but with
the whole German people. If the people
had not been behind Hitler this war
would never have occurred. We rejoice
to know that our men have joined the
colours in such large numbers to defend
their home and country. We are fighting
this war to maintain our freedom to live,
and if ever Great Britain entered a war
with just cause it is now. Time will
prove that England and her allies will be
the victors, and I hope that this war will
put an end to all wars. As one who has
sons serving with His Majesty's Forces I
feel that it is the duty of every man and
woman in this country to do his and her
part to help to win the war. Sometimes we
have to listen to speeches that are not
pleasing, but surely no hon. Member
would suggest that all the energy and
money at our disposal should not be put
into the hands of those who are out to
win the war.
The Gracious Speech deals with food
production, and to-day the farmers are
asked to play another important part in
winning this war. Although we played
a very important part in the previous.
war, history is repeating itself and the
Government has called upon the farmers
of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
to till every acre of land possible in order
to produce food for our people. I believe
the response to that appeal will be even
greater than anticipated by the Minister

wish to state that never from the time I

Sir BASIL BROOKE: All I have got
to say is that in the registry there is only

been gathered the hon. Member will
receive a reply signed by myself.
Mr. BROWN: I deny that statement.
Mr. SPEAKER: When a right hon.
Gentleman of the Front Bench gives his
word that a certain thing has happened
it is the custom of the House of Commons
that every hon. Member in the House
accepts it.
It may be wrong; it is possible for any human being to make a
mistake, but it is always accepted by
Members of the House of Commons, and
I hope the hon. Member will not deny it.
The difficulty of points of correction is
that very often there is a misconception.
In this case the right hon. Gentleman
stated that he himself signed the letter
or personally supervised it. In the case
of right hon. Gentlemen it is the invariable custom that acknowledgments to
letters are signed by their private secretaries, but the main letter which follows
the acknowledgment is, as a rule, signed
by the right hon. Gentleman in charge of
the Department. I think that is where
the misconception has arisen in this case.
Mr. BROWN: Thank you. The only
comment I have to make is that my word
is, in my humble opinion, as good as that
of the Minister. We are both sensible
men.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: We can leave
it at that. To deal now with the other
matters raised on the King's Speech. I
would like first of all to take the feeding
stuff question which is the most critical
and most difficult. Let me say at the
outset that I have been most agreeably
surprised at the manner in which the
various Members have presented this case
to me. I know the difficulties which every
farmer is up against owing to this
regrettable food shortage, and I know the
horrible position they are in having to
get rid of their animals before they are
finished and not being able to go on in
the normal course of preparing animals
for the market. That is all well known.
The reasons are, of course, that at the
beginning of the war you have disorganisation of traffic and disorganisation
of ships. You have set up a convoy
system which very often reduces the
number of voyages carried out by each
ship. That ship will probably do only
one voyage compared with two or three
in previous times. This part of the world
was in a rather worse position than
perhaps the other side of the water, and
the reason for that was because wheat
and barley had fallen in price and maize
meal had not fallen in price. The consequence was that merchants over the
country did not fill their stores with
maize meal anticipating a fall in that
product. That is one reason. A second
reason accentuated the difficulty because
we here depend on maize meal for feeding stuff. In England it is barley and
not maize.
20 DECEMBER 1939
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
The whole combination of circumstances
made it more difficult for our farmers
than for the farmers on the other side of
the water. I want to assure hon.
Members-I think no fewer than five
hon. Members asked me if I can
state that Northern Ireland is getting a
fair deal and a proper share of feeding
stuff I can assure them without any
hesitation whatever that we are getting
our fair share. I have only to refer
them to the answer which Mr. Morrison,
the Minister of Food, gave on 6th
December.
"Since the beginning of the war
Northern Ireland has received as large
a percentage of normal requirements of
feeding stuffs as other parts of the
United Kingdom, and every effort will
be made to ensure the continuance of
this policy."
That, I am satisfied, will be continued,
and I am satisfied that, although the
period of difficulty may go on for some
time, it will be shared by all parts of the
United Kingdom alike. The hon.
Member for Pottinger stated the case of
a ship which had not been unloaded at
the docks. As far as I can make out the
ship which he mentioned was carrying
wheat.
Mr. BEATTIE: It was the Earl Graf
and it was carrying maize-7,000 tons of
maize.
Mr. BEATTIE: The ship was the Earl
Graf. The Torr Head had three different
classes of cargo. It had to be held out
to allow the other ship up to the side to
discharge. They were waiting for discharge, and the Earl Graf could not get
in to the siding. The other ship had to
discharge. I say two or three days were
lost in the discharge. and it was very
important to the farmers.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: There was a
ship carrying wheat. It was actually
being used as a reserve. The same thing
applies to maize meal. It is impossible
for any port authority to know when
the next ship is coming in. In war time
they are not announced. In many cases
these ships are used as storerooms for a
supply of foodstuffs. Calculation has
been made by the Ministry of what is
going out in order to keep a more or less
continuous flow of products going to the.
retailers in the country. It is quite impossible for the Ministry to issue any
straight feeding stuffs. It has to be made
up in mixtures. If we used maize meal,
bran, and pollard, or anything of the
sort the balanced ration sent out would be
wrong. All the feeding stuff has to be
kept balanced and sent out as a ration.
It was not the delay in unloading the
ship. It was an intentional delay. That
ship was being used as a reserve store..
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I see the hon.
Member's point. I think he went rather
further, which is not my side of the
show. It is mechanical discharge and
hand discharge. Normally speaking that
is the procedure at the present time.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The first supply

hon. Members do not realise quite the
method that we intend to employ with
regard to the land army. We are not
training women for the land in the same
way as they are in England. The
difficulty we are placed in is this. Even
calculating that all the agricultural unemployed are absorbed, and if the
250,000 acres which we hope to see
ploughed before the end of the year were
producing a full crop, it would probably
require more men than are actually available. What I am proposing to do is to train
a few women for land work, using them
as a reserve and then on their instruction,
and with the knowledge they have gained
at these schools, they will be able to build

or three weeks a reserve of women who
will be able to handle the harvest. That

is the scheme. There is not going to be

Ideal with an emergency.
I think I have dealt with most of the
points raised except I want to say this,
and it is an important point. I am sure
the House will be gratified to learn that
over 130,000 acres of land will be
ploughed up in a very short time, but
there is in certain parts of the country a
distinct reluctance to plough up, and
that may be caused by a doubt of the
necessity of ploughing up and as to
whether these people will be compelled
to plough up. Now this tillage campaign
is under the Defence of the Realm Regulations and there are reasons why every
farmer should plough. First of all, he
is breaking the law if he does not plough.
Secondly, I want to warn him with all
the solemnity I can that if he does not
plough and does not produce feeding stuff
next year he will not be able to carry on
farm work. The feeding position as I see
it is going to be very serious for the whole
of the war. Unless we produce stuff here
it will not be available for the farmer
who will not plough the land. These two
reasons urge upon them not to delay any
further in ploughing their quota and
complying with the law. Having done
that they are in a position to help themselves. The vast majority have done a
wonderful work, and I think the fact
that 130,000 acres have been ploughed in
a very short time with the inclement
weather we usually have in this country
is very gratifying. I should like to
congratulate and praise these farmers for
the spirit of patriotism which they have
shown in the work.

C
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Mr. Andrews): The question of the
protection of persons in occupation of the
building at Stormont has on several
occasions engaged the attention of the
Cabinet, who consider that in the event
of an air-raid warning Members of Parliament and the staff should be left free
to choose between taking cover in the
grounds and plantations of the estate or
remaining in the building.
It has been decided that the corridors
of the second and third floors, which are
the safest portions of the building, shall
receive protection by fitting wire screens
and sandbags to the windows so as to
minimise the risk. This work is now
being carried out. Direction arrows
will be placed on the walls throughout
the entire building to ensure as far as
possible the rapid evacuation of all concerned, either to the grounds or to the
These corridors are ample
corridors.
to accommodate everyone in the building. The estimated cost of these works
is £450.
The Telephone Exchange must remain.
open during an air-raid and as it is
situated in a more exposed part of the
building a sum of about £250 has been
spent in providing protection.
First-aid equipment, special fire extinguishers, protective clothing for
wardens and members of first-aid and firefighting squads, have been ordered at
an estimated cost of £570. Some of this
equipment has already been delivered.

PRODUCE.
8. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime

the result of his negotiations with the
Imperial Authorities regarding the memorandum from the Ulster Farmers' Union,
asking the British Government to (1)
assure farmers an economic price for crops
raised under the Tillage Order during the
next three years; (2) take over the 1939
potato crop in order to recoup growers
their financial losses due to the stopping
of exports to foreign countries; (3) appoint the Ulster Ministry of Agriculture,
with certain outside assistance, to
administer the flax scheme, and at the
same time announce prices for the 1940
crop on a scale to be approved by representatives of growers, and (4) guarantee
a price for fat cattle and sheep.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have been
asked to reply.
Guaranteed prices for wheat, oats and
barley have already been the subject of
legislation by the Imperial Parliament
and these prices extend to Northern Ireland.
STREET LIGHTING IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
As regards potatoes an order will
shortly be made by the Ministry of Food
fixing minimum prices for potatoes grown
in 1939 in Northern Ireland and arrangements will also be made to deal with any
surplus potatoes remaining unsold at the
end of the season. In the case of flax,
as the House is already aware, guaranteed
prices of 178 6d to 22s 6d per stone have
been fixed by the Ministry of Supply in
respect of the 1940 crop. Finally I am
confident that all Members are gratified
that prices for cattle, sheep and pigs purchased by my Department on behalf of
the Ministry of Food have been fixed on
the same basis as in Great Britain.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked

Order recently issued, modified street

what extent the concession will be used is
a matter for decision by the local authorities concerned.

Under the existing system of grants
each mental hospital receives from the

1920.
This was an unsatisfactory arrangement from the point of view of mental
institutions, as it failed to take into

of the maintenance of these institutions
and, furthermore, the grants bore no

The Bill, therefore, in addition to

on the total number of patients
under treatment in each of them from
time to time.
I have had the advantage of consulting
various local authorties, and I think they
agree with me that this would be the
most equitable way of dealing with the
grant.
In moving this Bill I should like to
take this opportunity of expressing my

the various committees, and of the
excellent work carried on there with the
object of relieving the afflictions of the
unfortunate inmates who suffer from
mental trouble. I do not think it is
necessary for me to say any more on the
subject. I beg to move.

Prime Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
The PRIME MINISTER: I must, first
of all, tender my thanks to the hon.
Member for South Down, who has withdrawn the motion standing in his name
on the Paper. He has already explained
the reason, but, at the same time, I told
him that I intended in the course of my
statement to touch upon several of those
matters which were obviously from the
wording of his motion in his mind, and,
therefore, he would have an opportunity
of giving his views to the House afterwards.
It is very necessary for me from time
to time to make statements here which
will guide the people as far as possible in
those important works in which so many
of them are engaged, and to-day I choose
as the subject of my remarks agriculture,
and chiefly flax. The reason why I am
doing this instead of my right hon.
Friend, who could do it ten times better,
is two-fold. I do want to impress the
country with the fact that when a
Minister carries out a work and gives instructions and puts up posters and helps
in every way he can, he is not only speaking for himself on the subject, but also
for the Cabinet, as a whole. The Cabinet
are backing up the Minister of Agriculture in the gallant efforts which he and
his staff are making in order to fulfil the
slogan, "Plough more land." The second
reason why I am doing it is because there
is no more complicated crop, I
in
suppose
the world, than the flax crop, and it
brings in very many departments. It is
not altogether agriculture, and not only
departments here in Ulster itself, but
also under war conditions, various departments at Whitehall are brought in.
Consequently there is a cross-interest of
so many departments; for instance, commerce, and I thought it would clear the
air considerably if I dealt with the
matter instead of leaving it to the two
Ministers individually.
we
possibly promote further efforts on our
part here, and
welcome it most
heartily in order to find more employment for those who are at present out of
work. I am sure the people of Ulster will
give Mr. Burgin a fine welcome when he
comes, knowing the responsibility on his
shoulders and his anxiety to get on with
everything for the prosecution of the war.
In the first place, before I make a few
remarks, I should like to announce to the
House the coming visit at my invitation
of the right hon. Leslie Burgin, who is
Minister of Supply. I have asked him
to come over here and to do us the honour
of addressing a meeting and also, if
possible, to be brought into contact
with the captains of industry, and, if I
may use the expression, the sinews of
industry. If I can arrange an amalgamated meeting of that sort I think it may
Now if I may plunge directly into the
subject of flax every word is of such
importance that I have been most cautious
in what I propose to say. My colleagues
and I have had under active consideration for some time, in consultation with
the Imperial Departments, the question
of the best method of securing as large an
increase as possible in the acreage under
flax in Northern Ireland.
We have thought it desirable in the
first place to draw a definite line of
demarcation between the respective functions of our Ministries of Agriculture and
Commerce in regard to the problem of
flax development, and we have decided
that my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Agriculture will be responsible for all
matters connected with the production of
flax until it has left the hands of the
farmer, and that subsequent processes
will fall to be dealt with by my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Commerce.
In making arrangements which we
hope will secure a substantial increase in
the acreage under flax we have naturally
sought to obtain first a satisfactory price
to the farmer and a measure of security
to our linen industry. As a result of the
direct intervention of the Government
here with the appropriate Ministries at
Westminster the Ministry of Supply has
found it possible to guarantee prices of
from 17s 6d to 22s 6d per stone for the
1940 crop with an average of £1 per
stone.
I should like to say how much we all
appreciate the consideration which has
been given by the Imperial departments
and, in particular, the Ministry of
Supply in approving these prices which,
I may say, have been fixed at a level substantially higher than in the case of any
other comparable crop in order to
stimulate flax growing and provide the
necessary
raw material
which our
linen industry and the expansion of an
essential part of our export trade depend.
on
6 FEBRUARY 1940
Adjournment-—
Prime Minister's Statement
I believe that these prices will be
accepted by our farmers as satisfactory.
and, indeed, generous. They represent
an increase of considerably more than 100
per cent. above the prices realised for
flax in the last pre-war year. We have
to go back to 1929 to find a year in which
the average price of flax exceeded 10s per
stone. We must, therefore, from the
point of view of our Government, regard
the prices which have been announced as
absolutely final. Any attempt now to
. lead our farmers to expect further
financial inducements from public funds
will only create uncertainty in their
minds and result in delay in making
arrangements for an increased acreage
this year.
Having secured these prices for our
farmers it now behoves everyone
interested in flax and the production of
linen to work together to ensure that the
maximum advantage is taken of the
Imperial Government's decision, and to
assist my right hon. Friend and his staff
in the Ministry of Agriculture to obtain
the
necessary expansion in the flax
acreage. The Government are already
doing their part. Arrangements have
been made for the purchase of flax seed
from overseas; this has been no easy task
in view of the difficulties which will be
apparent to all hon. Members, but I may
say that we hope to obtain sufficient seed
for at least 50,000 acres. This seed will
be distributed through ordinary trade
channels at fixed prices ranging from
about 45s per cwt. to about 70s per cwt.
according to variety and as to whether
the seed is pedigree or otherwise. The
House will appreciate that these seed
prices are lower than those obtaining for
comparable seeds in 1937 and 1938.
We have also considered the question
of scutching facilities. As hon. Members
will be aware the Flax Development
Committee which was set up with the
approval of this House to consider ways
and means of improving the methods of
flax processing has already turned its
attention to the best type of turbine
scutcher which would be suitable for our
local conditions. Experimental work is
still proceeding on this matter, but in
view of the urgency of the problem we
have come to the conclusion that the most
practicable course is to renovate existing
scutch mills where necesary. Loans for
this purpose will be made available on
reasonable terms. We are satisfied that
existing mills, overhauled in some cases,
will be fully equal to the task of handling
the increased acreage anticipated during
the current year. The Government
propose to purchase a substantial number
of flax pulling machines, and negotiations
are at present being conducted with this
object in view. These pullers will be
supplied on hire or sold on a repayment
basis, and my right hon. Friend is
satisfied that these arrangements will be
adequate to cope with any shortage of
labour which may arise.
We are also aware that after prolonged
disuse flax dams and holes will in many
cases require cleaning out.
We propose
that, where necessary, grants up to 75 per
cent. of the total cost of labour involved
will be supplied from public funds. In
addition to the foregoing, arrangements
have been made for the training of suitable men in the processes of scutching as,
of course, it will be realised that, owing
to the decline in the acreage of flax, there
may be a shortage. in qualified scutchers.
The Government have also been working in touch with the linen trade, which
has now set up a committee consisting
of representatives of the spinning
industry. It is our hope that this committee will provide useful machinery for
profitable consultations with our Ministry of Agriculture and the Flax Development Committee on matters connected
with the flax growing industry. I trust
that with these arrangements now in
hand all interests will co-operate wholeheartedly and assist my right hon. Friend
in the vital problem of securing a very
substantial increase in the acreage of flax
this year.
I come now to feeding stuffs, about
which my hon. Friend behind me is very
interested and may take note. With
regard to feeding stuffs I am, as everybody else is, conscious of the difficulties
which many of our farmers have been
experiencing in connection with the
supply of feeding stuffs. It is not always
easy to appreciate the reasons which make
it impossible to get maize and barley and
other feeding stuffs in the quantities that
were, available before the war. We must
remember, however, that in this war
shipping is one of our very first lines of
defence. And it is our merchant shipping, more than anything else, which has
had to bear the fiercest and most in-

Unfortunately, it was necessary late

per cent. of normal. We weathered that
period successfully, and we may now look
forward almost immediately to a substantial increase in supplies up to twothirds of normal. That figure was
announced by Mr. Morrison at Westminster a fortnight ago, and we have the
definite assurance that in regard to supplies of feeding stuffs Northern Ireland is
receiving, and will always continue to
receive, her fair share in comparison with
Great Britain. That is the assurance
that my hon. Friend (Mr. Brown)
wanted.
within a few days to be able to release

maize meal as such. That deals with

The improvement in supplies which
will take place during February will, I
am confident, ease the position of our pig
and poultry farmers very considerably.
There is also the question of price. Prices
of feeding stuffs are governed by the
Maximum Prices Order made by the

being exceeded in Northern Ireland,
especially in the case of mixtures. Special
steps are, however, being taken by my

remedy any abuses. I am happy to be
able to say that the supply position is improving rapidly, and the Ministry expect
Coming to tillage the House will be
interested to learn that up to the end of

in the Ministry of Agriculture for the £2
per acre grant for the ploughing up of
old grassland in respect of no less an area
than 180,000 acres. I think that is a
great accomplishment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Thus, I think, we can
claim to be within measurable distance of

additional 250,000 acres under the plough
in the course of the present year. Hon.
Members will appreciate the precise effect
of this when I remind them that every

few months.
I am also glad to be able to inform
the House that the tractor position continues to be satisfactory. At the moment
there are no fewer than 1,100 tractors
operating or ready to operate in Northern Ireland. Up to date my right hon.
Friend has purchased 150 tractors and
ploughs, and another 50 are expected to
be delivered very shortly. In addition,
of course, tractors of various makes are
coming in steadily through the usual
trade channels.
With regard to seed, other than flax
seed to which I have already referred, our
Ministry of Agriculture is doing everything possible to ensure that adequate
supplies of seed of all descriptions will be
available for our farmers at reasonable
prices when seed time comes. I am not
in a position to-day to make any definite
announcement as to what those prices will
be, but I have every confidence in the
prompt response which our farmers will
make to the appeal to put into cultivation
the maximum possible acreage and ensure
the success of our "Plough for victory"
campaign.
That is all I have to announce with
regard to agriculture in particular, but,
in general, I would like to ask hon. Members on all sides of the House to hold up
the arms of my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Agriculture, during the

Mr. SPEAKER: In reply to the

House for ten days, five of which days

Member of this House moves that that

Mr. THOMPSON: When the report
of the investigators appointed by the
Minister of Agriculture came into my
hands last week I was so perturbed that
having seen the reports of the matter
printed in the Press I felt an opportunity
should be given at the earliest moment to
the House to get hold of the facts of the
present situation in connection with the
Pigs Marketing Board. So I hoped to
move the Adjournment of the House,
but I understand that other arrangements have been made. My purpose in
doing so was to enable the Minister to
put before the House more clearly his
reasons for the drastic steps he has
found it necessary to take within the past
week.
It is not my intention at the present
to enter into a debate on the merits or
demerits of such action, but I would just
say that if the incidents as set out in
this report are true a moral rot has set
into the public boards and must be
thoroughly investigated and got rid of not
matter what the cost may be. If these
statements cannot be fully substantiated
a very serious situation must develop in
the Ministry. I am quite sure that
when the whole matter has been brought
into the light in debate this House will
know exactly what to do in order that
the people may be assured that public
bodies will be run on sound business
methods, and that any kind of dishonesty
or corruption will be thoroughly dealt
with. That is all I want to say at the
moment, but I do look forward with
eagerness to the Minister's statement in
this House and I shall be glad if he will
now make that statement.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I am very
glad indeed to have been afforded this,
the earliest, opportunity of making a
statement to the House on the reasons
for and the events which have led up
to my amending the Pigs Marketing
Scheme in such a manner as to replace
the old Board by the one now in office.
I observe that members of the former
Board seek to make out that I and my
Ministry have no responsibility for the
Pigs Marketing Scheme. No statement
could be more at variance with the facts.
Apparently it is their view that
matter how inefficiently the scheme is
run, or how much producers' money is
squandered, I must not intervene, but
must stand back and watch with
equanimity the spectacle of mounting
levies. That is not my conception of my
duties to this House and to producers,
and I shall, therefore, first of all, try
to explain the essential facts as simply
as possible.
no
289 Pigs Marketing Board
Pigs Marketing Board 290
7 MARCH 1939
It is necessary to understand quite
clearly that the Pigs Marketing Board is
not an organisation set up by Act of
Parliament. Under the Agricultural
Marketing Act of 1933 my Ministry is
empowered to set up marketing organisations such as the Pigs Marketing
Board by means of a scheme brought into
force by an order, and subsequently submitted to this House for approval.
Mr. BEATTIE: Does that mean by
an Order in Council?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: If the House
approves it gives me power to set up a
scheme.
Mr. NIXON: By Act of Parliament.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The powers
conferred upon a marketing board
depended upon my discretion when framing the original scheme under the Act
of 1933, and Parliament has empowered
me to modify these powers by means of
an amendment to the scheme, which it is
possible for me to make by order.
I have mentioned this matter in order
to make it clear that the Pigs Marketing
Board derives its powers from the action
of the Ministry, and that in a very real
sense I am responsible to this House for
seeing that the powers conferred upon
the Pigs Marketing Board are properly
and efficiently carried out.
It is, however, important to remember
that once a scheme is in existence the
responsibility for the actual running of
the scheme rests entirely with the Board.
It is true that it is necessary for the
Board to seek the approval of the Ministry for the creation of any post and of
the salary and conditions attached to the
appointment, but I have no power to disapprove of the person appointed to the
post. The administrative levy imposed
by the Board on producers also requires
the Ministry's approval, while the trading levy is made by the Ministry to cover
the Board's losses. Subject to such
matters the Board is a free body and
does not require the approval of the Minisin the exercise of the powers conferred
upon them. My only means of checking
the Board should it abuse its powers is
by an Order laid on the Table of the
House amending the scheme the Board
has been set up to operate.
Having made the position clear I will
now deal with the facts and circumstances which led up to the present
position. In the summer of last year
certain rumours became prevalent as to
the sale by the Board of casualty pigs and
other irregularities. The Board set up a
committee of five of its members to inquire
into these and referred certain other
matters to the secretary and manager to
investigate, and the investigations were
clearly deemed to be of such importance
by the committee as to require the attendance of their solicitor and auditors.
There was some delay in sending the
minutes of the Board's committee of
inquiry to the Ministry, but when the
minutes did arrive they were found to be
completely uninformative-and indeed for
some considerable time past the minutes
of the Board itself had been singularly
lacking in information. In view, therefore, of the uninformative nature of the
report of the committee set up by the
Board and the persistence of the rumours,
I told the Board that I proposed to
appoint two officers of the Ministry to
inquire into and report upon
(1) The arrangements of the Pigs
Marketing Board, Northern
Ireland, in regard to the purchase
and sale of pigs, and the administrative and financial control of
those arrangements;
(2) The general administrative and
financial arrangements of the
Board.
to
I had no direct power to order such an
inquiry, although I was in a position to
force it by refusing to continue
approve of the levies made by the Board
After some show of reon producers.
luctance the Board agreed to this private
inquiry, and assured me that the Board
and the staff would give every assistance
in their power.
The only other point I need mention
here is that on the 13th October the hon.
Member for Antrim asked me if I was
making such an inquiry, and if I would
make the report available to Members of
the House. In reply I intimated that the
report would be made available to any
Member who asked for it. The investigation duly commenced on September
20th, but it soon became clear that certain
of the senior officers of the Board resented
it and were unwilling co-operators. One
striking illustration is detailed in the
291 Pigs Marketing Board
Pigs Marketing Board 292
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
report, and, as you will see, the Board
itself went out of its way to support its
officer in the recalcitrant attitude which
he adopted.
the
In the course of the investigation a
number of matters arose which seemed to
be of an irregular character.
As it was
difficult to imagine that they could have
escaped the eye of the Board's auditors,
the two investigators waited on
auditor, told him the points in confidence,
and asked if they might have the advantage of studying his notes and any reports
he had made to the Board or the members
of the Board's staff. The auditor quite
properly intimated that he would require
the Board's approval, and when the
matter was referred to the Board they,
despite the fact that they had promised
full co-operation, instructed the auditor
that he was not to make his notes available to the investigators. I must leave
the House and the producers generally to
place their own interpretation upon that
refusal.
As the investigation proceeded it
became desirable to examine the Board's
files dealing with the transactions and
correspondence with its solicitor, and here
again a request for access was declined by
the Board.
One further example will illustrate the
difficulties the two investigators had to
contend with. The Board has invested,
or is committed to the investment of,
approximately £80,000 of producers'
money in two bacon curing factories.
The money available for this purpose is
the accumulated surplus of the administrative levy of Is on all pigs sold under
the scheme. This administrative levy
requires the approval of the Ministry.
Nevertheless, when the two investigating
officers asked access to the Board's files
dealing with the factories the Board refused permission, and I had no power to
compel them to comply. I mention these,
to my mind, three vital matters as illustrating vividly the difficulties the investigators had to encounter. That the Board
was misguided in the action it took must
be manifest to everyone, and it is difficult
to escape the conclusion that some person
or persons desired to put formidable
obstacles in the way of the facts being
brought to light.
As the House is aware, half the Board's
supply of live pigs is sold in Great
Britain, and the investigating officers
deemed it desirable to examine the
circumstances and conditions under which
these operations were carried on.
As a
criminal charge against one of the officers
of the Board is pending in Great Britain
regarding these sales I am
am not in a
position to comment further on this
matter.
I did not propose to say anything regarding the report itself. It has been
circulated to members, who can form
their own judgment regarding the serious
position revealed. I find, however, that
members of the former Board have circulated a document which purports to reply
to a carefully selected number of points
in the report. I do not propose to trouble
the House with a detailed answer to that
memorandum.
Many of the so-called answers are to
points that were never raised, and the
remainder obvious evasions. Thus in the
reference in the late Board's memorandum to the sale of a copy of the Register
of Producers the case referred to by them
is not the one referred to in paragraph 12
of the report.
Again on page 5 of the late Board's
memorandum
following
sentence:
Occurs the
"The travelling claims. were not
extravagant, were frequently incurred
in conjunction with Board members,
and represented such out-of-pocket
expenses as could reasonably be
claimed."
This is the answer that the elected
members of the late Board see fit to make
to paragraphs 18 and 20 of the report.
One further example. On pages 6 and
7 the elected members of the late Board
deal with staff season tickets. This is too
obviously an attempt to prove innocence
of a charge never made in the reportan effort to side-track the whole issue.
The report does not accuse the officers in
question of not paying for the season
tickets which they obtained at very greatly
reduced rates by virtue of the fact that
they were purchased through the Board.
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps the right
hon. Gentleman will allow me to interrupt. The acoustics of this Chamber are
very bad, and there is difficulty in hearing. Perhaps if the right hon. Gentleman

In a statement issued by the former

"The laxity of control alleged against
the Board cannot in any way be responsible for the arrest of one of the
Board's staff. The Board had never
any opportunity of discussing what was
the position."
That statement does not bear examination. Let me tell hon. Members the
facts. The two investigating officers satisfied themselves, by a study of the records
in the Board's offices, that all was not
well in connection with the sale of pigs
in Great Britain, and if there had been
any efficient supervision in the Board's
offices that position should have been
obvious to the Board long ago. Accordingly, the two investigators visited certain
centres in England, and the information
they obtained there was, on the direction
of my right hon. Friend the Attorney-
General, forwarded to the proper quarter.
After my investigators returned the
Board instructed, on December 16th, its
marketing officer, accompanied by a member of their auditors' staff, to call on every
one of the firms of buyers who had been
visited by the Ministry's investigators.
They endeavoured to extract from these
buyers what information they had given
to the Ministry, and the secretary and
manager subsequently prepared a statement and sent it to these buyers asking
them to sign it. I leave the House to
put its own interpretation upon this, and
to weigh up the hollowness of the statement issued by the late Board which I
have quoted.
You will have noted that the solicitor

I would now like to deal with the action
I took following the receipt and my
acceptance of the report submitted to
me by the two investigating officers.
Conscious of
of the fact that I was
ultimately responsible to this House I
realised that it was incumbent upon me
to see that proper action was taken to
clear up the affairs of the Pigs Marketing Board, and that such action would
have to be of a far-reaching character.
I accordingly transmitted a copy of the
report to each member of the Board at
his private residence, and at the same
time asked the Chairman to come and
discuss the situation with me, an invitation which he declined. I may say that
the Chairman is appointed by the
Minister. I also enclosed with the
report a letter intimating that I was
gravely perturbed at the state of affairs
revealed by the report, inviting them to
meet me six days later, namely, on
Wednesday, 22nd February, and
intimating that I was sure they would
appreciate the necessity for immediate
action being taken, and expressing the
hope that when they did meet me on
the 22nd they would be able to submit
proposals which would be adequate to
ensure an immediate improvement in the
administrative organisation of the
Board. I met the Board on Wednesday
afternoon, the 22nd February, when I
found that the Board not only had no
proposals to submit, but were anxious
to be given more time to consider the
matter.
I accordingly tabled three proposals.
which I asked the Board to accept, and
told them quite frankly that I thought
they should have no difficulty in coming
to a conclusion within an hour. These
proposals were: —
(1) The immediate dismissal of the
secretary and manager (the responsible
officer of the Board), and of the
accountant, with the appropriate salary
payments in accordance with their terms
of appointment in lieu of notice.
(2) The appointment in their place
as a temporary measure of two officers
seconded by the Ministry, and that these
two officers be responsible for the whole
of the administrative and accounting
arrangements of the Board and be
instructed to prepare and submit to the
Board proposals for the reorganisation
of the Board's staff and for the proper
conduct and supervision of the work.
(3) The appointment of the Comptroller and Auditor-General as the
Board's Auditor. At the same time I
made it clear to the Board that if they
could
not accept these conditions I
should have no alternative but to deal
with the Board by amending the Scheme.
When I returned to the meeting the
plea for time was again emphasised, and
I agreed to give them two further days,
that is, until Friday, to consider the

request to extend the period till Monday, a further five days; time which the
Board appear to have utilised, not in

I should point out, moreover, that at

the Board had entered into an agreement

three years' period. This vital information was withheld from me, although it
obviously affected the course of action

I again met the Board on Monday,

to represent producers.

As I have already indicated, one day

manager in regard to the investigation,
so that the Board were fully aware of

bound to tell you that this action of the

was taken despite the fact that the

and manager over a period of years.
They were then told that such a proposal

That matter was never again raised

When I suggested to the former Board

How were they to justify the expenditure of £4,500 of producers' money to

Before concluding, I should like to say
word regarding the position. of
individual members of the former Board,
of whom three are Members of this
House. I make no charge against them

They had every right to expect their

But when the report was sent to members of the Board indicating the laxity
of administration which existed I found

Finally, may I recapitulate the points.
I wish to emphasise to the House? I
am responsible for the Pigs Marketing
Scheme. The scheme is the creation of
my Department. To suggest that I
cannot intervene to dispose of the Board
that administers the scheme badly is like
suggesting that a parent cannot dismiss
an inefficient tutor who has charge of
his own son.
Members of the Board were perfectly
aware that rumours and criticism existed
regarding the affairs of the Board.
They had appointed a Committee to go

that arose in the course of the Ministry's
investigation were raised with the staff
and with the Board, who were fully

Nevertheless the Board refused to

accountant, on payment of the appropriate compensation to which they were

Instead of co-operating with me in

three years' agreement with their
secretary, and in these circumstances I
am convinced beyond a shadow of doubt
that had I done less than I have done
I should have failed in my elementary
duty to producers and to this House.

I regret very much that Members of
this House have been units in a combination that has gone a long way to
destroy the principle of public control
and regulation, but I am not surprised
when I hear the statement made by the
Minister. The members of a Board are
not always conversant with everything
the officials under the Board do. I was
pleased to hear the right hon. Gentleman making the special reference to the
three Members of this House who were
members of the old Pigs Marketing
Board. I think every Member of this
House can agree with that reference. I
was very much impressed by the statement of the Minister that in secrecy
these Members, along with their

agreement to retain the services of the
manager and secretary of the Board for

retaining the services of the manager

realised how much of that £4,500 the
working classes were asked to pay.
I am not viewing this matter from a
political or a personal point of view. I
would very much regret it if I thought
I had touched on a personal note during
my remarks. When this Board was
being established by the Minister of
Agriculture in this House I, as chairman

result of this has been shown in the

Year by year the accounts of other

supervised in the same way as the

I do regret very much the attitude of

From my knowledge of certain members

It is quite true to say that it is an

That in itself called for the interference

That in itself is not an answer. I feel

find a

are
The Pigs Marketing Board regarded
itself as a body elected by producers to
secure the advantages offered to producers by Parliament-not by
by the
Minister of Agriculture-under the
Agricultural Marketing Act. For the
first time in farming history, farmers
were given the right to organise themselves for collective action and to secure
for themselves the benefits of bulk purchase, bulk sale, and a stronger bargaining position in price negotiations.
Parliament having given the powers, the
Ministry of Agriculture have spent five
years in trying to take them away.
The Board has aimed at directing pig
supplies into the channel yielding the
greatest return, and at the maintenance
of level supplies to the more valuable
outlets. It has sought to regulate and
cheapen transport, and to give a service
to the farmers in the collection and
delivery of their pigs at the least cost.
How far has it been successful? By the
establishment of 30 collecting depots
throughout the country the Board has
placed at the farmers' disposal the best
method yet devised here or in Great
Britain for the handling of a live pig
trade. The cost of this regional marketing organisation in commissions to those
operating it has been reduced year by
year. In 1935 the cost was 22.66d per
pig, and it has since been steadily
brought down until in 1938 the figure
was 9.08d per pig. On the number of
pigs handled in 1938 this meant a saving
in that year alone of over £17,000 as
compared with the amount paid in
1935. The Board had under consideration a scheme which would have removed
even this cost from the farmer, and
which would have delivered his pigs
from farm to factory at no cost at all,
thus saving thousands of pounds to the
industry.
Year by year the control of pig
supplies has enabled the Board to secure
lower and lower freight rates. In 1932
rail rates for the carriage of pigs varied
from 2s to 3s per pig. In 1935 it was
1s 1d per pig; in 1938 it was down to
94d per pig. Over comparable areas
this is the lowest transport rate in Great
Britain or Eire, and represents a saving
of many thousands of pounds to the
industry.
Under the powers of producer control
at present held by the Board, direct
price negotiations with curers have
resulted in a vastly improved position.

cwt. less. In 1937 the prices paid were
variable, and in 1938, I am glad to say,
the Wiltshire curers paid the full Great
Britain price.
As compared with the 1935 price
basis, the improved arrangements made
by the Board represent an
increased
return to the farming industry of not
less than £56,000 up to the end of
September last. Nor is that all. The
ownership of curing factories by the
Board has recently enabled it to secure
a pig price, that in the seven months,
December, 1938-June, 1939, will yield
to the producers of Northern Ireland
£30,000 more in additional curers' prices
than they could have otherwise got.
Cheaper marketing costs, substantially
lower transport rates, vastly improved
curer prices, continuously improving pig
prices, an assured market for all pigs of
whatever class or type, are among the
achievements of the Board. But, in the
investigations that have been made, no
reference is to be found to what the
Board has been able to accomplish. In
this connection I should like to say that
at the moment practically the only
other Board in existence is the Board
set up by the Government through the
Ministry of Home Affairs-the Transport
Board-which has already squandered
two or three millions of the taxpayers'
money, and not one word of perturbation has been heard from the Minister
of Agriculture about that. For five
years the Pigs Board, unlike some
others, has enjoyed the complete confidence of producers. That the industry
has appreciated the vastly improved conditions that the Board has brought
about, and that due to producer control
so much has been gained and so much
saved, is evidenced by the present
position of the industry.
Imports of bacon into Northern Ireland have dropped from 94,000 cwt. in
1925 to 36,000 cwt. in 1936. The output of pigs in Northern Ireland has
increased from £290,000 in 1926 to
£770,000 in 1938. In the years
immediately before the Board the output yearly of pigs was in the region of
£400,000. In 1938 the figure was
£770,000. The value of the output of
pigs in pounds sterling as compared with
the total value of the whole of the agricultural output of Northern Ireland has
risen from 9.1 per cent. in 1931-2 to
20.6 per cent. in 1935-6, owing to the
operations of the Pigs Marketing Board.
From one of the smallest sections of Northern Ireland agricultural output and
one of the least value in exports, it has
risen under the Board's administration
to more than double its value, and is
now the largest section of the farming
industry with the highest annual output
in pounds sterling.
Whilst the pig industry was thus
thrusting its way into the foremost place
agriculturally, almost every other agricultural commodity had declined in
value or had remained stationary.
Dairy produce and milk, administered
by a Board controlled by Stormont,
declined in value from 24.6 per cent.
of the total value of Northern Ireland
agricultural produce in 1932-3 to as low
as 16.5 per cent. in 1935-6. These are
the achievements of a Board and staff
whom this report condemns. Is there
another marketing scheme in Great
Britain or Eire that can show a record
like the Pigs Marketing Board of Northern Ireland? I notice that the Members who are laughing are those who
supported and voted for the Transport
Bill. If they would look at the operation of the Transport Act they would
have sufficient to do without laughing
at the Pigs Marketing Board.
Mr. NIXON: The water wheel.
Mr. ELLIOTT: The enforcing of an
unworkable price arrangement in 1937
meant to the Pigs Marketing Board, not
the Transport Board, the closing of Wiltshire factories in April, May and June
of that year at a cost to the producers of
between £20,000 and £30,000.
Within the past two years the Ministry have sought to introduce Bills into
this House to deprive the Board of its
powers and hand them over to Stormont.
One of those was withdrawn because the
Board would not have it, while one was
never introduced for the same reason. The
Board has been put to considerable and
unnecessary legal expense in defeating
these Measures in the interests of the farming community. I should say that twothirds of the Board's legal charges are
made up in this way.

as levies have to be paid on my own pigs
I feel pained by the fact that a levy has

We have been told that we lost money

(1) Price incentive of 5s to 6s per cwt.
above roll price to bring forward Wiltshire supplies; (2) shipping of Wiltshire
pigs when the factories closed down and

Of the £44,151 stated by the Ministry

Wiltshire factories the Pigs Marketing
Board is interested to the tune, I think,

interests of the pig producers. As a
director of these Wiltshire factories he
had a duty to safeguard the interests of
those concerns, and those two concerns
are private companies.
Here we find a gentleman in a public
position, under a public Board, responsible to the Minister, holding two
positions which are irreconcilable, and
which necessitate a conflict of interest.
Has the Minister no responsibility in that
regard? Can it be rolled from his
shoulders on to the Pigs Board? Can it
be assumed for a moment that this Board
had been in existence for years past and
the Minister knew nothing of this
anomaly. I doubt if a parallel can be
found for such conflict and irreconcilability of interest and attitude on the part
of a high official of a Board constituted
under Act of Parliament, and having
indirect responsibility to the Minister of
Agriculture.
The unliquidated trading losses of this
Board amounted to over £31,000, and to
recover that a levy of 4s per pig is
required. The investigators of the Ministry say they found in the administration
of the Pigs Board inadequate records and
gross carelessness. They say they sought
for light in regard to these matters, and
they say the Board refused to give to the
investigators access to the auditor's notes
of meetings with the Board's executive
staff. I do not understand that procedure. I have found no reason for that
attitude of the Board. I think it very
unwise, and very short-sighted. They
say the published accounts of the Board
are misleading. What does that mean?
Here is a Board dealing with public
moneys, because, after all, producers'
money is public money, and the Board is
simply a trustee of these moneys. Every
penny it receives it holds in trusteeship,
and the grave allegation is made that the
very accounts as published by this Board,
and guaranteed to this House and the
public as being accurate, are in fact misleading.
They proceed to give details of that.
Some of them may be trifling, but, after
all, when you are dealing with public
moneys, these matters are not trifling,
because if they exist here they may exist
elsewhere, and may be typical of what is
taking place elsewhere. I do not say it
is, but there is the danger, the possibility,
that it may be typical of what is taking
place in other departments. For instance,
there is an allegation that the refreshments each morning for the members of

those strangers are paid for out of the
Boards' money

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: One shilling,
as has already been pointed out, of the

do not want to repeat any single word

rest of the shilling per pig of the administration fund has been steadily and consistently put into a reserve fund, and it
