That is the use to which
the shilling administration levy has been
put.
That brings us to the other part of
this levy, and I would just like for the
information of hon. Members to say that
they should try to think back to the
position before this scheme was brought
into operation. Up to that point we had
only one class of curing in Northern
Ireland. It was the roll and ham curing.
It was at all events a luxury trade, and
it could command a very good price so
long as it did not glut its own market.
But when the fuss arose over this new
pigs marketing scheme that was going to
make all the farmers rich the people
started to increase the stocks of pigs as
quickly as they could, and inside twelve
months the roll and ham trade was unable
at an economic price to absorb the number
of pigs that were coming forward. That
meant that some other steps had to be
taken to find a market for the increased
supply of pigs. Immediately the Ministry
put up a suggestion of Wiltshire cure.
The Wiltshire factories of to-day were
originally the Ministry's own baby, and
we as a Board have been nursing it from
the day they handed it over till this day.
I was not one of those who believed
that the establishment of Wiltshire cure
in the North of Ireland was going to
solve all the pig producers' difficulties,
but I readily fell in with the ideas of the
Ministry up to a point, and we as a Board
took over this idea of Wiltshire factories
to find what? To find that it could not
compete at all most of the year in price.
with the roll and ham factories, to find
further that the pig producers of Northern Ireland did not like bringing their
pigs forward at Wiltshire weights, and
would insist on going on in their own
way and feeding them into the weights
that were no use for Wiltshire. That
faced the Board with two difficulties, the

Pigs Marketing Board

difficulty of bridging the gap between
what the Wiltshire trade would pay and
what the roll and ham trade could pay

It necessitated a step to provide an incentive or inducement to the producers
to switch over from the roll and ham
pigs and produce a certain percentage of
Wiltshire pigs. The gap between the

If hon. Members will keep these facts
in mind it is in the internal trade of
Northern Ireland they will find the real
reason for this so-called trading loss or
trading levy. The Board had to step in
and find the money to fill that gap. We
did so by putting on this so-called trading
levy. We put that trading levy on everybody who produced pigs at so much per
pig, and we claim we were acting equitably in putting on that levy, because time
and again we tried as a Board whether
we should get more pigs into the roll and
ham trade, and immediately we tried that
with half a million pigs down went the
price. On the other hand, the Wiltshire
producers could not blame us because we
were then on an equality with the
suppliers of roll and ham and giving them
a handsome inducement on the top of that
for producing Wiltshire pigs. I would
like the House to understand that this
trading levy in respect of these factors
was not a necessity all the time. There
were times in the year when these two
different sets of prices practically met.
Sometimes they passed each other and
then receded to the old position.
There is a third factor that comes into
this trading levy, and that is the pigs.
that are shipped. The implication in
this report is that we persisted in shipping these pigs across to England and
selling them higgledy-piggledy, that we

early on in the activities of the Board
that necessitated this trading levy.
That is not the only story. In March,
1936, I think it was, having had considerable experience of the working of this
trading levy we approached the Minister

It seems to me that in years to come

Then there is the question of refreshments for the staff. When this matter
was looked into some years ago it was
found that the staff was paying for its
own refreshments and it seemed as if the
kettle was never off the hob. We thought,
as a Board, it was about time that some
regulation was laid down, and at the
suggestion of the secretary and manager
the Board actually decided that the staff
would be allowed just fifteen minutes, at
11 o'clock, each day in which to take a
cup of tea and a biscuit. To sweeten this
regulation a little bit, the Board decided
that it would bear the cost. From inquiries I have made I find that the
outlay would not amount to 50s a month
for the whole staff.
I wonder that another item is not included in this report. Speaking from
memory, I think that on three occasions
the Board members who were receiving
this handsome fee that the hon. and
learned Member for Central Belfast (Mr.
Campbell) has stressed so heavily, found
that if they adjourned for luncheon in
the middle of the day it would involve
their coming back on another day, as
they would not be able to finish the business on the agenda. A messenger was
sent out to one of the restaurants near
by to bring in sandwiches and coffee,
and we worked while we ate. We
thereby saved the expense of coming
back the next day and the fees
for attendance. We saved those
luxurious travelling expenses for the pig
producer, and the total cost of the sandwiches and the coffee came out of the
funds of the Board. Then there is the
matter of laxity in the petty cash, the
terrible laxity that is spoken of. It seems
as if we were running a bank, that the
secretary and manager borrowed continuously, certainly very regularly, from
this cash box, and that there is no

infallibles who have a great deal to query,
say they found no trace of the secretary
and manager having liquidated his

never asked? If hon. Members will turn
up the statement which was circulated
they will find a list of dates. The amounts
of those cheques are available, but they
were never requested.

in-
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The
creased provision under subhead C has
been necessitated by the Ministry's purchase of the late Mr. Tenison Groves's
collection of Irish records. Mr. Groves
in his life was a professional record
agent, and on his death his executors
offered to the Ministry practically the
whole of his collection of copies of
records and of the notes he had taken,
a great deal of which came from the
collection of the Public Record Office
in Dublin which was destroyed in the
fire at the Four Courts in 1922.
Material concerning Ulster is to be
found throughout the general collection,
which includes 6,000 copies of wills and
copies of or extracts from hearthmoney
and subsidy rolls, freeholders' lists,
parish registers and the like. The price
paid for the collection was £150 and
this cannot be regarded as anything but
reasonable, having regard to the fact
that the Groves collection is the
largest extant body of matter from the
destroyed Irish records, and is probably
the last of its kind obtainable.
As regards subhead F, the additional
provision is required on account of the
unexpectedly rapid progress made with
work of restoration. I beg to move.

which up to date is one acting principal,

especially those of the class who brought

when the mother takes this up the

Minister do the same. Supposing
you had a daughter who had to

Then when you come home from your

doing this embroidery or whatever kind
of work it is. It means she is slaving all
day without getting as much in a week as
would be got from a couple of days' work
with a decent employer.
Is the home a proper place to have an
industry? You know what these little
homes in the country are. There is the

the drawing room, the dining room, the

Oral Answers to Questions.
BLENDED WHISKY.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Commerce whether representations
have been made by his Ministry to the
British Government with reference to the
British Excise Authorities declining to
certify the mixture of half Scotch and
half Irish whisky as blended Scotch
whisky and the consequent refusal of the
Federal Alcohol Administration to admit
such whisky into the U.S.A.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): Representations have
been made to the British Government on
the general question of safeguarding the
outlet for Northern Ireland grain spirits
(which I understand are virtually of a
neutral character), provided by the practice which has grown up of exporting
such spirits in bulk for the purpose of
blending with Scotch malt whisky.
The hon. and learned Member will be
aware that the question of the description of such blends has been the subject
of litigation both in the United States
and in Great Britain. It is, I understand, sub judice.
MANUFACTURE OF ALCOHOL.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Commerce whether he can state if
the Government have had under consideration a grant or loan for a site and
new premises for an undertaking under
the New Industries Act, 1937, for the
manufacture of alcohol-both pot and
patent still-and industrial alcohol byproducts; whether this undertaking will
be entitled to an exemption for rates;
whether such concessions will enable it to
produce cheaper whisky than competitors
here; whether the wholesale whisky
trade has been consulted at any stage by
the Ministry; whether the stocks of potable whisky in Ulster 17 or 18 years old
are so large as to provide ample supplies
for all markets for the next ten or fifteen
years; whether a long-established distillery has been recently closed; and
whether trade depression has left only
about forty workers directly employed in
the process of whisky distillation in
Belfast area.
Mr. BARBOUR: Facilities under the
New Industries (Development) Act,
1937, have been offered to the promoters
of a company proposed to be formed for
the purpose of the manufacture in Northern Ireland of industrial alcohol and
other alcohol solvents, and the grant of
such facilities would enable the local
authority, if they thought fit, to exempt
the premises from the payment of local
rates.
The Ministry understands that the
operations of the proposed new undertaking may include from time to time the
manufacture of potable grain spirit to
the order of an associated company.
In dealing with applications for assistance under the New Industries (Development) Act (Northern Ireland), 1937, the
hon. and learned Member will be aware
that the main condition to be satisfied by
the applicant is that the new undertaking
will provide and maintain substantial
additional employment of a continuing
nature, and I am advised that there is
every reasonable prospect that the proposed new undertaking if it is proceeded
with will satisfy the conditions laid
down in the Act with regard to employment, as well as providing the
Province with a new basic industry from
which many other manufacturing activities may be developed.
As regards the remainder of the hon.
and learned Member's question, he will
be aware that all applications for assistance under the New Industries Act are
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
subjected to careful scrutiny by a statutory Advisory Committee who before
making any recommendation satisfy
themselves that the various statutory requirements have been complied with. He
will also be aware that in recent years
five or six distilleries in Northern Ireland have been acquired by outside
interests and subsequently closed down,
a step which has prejudicially affected
employment in Northern Ireland.
VOLUME OF WHISKY EXPORTS.
3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Commerce whether he can furnish
the statistics upon which Mr. Robson
based his forecast of the volume of
whisky exports of the alcohol factory
envisaged under the New Industries Act
when he is reported to have informed
the Belfast Rotary Club last year "they
may put in a still to make a little whisky
-this is where the market comes in again
-the market is thirsty and if a few
gallons of Irish whisky can be exported
to America we will have the employment
and the Americans the good whisky."
Mr. BARBOUR: I understand, from
the officer of the Ministry to whom the
hon. and learned Member refers, that the
reference to potable spirits in his speech
was not based upon specific data, but
was merely intended to be a general indication of the form which, in his opinion,
the projected new undertaking might
eventually take.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Could the right
hon. Gentleman, who has recently been
in the States, say whether there is a
thirst for Irish whisky being cultivated
among the public there?
Mr. BARBOUR: My inquiries did
not lie in that direction.
Mr. NIXON: About the thirst in
America for whisky, has that official's
statement anything to do with his promotion yesterday?
STUDENTS OF IRISH IN
NORTHERN IRELAND SCHOOLS.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she can state the
numbers for the year ended 31st Decem
ber, 1937-(1) of pupils in public ele
mentary schools in Northern Ireland
and how many were studying Irish; (2)
of pupils in secondary schools, and how
many were studying Irish; (3) of pupils
in junior technical schools, and how
many were studying Irish, and (4) of
pupils in teachers' training colleges, and
how many were studying Irish.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mrs. Parker): On
31st December, 1937, the number
pupils enrolled in public elementary
schools was 194,347, of whom 9,391 were
learning Irish.
The Ministry has no information as to
the number of pupils in secondary schools
who learn Irish, but it may be of assistance to the hon. and learned Member
to know that of the 3,640 candidates at
the Secondary Schools Certificate Examinations, 1937, 931 offered Irish as a
subject.
During the school year 1937-38, 2,903
pupils were enrolled in the day technical
schools and of these pupils 261 attended
classes in Irish.
As regards the colleges for the training of teachers, on 31st December, 1937,
of the 314 students in training under
this Ministry 52 at St. Mary's College,
Belfast, and 26 at St. Mary's College,
Strawberry Hill, London, were learning
Irish.
THE POSTPONED ROYAL VISIT.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if, at or
about, the time of the proposed visit of
the Duke and Duchess of Kent to Northern Ireland was announced he publicly
stated that the Duke was inviting himself; whether on or about the 6th of
February, 1939, the following official
statement was issued on behalf of the
Government: "On the advice of the Government of Northern Ireland the Duke
and Duchess of Kent have agreed to
postpone their visit to Northern Ireland
until later in the year;" whether the
Duke and Duchess have arranged to go
to Australia in October next to take up
his appointment as Governor-General of
the Commonwealth of Australia, and
whether the Prime Minister will explain
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
9 MARCH 1939
the motives which prompted the Government to tender this advice to His
Majesty's brother and representative.
The PRIME MINISTER: The
answer to the first three parts of the
question is in the affirmative. As regards the fourth it is not in the public
interest to reveal the reasons which
actuate the Government in tendering
advice on occasions such as that to which
reference has been made.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not part of the
policy of appeasement and surrender and
has not gelignite won again? And, by
the way, when I am on my feet I give
notice that I will raise this question on
the adjournment on some suitable
occasion.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think
that the question is a very inappropriate
one and even if it is raised on the
adjournment I will be able to add
nothing to what I have said. I consider it is not in the public interest to
give information of the kind required by
the hon. Member.
Mr. NIXON: Why are you giving the
world a false impression?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think it
is only people like the hon Member who
get a false impression.
Mr. NIXON: No. I am talking
about the world.
PERSONATION IN BELFAST.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Attorney-
General whether Henrietta Freeman,
Wigton Street, pleaded guilty at the last
July Assizes of the felony of personation at Northumberland Street Polling
Station on 9th February, 1938, and
received a recorded sentence from the
late Lord Justice Best; whether two of
the presiding officers on duty at the booth.
on the occasion of the personation refused to give a statement to the police
detective charged with investigating the
case; whether this refusal constitutes the
offence of "Misprision of Felony" or
some kindred offence; whether the two
presiding officers referred to were men
with large election experience; whether
several people in Northern Ireland have
been prosecuted for "Misprision of
Felony," and now that the matter has
been brought to the notice of the
Attorney-General will he consider it.
The
The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
facts as to the plea of guilty of Henrietta Freeman and the recorded sentence
imposed by the learned judge, are as
stated in the first part of the hon. Member's question. I have not been able, in
the time at my disposal since this qustion
was put down, to ascertain the facts to
which the hon Member refers in the
subsequent part of his question. If,
however, the hon. Member will supply
me with the name of the detective officer
referred to, I shall have further inquiries
made and communicate the result to the
hon. Member.
I may say that prosecutions for misprision of felony are extremely rare,
and, according to Lord Westbury in
1866, "have now somewhat passed into
desuetude."
Mr. NIXON: Has the Attorney-
General ordered a successful prosecution
in Northern Ireland for misprision of
felony in connection with the police.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I certainly ordered one which was unsuccessful.

does not appear to be aware of the legal

DETAINED UNDER SPECIAL
POWERS ACT.
8. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state how
long he proposes to detain in prison,
under the Special Powers Act, without
any charge being preferred against them,
the men who were arrested in Belfast at
Christmas.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question
raised by the hon. Member involves considerations of policy.
I think it well again to emphasise the
views of the Government in regard to
this matter.
At the present time we in Northern
Ireland are being attacked by the I.R.A.
and other illegal organisations-emanating mainly from Eire-by methods involving damage to life and property, and
having for their object the disruption of
the Constitution.
So long as this condition of affairs continues the Government is fully prepared
to use all the powers entrusted to it by
this House in defending the lives and
property of our people and in maintaining law and order.
The hon. Member asks me when the
men at present detained will be released. In reply, I would suggest to him
that he should ascertain from his friends
in Eire when these attacks on Northern
Ireland to which I have referred are
going to cease.
Mr. BYRNE: Is it not a fact that
some of the arrested men have been released and no charge found against them?
There may be others in the same
position.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I have
already stated, the men interned have
the right to make representations to a
committee of which a legal gentleman is
chairman. One of these men did so and,
on the representations he made, he was,
after a further investigation into the
facts, released.
Major PANTER: Is it not a fact that
it was entirely due to the active and immediate steps taken by the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs,
that we had no bombing outrages at
Christmas and that his action was well
justified? (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
UNSANITARY HOUSES IN
BELFAST.
9. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether there are
2,000 unsanitary houses in Belfast, as
reckoned in the annual report for 1938
of the Irish Regional Council of the
Federation of Building Trades Operatives.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have not
seen the report of the Irish Regional
Council of the Federation of Building
Trades Operatives, but the figure
mentioned
agrees with that given in the
annual report of the Medical Superintendent Officer of Health for Belfast.
PENSIONS FOR MUNICIPAL
EMPLOYEES.
10. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
Oral Answers
9 MARCH 1939
Oral Answers
when the introduction of the Belfast Corporation Enabling Bill to provide
pensions for municipal employees will be
presented for the first reading; whether
he will expedite this Measure so as to
secure pensions for the workers on and
from the 1st April, 1939.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member will understand that the promotion of legislation providing particular
powers for the Belfast Corporation would
be a matter for Private Bill legislation
by the Corporation. I do, however, propose to introduce a general Bill enabling
local authorities to superannuate any
officers who may have been compelled to
retire under an age limit before they
have completed 20 years' service, and
this provision will enable the Corporation to deal with certain difficulties that
have arisen in their case.
If, however, by "employees" and
"workers" the hon. Member has in mind
persons paid by weekly wages as distinct
from "officers" I have to inform him
that it would not be possible to cover
the case of such persons in the Bill which
I propose to introduce at once.
I hope,
however, to introduce a Measure at an
early date dealing with the whole question of superannuation for local Government employees, and the case of these
persons will be carefully and sympathetically considered in the preparation
of this Measure.
Mr. BEATTIE: Do I understand that
the representations made by the trade
unions and the Belfast Corporation for
an enabling Bill to allow the Corporation
to bring in a scheme of pensions from
the 1st April, 1939, is now abandoned,
and that they have got to wait on the
general scheme which will be introduced
at an early date? I would like to ask
the Minister is he aware that the weekly
workers in the Belfast Corporation are
expecting to have this pension scheme
operating from the 1st April? Is he also
aware that the Belfast Corporation has
made provision in its budget to meet the
liability of this scheme? In view of this
position will the right hon. Gentleman,
if there is an emergency Bill, give power
to the Belfast Corporation to carry out
the scheme?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the
hon. Member is under a misapprehension.
As I have already explained, the Government gave every possible facility to the
Corporation to deal with this matter.
Those facilities were not availed of by
the Belfast Corporation. While it would
be impossible for us to frame a Bill to
deal with the Belfast Corporation alone,
the Government is prepared to provide
an enabling Bill to deal with all local
authorities which will meet the case of
the hon. Member.
Mr. BEATTIE: Do I take it that the
onus of responsibility for an emergency
Bill on behalf of the workers of the
Belfast Corporation falls on that body?

TYPHOID AT ANTRIM MENTAL
HOSPITAL.
11. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of persons in the Antrim Mental
Hospital who contracted typhoid fever
some time ago; whether the carrier was
traced; whether he will state the salary
and emoluments of the medical superintendent of the institution; whether the
position of medical superintendent is a
full-time post, and whether the officer in
question holds the D.P.H. qualification.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I assume that
the hon. Member's question refers to the
outbreak of paratyphoid fever which
occurred in the Antrim Mental Hospital
towards the end of 1937 and the beginning of 1938. This outbreak affected 36
inmates and three of the nursing staff.
The paratyphoid fever is believed to
have originated with a female patient.
admitted a short time before the outbreak took place, and seven patients are
still isolated as carriers of paratyphoid
infection.
The resident medical superintendent of
Antrim Mental Hospital is in receipt of
a salary of £1,000 a year, with emoluments valued at £150 a year. The post
is a full-time one, and the resident
medical superintendent does not hold the
D.P.H. qualification.
I am glad to have this opportunity of
paying a tribute to the energetic steps
taken by the Committee of Management
and by the medical and nursing staffs to
control the outbreak.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that the
resident medical superintendent undertakes work outside the institution?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the hon.
Member wishes to make an attack upon
this gentleman perhaps he will give me
notice.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is that about the
water wheel?
VOLUNTARY INSURANCE.
12. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Labour whether in regard to the
Ministry's leaflet on Voluntary Insurance
for Widows', Orphans' and Old Age
Pensions, contributors removing to any
of the overseas Dominions can continue
to pay contributions and eventually draw
their pensions in the Dominions, and
whether in view of the fact that pensions
are not payable elsewhere than in Northern Ireland, Great Britain and the
Dominions, the Ministry have decided
whether Eire is a Dominion for such
pension purposes, and whether the Ministry have decided if a resident in Northern
Ireland insures under the Contributory
Pensions Act, 1937, and pays contributions for years or until benefit becomes
payable, and through family, health or
other reasons has to go and reside in
Eire, such change of resident will involve
(a) loss of benefit, or (b) both loss of
benefit and of contributions towards
benefit.
Payment to Members
Payment to Members
9 MARCH 1939
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): Eire is part of His Majesty's
Dominions, and so long as it remains so
a voluntary contributor moving there
can continue to pay contributions, can
become entitled to pensions from Northern Ireland, subject to the usual conditions, and if he removes to Eire after
reaching pension age, can continue to
draw his pension there.
Mr. NIXON: If Eire is part of His
Majesty's Dominions why did the Government of Northern Ireland forbid the
King's brother to carry out his visit here.

"That in the opinion of this House, so
much of the Resolution of this House on
the sixth day of June, nineteen hundred
and thirty-five (relating to payments to

twentieth days of December, nineteen
hundred and thirty-eight, to report on
certain matters in regard to public transport in Northern Ireland."
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): The purpose of
this Resolution will be clear to hon.
Members without a great deal of explanation on my part. As hon. Members are
aware, the total amount payable to a
Member of this House in respect of attendances at meetings of Committees of this
House or Joint Committees of the Senate
and of this House is restricted by a
Resolution of this House to fifty guineas
per annum.
When this limit was introduced I am
sure that the House did not visualise that
an occasion would ever arise when the
sittings of a Joint Committee would
involve the unremitting attendances
which the Joint Select Committee on
Transport has entailed. Representations have been made to my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, that the
application of the limit in respect of this
particular Committee would be unreasonable, and with this view the Minister
and the Government as a whole fully
concur. I beg to move.
Mr. BROWN: Arising out of this
Resolution, I submit that the decision of
this Committee, whose expenses we are
dealing with to-day, has been anticipated.
Mr. SPEAKER: That matter can be
discussed on another occasion. The only
point here is as to the payment mentioned
in the Resolution.
Mr. BROWN: There was another
matter I was going to raise now, but
I will wait and do so on the Adjournment of the House to-day.

Manufacture of Alcohol.
The Pigs Marketing Board.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."
(Sir Wilson Hungerford).
Mr. CAMPBELL: I wish to take this
opportunity of diverting the House for a
few minutes from the marketing of Irish
pigs to the manufacture of Irish whisky,
both the pot still and the manufactured
end, and I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will say, "For this relief, much
thanks." The wholesale and manufacturing end of the whisky trade in Northern Ireland is watching with some
anxiety the encouragement by the Government of a new alcoholic venture.
is a venture for the manufacture of
whisky, both pot still and patent still,
for consumption, with its industrial byproducts. The encouragement is to be
given through the machinery of the New
Industries Act, 1937. That Act provides
for grants or loans to approved undertakings, and also for help to those undertakings towards the payment of income
tax and in the way of relief or exemption
from rates.
The position as developed is Gilbertian,
because on the one hand the Government
have put on the Statute Book, and are
keeping on the Statute Book, the most
drastic statute extant in any Statute Book.
There is no parallel with our Northern
Ireland licensing code in its severity.
Yet, on the other hand, Sir Roland
Nugent, chairman of the Ulster Development Council, speaking at the birthday
luncheon of that Council last December,
in the presence of three Cabinet Ministers, and I dare say with their approval
and applause, said that this alcohol
venture would provide a basis for extending the range of all industrial activities,
founded on the alcohol we produced. He
said also that it was likely to become the
biggest industrial unit in terms of factory
employment of those so far established.
So we are building on the strong and
firm foundation of alcohol. I submit to
It
Manufacture of Alcohol 434
Manufacture of Alcohol

the House as a matter of administration
that the State backing-because it comes
to that to one privileged enterprise, one
preferred venture, is unfair to the local
trade, which has been passing through
hard times.
I have been looking into this matter
with some curiosity, and I believe that
forty or fifty years ago Irish whisky was.
all the rage. Then a change set in.
Scotch whisky came into vogue, and was
distributed to the fighting forces during
the War in preference to Irish whisky.
Then it was widely and cleverly advertised. The public were attracted, and,
of course, in exercising a preference
for Scotch or Irish whisky, they
were guided only by the factor
of palatability. They say whisky in
pot still in Scotland is unique, and
is impossible of reproduction elsewhere.
The pure unblended Scotch whisky,
owing to its characteristically marked
taste and aroma, has gradually become
more acceptable to the taste of the
public.
So widespread has the popularity of
Scotch whisky grown that enterprising
Japanese merchants in far away Japan
have named a town in Japan, Aberdeen.
They gave it a new orientation, a new
name, unpronouncable, but in the home
and American markets it is recognised
as Aberdeen. They set up this new town
of Aberdeen, and this Aberdeen whisky
from Japan found its way on to the
market, and is making its way on the
market. Owing to the change of taste
the demand for Irish whisky has fallen
off, and this is particularly noticeable
in the case of the United States.
I
One of the hopes held out in regard
to this new venture is that there is a
thirst in the United States for Irish
whisky. I appeal to the Minister of
Commerce, who has been in the United
States recently, as to whether there is
any foundation for that statement.
take it from his silence that he thinks
there is no foundation for that statement. As a matter of fact, far from
there being a market in the United
States for Irish whisky, Irish whisky is
finding it more difficult to find a demand
there. There are tariffs and legal limitations against it, and to sell it in the
United States is almost impossible. Yet
one of the hopes of this new venture is
that there will be a market in the United
States for Irish whisky, a great deal of
which comes from Northern Ireland.
I understand that only two distilleries
are operating in the Belfast area as
against three a short time ago, and that
of the distilleries in Eire one was recently
shut down. I also understand that local
stocks for the available markets are abundant for years ahead. What chance has
an alcoholic venture, even with the powerful resources of the Government behind
it, of making any headway in the United
States of America? I do not enter upon
the moral aspect of this question. There
may be hon. Gentlemen on the back
benches opposite who may not think it
right or proper to facilitate this particular form of manufacture, and to
send out from Northern Ireland an overflow of alcohol to circulate in the
American markets. But I do submit to
the House that it is not a sound and wise
policy to utilise public resources for the
benefit of a new venture to the detriment
of old long-established firms who can find
no ready outlet for their products. If
the help that is foreshadowed is given,
then in a few years, thanks to public concessions and preferences, this venture
may be able to put on the markets
whisky cheaper than its competitors can
produce. What do the temperance party
think of this state of affairs? As to the
likelihood of success attending the byproducts part of the venture, can the
Minister hold out any reasonable expectation of it ever fructifying commercially or industrially?

returns, and other infor-
Do not let there be any mistake about
this question. It was Parliament which
laid down the relations which were to
exist between Marketing Boards formed
by me under the Act of 1933. We have
heard from the hon. Member the way in
which the Board sought to evade its responsibility in this matter of their
minutes. The hon. Member suggests
that this was to avoid interference by the
Ministry. But do not forget that there
was no matter in the affairs of the Board
with which my Ministry could interfere
except where Parliament had given my
Ministry express powers to exercise supervision over the affairs of the Board. For,
as I have already explained to the House,
although I and my Department had
power to create the Pigs Marketing
Scheme, to endow the Board with powers,
and subsequently to amend or even wind
up the scheme, my Ministry had only
very limited functions in regard to the
supervision of the scheme whilst in
operation. It is true that certain matters,
such as the approval of the salary and
employment of staff, the approval of
levies, the grading of pigs, and the regulation of the export of pigs from Northern Ireland, were expressly reserved to
my Ministry under the Act of 1933. In
some cases, however, the Ministry
exercised its powers solely in consultation
with the Board. Let me take the case of
the trading levy. The hon. Member
made considerable reference to how the
Board came to impose this levy. What
does he say?: "We put on this so-called
trading levy."-I am quoting from
Hansard "We put it on everybody."
In fact, we did this and we did that.
Listening to him I am sure the House
formed the impression that the trading
levy was entirely a matter for the Board.
Actually it is entirely a matter for the
Ministry. Let me quote the statute :-
(3) The Ministry may by order require the Board administering a scheme
to impose a special levy or levies;
(a) For the purpore of securing that
the provisions of the scheme operate
equitably as between all classes of
producers; or
(b) For the purpose of covering any
loss which the Board have experienced
in trading under the scheme.
In practice, however, the Ministry has
always consulted the Board with regard
to the trading levy. Not once has the

exercisable by my Department, and not

in Northern Ireland, and so long as I

Infanticide Bill--
Second Reading
14 MARCH 1939
Infanticide Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In moving
the Second Reading of this short
Measure I feel confident that I shall have
the support of Members in all parts of
the House. A mother who has killed
her infant child has always been emphatically an object of sympathy and pity
rather than a subject for punishment.
That it should at times be necessary to
bring such a person to court charged with
murder, and to impose upon her a death
sentence, is harrowing in the extreme to
the presiding judge, and in indeed to all
concerned in the administration of justice.
It is true that a reprieve might arrest
the direct consequences of the law's
decision, but it cannot compensate for the
suffering caused to the mother or the
acute discomfort felt by all those who are
compelled to assist in framing the charge
against her.
In 1922 the first step was taken to
mitigate the unhappiness caused by these
sad cases, when the Infanticide Act of
that year passed the Imperial Parliament and was applied here by the
Uniformity of Laws Act. By this
Measure a mother who caused the death
of her newly born child while the balance
of her mind was disturbed by the effects
of childbirth, was to be guilty of
infanticide, and to be punishable for
manslaughter and not for murder.
This Act represented a great step forward in the treatment of cases where the
destruction of the child followed immediately on its birth, and in dealing with
matters brought before them under its
provisions judges showed all the mercy
and humanity which ought to characterise
the administration of justice. Judicial
decisions in England and in this country,
however, laid down the principle that
the words "newly born" could not include
children whose age exceeded one month.
Distressing cases still arose from time to
time where a mother did away with a
child of more than a month old, her
mental condition being still affected by
childbirth, and at such times the protection intended by the Act of 1922 could
not be extended to her.
Accordingly, last year steps were taken
by the Imperial Parliament to repeal and
re-enact the original Measure in a form
which defined a newly born child as one
under 12 months old, and protected the
mother from the finding of murder while
the balance of her mind was disturbed,
not only by the effects of childbirth as in
the Act of 1922, but also by the effects
of lactation consequent on the birth of
the child. This Bill reached the Statute
Book as the Infanticide Act, 1938. It
did not apply to Northern Ireland, but
the present Bill is framed on the same
humane basis, and will, I hope, speedily
reach our Statute Book.
While I am glad to say that few cases
arise in Northern Ireland to which either
the original Act or the present Bill would
apply, I feel that this short two Clause
Measure will command general approval.
We all recognise that motherhood should
normally be a state of happy emotion,
and where for any reason a mother is so
distraught as to destroy what should have
been the centre of her affections, the State
should mitigate as far as possible the legal
consequences which must inevitably
follow the taking of any human life. I
beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time.'
my

I would be very surprised if there was

would hold the mothers to be responsible

will give the human touch to that kind
of person and I hope it will meet with
no opposition.

Mr. BYRNE: In proposing the
Second Reading of the Hairdressers Bill
I will be very brief because a similar
Bill was debated in this House on a
previous occasion. Since that time the
Bill has gone through another place. I
should like to mention a few of the
objects of the Bill. It is brought in in
the interests of public health. I am
sure every Member of the House wishes
to see the health of the public safeguarded. That is one of the principal
objects of this Measure. Hairdressing
is a service which is used by young and
old, rich and poor, and, therefore. it
applies to all sections of the community.
On a previous occasion I stated that I
had in my possession letters from practically every local authority in this area,
and each and everyone of them approved
of the Measure. That is one of the
reasons why I took this matter up and
introduced this Measure as a Private
Member's Bill.
It is left to the option of the local
authorities whether they put this
Measure, if it becomes law, into operation or not. Bylaws can be made by
the various local authorities in consultation with the members of the Hairdressers' Association, and that, I think,
guarantees that no hardship will be
placed on hairdressers. It was mentioned on a previous occasion that a
Measure of this kind might be injurious
to the small man. In my opinion it
will be in his interest, and will guarantee to each and everyone of his
customers that the service they receive
will comply with public health requirements. The cost of carrying out the
provisions of this Bill was also mentioned
on a previous occasion. I have gone into the matter carefully and find that the
cost of registration, insurance, etc., will
amount to 6d or 7d per week. In my
opinion it will be of immense advantage
to the small man, because it will help
to increase his business.
So far as inspectors are concerned the
local authorities need not be put to any
expense. The inspectors at present employed by them could easily discharge
this duty without any extra cost. It
would only take a very short time to
visit all the hairdressers in a particular
area. Therefore, there can be no complaint so far as expense is concerned.
In introducing this Measure we are
only going step by step with local
authorities across the water. A similar
Measure has been in operation across
the Channel for some time, and so far
as we can find out there have been no
complaints. In certain localities the
Hairdressers' Association has requested
the local authorities to put this Measure
into operation. Therefore I would ask
the House to give this Bill a Second
Reading. We will be prepared to accept
any reasonal amendments that may be
put forward by any Member of the
House. I beg to move.
Mr. HENDERSON: I have pleasure
in seconding the Motion so ably proposed by the hon. Member for Falls.
It would not be fair for me to take
up the time of the House in regard to
this matter, because I know everyone
is anxious to support the hon. Member,
more especially in view of the very able
way he has handled this Bill since its
inception. It would not be fair to put
forward any more amendments than
those introduced on the previous
occasions. I think the Government
moved 54 amendments. However.
they were reasonable amendments. I
appeal to the House to give the Bill a
Second Reading.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews) I wish to make it quite clear at
the beginning of my remarks that, in my
opinion, it is not a question of some
Members of this House desiring to help
our farming community more than other
Members wish to do. We all desire to
help our farmers to the greatest extent
in our power. It is, therefore, simply
a question of how can our farmers best
be helped. We all appreciate the diffi
culties with which our farmers have got
to contend; we all know the disappointments they meet, and we also realise that
any decline in the farming industry
would have very serious results to Northern Ireland. After all it is our chief
industry; there are more engaged in it
than in any other industry, and to a
considerable extent the security of the
United Kingdom rests in the hands of
the farming community. It is therefore only natural, as I have already said.
that we should all wish to help the
farmers.
When I was Minister of Labour for
more than 16 years I always held, with
the approval and support of my
colleagues, that the best that could be
done for our industrial classes was that
they should, as regards social services.
receive the same benefits which their
fellow countrymen receive in the rest of
the United Kingdom. Therefore I feel
I am quite consistent in urging that the
same policy should be adopted in regard
to the farming community; in other
words that they should receive, by means
of subsidies, and in every other direction,
the same advantages which the farming
community across the water receive.
You will, however, agree that equality
does not mean that they should receive
privileges. If we urge that our farmers
should be placed in a privileged position
in one direction we would probably do
them very substantial injury, due to the
fact that the British Government would.
in my opinion, be justified in saying
that in other directions we
entitled to claim equality.

Land Annuities
Land Annuities
14 MARCH 1939
annuities came to be payable. It was
found that the old land system could
not continue for this reason. In Ireland,
to begin with, the landlords owned the
land and all upon it, and many landlords, there were some notable exceptions, left the improvements to be made
by the farmers. Then, in some
instances, the tenants were rented on
those improvements which was a thing
no one could stand over. Many landlords agreed to give their tenants what
was called the three F's-fixity of tenure,
free sale and fair rents.
As regards fixity of tenure there was
no difficulty. It simply meant that no
farmer could be put out of his holding
so long as he wished to remain in it
and paid the rent. Free sale simply
meant that when the farmer wished to
give up the farm, or his discendants
wished to sell, they could put it up for
sale and sell the improvements which
had been made on the farm by the
tenant-not by the landlord-to the
highest bidder. The difficulty arose of
fixing what was a fair rent, and although
the Land Commission was set up in order
to fix rents it proved to be unsatisfactory. The British Government, in
their wisdom and generosity, decided
that this dual ownership would have to
end. A succession of Land Acts were passed
ending in our own Act of 1925, which
was a compulsory Measure and which
practically put every farmer in Norhern Ireland who had a purely agricultural holding in the position of owning his own farm, subject to the payment
of the annuities which we are discussing
to-day.
Now, the hon. Member for Woodvale,
who moved this Motion in the first
instance, did not seem to be very
definite in his opinions, because in his
Motion he asks that the land annuities
should be remitted in whole or in part.
That was a fairly flexible term. But it
simply means this in any case, that if
the whole of the annuities were to be
done away with the farmers would receive a gift of the balance of the
annuities payable, and if only a part
were to be remitted, according to this
Motion, the farmers would receive part
of the balance payable, because the hon.
Member did not go on to say that he
proposed that the time for payment
should be extended.

promptly and willingly by the vast
majority of them, and it is only a small

The British Government raised the

from their landlords. Further, there
was a gap between what the landlords
could be expected to accept and what the
tenants could be expected to give, and

that these land purchase schemes should
be carried through. That is the position
beyond all doubt. Great Britain is still
responsible for redeeming the loans for
both the old and new land annuities and
for paying the interest in the meantime.
Therefore it must be obvious, even to
the hon. Member himself, that it is only
the British Government that could do this
thing, and it would require an Act of
Parliament in order to enable it to be
done.

help our farming community-both the

turbed to find recently that four members of the Butter and Cream Marketing
Board had resigned from that Board, and

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The circumstances
in which four of the elected members
of the Butter and Cream Marketing
Board have resigned may be stated very
simply. In November and December
last fines totalling £700 were imposed by
this Board against one of their
gistered producers, namely, Armaghdown Creameries, Limited, of Newry.
The Board had a perfect legal right to
impose this fine under the provisions of
the Butter and Cream Marketing

Scheme. I consider, however, that the

is
the treatment of Armaghdown
Creameries, Limited, by the Board.
To appreciate the full significance of
the recent action of the Board towards
this creamery it is necessary to recall
a number of events which may have been
forgotten by Members of the House. The
matter, indeed, goes back to the end of
1934, and the beginning of 1935, when
the firm of Armaghdown Creameries,
Limited, commenced operations in Newry.
This firm, which had had considerable experience in butter manufacture and dairy
production in the South of Ireland, decided
at the end of 1934 that they would
be glad to commence operations in the
North of Ireland and to start a creamery
in this area. At that date there was
not a single creamery operating in the
whole of County Down, and Armaghdown Creameries decided that they
would commence operations in Newry.
I welcomed this development, not alone
on account of the fact that it meant the
development of creamery facilities in an
area in which such facilities had been
absent in the past, but also because of
the employment which would be afforded.
in the town of Newry. As soon, however, as it was learnt by the Ulster
Agricultural Organisation Society that
Armaghdown Creameries were commencing operations in this area, this
organisation came to my Ministry and
offered to start a creamery at Loughbrickland. They urged in the very
strongest manner that preference should
be given to them, because they would
be a co-operative concern, and that I
should refuse a licence to Armaghdown
Creameries.

Similarly Mr. Johnston, secretary of
the Ulster Agricultural Organisation
Society, was also appointed as secretary
to the new Butter and Cream Marketing
Board, and of the five elected members
of the Board no fewer than four were
members of the committee of the Ulster
Agricultural Organisation Society.
Armaghdown Creamery had a contract
for the supply of cream to a purchaser
in Great Britain who had never in the
past purchased regular supplies from
Northern Ireland. This contract was
duly registered by the Butter and Cream
Marketing Board in July, 1936. Deliveries were continued until June, 1938,
when there was an interruption in
supplies for a few weeks until April. The
Board, which did not like such contracts,
claimed that this interruption in supplies rendered the contract void, and
fined Armaghdown Creameries £20. The
matter was submitted to an arbitrator
appointed by me. The arbitrator found
that the contract had been broken by
the interruption of deliveries. Since,
however, the sales had been made under
the same conditions as when the contract
was in force, the arbitrator further decided that each side should bear their
own costs.
The award of the arbitrator was made
on the 21st October, 1938, and copies
of his award were despatched by the
Ministry to each party on the 25th
October, 1938. The Board thereupon
demanded that Armaghdown should
forthwith cease selling to Messrs. Henry
Edwards, and on the 22nd November,
1938, imposed a fine of £350 upon
Armaghdown for continuing to do so.
On the 2nd December, 1938, Armaghdown submitted to the Board a new
contract similar to the one the Board
had approved on the 16th July, 1936.
The Board refused to accept this contract,
and on the 14th December, 1938, imposed
a further fine of £350, making the aggregate of the fines imposed on this creamery
£700. Incidentally on neither occasion.
was a representative of Armaghdown
Creamery invited to be present at the
Board to state the case for the defence.
In both instances this creamery was fined
without being heard in its own defence
and without being invited to make any
defence.
At this stage I considered it necessary
to intervene. I regarded the offence
committed by Armaghdown as largely a
technical one. There was no question of
price cutting, and, that being so, in
my view the question whether cream was
sold direct to an English buyer on a
contract or through the agency of the
Butter and Cream Marketing Board was
of little moment. Both methods are perfectly legal under the scheme. My
anxiety is to see as much Northern Ireland cream as possible sold in Great
Britain, and which of the two methods
of sale is adopted seems to me essentially
matter for creameries and their
customers to decide.

Accordingly, I indicated to the Butter

The Board urged that for the sake of

I acceded to this request, and

"I acknowledge receipt of your

and Cream Marketing Scheme, Northern Ireland, has appointed an assistant

"In view of the expressions of

will not allow their rights and justice
to be exercised in this way. I will
also advise the Board that they should

I am confident that members of the
House will be surprised at the tone of
the letter received and at the suggestion
of the solicitor to the Board that he
would instruct the Board to take certain
action if I failed to respond to the threat
contained in his letter.
I greatly deprecate the way in which
this dispute between the Butter and
Cream Board and Armaghdown has been
forced to an issue at the present time.
I think the House will agree that the
mere mention of the amount of the fines
imposed-£700-for what was after all
a purely technical offence is sufficient to
indicate the extremity of the Board's
action. I am at present considering the
whole future of the Butter and Cream
Scheme in the light of the situation that
has been created. I have not yet decided
what steps I shall take to deal with the
situation, but of one thing I am at least
certain. It has been borne in upon me

Marketing Scheme of allowing a Board.
to impose monetary penalties upon its
registered producers has proved a failure.
I am regretfully driven to the conclusion
that the power of self-discipline given to
producers under the Agricultural Marketing Act is one which representatives of
producers have not yet learnt to exercise.
with wisdom and moderation, and that
in future power of imposing penalties

of law.

Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move:
"That this House deplores the fact that
over approximately 90,000 persons are
workless; it views with grave concern the
evidence of widespread and serious malnutrition and is of the opinion that
immediate improvement in their standard
of maintenance is urgently necessary;
it regrets that the continued failure of
the Government of Northern Ireland
either to produce definite plans for the
provision of work and wages under the
present system or to initiate a policy
whereby old-age pensioners would receive an increased income; it is of
opinion that all able-bodied unemployed
should be taken away from the poor law
unemployment
system and placed on
assistance, thereby relieving the local
authorities from a national responsibility
and that unemployment assistance grants
should be substantially increased."
I move this Vote of Censure with a
feeling of my responsibility to the masses.
of the people, who, for the past 18
years, have looked to the Government for
some assistance and support. And after
reviewing that period of time which was
occupied by the Unionist Government in
our area, I came to the conclusion that
there was only one thing that I should
do, and which it was my bounden duty
to do, and that was to frame a Motion
such as you see on the Order Paper and
place it there as a Vote of Censure.
Now, much can be forgiven to the Government even if it fails and blunders,
provided only that it has tried to succeed.
For nearly eighteen years the Northern
Government has passively watched the
unemployment figures slowly rising. It
has not merely failed to overcome unemployment; it has not tried. There is
no attack being made on the evil of unemployment in this country. There are
no men, no civil servants detailed for

There is no economic sub-committee

is fired, not a command is given. Such is

I say the country's need now is for a

I have been thinking recently of the
fundamental causes of unemployment.
In this House we generally relate it to
such things as trade cycles, tariff barriers
and fluctuations in the balance of trade.
I believe if we want to seek a real solution we need to go deeper still. The
thing that is holding up trade and commerce at the moment is not primarily
economic barriers but a lack of trust and
confidence between man and man. And
that is not due solely to international
unrest. It is often due to personal feelings that are not unknown even in this
House. We need to-day a new spirit in

will work together and where Government departments and local authorities

Kingdom depends to a large extent on

necessarily await some general amelioration in the relations between the great
trading nations before we can hope to
witness the rehabilitation of our export
trade.

Nevertheless, it has been the constant
endeavour of the Government, to the
fullest extent within its power, to maintain and, if possible, to develop our
position in overseas markets. There has
been built up in the Ministry of Commerce an efficient commercial intelligence
service through which local exporters
are kept regularly in touch with overseas markets, trade openings abroad, and
the exchange position in various
countries of the world. This service is
at all times available to assist any
individual firm to develop new markets,
and to make new contacts in existing
markets. Moreover, while the Ministry
of Commerce can take no direct part in
the conclusion of trade agreements with
overseas countries, regular contact is
maintained with the Board of Trade in
connection with the negotiations leading
up to such agreements. To mention one
example, the Anglo-American Agreement concluded last year, which incidentally provided a striking departure
from the prevailing tendency towards
economic nationalism, took particular
account of the importance of our linen
trade with the United States. In passing, I should say we owe our gratitude
to the President of the Board of Trade

R. S. Hudson, for the efforts which were
made on our behalf, and for maintaining the closest possible liaison between
the British negotiators in New York
and the Ministry of Commerce in Belfast during the progress of the
negotiations.

scheme; whether he has formed any
estimate of the amount of fire brigade
emergency equipment necessary for
effective fire-fighting in Belfast under
assumed modern war conditions, and, if
so, what progress has been made towards
the purchase of this equipment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to
the first part of the question is in the
negative.
for
An estimate of the necessary fire
brigade emergency equipment
Belfast has been prepared by the Corporation, and I have had the benefit of

The purchase of the necessary equip
ment is at the moment under consideration by the Government.
ALTERNATIVE TO DEEP
SHELTERS.
3. Mr. CLARK asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state, in
view of the impracticability of Belfast
to deep air raid shelters, what alternative shelter policy the Government have
in mind; how many gas masks were
ordered for Northern Ireland and how
many of these have been delivered to
date.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This is one of
the many difficult problems with which
the Government is faced in connection
with air raid precautions, more especially
in view of the nature of the Belfast
sub-soil, and I am not in a position at
the moment to express any opinion as to
what the decision of the Government in
this matter will ultimately be.
.

One million four hundred thousand

the next few days.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the right

AN A.R.P. ADVISORY
COMMITTEE.
4. Mr. CLARK asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has considered
the appointment of an advisory committee and technical sub-committee to assist
him in the effective administration of
the A.R.P. Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, Sir.

an advisory committee and technical
sub-committee would serve a most useful
purpose.
POSITION OF HOSPITALS.
5. Mr. CLARK asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has been
approached by hospitals or institutions.
asking his advice on the evacuation
question in time of war, and whether
any advice
was given; whether the
Ministry has received any plans from
the Belfast Corporation with a view to
the possible accommodation of many of
the casualities that might be expected
from a modern air raid.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer
to the first part of the question is in
the negative.
As to the second part of the question,
I am aware that the Belfast Corporation
have under consideration the number
and location of first aid posts for the
city. The question of hospital accommodation for casualties subsequent to
treatment at a first aid post is one to
be dealt with by the Government, and
I am glad to be able to record that,
in considering this matter, I am receiving the co-operation and assistance of the
Northern Ireland Branch of the British
Medical Association.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of
that, will the right hon. Gentleman tell
the House how he is going to utilise the
offices vacated by their friends, the members of the Belfast Poor Law Guardians,
who have since been dissolved?

A HILLSBOROUGH BUILDING
CONTRACT.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of labourers' cottages recently
built by
by the Hillsborough District
Council and the agreed contract price of
each cottage; whether the specification.
stipulated that each cottage should be
plastered outside with a three-quarter
coat of Portland cement and a finishing
coat of Snowcrete or Atlas cement;
whether the job was carried out according to specification, and, if not, what
penalty, if any, was imposed on the
contractor; whether the money to build
these cottages, or any of it, was
borrowed from the Ministry of Finance;
and whether any complaint in respect to
the matter has been made to the Minister
of Home Affairs.
Sir DAWSON BATES: A scheme for
57 cottages is being carried out by the
Council, the average cost per cottage
being £309. A loan of £21,741 was
sanctioned by the Ministry and the
amount borrowed from the Government
Loans Fund.
The original specification was as stated
by the hon. Member, but the architect,
with the approval of the Council,
amended the specification by omitting
Snowcrete in favour of cement plaster,
whitewashed. No penalty was imposed
on the contractor as the amended specification was made by the Council, but the
latter will get the benefit of a saving of
about £103.
A complaint was made to the Ministry on the subject by the Joint Council
for the plastering industry and this was
investigated by the Ministry's inspectors
who were satisfied with the work carried
out in accordance with the amended
specification.

Mr. BEATTIE: This seems to be a
very big burden for an area such as we
represent, but I presume that economy
is being brought to a state of efficiency.
Sometimes economy might interfere with
efficiency. I take it from the right hon.
Gentleman and his Financial Secretary
that efficiency in service has not been in
any way interfered with. I think myself that there has been a little cheeseparing in some ends of the service. Take
the question of unemployment, which
was dealt with so widely yesterday; the
question of education, the question of
the school-leaving age and the question
of grants to local authorities, who are
really administrative bodies acting on
behalf of the Government. I feel that
many of our social services are being
asked to bear too large a share of this
enormous amount of £4,134,300.
Having said that, I would like to know
from the right hon. Gentleman what
provision is made in this huge amount
for education over and above the standard that education was allowed in the
past. We have now a system of education extending the school leaving age to
15. Our educational system was impoverished for half a generation or more,
and we did think when the Act of 1893
was brought forth that education was
going to be open from the elementary
school to the university. We discovered
that was only a myth, it was not real.
We found that as far as the working
classes were concerned education was
going to be limited, and this limitation
was because of the financial responsibility
of widening it to any great extent. I had
hopes, and still have hopes, that there
were amongst the working-class population some brilliant boys and girls who, if
given a reasonable opportunity by State
financial assistance, might be able to
place Northern Ireland on a very high
pedestal educationally throughout the
world.
We have a system operating to-day
that does not encourage to the greatest
possible extent the use of the machine
known as education. I will be told that
the educational costs in Northern Ireland
are very high as compared with Great
Britain, but educational costs could
never be too high. Perhaps if the
peoples of the world had been educated
by proper methods the world would not
be in the state it is in to-day. I believe
no area in the world requires more attention from the educational point of view
than the area we represent. I would like
this area to be in a position of honour,
Supply--

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
but we have not got near that region of
educational facilities I would like to move
in. I can see in the Estimates a very
drastic limitation of assistance to the
children. Just imagine putting a boy
into learning the craftsmanship of carving. He looks upon the practical carver
doing his work of art. The boy himself
would like to perform a similar task,
but, owing to the poverty of his parents
he is not in a position to provide the
tools to do a craftsman's work. Is that
not the position of the child in the school?
He can go to school and take instruction
from the teacher, but owing to the
poverty of his parents he has not the
tools, the school books, that are needed.
Like the apprentice he is only a lookeron, and the benefit he should get from
education is not received.
I would like the Minister under our
educational system to provide for the
granting of free books to all the elementary schools in Northern Ireland. I
think a duty devolves upon the Government to make that provision. If they
are prepared to allow the local authorities to make that provision they are
putting them up against a very high
obstacle because they must make that
provision from the rates, and whilst some
local authorities have endeavoured to
help to the best of their ability they
have only touched the fringe of the
problem of equipping the child with the
necessary books.
Then I think the policy of the Government is wrong in respect to its management. I hope that "Justice for all and
privilege for none" is their motto, as
it is mine. The banner that I carry
bears those words. But is that the motto
of the Government? Their policy is to
try to make provision for a quid pro quo.
They give out one or two contracts of a
serviceable kind to certain classes of
industry. There are only a few privileged printing firms in Northern Ireland
allowed to do the good class of work
which this Government requires. That
policy is a very unwise one. The
Government may get newspapers both
evening and morning to be their mouthpieces. That is a privilege they give to
two units in the newspaper world. I
think it is wrong, unfair, and unjust.
I do not think they are entitled to
take the position which they occupy and
use it for the purpose of propagating
the ideals they represent. That has been
a noted factor for the last number of
years in this part of the world and a
recent increase in that propaganda has
been shown by at least two newspapers
in this city. I have an idea that I could
spot the winner in the competition. We
have the morning mouthpiece giving out
and we have the evening mouthpiece
giving out. I want to tell you that
you
represent all classes of the community,

NORTHERN IRELAND AND THE
WORLD'S FAIR.
the
1. Mr. HENDERSON asked
Minister of Commerce whether he can
state if the Government of Northern
Ireland have a stand at the World's Fair
to advertise the goods manufactured in
this country, and, if not, can he state
the reason why.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): As soon as plans for the
New York World's Fair were made
known my Department communicated
with the appropriate Department in
London on the subject of Northern Ireland participation. It was ascertained
that, apart from a central prestige exhibit, His Majesty's Government in
Great Britain contemplated an exhibit
for the United Kingdom on an industrial and not on a geographical basis.
Accordingly, the Irish Linen Guild, with
the financial support of the Government
of Northern Ireland is organising a display of linen goods for inclusion in this
British industrial exhibit.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
adequate separate representation. for
Northern Ireland could only be achieved
at a cost altogether disproportionate to
the potential advantages to be secured.
I am satisfied, moreover, that it would
be prejudicial to the linen exhibit to
deprive it of its place in the great Hall
of British Industry which will be one
of the important features of the Fair.
Mr. HENDERSON: Does the right
hon. Gentleman not think that this is
against the best interests of the Ulster
manufacturers? It is no good to say
that the linen trade will be represented.
What about the shipping firm of Harland
& Wolff, the manufacture of tobacco and
of other things. The question of cost
should not have entered into the matter
at all. I am not quite satisfied. The
Free State Government will have a
stand and we should have a stand there
too representing Northern Ireland manufactured goods.
Mr. BARBOUR: Of course there is
room for a diversity of opinion on this
subject. I think a great number of
people in Northern Ireland will only be
too glad to welcome this opportunity of
demonstrating in this way that we are
part and parcel of the United Kingdom
of Great Britain and Northern Ireland,
and certainly we should not have wished
to take advantage of this opportunity
to show a separate identity in any way.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman whether the experience
at Glasgow Exhibition has not taught
his Department a lesson in so far as
advertising linen is concerned? Is he
not aware that any person who is looking for an exhibit of Irish linen will
never dream of going to the British
industries. He will go to the Irish space
to look for Irish linen, and it will be
known as Eire. In view of that position
arising in the World's Fair, does he not
think it would be in the interests of
Ulster industries if Northern Ireland
had a space let out for advertising goods
produced in Ulster?
Mr. HENDERSON: Might I ask the
right hon. Gentleman to tell the House
whether the advertising of this stand will
be in the name of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland?
Mr. BARBOUR: Again there is a
difference of opinion on this point, but
a great number of industrialists, the
people really interested to see the exhibit
of linen, would go to the section of the
exhibition which is devoted specially to
textiles, and exhibits in such section are
made to much better advantage by those
firms manufacturing these goods and
able to have attendants there who are
able to explain and give information to
potential purchasers as to where they
can get the goods, and as to prices and
things of that kind.
Mr. JOHNSTON: Is it not a fact
that linen has been selected as one of
the four textiles to be exhibited in the
British section of the Fair and is to be
placed in the most favourable position?
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes.

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): The

authorities?
DEATH IN A POLICE CELL.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
circumstances of the death of the late
Thomas Stanley Stewart, 225
225 Mayo
Street, who died in the police cell on
13th June, 1938, from the effects of a
fracture of the skull caused by falling
off his bicycle; whether it is admitted
that there was a mistake made by the
police on the occasion inasmuch as they
thought the boy was drunk, while in
fact he never took drink in his life;
whether when this boy was dying in the
police office any word was sent to his
parents, and what steps, if any, have
been taken, or will be taken in the
matter.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Warnock):
In the absence of the right hon. Gentleman, may I say the circumstances of the
case referred to by the hon. Member are
as follows:-
At 11-30 p.m. on the 13th June last
two constables on duty in Albert Street,
Belfast, found a man, later ascertained
to be Thomas Stanley Stewart, sitting
on the footpath with his back against a
wall, and as he smelt strongly of intoxicating liquor, was unable to speak or
stand up, and had every appearance of
intoxication, he was brought to barracks
on a charge of drunkenness.
At 11-55 p.m. he was conveyed to the
police office and he spoke both on getting
into the police van and later when being
searched in the police office. While in
the cell he seemed to be suffering from
sickness as a result of intoxication, and
he moved about the cell until 4-15 a.m.
the following morning, when he
apparently went to sleep.
on
At 4-50 a.m. he became very ill, and
the medical attendant, who arrived in
about 18 minutes, treated him for weakness of his heart. His condition then
deteriorated so fast that he could not be
moved to hospital, and he died about
6 a.m.
On the same day a post-mortem
examination was carried out at the
Coroner's instructions, but no indication
of the presence of intoxicating liquor
could be found, the doctor stating that
death was due to a fracture of the skull
such as could have been caused by a fall
from a bicycle. There were no external
indications of this fracture, and the
doctor stated that the effects of an injury
of this nature were similar to those
arising from intoxication. The Coroner
found that Stewart "died from coma
following a fracture of the skull, caused
by an accidental fall of his bicycle."
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
It subsequently transpired that after
Stewart had fallen from his bicycle, and
prior to the arrival of the police, a
civilian had given him brandy in an
attempt to revive him, and it was the
smell of the brandy, together with the
effects of the injury, of which, as I have
stated, there were no external indications, that misled the police and
resulted in the charge of drunkenness.
I
The Coroner at the inquest said,
cannot find that I can attach any blame
at all to the police. It was a regrettable
mistake, but, at the same time, it was
a most natural one, and, as the doctors
have stated in evidence, had they been
in the shoes of the two policemen, they
might have made the same mistake
themselves."
Having given the hon. Member the
facts of this case, I should like to say
at once that I am very glad it has been
raised in this House, because it gives
me the opportunity to testify to the fact
that Stewart, at the time of his accident,
must have been perfectly sober and that
he bore a most excellent character in
every respect. The deceased's parents,
very properly, obtained professional
assistance to clear up the cause of death
and to remove, once and for all, any
suggestion that Stewart was suffering
from the results of intoxicating liquor.
On the matter being brought to the
notice of the Ministry, it was felt that
the parents should not be put to any
expense in doing what any other parent
would do in like circumstances, and,
accordingly, an ex gratia payment was
made to meet the actual expenses incurred by them in being represented at
the Coroner's Court.

21 MARCH 1939
MILLISLE WATER SUPPLY.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state what steps are being taken by the
Down County Council to have a proper
water supply and sanitary system carried
out in Millisle in order to promote the
health and well-being of its residents and
visitors, and to provide suitable and useful work for the unemployed in that area.
Mr. WARNOCK: The hon. Member
will recall that when he last put a question about this matter in October, 1936,
I explained that serious technical difficulties stood in the way of the development in which he is interested. I then
also mentioned that the Newtownards
Rural District Council were considering
various alternative solutions of the
problem, including that of securing the
necessary water from local wells.
The present position is that the
Council have sunk a well at Millisle. It
will be necessary to have this well tested
so as to ascertain whether it is capable
of providing a sufficient supply of water.
The tests have been delayed by the recent
rains, but it is hoped to have them made
as soon as the weather improves. Should
they give satisfactory results a gravitation supply by means of a pump and
tank is in contemplation.
The provision of sewerage facilities
must naturally await the installation of
the water supply, but in the meantime
the Council have decided to provide a
public sanitary convenience at Millisle
for the use of residents and visitors, and
they hope to proceed with the erection of
this convenience at an early date.
FOUND DROWNED.
5. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he can state the
number of persons "found drowned" in
Northern Ireland during the last four
years, and how many of these people
were unemployed.
The PRIME MINISTER: In reply
to the hon. Member's question, I find
on inquiry that apart from cases of
accidental drowning the total registered
deaths from drowning in Northern
Ireland in the last four years was 70, of
which 47 were returned as "Found
drowned-open verdict," and 23 as
suicidal. Of these 70 cases seven were
recorded at the Labour Exchange as unemployed.

657 Local Superannuation Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
Local Officers Superannuation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
cases
Mr. WARNOCK: As the House is
aware, an officer of a local authority is
only entitled to a superannuation allowance where two conditions are satisfied:
First, he must have attained 60 years;
and secondly, he must have had 20 years'
service. There are exceptional
where retirement is due to ill-health, but
the general rule is as I have stated. The
Belfast Corporation last year adopted a
scheme giving terms and conditions of
service for its officers, and under that
scheme all officers must retire at 65. As
a result of the operation of this scheme
a number of officers have been, or will be,
compelled to retire at 65 without having
attained 20 years' service. Under the
existing Statutes they would be ineligible
for pension. When they entered the
Corporation service there was no
compulsory retirement rule, and normally
they would have been permitted to remain until they had completed their 20
years. It appeared inequitable that
these officers, compelled to retire, should
be denied pension rights, and the Ministry agreed. The object of this Bill is
to enable the local authority to superannuate such officers. It only applies
to those officers who were there on 31st
March, 1939. I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. BEATTIE: I regret very much

That in no way interferes with the

authorities outside Belfast. Unfortunately that enabling Bill is not forthcoming, for what
I am not
aware.
reasons
