Investigation into Various Boards.
Mr. BROWN: I beg to move, "That
in the opinion of this House a Select
Committee, representative of each of the
Six Counties of Northern Ireland, should
be set up forthwith to conduct an independent investigation into the working of
the various Marketing Boards in Northern
Ireland, with particular reference to the
Pigs Marketing Board and the Butter
and Cream Marketing Board, and at
the same time to hear evidence from all
parties interested in the Bacon Industry
Bill and to make recommendations
regarding the proposals contained in
same before it is placed on the Statute
Book."
As the House is aware, we have had
a considerable amount of discussion on
this subject already, and it is my desire
and wish to avoid going over ground
that has already been covered, but this
is an occasion on which I think the
House cannot and must not shirk its
responsibilities and duties in the matter.
The first question involved is the question of the privilege of Members of this
House. I suggest it is a question of
privilege no less important than the
question of privilege involved in the
famous Duncan Sandys case in Great
Britain a short time ago.
The question of privilege involved here is no way
smaller as far as we are concerned. We
must approach it from that angle to
start with.
What is the question of privilege?
The question of privilege is this. We
have a Board which has been dissolved,
the Pigs Marketing Board, and on that
Board were three Members of this House.
Certain charges have been made against
the members of that Board. It is not
for me to say whether they were right
or wrong, nor is it necessary for me to
say whether the Minister of Agriculture
was right or wrong.
Mr. ELLIOTT: On a point of
correction, may I say that no charges
were made against the members of the
Pigs Marketing Board?
Mr. BROWN: I do not want to enter
into conflict with the hon. Member for
South Tyrone in this matter because I
am as anxious on his behalf as I am
on behalf of the Government that all the
facts should be brought out. I am
661 Investigation into Boards

to condemn three Members of this House

To get back where I left off when the

or wrong in dissolving the Board is not

I have said I do not

If we
are prepared to condemn Members of
this House unheard on the written

It is an axiom and principle of democratic Parliamentary institutions that
there should be no taxation without representation. This is taxation without
representation, and I am going to oppose

myself. These Committees are
a vital

I suggest that in future it would be

it should be possible to give representation to each county. Such representation is the very basis of democratic
government. I suggest that this Motion

the people of this country there will soon
be no country to fight for.
I feel I must give the Prime Minister
an opportunity to tell the country what
is going to be done to assist the overburdened taxpayers, and so I am going
to resume my seat. Before doing so, I
would appeal to the Members on the
other side of the House to take some
interest in the affairs of this country,
because some day there will be an
Opposition in the British House of
Commons who will ask questions in
regard to the finances of this country,
and if that is done I am afraid the
answers will not add to the dignity of
Northern Ireland.
I protest against the huge amount
asked for this Consolidated Fund. I feel
the Ulster people are not getting value
for their money, and that will continue
until they are intelligent enough to vote
in the right manner. In the meantime,
I protest formally against this sum
being asked for in view of the fact that
the Government have added to the
burden of the ratepayers by foisting
upon them responsibility for the unemployed. If that had not been done the
Government would have asked for
another £5,000,000 at least. The same
thing applies with regard to education.
By that means the expenditure of the
Government is reduced considerably, but
that is not taken into account. I appeal
to the Prime Minister to let the House
know what steps are going to be taken
to economise more in the future than has
been done in the past.
Mr. NIXON: It is regrettable, but we
are undoubtedly getting into an economic
mess in consequence of over-spending, as
illustrated by these Estimates. Coming
here I travelled by two roads which were
the most prosperous in the city in former
times, the Shankill Road and the Newtownards Road. Every couple of perches
there are vacant shops. Whole blocks
of shops are vacant. That is the greatest
sign of Government extravagance, because the tenants are not able to carry
on business and pay the rates and
income-tax. The rates are 10s 6d in the
£ and income-tax, which is based on the
valuation, is 5s 6d, that is 16s in the £.
There is nothing for hundreds of these
people but to close down their businesses
and clear out.
Nearly every day I am here I come.
across new Boards set up by the Government which I have never heard of
before. There is one called the Pig
Industry Council set up by the Government. The nominated chairman is Sir
Dudley McCorkell, who is paid between
£20 and £25 every time he presides at
a meeting. Then there is the Bacon
Board. I am here all the time, and I
pay considerable attention to what is
going on, but I could not tell the number of official Boards set up in Northern
Ireland. When a Board is set up it gets
its own staff, its own solicitor, and its
own premises. These gentlemen flourish,
as they must when the chairman gets up
to £20 or £25 every time he presides.
And the people who pay have to go out
of business. I said before when the
Prime Minister was not present that I
honestly believe I have been one of the
greatest friends the Government have
had in this House for the past ten years,
because if they had taken my advice they
would have had very few of these Boards,
very little trouble, and not so many
vacant shops.
The hon. Member for Shankill referred
to elections. I know the Government
are not responsible for the way elections
are conducted in Northern Ireland. In
Victoria Division something like 150 more
votes came out of a box than were cast.
How did those votes get into the box?
Everyone knows that the presiding
officer keeps blocks of the votes issued,
and when more votes are taken out of
a box than there are blocks in the hands
of the presiding officer, then there has
been maladministration. The only possible way they could get into the box
is that there were extra blocks of votes
-it is not hard to get the stamp-and
a voter in going forward with his own
vote gets one or more of these extra
votes to put along with his own. That
was in the Press and cannot be disputed.
When I am talking about administration and maladministration, in case I
should wrong any person, I must say

that the Royal Ulster Constabulary are

that, but when the police who had

He was fair enough, but said he was
told at Glengall Street not to make a
statement, and I know he was telling
the truth.
There you have men who get three
guineas a day and are sworn to carry
out their duty impartially, and when the
officers of the Crown who are charged
with seeing justice done between man
and man, go to these gentlemen, these
political hacks, who should not be let
near a ballot box, they are refused information. I only mention this matter in
order that something will be done at
future elections to prevent gentlemen of
this class getting behind boxes. I spoke
before of the great impartiality of the
Attorney-General's Department and of
the police, but they cannot control these
gentlemen, and if I did not now say
something about it the Returning Officer
might not hear of it. That is why I
mention the matter here.
I do not believe for one moment that
the Returning Officer would stand for
anything of the kind, because if that
went on you might as well stop elections
altogether. I can assure you that I
could hardly stop personation, and
when I could hardly stop it, where does
the ordinary man come in? In that
respect I classify myself as being better
able to stop it than anyone else. In
one division I noticed a gentleman called
the Captain. Every now and then he
went in and stood behind the personation
clerks, made notes, and then came out.
I went behind him and took the notes

While I hold no brief for the workhouse master, I think it is going quite
too far to deprive him of his living and

ing him of his living for all time,

Another thing the
Secretary said is that he would see that
the guilty were punished in respect of
what took place in the union. We will
wait to see what he will do in that respect, but I do say this, let the punishment fit the crime, let the crime be
reproved before a proper tribunal. But
punishment such as has been inflicted
upon the master, which is equal to a fine
of £400 or £500 a year for all the days
of his life, and which will fall more
heavily on his wife and family than on
himself if he has a family-I do not
know personally-is not what we used to
get under British justice and fair play.
Let the punishment be suitable to the
crime. In to-day's papers it was
ported that he would get no pensionthat is what I am going on-that the two
Commissioners said he was not entitled
to a pension. Let the punishment be
suitable to the crime. If he is retired
on a reduced pension that he can live on,
and he is losing £700 a year-that is
punishment; but you might as well
murder the unfortunate man
as take
away his living altogether. That is all
I wish to say at the present time.

REARMAMENT WORK FOR
NORTHERN IRELAND.
3. Major SINCLAIR asked the Prime
Minister whether in view of the publicity
recently given in the Press to the share
of rearmament work allotted to Scotland,
said to total about £20,000,000 of which
no less than £5,500,000 will be spent
in the next twelve months on the construction of new factories alone, he will
give the House some information about
the value of this work shared in Northern Ireland, and whether he can state
what progress has been made in the
negotiations for the establishment of a
Government factory in this area.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
The hon. and gallant Member will
appreciate that information as to contracts under the rearmament scheme is
normally of a highly confidential nature
and cannot be divulged. He will be
aware, however, that a substantial
amount of work in the production of
aircraft and warships, armaments and
munitions, has been allotted to Northern
Ireland firms, and that, moreover, the
expenditure on Defence Service developments, such as the construction of new
barracks at Ballymena and Lisburn and
the extension of the Aldergrove aerodrome, is not inconsiderable.
I should like to assure the hon. and
gallant Member that while it has not been
found possible to secure the establishment of a Government factory in this
area, the question of Northern Ireland's
share of the rearmament programme is
receiving the unremitting attention of
the Government.
Mr. BROWN: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if the Government is
prepared to consider the question of
sending a deputation of Members of this
House to Westminster in order to reinforce the appeals of the Government for
a greater share for Northern Ireland of
the thousand pounds per minute, day and
night, being expended on armament work
in Great Britain?
Mr. BARBOUR: No.

NEW INDUSTRIES.
4. Major SINCLAIR asked the Minister of Commerce whether his attention
has been drawn to the fact that in
certain areas in Great Britain steps are
already being taken to attract new industries with a view to the absorption
in them of workers thrown out of employment by the eventual slowing down
of the rearmament programme; to what
extent a similar problem will arise in
Northern Ireland, and what action he
proposes to take to counteract any increase in unemployment therefrom.
Mr. BARBOUR: It is difficult, if not
impossible, to assess the probable industrial effect of the slowing down of rearmament, but the hon. and gallant
Member will be aware of the constant
activities of my Department under the
New Industries (Development) Acts. It
is hoped that the type of work attracted
hitherto, and that represented by several
applications now under consideration are
not such as will disappear with
slackening of rearmament, but will constitute, I trust, a permanent and expanding addition to the industrial
structure of Northern Ireland.

The PRIME MINISTER: I must
apologise again to the hon. and learned
Member (Mr. Campbell) for the delay
in giving an answer to the very proper
question he put down on many occasions
in connection with the debate that is
to take place to-day. I think I should
reply to his question before proceeding
to make any further remarks.
reason for the delay was that I felt that
the questions at issue were very wide
and required most careful consideration.
The point he put forward was that the
Government might set up a judicial committee outside the House, free from all
influence in the House, in order to go
into the whole matter that was
dispute.
In the first instance it may clear the
air a bit if I explain that Members of
this House who became members of a
Board outside the House by specia!
election have no special privileges
within the House. I think it 18
not perhaps generally understood that
in discussing this matter to-day we are
not discussing the conduct of three Members of this House but the conduct of
the Board as a whole, from whom they
cannot be, and I am sure have no desire
to be, dissociated.
With regard to a public judicial
inquiry, it would to-day be impossible
for me to set up such a tribunal to be
effective. When I say "to be effective"
I mean that it would not have power to
send for persons and demand the production of
papers and documents.
Therefore, it would require legislation
in this House in order to enable the
Government to entrust the inquiry to a
judicial committee. I want to make
that perfectly clear. I should also say
with perfect honesty to the House that
even had it been possible to set up a

judicial committee I would not have been

The
The difficulties would be very great.
May I mention the fact that some time
ago a Resolution was put down on the

referred. A Motion was put down asking for a judicial inquiry to be held, but
it did not limit it in any way.
inevitable consequence would be that

questions of policy before any tribunal
outside the House in my opinion would
be derogatory to the powers of Parliament itself. Parliament should be the
supreme authority for giving a decision
on matters of policy and on what any
individual department of the Government should decide to do.
Another great objection which will
appeal to the House is this. We have
already had a long discussion on
matter of the dismissal of the Board.
Both sides have been heard. My right
hon. Friend the Minister of Agriculture
has spoken. He is a gentleman in whom
I and, I believe, the vast majority of
the farmers of this country have ample

hear.) So have also my right hon.

me. That Report has been aired outside and inside the House, and the House
having heard all sides of the question I
think should be able to come to a conclusion and vote, I trust as unanimously
as possible, for the Resolution standing
in my name.
If this speedy and constitutional way
of determining the matter were deviated
from by having to introduce into this
House a special Act of Parliament empowering the Government to set up a
judicial committee it would mean such
an intolerable delay that I do not think
any of us could stand for it. There
would first of all be the process of preparing the Bill. Then there would be
the First and Second Readings, the
Committee Stage, and the Third Reading in this House, after that the Bill
would have to go to the Senate and pass
through there, and then come back here
to get the Royal Assent. That in itself
would require a considerable amount of
time.
During that period matters would be
dealt with in various directions to which
I will refer later, but even if we had
the powers, probably in the summer
time, to set up this judicial committee it
would require at least, judging by other
similar inquiries, six or eight months to
carry out its duties. It seems to me that
that added to the preliminaries which
would be necessary, and then the consideration by the Government of any
report that was received, also bringing
it into this House to ask its opinion on
the subject would add still further to the
long period that would be necessary
between now and getting the matter
finally decided.

In doing so, the first thing I want to

I am

It took years of agitation and effort
on the part of the farming community
in Great Britain and Northern Ireland
to secure for themselves the right to control in a democratic way the marketing
of their own produce. To me it is
the
alarming that

When we had achieved a good measure

that if irregularities should arise they

secure that if grave abuses do arise they

the business of the ratepayers to secure
the

Votes of Censures.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have been asked
to give a ruling on the Notice of Motion
which was on the Order Paper last week
in the names of the hon. Member for
North Tyrone and the hon. Member for
North Derry. The House will remember that a vote of confidence was put
on the Order Paper last Thursday by
the Government, which subsequently
became a vote of censure owing to the
terms of the Amendment which was proposed. This Motion was discussed, and
the House decided in the negative against
the Amendment. I had to consider the
implications of the debate which took
place on Thursday, and after carefully
considering them I decided
I decided that it
definitely did amount to a vote of censure.
Then noticing on the Order Paper this
Motion, which stood in the names of my
hon. Friends, I had to come to a conclusion whether that was a vote of
censure too. On examining the matter
I found definitely that it was. Right
hon. and hon. Members will understand
that the House, having taken a decision
on the vote of censure on Thursday,
could not possibly take a vote of censure
on Tuesday.
Further, the procedure is that on a
vote of censure those who wish to move
such a vote must ask the Government for
time to discuss it, and of course it is
up to the Government to decide whether
they will give that time or not. The
principle I would like the House. to consider is that on matters of administration there are ample opportunities for
discussion. For instance, on the Vote
on Account this matter could have been
discussed, it can also be discussed on the
Adjournment on any day. On Class 1.
Vote 1, of the Estimates an Amendment
can be moved to reduce the salary of the
Minister in order to draw attention to
certain matters of administration, and a
vote can be taken. Then, when the
Appropriation Bill comes forward the
matter can be discussed and voted upon.
I think the House will understand that
it is undesirable, except in very exceptional circumstances, for votes of censure
to be moved indiscriminately by Members of the House. For these reasons I
have to rule the Motion out of order.
Mr. NIXON: I am quite aware that
it is not competent for me to question
Local Superannuation Bill. 808
Votes of Censures

or argue with your ruling, and that I do
not propose to do. I never do so. Is
it your ruling that the Minister, so to
speak, having been acquitted of one
offence it is not competent for the House
as it were to try him for another offence?
I do not mean it in that way, but I
know it used to be competent under the
criminal law-if a man is acquitted on

I am not saying that ruling here should
follow that principle, but is that the
ruling? How long is the Minister to be
immune from a vote of censure? How

he is acquitted?
Mr. SPEAKER: I would say if the
right hon. Gentleman committed a crime

Mr. GAMBLE: I must bow to your
ruling, Mr. Speaker, but I cannot say

later date.
Mr. HENDERSON: I think the
decision is a wise one, and will give the

The public will then not be one bit the

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
you, in view of your ruling, whether it
is right and proper for one Minister to
be selected from the Government and be
subject to votes of censure? Would
this vote of censure not be more in keeping against the Cabinet, who are the
rulers and guides of the Government's
policy, and not against one particular
Minister? The Minister's action, I am
sure, was subject to the Cabinet's confirmation and approval. I would be
inclined to ask you on a vote of censure
of this kind is it not within the rights
of Members of the House to table Motions
as votes of censure against the Government, and ask the Government that time
be given to them, instead of selecting one
man out of the Cabinet to be subject to
a vote of censure?
Mr. SPEAKER: A vote of censure
can take two phases. First, it can be
taken as a definite vote of censure against
the conduct of a particular Minister.
The more reasonable way, however, as
the hon. Member has said, is for the
responsible leader of the Opposition or
the Opposition in a body to put down a
vote of censure against the Government.
If it is a responsible body the Government accepts that vote of censure and
finds time for it, but the Government is
not obliged to find time if it chooses not
to do so. Pressure of business may be
such that there may not be time to allow
a day for discussion.
Mr. BROWN: As one who considers
that the Minister of Agriculture could
have done nothing else in this matter,
as it might have resulted in closing down
a valuable industry, I desire to-
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is
entitled to ask the Speaker for a direction, but he is not entitled to give his
views at this stage.

Mr. WARNOCK: In introducing this
Bill my first word naturally is to express
my own deep regret, which I am sure
will be shared by every Member of the
House, that the Minister of Home Affairs
is not able, through indisposition, to be
here to move the Second Reading. He
has taken a great interest in this
Measure, and I am sure it is a matter

of great regret to him personally that he

I do not propose to occupy the time
of the House in advancing arguments
or stating facts to show the necessity
for further proposals for better housing
for the working-class people of Northern
Ireland. It is safe to assume that there
is unanimity in the House and in the
country that the improvement of housing
conditions is an obligation, and a continuing obligation resting upon every
Government which may be in power for
many years to come.
The Measure which is submitted to-day
to the House is merely a step along a
road which we will be travelling for
many a day until all our people are
suitably and adequately housed. I need
not enter into any controversy as to
which of our social services is the most
important or confers the greatest benefit
upon our people. Whatever view the
individual may take, it cannot be denied
that the provision of good housing is one
Housing Bill—
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
of the greatest factors in raising the
standards of living for our people. Nor
need I advance arguments to show the
necessity for or the desirability of
assistance from public funds. The
principle of State assistance for housing
has been recognised in this country for
with the
beginning
many years,
Labourers Acts and continuing with the
Housing Acts which from 1923 onwards
authorised the payment of subsidies to
private individuals who built houses of
specified types and dimensions.
With building costs as they are to-day
it is financially impossible to build
houses of the kind demanded by present
day standards which will let at rents
which are economic and at the same time
within the resources of the class of
tenants for whom we desire to provide
housing. I referred a moment ago to
the subsidy system. Thirty-six thousand
house were built since 1923 under the
Housing Acts which granted subsidy,
and 3 million pounds of public money
was expended in providing them.
The subsidy system has been severely
criticised, sometimes not without justification, but it served its day and achieved a
great deal. The intention of the Statutes
was to provide accommodation for working-class people at rents which they could
afford to pay.
But economic factors
operating at the time, mainly the law.
of supply and demand, forced the rents
of many of the subsidy houses to levels.
beyond the capacity of the great bulk
of working-class people. The lowerpaid workers, who form a very large
block, were not able to take advantage
of the new houses to anything like the
extent anticipated by Parliament when
the legislation was passed.
These houses, or the majority of them,
came into the possession of the highlypaid artisans and the lower-paid black
coated workers. Although the Subsidy
Acts did not operate exactly as Parliament intended they did secure 36,000
houses and this provision has been a very
great advantage to the community. It
removed the shortage which was causing
hardship to the very numerous and
important sections to whom I have
referred. It freed an approximately
equal number of houses which eased the
situation considerably for the main
body of working people. But the subsidy houses have not done very much to
solve the difficulties of that very large
part of the population whose incomes are
insufficient to pay the rents which must
be charged for satisfactory houses in
private ownership, and who are compelled to inhabit houses which could
not be called satisfactory.
The position to-day-I hope I am
stating it correctly-is that while a substantial improvement in housing facili
ties for the higher-paid and mediumpaid workers has been effected, enough
has not been done for those people in
town or county who have to live in the
worst type of houses, the people who are
the most poorly paid of our workingclass. This Bill is designed to do something for these people. To remedy their
situation new houses are necessary and
they can only be supplied, at rents which
they can pay, if a considerable Measure
of State assistance is forthcoming.
The first part of this Bill is designed
to assist in rehousing those people in
urban areas who are at present living
in houses which have been condemned or
which ought to be condemned as unfit
for habitation. This part of the Bill
does not aim at increasing the actual
number of houses available. Its purpose
is to clear away a large number of the
old unsanitary and unsatisfactory houses,
and to replace them on the site with
good houses to be let to the present
tenants at rents which they can afford
to pay. If we are to succeed in this scheme
we must rely upon the local authority
rather than upon private enterprise.
This is essential for a variety of reasons.
One is to keep down the cost, and
another to control the rents and the
conditions of letting.
The local authority will require
financial assistance from the Government. Housing is not the concern of
any one section of the community; it is
in the national interest that our people
should be well housed. It is in the
interests of the local authorities responsible for the administration of the
area that the people in their areas should
be well housed, and, as is obvious, it is
in the interests of the tenants who are
going to occupy the houses. The three
parties concerned are the Government,
the local authority, and the tenant, and
it is hoped that the cost will be equally
distributed over the three parties
concerned.
Housing Bill—
Second Reading
28 MARCH 1939
The first and main proposal is that a
contribution of one-third of the cost of
each new house erected by an urban
authority to rehouse people displaced
from a house condemned as unsanitary
or overcrowded shall be made by the
Government. This contribution will be
made subject to certain important conditions. The schemes and their execution will be subject to the approval and
supervision of the Ministry. Rents will
be strictly controlled and those who are
eligible to be accepted as tenants are
specified with definiteness. We have
fixed the upper limit of contribution at
£150, that is, one-third of £450, which we
regard as a fair maximum for the cost
of the kind of house which we have in
view.
In some cases it may be necessary to
spend more than £450 per house. In
such cases the additional cost will be
borne between the local authority and
the tenant, the latter's share taking the
shape of a slightly higher rent. The
permitted rent where the cost of the
house does not exceed £450 will not
exceed 4s per week, and the maximum
permissible where the cost exceeds £450
is 6s. We contemplate building schemes,
and the basis of calculation of the cost
of the house will be the total cost of the
scheme divided by the number of houses.
This part of the Act, as I have said,
deals with the rehousing of people now
living in very poor classes of houses.
Up to now it has been obligatory on
local authorities to provide alternative
accommodation before displacing the
occupiers. The result has been that it
has been necessary to build new houses
on some other site before clearing any
area. This has had, not only here but
throughout the Kingdom, unfortunate
results in many ways. It has meant the
displacement of population to areas some
distance from their work. The rents of
the new houses have been higher, and
this, coupled with increased travelling
costs, has in many cases depleted the
family fund to an extent which was very
undesirable. In the case of the class we
are dealing with, the most poorly-paid,
we think this additional expense would be
undesirable.
This Bill contains an innovation in
this regard. A power is conferred upon
local authorties to provide temporary
accommodation before displacing the
occupiers, who will be reinstated in the
new houses erected on or about the old
site as soon as they are ready for
occupation. Before passing to Part II.
there is one other matter I must
mention.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the
Parliamentary Secretary if it is compulsory on local authorities to provide

one other matter which I might refer

Some time ago Mrs. Harold Barbour
made a munificient gift of £20,000 to
the Belfast Council of Social Welfare
for the purpose of assisting in the
housing of the working classes. The
object of this gift is closely analogous to
that of the Government's present proposals, and when the Welfare Council
approached us and asked that provision
should be included in our present legislation for extending to them any benefits
in the way of State assistance which we
had in mind for local authorities the
Government decided to do so. I think
it is the intention of the Belfast Council
of Social Welfare to administer their
scheme through a public utility company, which as the House knows, must
be a non-profit-earning corporation.
Accordingly, in this part of the Bill
provision is made that if a public utility
society or housing trust prepares
schemes for the erection of houses similar
in nature and purpose to those which the
Bill contemplates being erected by local
authorities, a contribution will be made
out of public funds to the society or trust
as in the case of a local authority.
The provisions contained in this part of
the Bill will, I hope, go some way towards
solving one part of our housing problem.
It does not profess to be a complete
solution. It is only a step on the road
as I said before, and I hope the House.
will think it is a good step and one which
they can accept.

To-day I visited some of the old-age
pensioners in the Belfast side streets.
If 80-year-old Mrs. Mary Lofty,
"Grannie" to hundreds of children

Brookmount Street, had another 10s a
week she could live in comfort.
The extra money would mean meat
for her meals during the week, new
shoes, heavier blankets, and even a few
luxuries.
The rent of her home is 5s 3d a week,
but she rents two rooms to a city workman. To-day she showed me the two
small cakes she had bought for dinner.
They cost her 1d each.
The glow of her coke fire usually has
to light her room.
Mr. William James Beggs, 67 years
old, once earned a regular £3 15s a
week. But the ex-shipyard fitter has
been an old-age pensioner for two years.
His total income
now is a 10s
pension and 2s 6d a week, which was

Sitting before his small fire he

and butter, but twice a week I buy

That has to make two meals.

again. If eggs were cheaper I would

each, and that's much too dear for
me..

that will give an individual a decent

class conditions an Act granting old-age

I want this House to give its serious

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Warnock):
When half-past Four descended upon me
yesterday I had just finished dealing
with Part 1 of the Bill, which undertakes the rehousing of the working-class
people occupying the worst type of
house in the city. I want to go on to
Part 2, dealing with grants towards
the repair of houses both in urban and
rural districts which are very unsatis
factory. There are throughout Northern
Ireland great numbers of houses which in
their present state are scarcely fit for
human habitation, but which are capable of transformation into satisfactory
dwelling-houses at a cost much less than
that of demolition and rebuilding. The
number of such houses tends to increase,
because when once a house reaches a
certain age the cost of repairs to rehabili
tate it increases rapidly.
Here, again, the matter affects a
variety of interest. As before, the Government and the local authority are concerned and the occupier is concerned.
But in the case of a house reconditioned,
the owner, when he is not the occupier,
is also concerned. We have devised a
scheme whereby the actual cost of reconditioning shall be shared between the
Government, the local authority, and the
owner, at the same time making it possible for the due share, but only the
due share, of the cost to the owner being
passed on to the occupier.
was a
That
local
We are not without experience in this
matter, because in 1926 the Housing
(Rural Workers) Act, was passed in
England, a Measure on lines very similar
to those in this part of the Bill.
Measure enabling the
authorities to make grants towards the
reconditioning of houses, just as we are
seeking to do, where it is possible to ge:
good houses at a cost which will be much
less than that of demolishing the old and
rebuilding the new. Scores of thousands
of houses have been reconditioned in
England, and that Act, which was passed
for five years and was a purely experimental Measure, has been sufficiently
satisfactory to justify the British Parliament in continuing it, with small modifications, and it is still operating in
England to-day.
The proposal is that when a house in
private ownership has been condemned
as unfit for habitation, but is adjudged
suitable for reconditioning at reasonable
cost, the owner of the house may apply
to the local authority for assistance
towards the cost of the work necessary
to make the house a satisfactory dwelling. If satisfied, the local authority
may agree to assist and the assistance
may take the form of an out and out
grant or a loan at a low rate of interest,
or a combination of both.

what we propose to do is to extend the
scope of that definition by making
eligible as tenants of the houses certain
classes of people who are not now
eligible. At present if an agricultural
labourer in occupation of one of these
houses dies leaving a widow she can be
ejected from the house, because she does
not come within the definition of a

labourers as defined to continue in occupation. This amendment will be more
apparent than real, because throughout

to eject widows. This provision will
enable them to become eligible, and
strictly eligible, for cottages provided
under the scheme.
We think that £150 would be a fair
maximum to allow as the cost of repair.
If the house ultimately is not to be
worth more than £450, it would hardly
seem right to expend more than £150 in
reconditioning. It would be bad business to spend more than £150. It would
probably be better to let the house go
and have a new one. We have, therefore, fixed the maximum grant which
may be paid by a local authority in
respect of reconditioning any one house
at £100. Of this £100 the Government
will repay to the local authority £50.
That would leave £50 to be paid by the
owner of the property. This, in effect,
is that the Government, the local
authority, and the owner will each pay
one-third. Unless the owner of the
house can pass his share on to the tenant
there will not be much inducement to
him to recondition. We propose to allow
the owner to add to the pre-repair rent
an amount equal to 4
per cent.
per
annum of the owner's share of the cost
of reconditioning.
May I illustrate the effect? Take a
man occupying a house at 3s 6d per
week, and £150 is required to put the
house into satisfactory condition. The
owner gets £100. He must find the
other £50. When the house is completed he will be entitled to raise the
rent by about 10d per week. The tenant
who was paying 3s 6d for a house unfit
for habitation will thereafter pay 4s 4d
for a satisfactory house. It seems to me
that that, from the point of view of the
tenant, will be good business.
Part 1 has dealt with the erection of
houses in urban areas. Part 2 deals with
reconditioning in both urban and rural
areas. There is another phase of this
problem, that is, the provision of new
houses in rural areas. This is, to some
extent, covered by existing legislation.
Under the Labourers Acts, Rural District Councils are empowered to provide.
cottages for agricultural labourers.
Towards the cost of these the Government contributes very substantially.
Grants amounting to 40 per cent. of the
annual loan charges incurred by the
Councils are in fact paid as Government
grant. Up to date 8,000 cottages have
been provided and further schemes are in
preparation for about 4,000 more.
But the statutory definition of agricultural labourer presents a difficulty, and
Next we propose to include persons
living in rural districts but who have
secured employment in another rural
district or neighbouring town. Once
again, under the Labourers Acts, when
they ceased to work in a rural district
they ceased to be. eligible to get a cottage.
Then we hope to include persons of
limited incomes presently living in unsanitary houses. We also propose. to
make eligible smallholders whose land has
a net annual valuation not exceeding £4.
I think it will be within knowledge that
this latter class includes many of the
worst housed people. in the country.
Occupying very small holdings, they have
not sufficient means to enable them to rebuild the houses in which they live. Those
are the three, main heads of the Bill.
Part 4 deals with matters which are
mainly consequential. We intend that
those who are to benefit by the provisions
of this Act shall be our own people. We
have provided that a local authority shall
not accept as a tenant any person other
than a person born in Northern Ireland,
or who has lived in the United Kingdom
for seven years. This provision does not
apply, and of course could not apply, to
persons being rehoused under the provisions of Part 1, and for whom no
alternative accommodation is available.
Subject to that limitation the question of
persons who shall be accepted as tenants
will be laid down by the Act.

given by the Minister to the trade unions

There is a possibility of deceit and

The life of these bricks varies very considerably. Many builders in the pastthey may have all gone now-adopted

on the other side may not be eligible for
the simple reason that the local authority
for his district is not a progressive
authority. I suggest the Bill should be
revised in order that those who desire
to avail themselves of this grant could,
if the local authority does not take the
matter up, go direct to the Ministry and
receive a grant from them, the half of
which the latter could afterwards recover
from the local authority. If that is not
done many anomalies will exist.
In one particular district the standard
of local government may not be progressive, and the inhabitants of that area
may not receive any benefit from the
Measure. This House should see to it
that the provisions of the legislation it
passes are made available to every member of the community in the entire Six
Counties. It should not be possible for
any local authority to render this Act
a complete dead letter, as they can do as
it at present stands.
29 MARCH 1939
Housing Bill—

Second Reading
I welcome this Bill because it will
render a great service to the poorest of
the poor in this city. The Medical
Officer of Health for Belfast has condemned about 2,000 houses as being
unfit for human habitation. There is
no place to which these people can go.
The majority of the houses they are
occupying at the present time are rented
at from 2s 9d to 4s per week. If they
have to leave these houses the only ones
they can get cost about 9s 7d per week.
The only hope these poor people have
when they are evicted from or leave
their homes because of their dangerous
and unsanitary condition is to rent one
at 9s 7d per week. This Bill will render
a great service to these people.
The hon. Member for Pottinger dealt
with the question of jerry-built houses.
I think he will agree with me when I
say that, in many cases, the clerk of
works was not a tradesman. A revision
should be made in this regard. The
clerk of works should be a tradesman, a
man of experience and one who knows
what he is supervising. We have men
filling these positions who have not
sufficient knowledge to enable them to
carry out the work satisfactorily. I
should like to ask a question. I wish to
know if private builders will be eligible
to operate under this Act. I know it
refers to building societies and local
authorities, but I am not sure if private
builders will be eligible to carry out
schemes under the Act. I am sure the
Parliamentary Secretary will give some
information on that point. All contracts
under this scheme should be guaranteed
by a bond obtained through
an
insurance company. I have known
of cases where the local authorities
have been mulcted and put to very considerable expense owing to the absence
of such a bond. With these few explanations and suggestions which I put
forward with the object of improving the
Bill, I once more wish to congratulate
the Government on their attempt to deal
with this problem. I wish the Bill every
success.
Mr. BYRNE: I wish to congratulate
the Government on introducing this Bill.
I have had many years experience in
regard to housing as I am a member of
the Housing and Estates Committee of the
Corporation. I know something about
the difficulties with which the people
have to contend in regard to housing
accommodation. It is quite true
that the Government have in the past
given grants for the building of houses,
but the unfortunate thing was that they
had no power to control the rents
charged for those houses. There
many people in the city of Belfast on the
dole who have to pay very high rents
for the houses they occupy. They are
suffering very severely. From time to
time it is my duty, as a member of the
Estates Committee, to visit houses in
which these people reside. I know something about their complaints. People
were very glad to get into the houses,
but, unfortunately, they soon found they
could not pay the higher rents.
are
When a Housing Bill was being passed
in the British House of Commons some
time ago I, as a member of the Housing
Committee, approached this Government
and asked them to give grants for the

with what was proposed in the
English Bill, that is for each person

the Government were unable to give that

the houses will be erected in or convenient to the district where the people
at present reside. That will confer a

Neither the Government nor the Corporation should have any hesitation
in giving decent grants towards the

it will be repaid a hundred fold. For

great amount of that disease is caused
by bad housing accommodation.
larger sums had been expended on the

would not be a demand for such an

The repairing of houses is a matter

I do not approve of houses being
repaired, but I know there are several

The work could be carried out at less
than it would cost to build new houses.
I am glad to know that the tenant will

is spent on these houses. I understand

receive 4 per cent. on his expenses. That

rent.
Another point in this Bill is that the

to take over
other buildings in order to accommodate

houses at a rent of about 4s per week.
To-day many are paying 7s a week for
a single room. It will be a great relief
to them when they can have a house of
their own for 4s or 4s 6d per week. I
hope that this Measure will soon come
into operation. No Bill introduced into

House. There is great need for good
healthy houses. The Parliamentary

the commencement. I sincerely hope

when

reconditioned in Great Britain under the

worth while to give this measure a fair

The Ministry, I hope, can be trusted to

show that only such houses as are suitable for reconditioning and are proper
to be reconditioned are eligible for the

the beginning, and now I unreservedly
and humbly apologise to that gentleman,
and withdraw anything I said about his

During the short time that we had the

found in various parts of the country,

that statement on the authority of

I have to raise a matter of this kind,
and I am glad that the Speaker is going
out. The Speaker of this House and I
am not saying this in a disparaging way
-made a speech at the Chamber of

Major Reilly's Resignation
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. HENDERSON: I am referring
to him as an ordinary Member of this
House.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: You cannot do that. He is not an ordinary
Member of this House. He is the
Speaker of this House.
Mr. HENDERSON: Very well, then,
we will forget about it. Certain persons
who hold high positions in this country
spoke at the Chamber of Trade dinner.
One of them made a very important
statement, and that was that A.R.P. in
Northern Ireland was in a terrible condition, and that nothing was being done.
In fact, he went on to say—and I was
amazed at the statement in view of what
I know about A.R.P.-that in his mill
or factory, if there were an air raid, he
would not know what to do. I can tell
this House that Murray's Tobacco
Factory, Gallaher's Tobacco Factory,
and many of the mills and factories
throughout the city have made absolutely
perfect preparations for dealing with
their workers in the event of an air
raid.
I feel this matter very much. Here
is a gentleman who gave great service
to his country, a man who was a very
distinguished and gallant officer of His
Majesty's Forces in the Great War.
When the country needed his services in
time of war, he gave those services, and
he came here when his country needed
him again. A Member of this House,
after that speech by a Member of this
House in an outside place, put down a
question. In view of the prominence
given to the statement made at the
Chamber of Trade he had no alternative.
In fact, I myself put down a question,
and it was ruled out of order. I think
it is unfortunate that things like this
should be allowed to get past without an
opportunity of contradicting them,
unless one takes a hall. I could not
afford £20 or £30 to engage a hall in
order to get an opportunity of contradicting the statement to which I have
referred.
In fairness to this gallant officer, I
must say that in my opinion he has
been driven out of his position owing to
those speeches. The hon. and gallant
Member for Cromac (Major Sinclair) put
down a question asking whether in view
of the serious situation, so far as A.R.P.
is concerned, this man had not been
relieved of his appointment. Is it not
true to say that practically nothing had
been done in Northern Ireland, as far
as A.R.P. is concerned, when this
gentleman took up his position two
months ago? It is not Ulster-like, it is
not British-like, to drive a man out of
office before he gets the slightest opportunity of proving his worth. I am quite
satisfied, from the inquiries I have made,
that this very honourable and very
gallant gentleman would have given 100
per cent. service to his country, and
would have done many things for the
protection of the civil population, if he
had been afforded the opportunity. He
had great experience of A.R.P. work.
I believe that it is due to those
speeches that we have lost his services.
Those speeches have caused a great sensation throughout the length and breadth
of the country. We have been told by
people who should know better that
nothing has been done so far as A.R.P.
services are concerned. I say that is
wrong. With the assistance of Major
Myles Reilly, M.C., and Major Hamill,
of the Belfast Corporation, great work
has been done in Belfast. Much work
has yet to be done to put A.R.P. services
on a sound basis. I think this gallant
officer has been treated most unfairly.
He has had only two months in order
to pick up the threads, when it is stated
that nothing has been done. I know
from the statements of the A.R.P. experts that we could not have had a
better man for the job than Major Myles
Reilly; we could not have got a better
man in any part of the British Empire.
I stand for justice. At first I criticised this as a political appointment, but
in the absence of the Prime Minister I
have withdrawn that statement. The
people responsible for making these
speeches outside should be careful what
they say. In view of the question put
down by the hon. Member for Cromac-
I am sorry he is not here-Major Reilly
had no other alternative but to resign.
All honour to him. Perhaps the British
Empire may have a far more important
position for him to fill. I sincerely
trust, although Ulster has been denied
the services of this gallant gentleman,
that there will be greater honour in
store for him, especially in view of the

The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I do not
quite follow the hon. Member in regard
to the £40,000,000 for sugar beet because
the subsidy for that industry has not
been in existence for fifteen years. So
far as flax is concerned the Government,
under my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Commerce, has set up a
Committee composed of farmers, spinners
and all those interested in the industry,
in an endeavour to discover what is the
best method of assisting the further production and a greater acreage of flax in
this country.
I will just cover one or two points
raised by the hon. Member. It would
be very unwise at this stage for the
Government to produce a stop-gap
method to try to increase flax production, because it is hoped that in a comparatively short time the Committee will
make its report.
The hon. Gentleman has made two
points. He referred to the wheat subsidy and the sugar beet subsidy-which,
admittedly, are not a particular help to
Northern Ireland; in fact the sugar subsidy is of no value. I would point out,
however, that so far as oats and barley
are concerned, we get about one-twelfth
of the total subsidy granted in Great
Britain, although we only represent
one-fortieth of the population. So far
as the cattle subsidy is concerned I cannot give the exact proportion, but we
are getting a very large share. In
regard to pigs I am hoping that shortly
we shall have an output equal to onethird of the whole of the United Kingdom. It will be seen, therefore, that
Northern Ireland is not doing badly.
The oats and barley subsidy this year
we calculate will be somewhere about 10s
to 12s 6d an acre, and a further increase,
which I cannot divulge, is promised for
barley.
It must be obvious that we cannot have
a policy of in and out. We have to
accept the general principle of assistance
for agriculture. In some cases what
suits one part of the United Kingdom
does not suit another part. In the
North and other parts of Scotland they
make the same claim. Wales makes the
same claim. If we do not benefit in one
particular we get other subsidies which
are more suitable for our particular type
of agriculture. I am glad the hon.
Member has given me an opportunity of
making this statement, but, at the same
time, he must face the fact that we are
getting benefit in other directions.

interests of this country and of Great

in time of war.
I hope the Minister will
give the House some information regarding the policy of this Flax Development
Committee.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): Speaking as
Speaking as a flax
spinner, as one vitally interested in the
cultivation of flax, and as one largely
interested in the world trade in linen
manufactures, I look at this matter from
a somewhat different aspect to those hon.
Members who have just spoken. I think
I am speaking for everyone engaged in
the linen trade in Northern Ireland when
I say that our great anxiety is how to get
orders for our products. It is not so
much a question of the narrowing
markets in which we can get our raw
material, but the narrowing markets in
which we can sell our finished goods.
Unfortunately many markets to which we
used to ship our linen manufactures are
now controlled either by lack of currency
with which they used to make payment
for goods, or by a strict system of
licensing under which we have to ship our
goods. Even in some of the Dominions
of the British Empire restrictions are
being imposed on imports even from this
country.
The Flax Development Committee was
not one of my appointments. The proposal to appoint this committee was
adopted by this House, and we decided
that, as a matter of this kind requires
great technical knowledge, we could not
do better than entrust this very important
matter as to how best the growing of
flax could be developed in Northern
Flax Production
Flax Production
29 MARCH 1939
Ireland, to those experts who have
devoted their whole life to the study of
the linen trade, from the growth of the
fibre to its manufacture and its subsequent weaving and merchanting, so
that they could study the problem and
advise as to the best means of promoting
the industry in which they are so vitally
concerned. This House made the grant
of £50,000 a year for three years, contingent on the people who are interested
in the trade raising 10 per cent. of that
amount, and on their doing so they get
proportionate grant from the
Exchequer.
a
We then decided that the spinning
trade, the farmers, and the scutch mill
proprietors should appoint a committee
to carry out this important work. It is
a very difficult subject. I think that our
hope lies in the improvement in the
methods of retting and scutching that
will enable the farmer to get a very much
higher price for his flax than he does at
present. It is in the adoption of Continental methods that our hope for the
extension of flax growing in Northern
Ireland lies. I may say that personally
I approve entirely-it might not be. so
much in detail-but as to the manner
generally in which this committee have
gone about their work. They have
approached it most earnestly. They have.
studied not only the proposition here in
Northern Ireland, but they made a visit
to the Continent in order to study the
methods practised over there.
And really we must remember that in
the olden days it was to the introduction
of experts from Flanders and Belgium
that we owed the prosperity in the linen
trade which we have enjoyed for many
years.
I do not think it is a retrograde
step at all if we turn our eyes once again
to that country which produces the very
highest quality of flax grown in any part
of the world, and where it is handled
with a skill which I do not think is
approached in any other part of the
world, in order to benefit by their
guidance and in order to teach our
farmers and scutchers how best to handle
flax in Northern Ireland. It is these
experts that we hope will train our own
people to establish such methods over
here as will enable us, as far as raw flax
is concerned, to hold the same position
that we undoubtedly do in the skill and
quality of the finished article which the
weavers in Northern Ireland produce.
As to how the committee carry out
their work is a matter for themselves,
and any complaint ought to be addressed
to them rather than to this House. We
have entrusted this task to them, and we
must feel confident that they are the
parties most interested in achieving success. Naturally they will pay attention
to the different contributory factors to
attain that end. It is rather early as yet
for them to be able to report any results,
but I have every confidence that as time
goes by, from the manner in which they
are approaching the subject, that they
I will be able to confer substantial benefits
on this industry in Northern Ireland.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Ten
minutes to Six o'clock until

suant to the Resolution of

opened in Belfast under the name of
fun fairs, which contain automatic

is expedient-
(1) to authorise a charge upon the

housing associations providing

(a) the principal of and interest on

(2) to authorise a charge upon

(3) to authorise a charge upon

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): The. Resolution which appears on the Order Paper
provides for Exchequer contributions to
local authorities who undertake schemes
for rehousing or improving the housing
of the working classes. As explained by
my hon. Friend on the Second Reading
of the Bill, the object is not to provide
additional houses, but to replace unsatisfactory houses with better dwellings.
In the case, of housing associations, however, Exchequer grants will be given for
new houses erected by such associations
under schemes approved by the Ministry
of Home Affairs.
The Resolution contains the usual
charging Clauses, placing on the Consolidated Fund or Parliamentary Votes
the liability for the proposed expenditure,
to which I need not refer.
The paragraphs containing the actual amounts of
the proposed State contributions are those
numbered 1 (a) and 3 (b). Paragraph
1 (a) governs the making of Exchequer
contributions to local authorities in
urban areas for the building of new
houses to replace unsanitary houses, or
contributions to housing associations for
the erection of new houses. In each
case the Exchequer contribution is
limited to £150, that is, one-third of
£450, which is regarded as an equitable
maximum figure of cost for the type of
house required. If the house costs less
than £450, one-third of the lesser cost
is payable by the Exchequer, and if more
than £450 the full additional cost above
£450 falls upon the local authority.
The other limiting condition is that
grants are to be made only for a limited
period of time, that is, in respect of
schemes approved up to the 1st January,
1945. The object of this is that, if rehousing is to take place, it should do so
at an early date and without any undue
delay. Paragraph 3 (b) of the Resolution deals with the State contribution for
the repair of working-class houses in
urban and rural areas. Such contributions may be made to local authorities
in either of two sets of circumstances:-
(1) where a local authority makes a
grant to a private individual to reconstruct or repair his house; or (2) where
a local authority acquires a house for rehousing purposes and itself executes the
repairs.
In each case the maximum State grant
is £50, that is, one-third of the sum of
£150, which is thought to be a fair
maximum figure for repairs to a house,
the total value of which does not exceed
£450. In the case of a house acquired
by a local authority, the maximum cost
to the authority on repairs costing £150
would be £100, and in the case of grants
made by local authorities to owners of
houses the maximum cost to the local
authority would be £50, that is, the
State, the local authority and the owner
each pay one-third of the cost.
It is, of course, impracticable to give
any estimate of the total amount of State
expenditure which would be involved, as
this depends entirely on the extent to
which local authorities avail themselves
of the provisions of the. Act. Parliament
will, of course, have an opportunity each
year, when the Estimates are presented,
of voting in the form of annuities the
amounts required for the contributions
for rebuilding schemes-which expenditure is to be funded; as regards the repairs to houses, Parliament will be asked
to vote. each year the actual amounts
payable as contributions to local
authorities.
Paragraph 3 (c) provides for the extension of the Labourers Act Code for a
further period of five years to the 31st
December, 1945, and this extension will
involve an increased charge upon public
Housing (Money)-

moneys by reason of the fact that a proportion (40 per cent.) of the loan
charges for the building schemes is payable by the State. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: This Money Resolution is really going to be the kernel of
whether the Housing Bill will be a success or failure. I am inclined to think
the question of money will be the factor
in deciding whether the people, will have
housing accommodation or not. I am
satisfied in my own mind that if this
Resolution is accepted by the House as it
stands there will be no houses built in
Northern Ireland for the people, who require them, because at the moment there
is a cry-out from all local authorities as
to the heavy burden that is being borne
on the rates. Householders and ratepayers are also raising a storm of protest
against various local authorities owing to
increased rates. If the Housing Bill is
passed is there a possibility of getting
these local authorities to meet the
financial obligations included in the
Money Resolution? I believe that the
answer would be no. If we are trying
to accommodate our people with better
houses why are we deviating from the.
step-by-step policy with Great Britain?
All these grants that are to be made
will be taken out of the general revenue.
of Northern Ireland. If we are saving
money as far as the local authorities are
concerned on this question of housing
then we are handing over that saving in
our Imperial contribution.
That is the effect of the economy that
has been introduced by the Financial
Secretary in this Resolution before the
Committee. I cannot understand that
way of management, because I think we
here are a poorer area than Great
Britain, and the farming community,
industrialists and business people are at
the moment struggling to exist. I am
satisfied that the county council in whose
area the Financial Secretary lives have a
grouse against the financial conditions
attached to the Housing Bill. They
say "The least we should expect and
should receive is what is provided in the
English Act." That is a reasonable and
justifiable claim, and one that the
Government should not overlook. Why
impoverish our area more than necessary?
Why take from the local authorities the
financial assistance which they require?
If we are to continue with this Resolution in its present form then we may as
well say here and now that the Housing
Bill is dead. If the Minister of Finance
strangles this Bill by refusing to apply
the same conditions in Northern Ireland
as apply in Great Britain, well then, he
is going to be the executioner of the
Measure which the House so highly
approved of.
Other Members of the Committee
should speak their minds in regard to
the grant. As I live in the city of Belfast
this does not affect me very much, but it
will affect the rural and urban areas.
The representatives from those areas
should express themselves as to how their
local authorities are being treated by the
financial provisions of this measure. I
am satisfied that the basis of contribution of 40 per cent. of the total cost of
houses here would not be in parity with
England. An important thing is set out
in a document I have here. The annual
charge to be borne by the local authorities amounts to £3 15s per house, or
exactly half what is proposed to be placed
on the local authorities in Northern
Ireland. In England the Government
contribute £2 5s per person in house,
which on an average of five persons in a
family works out at £11 5s per house,
while the contribution from the Government here is calculated at £8 2s 4d per
house, which figure may be reduced to
£6 7s 6d if the Government apply the
same repayment terms as is proposed to
be adopted by the local authorities for
a 60 years' loan annuity basis.
That is a very serious position. The
least we should get is the figure applicable
to England. We want houses, and we
want to try to accommodate. our people
in that respect, but I am satisfied in my
own mind that if this Money Resolution is accepted then our Housing Bill,
which the House gave time and attention to and supported, will be a failure
and will not meet the desired needs of
the people of the rural and urban areas
as expected when the Bill was sent out
first and foremost.
Mr. AGNEW: The financial assistance to be rendered by the Government
in the building of houses will not meet
the requirements at all. We who
live in the provincial areas know the
present conditions. In the city of
Housing (Money)——

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
Armagh there are at least 400 houses
needed, and if we take the area of South
Armagh we will find that the housing
conditions there are very bad, but when
it comes to a question of providing the
necessary capital the result will be that
the county, rural and urban councils
will not be pleased or willing to add any
further liability on the rates no matter
what the demand for housing will be.
The amount allocated by the Government
will not meet the needs as they stand
to-day. It is far too low, because it is
actually placing what we might call the
real responsibility of housing on the local
authorities, which are already overburdened. They are not in a position
to raise any further money, and if the
Government is going to place an additional burden on them it will mean that
the local authorities will not act in
accordance with the Bill.
Therefore, there is only one way out
of the difficulty, and that is that we.
should take the responsibility of housing
on the same basis as in Britain, and face
up to the realities of it. We should take
the full financial responsibility of a State
housing scheme. That is the only way
to meet the needs of the people affected,
because money spent on suitable houses
will be spent on behalf of the working
classes who need them. Unless you give
serious consideration to the amount to
be granted and take full responsibility
at least there will be grave disappointment, and we will find the local authorities will say, "We are not in a position
to build houses." The financial issue is
the main one, and it lies with the
Government to see, as far as the workers
are concerned, that money will not be an
obstacle in giving them decent homes.
Mr. NIXON: There is in Belfast an
undoubted scarcity of working class
houses, but there are far more than are
required of the big terrace and semi-villa
types. Anyone passing along the
streets of the city can see that. I
would like the Government to bear that
in mind. There is no sign of there
being a surplus of working class houses.
I have been reading through the Bill,
aud in regard to the intention of the
Government to provide assistance for
repairing houses that have been condemned by the competent authority, I
do not see much wrong because the
owner of the house is to be allowed 4
per cent. of whatever money he spends.
I would like to see some provision in
the Bill which would enable the owner
of a house in making these repairs to
put in a certain amount of electricity.
I see nothing about that in the Bill. I
think in a working class house it would
be a great acquisition to have a plug
for smoothing, and also a plug or two
in the bedrooms. If a person is sick
in the winter time there is rarely a
suitable fireplace upstairs in these smal
houses, and if there was a plug in the

I cannot conceive of anything that would

NEW CLAUSE (Removal of limitation
on borrowing powers).
Money borrowed by a rural district
council for the purposes of the Labourers
Acts, whether borrowed before or after
the passing of this Act, shall not be
reckoned as part of the debt of the
council for the purpose of the limitation on borrowing contained in section
two hundred and thirty-eight of the
Public Health (Ireland) Act, 1878.
Clause read a First time.
Mr. WARNOCK: This Clause is designed to remove the limitation which at
present exists in respect of borrowing
powers. The borrowing powers of rural
district councils are limited to a total of
twice the net annual value of the premises, and in the case of urban authorities
up to three times, but in certain cases
houses and small dwellings are excluded.
The purpose of this Clause is to provide
that money which is borrowed by a rural
district council for the purpose of the
Labourers Act shall not be reckoned as
part of the debt of the council for the
purpose of the limitation on borrowing
contained in section two hundred and
thirty-eight of the Public Health (Ireland)
Act. It is remunerative work, and it is
in accordance with the Small Dwellings
Act that money borrowed is not taken
into account.
Clause read a Second time and added to
the Bill.

bring before the House a matter of great
importance to this part of His Majesty's
Dominions. A duty has been cast upon
the Minister of Labour and certain members of his staff with regard to the
National Service Scheme. When I last
referred to this matter some months ago
the Minister will recollect that I said I
would say very little. in case I should
make his position more difficult than it
was. We must regretfully admit that
through no fault of the Minister the
scheme has been anything but a success.
What I am about to say is not to be
taken as referring to A.R.P. nor to the
Anti-Aircraft Brigade, for which recruiting is going on. I am not referring to
them as being unsuccessful; I rather
think they will be a great success. The
National Service Scheme as a whole has
not been a success.

A meeting was held in County Down

Empire, I would not be doing my duty

letting it be known, so far as I can, that
the present attitude is only fiddling with
the question and endangering the whole.
British Empire. It has got a trial, but
I knew from the start it would not be
a success; in fact, the particular gentleman who is responsible for it never did
draft anything successful in his life.
There are not many hon. Members more
in touch with the class of young men
you would expect to join than I am.
think I am justified in saying that if they
are not volunteering it is not because they

is worth fighting for, and if there is
fighting to be done every person should
do his share.

A certain gentleman promised to eat.
his hat he was of the very highest-if

already made. That is not history at
no

food campaign. There should be a clearcut direction from this House or the

The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

his warrant to the Clerk of the Crown
to make out a New Writ for the electing
of a Member to serve in the present
Parliament for the City of Derry in the
room of Edward Sullivan Murphy, Esq.,
K.C., who since his election for such
constituency has accepted the office of a
Judge of Appeal in His Majesty's High
Court of Justice in Northern Ireland.'
-(Captain Dixon).

CLASS VII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £26,773 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1940, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
