£13,000 has been voted on account).
—
The CHAIRMAN: There are two
Votes and I will follow the usual procedure of allowing discussion of both
Estimtes on the first Vote and then the
second Vote will be put formally.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): At probably no time in
the world's history has SO much
attention been directed to the question
of international trade. Despite the fact
that aviation and wireless have annihilated distance, it is unfortunately the
case that the year which has gone has
seen growing difficulties in trading and
economic relationships, with consequent
serious repercussions on world trade. As
hon. Members will be aware, all our
major industries are largely dependent
on export trade, a fact which is borne
out by the estimated value of exports
from Northern Ireland, which during the
year 1937-the last year for which detailed figures are available-amounted to
no less than 54 millions sterling. This
means that for every person in Northern
Ireland-whether adult or juvenilegoods to the value of £42 were exported,
a figure which contrasts with £34 in the
case of New Zealand and £8 in the case
of Eire.
Northern Ireland export trade has not
emerged scatheless from the general world
unsettlement. During 1938 the Sino-
Japanese War and the trade recession in
the United States provided two major
factors in the curtailment of our exports
of linen. For the United Kingdom as a
whole the value of linen goods exported
declined by 30 per cent. from the figure
reached in 1937, while the shrinkage in
the number of new orders for ships, a
natural consequence of the decline in
international trade, has been felt in
Northern Ireland, as in every shipbuilding area in Great Britain. Hon. Members will have noted from Press reports,
however, that there is already evidence
in the case of our great shipbuilding yard
of the beneficial results from the
Imperial Government's shipping subsidy
scheme.
as
Until peace is assured, overseas trade,
we know it, cannot revive. Recent
developments in Europe will, I think,
have convinced all parties of the difficult
task which faces the Government of a
country depending predominantly on export trade and likely to be affected by
any
action calculated to disturb the
normal channels of international trade.
I hope, therefore, that the House will
treat this problem of declining exports as
a question demanding the earnest consideration of everyone without regard to
one's particular political aspects or sympathies. I, for my part, would be pleased
to examine constructive suggestions com-
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
19 APRIL 1939
ing from any quarter which might
counteract in any degree the present
depression in our overseas markets.
Bearing all these unfavourable circumstances in mind, there are, however,
certain factors which justify me in
saying that if the position is not all we
should like it to be, it has certain reassuring factors. The market in Great
Britain continues to be a stabilising
factor in the economy of Northern Ireland. The extent of this market cannot
be accurately assessed, nor have I as yet
the guidance of Northern Ireland's trade
statistics for the year 1938, which are
still in course of preparation. Statistics,
however, showing the tonnage of goods
exported and imported through Belfast
Harbour, which are now available, indicate that the trade passing through our
principal port during 1938 declined by
less than 7 per cent. as compared with
the previous year's figure. Part of the
traffic passing through the Port of
Belfast consists of goods consigned
abroad, and as the decline in overseas
trade almost certainly fell by a considerably greater proportion than 7 per cent.,
We may assume that our trade in the
British market was fairly maintained
during 1938.
The increasing importance of this
market has been recognised
by the
appointment of a Northern Ireland agent
in Great Britain. The agent and his
staff are in a position to deal not only
with trade inquiries, but also to undertake the preliminary investigation of
inquiries regarding the facilities available under the New Industries Acts.
The London Office acts as a clearing
house for commercial inquiries
London, and also as the medium through
which the Government obtains for Northern Ireland and its industries publicity
of the kind which has now come to be
regarded as indispensable to an industrial
country such as ours.
in
I think that perhaps we may find some
consolation for the setbacks during 1938
in the Trade Agreement concluded between the United Kingdom and the
United States. As I have explained on
previous occasions, the Government of
Northern Ireland can take no direct part
in the negotiation of trade agreements,
but hon. Members will be aware that in
negotiating such agreements the Board
of Trade invariably consult my Ministry
at every stage of the negotiations where
Northern Ireland's interests are affected.
This was particularly the case in the
negotiation of the Anglo-American Agreement, where Northern Ireland's principal
manufacturing industry was so vitally
concerned. Successive increases in the
U.S.A. Customs duties since the end of
the Great War had seriously curtailed.
our trade with that country. The concessions which the linen industry was
accorded under the Agreement concluded
last year were so substantial that the
duties on most of the linen items, in
which Northern Ireland is particularly
interested, are now as low as, and in
many cases lower than, the pre-war
I am confident that, given a
favourable atmosphere, the trade between
Northern Ireland and the U.S.A. would
expand considerably as a result of this
Agreement. At a time when economic
nationalism appears to hold the field, this
Agreement will stand out as the one
liberal tendency in the economic history
of the year.
duties.
One other Trade Agreement concluded
last year was of considerable moment to
Northern Ireland. I refer to the Anglo-
Eire Pact. In considering this Agreement I would particularly remind hon.
Members that it should be regarded in its
true perspective as an economic arrangement between Eire and the United
Kingdom as a whole, in which the particular interests of Northern Ireland have
necessarily been balanced against what
may have appeared to be weightier considerations to the British Government.
Naturally, however, once, a pact of this
kind is negotiated we are bound to
examine it in its particular effect on
Northern Ireland. So far as I can judge
at present the Agreement has had the
effect of increasing slightly the export
trade from North to South, although
there is, of course, considerable leeway
to be made up in that direction. What
is of immediate importance to us, however, is the spirit in which that part of
the Agreement providing for consideration by an Eire Prices Commission of the
existing duties and restrictions will be
implemented by those in authority in
Eire. It is yet too early to pass any considered opinion upon this aspect of the
Agreement, but I may say that discussions, of which my Ministry is kept
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
fully informed, are proceeding between
London and Dublin, and every assistance
is being given by my Ministry to our
manufacturers in presenting their claims
to the Eire Prices Commission.
In introducing the Estimates last year
I referred at some length to the administration of the New Industries (Development) Act, particularly to the functions
of the Statutory Advisory Committee and
the Ulster Development Council. I propose on this occasion, therefore, to confine. myself in the main to the actual
progress recorded in the attraction of new
industries. I should like to say, however, that the Ulster Development
Council, which was appointed for an experimental period of a year, has been
reappointed for a further term, and continues to render valuable service, particularly through its Executive Committee, which meets at regular intervals
and maintains close contact with the
work of the New Industries Branch of my
Ministry.
The Statutory Advisory Committee has
continued to meet once a week ever since
the passing of the 1937 Act, and I must
once more express my indebtedness to its
members for their invaluable. help and
the readiness with which they have
devoted so much of their time to this
work.
Since its first meeting in December,
1937, the committee has considered 85
formal applications for assistance, of
which 33 have now been finally approved
by my Ministry and the Ministry of
Finance, 12 are still under consideration, and the remainder have been refused. Of the 33 applications approved,
six have since been withdrawn or
indefinitely postponed. It is estimated
that the remaining 27 will, when in full
production, provide employment for
2,500 persons. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
When considering the actual results
achieved in the form of employment
already provided, it is necessary to bring
the earlier New Industries Act of 1932
into the picture. Seven firms, giving
employment in all to some 6,000 workers,
were established with the assistance of
that Act, and while progress under the
1937 Act is less substantial, 12 firms,
giving employment to 530 persons, are
now in operation. To these will shortly
be added another, which will, in the
initial stages, provide work for a further
150 persons, and factories are at present
being prepared for other important
concerns.
In addition to the ordinary schemes of
factory production, two home industries,
which do not come within the strict
terms of the new industries legislation,
have been specially approved. In this
way provision has been made for the employment of 1,300 women and girls in
their own homes. One hundred and fifty
workers have already been trained, and a
further 300 are undergoing training.
In all, since the inception of the new
industries campaign, work has been provided, therefore, for almost 7,000 persons.
representing an average annual wages
bill approaching one million pounds. In
view of the recent trade recession and the
fact that the past year has been one of
recurring crises, this result cannot be regarded as unsatisfactory.
It must be borne in mind that the
new industries campaign forms part of
the Government's long-term policy to reduce unemployment, and that some years
must necessarily elapse before the ultimate effect of the. campaign in terms of
additional employment becomes fully
apparent. To the figures of direct employment must, of course, be added the
indirect employment due to such factors
as the erection and adaptation of premises
and, at a later stage, the additional work
in various trades following on the
increased spending power of the community.
The view has been expressed at various
times that Northern Ireland's share of
Government contracts arising out of the
rearmament programme has been far
from adequate. This is a question of
some delicacy but it will be within the
knowledge of hon. Members that substantial contracts for the Navy, Army
and Air Force are now being carried out
by local firms. Moreover continuous contact is being maintained with the Service
Departments with a view to ensuring the
more adequate utilisation of the available local man power.
I now turn to certain aspects of
publicity for our industrial and agricultural products. In collaboration with
the Ministry of Agriculture, the Minis-
Ministry of Commerce
Estimates-

19 APRIL 1939
try will continue to participate in
exhibitions which are staged periodically
in Great Britain. These include the
Imperial Fruit Show in London during
September and October, the Smithfield
Cattle Show in December, and the British
Industries Fair in February and March
of next year, together with an exhibition
at Nottingham next month.
The establishment of the office of the
Agent for Northern Ireland in Great
Britain has, moreover, provided a suitable centre. in London for an extension
of the exhibition programme to a number of displays which lie outside the
normal range, and thus the Youth Hostel
Association of Northern Ireland has been
given facilities in the London Office, for
staging a display of photographs, paintings and posters, illustrating the attractions offered in Northern Ireland to
tourists and members of Youth Hostel
Associations. In June next there will be
a display of the handicrafts and artwork
of Ulster school children.
At all these exhibitions information is
available regarding the facilities for the
establishment of new industries in
Northern Ireland, and at the British
Industries Fair in February and March
of next year it is hoped to include in an
extended form the display of products of
new industries established in the
Province, which formed so striking a
feature of this year's exhibit.
Satisfactory progress continues to be
made in the development of the supply
of electricity throughout Northern
Ireland. During the year 1938 approximately 203,100,000 units were sold by
statutory undertakings as compared with
189,600,000 units in the previous year,
that is, an increase of over 7 per cent.
During the year 1931, when the Electricity Board was established, the total
sales by statutory undertakings amounted
to only 75,454,582 units. It will be
observed that consumption has increased
by no less than 169 per cent. during the
period of seven years, thus emphasising
the point that the policy of the Government in securing by legislation the coordination of supplies has been amply
justified.
Development has by no means
approached saturation point, and the
Electricity Board continues to establish
new development areas and to extend
main transmission lines to the more remote districts of the Province.
The Electricity Board purchased during the year 1938 from the Belfast Corporation approximately 44 million units
and five million units from the Londonderry Corporation, as compared with 42
million units and four million units purchased respectively from these two undertakings during the previous year. The
Antrim Electricity Supply Company,
which undertakes the development of
supplies in County Antrim and South
Derry, purchased from the Larne
generating station 9.1 million units, as
compared with 8.08 units in 1937, and
6.7 in 1936. This company extended its
main transmission system from Ballymena to Portglenone and Innisrush;
from Coleraine to Castlerock, and from
Portrush to Bushmills and Portballintrae. The Antrim Electricity Distribution Company, which is a subsidiary
company of the Antrim Electricity
Supply Company, also afforded supplies
during the year in various towns and
villages.
•
With regard to fisheries, I regret that
the improvement in the herring fishing
to which I referred a year ago has not
been maintained. The quantity landed
last season was 35,000 cwts., valued at
£11,600, as compared with 47,000 cwts.,
valued at £16,000 in 1937. Although the
landings were. considerably less than in
1937 the average price fell to the lowest
recorded level of 6s 7d per cwt. In contrast to the previous season, the greater
part of the landings of herring was made
by ring-net boats, as conditions favoured
this type of fishing.
On the other hand, the catches from
Danish seine-netting during the winter
showed a considerable increase. Landings
of whiting increased from 7,500 cwts. in
1937 to 17,000 cwts. in 1938 valued at
£5,905 and £11,565 respectively. On
account of the good results from this
type of fishing, the total landings of
sea-fish on the coast of Northern Ireland for 1938 were almost up to the
1937 level of £57,000.
Provision is made in the Estimate for
grants to local fishermen for the purchase of new boats complete with Diesel
engine and gear adaptable to both
herring fishing and Danish seinenetting for white fish. Under this
scheme the Ministry is prepared, in
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
approved cases, to make a free grant
of one-third of the total cost of the new
boat, including engine and gear. Of
the remaining 66 per cent. the applicant will at the time of purchase be
required to make a cash payment of at
least 10 per cent. of the total cost and
the balance will be advanced by the
Ministry as a loan repayable within a
period of 15 years with interest at 37
per cent. The total cost of a boat of
this type with gear would be approximately £1,800, of which £600 would be a
free grant, £180 cash payment by the
fisherman and £1,020 a repayable loan.
The Ministry is also prepared to entertain applications for assistance by way
of grants and loans in the case of
second-hand boats of modern design and
of new engines for installation in
existing Northern Ireland boats which,
in the opinion of the Ministry, are
capable of being successfully adapted to
meet present-day requirements.
As regards salmon fishing, 1938 was
an exceptionally poor season, the take
by drift nets and fixed nets being even
smaller than in the previous year. I
am informed, however, that this condition of affairs also applied to many
of the salmon fisheries in Great Britain.
During the breeding season of 1938-39
the Northern Ireland rivers appeared
to be well stocked with spawning fish
and the conditions in most rivers
favourable.
There has been some improvement in
both eel and pollan fishing in Lough
Neagh. The Ministry is providing a
small measure of financial assistance to
an inquiry into the nature and habits
of pollan and the causes of the decline
in the stocks in Lough Neagh. The
inquiry is being carried out by
graduate of Queen's University under
the supervision of the Professor of
Zoology. I beg to move.

It is about time the Government had
a central purchasing department for the
purchase of all motor-cars and lorries
required by Government departments. I
can give you this tip for what it is
worth; that if a central authority purchased all motor vehicles for the use of
Government departments the Government
would save a considerable amount of
money. The motor manufacturers have
in operation what are called fleet rates,
which are given only to those who own
ten motors or more. That fleet rate is
about 10 per cent. less than the lowest
rate at which you could buy a motor

Again I want to say it is a crying

Development Committee should use their

I have mentioned before the names of

conditions imposed by the members of the

subject to fair wage conditions for the

Wages Clause, but in this case we part
with £150,000 and allow the workers

a week that is paid in connection with

The least
wage you should have
sanctioned is the agricultural rate in the

With regard to linen publicity, we
have heard about the Eire Agreement
and the statement made by Mr. Hudson.
We know the real cause of the backward
state of the linen industry, and I do not
think money will revive it to such an extent that the normal condition of the
industry will be restored. Money may
help to give it publicity, but publicity is
one thing, and the purchasing of linen
is another. We must get our markets
back, and as you are now in consultation
with the Eire Government you might be
able to help the linen industry by coming
to some arrangement about the American
market. We can still produce and
market linen at a reasonable figure, and
I would like the right hon. Gentleman
to tackle this question not so much by
publicity as by getting the real factor
which disturbed our linen markets
removed.

If your

Then the hon. Member for Pottinger
Isaid that in connection with flax we had

As regards the Anglo-Eire Pact to
which the hon. Member for Woodvale
referred, in my speech I said that, being
part and parcel of the United Kingdom,
we have to regard that- Pact as it affects
trade between the United Kingdom of
Great Britain and Northern Ireland and
Eire. We cannot expect that an arrangement of that sort should be concluded
entirely to suit Northern Ireland. There
were, from our point of view, certain
features of the Anglo-Eire Pact which
did not appeal to us at all. We must
admit that the British Government took
us into their confidence and studied the
extent to which we might be affected by
the Pact. I may say they were very
anxious so far as was consistent with the
success of the scheme as a whole to protect the interests of Northern Ireland.
There is a provision whereby if industrialists in Northern Ireland consider
that the Pact bears too harshly on them
they may go to the Eire Prices Commission and make representations with a
view to having the duties reduced on
goods going from Northern Ireland. But
it is too early to say how the whole thing
is going to work out.
As regards the hon. Member for South
Armagh, I am entirely in sympathy with
him that we should do all we possibly
can in getting new industries into the
country districts rather than have them
all centred round Belfast. But I think
the hon. Member must realise it is very
hard to prove to an industrialist coming
over here with the idea of starting an
industry, the advantages of going into
the country rather than enjoying the
amenities and facilities which
doubtedly exist nearer the port of arrival
and despatch from Belfast.
un-
Our sympathies are entirely with the country districts, and we have repeatedly brought
such arguments as we can before industrialists who come
over here to start
industries.
With regard to the price of electricity,
the service of electricity throughout
Northern Ireland must be carried on on a
self-supporting basis. If the hon. Member will look into the accounts of the
Electricity Supply Board, recently published, he will see that we are working
on a very close margin. As a matter
of fact, after giving a careful study to the
rates charged I think there is no doubt
that the more populous districts do bear
a burden of the cost of the supply of
electricity.
I do not know that any
advance could be made on what is being
done already.

TRAINING IN INSTRUCTION
FACTORIES.
1. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister of Labour whether he can state how
many young men have been admitted
into the Imperial Government Instruction Factories for training during
the past year from Northern Ireland;
how many have found employment after
training and the nature of the employment; how many can be taken from
Northern Ireland in any one year, and
if, having regard to the increased opportunities for placing men in engineering
works, any steps are being taken to see
that the quota for Northern Ireland will
be substantially increased in the near
future so that an outlet may be given
to young men who find it impossible to
obtain work in Northern Ireland at
present.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I am pleased to inform the
hon. Member that during the year ended
31st March last the number of men
admitted for training from Northern Ireland was 196, of whom 79 have been
placed in employment. Eighty-three are
still in training and the balance either
found work on their own account or
dropped out through leaving voluntarily,
sickness, or other cause. Of the 79
placings, 54
54 were in the engineering
trades and the remainder in other suitable occupations.
The course of training lasts six months,
and under present arrangements up to
200 trainees can be taken from Northern
Ireland in a year. My Department is
at present considering the advisability of
an increase in this number.

COMPANY.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

overflow pipes by the Concrete Piling
Company in McClure Street and other

job; whether the men on the air spade
in this job are getting the ld extra per
hour usually paid for this class of work
on Corporation and other subsidised jobs
in the City of Belfast involving the use
of air spades.
Mr. GORDON: The work referred to
by the hon. Member forms part of a
scheme which has been approved for
relief grant by my Department. I am
informed that no extra payment is being
made by the contractors to men operating air spades, nor is it customary, so
far as I have been able to ascertain, for
an extra payment to be made to men
on this class of work.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that and
before the Minister closes the subject, will
he ascertain from the Belfast Corporation
whether it is or is not customary to give
ld an hour for men employed on what
are known as air spades?
Mr. GORDON: We made inquiries.
from Belfast Corporation and I think we
discovered that only one person operating
a drill was paid 1d an hour extra because
the work is what is known as dirty work.
Mr. HENDERSON: In view of the
fact that these machines have a serious
effect on the health of the men, should
a man on this job not get the same pay
as the men using the drill?

CIVIL SERVANTS AND POLITICAL
ORGANISATIONS.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if members
of the Civil Service are permitted to
belong to and hold office in political
organisations.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Mr. Andrews): In a circular letter
issued by my Department in 1926 it was
laid down that no member of the Civil
Service is permitted to undertake remunerative work identified in any way
with the activities of a political party,
group or organisation. There is an unwritten, but none the less general, rule
that civil servants must maintain a
reserve in political matters.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister
kindly undertake to send round another
copy of the letter.
Mr. ANDREWS: Yes.
APPOINTMENTS IN THE
NORTHERN GOVERNMENT CIVIL
SERVICE.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can outline the
various systems for admission to the
Northern Government Civil Service:
whether there is in force a system by
which certain young men are brought
across from some of the English Universities and appointed assistant principals
over the heads of officers who have given
effcient service for years, and whether it
would be competent to select these
higher officers from men of proved
ability in the Civil Service in the same
way as His Majesty's judges are
appointed from distinguished legal local
men.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
20 APRIL 1939
Mr. ANDREWS : Administrative
clerical and typing posts are filled by
open competitive examination. Posts
requiring professional or technical qualifications are filled, after advertisement in
the public Press, by selection of the
official Selection Board. Temporary
posts in the lower ranks are filled from
suitable candidates obtained through the
medium of the employment exchanges.
Assistant principal vacancies, which
are of course very few in number, are
filled in one of two ways—either by
selection from serving officers in the
more junior ranks who have demonstrated that they possess special qualities
of an administrative character, or from
successful candidates at the
open competition for junior administrative
appointments conducted by the Imperial
Civil Service Commissioners on behalf of
the Civil Service Commissioners for
Northern Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
certain young men are selected and
brought over from some of the universities in Great Britain to fill these higher
positions over the heads of your own
trusted, tried, reliable, and proved men?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am afraid that
my hon. Friend does not understand the
position.
Mr. NIXON: I will let you know
what I understand.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is perfectly true
that young Englishmen and Scotsmen
can get positions here. It is equally
true that young men from here, for
instance, from our University can obtain
positions not only in Great Britain, but
throughout the Dominions. If we were
to be foolish enough to shut the door
to young persons coming from Great
Britain and if they were to retaliate
against us it would be very much to the
disadvantage of our young people here.
This is a kingdom. I do not think that
should be forgotten.
Mr. NIXON: Was that how Mr.
Plumb got in? His name has been
mentioned scores of times.
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not think it is
fair to mention the name of a particular
civil servant.
Mr. NIXON: I will raise this matter
on the Adjournment, because he is a
disgrace to the community, and to the
head of the Civil Service.

HIGH LEVEL DRAINAGE IN
BELFAST.
the

CLASS V. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF EDUCATION.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £46,332 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1940, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Education."- (Note
£24,000 has been voted on account.)
The CHAIRMAN: If it is agreeable.
to the Committee we will follow the usual
procedure and discuss the two Estimates
together.
Mrs. PARKER: In introducing these
Estimates I propose, with the permission
of the Committee, to adopt the customary
Ministry of Education 1014
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker.]
course of dealing with Votes 1 and 2
together. Last year the net total of the
two Votes was £2,256,111, and this year
the net total is £2,329,560-an increase
of £73,449-the main causes of which I
will refer to in detail as I proceed.
Dealing first with Vote 1 for the
salaries and expenses of the Ministry of
Education, I think that the Committee
will agree that the net increase of £698
calls for little comment. Certain savings
have arisen owing to changes of personnel
amongst the staff, but these have been
more than offset by the cost of increments
and by the appointment of an inspector
of physical training in connection with
the administration of the Physical Training and Recreation Act and the general
organisation and supervision of physical
training in our schools.
I cannot leave Vote 1 without referring
to the illness of Mr. Bonaparte Wyse,
the Permanent Secretary. He is greatly
missed in the Ministry, and by no one
more than by myself. Ever since I
became Parliamentary Secretary, Mr.
Wyse has been the kindest of friends and
advisers. His wisdom and the broadness
of his outlook have always been a source
of strength to us all. We wish him a
speedy and complete recovery. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Turning now to the figures included
in the Estimate for Educational Services,
it will be found that the net sum required
is £2,259,228, which
represents an
increase of £72,751 over last year's
figure, and I propose to refer seriatim
to the main items making up this
increase. In order, however, to determine the total estimated expenditure on
educational services which has to be. met
from public funds (that is, from Parliamentary grants and from rates) it is
necessary to add to Vote 2 (£2,259,228),
firstly, the portion of the net expenditure
of local education authorities which falls
to be met from rates under financial
schemes approved by the Ministry and,
secondly, the contribution from rates
under Section 3 of the Finance Act of
1934. The former figure is estimated at
£198,000 and the latter at £231,000, thus
making a total charge on rates of about
£429,000. The total estimated cost to
public funds of education in Northern
Ireland is, therefore, £2,688,228, of
which about 16 per cent. is met from
rates and about 84 per cent. from Parliamentary funds.
Under subhead Al it will be observed
that there is a decrease of some £1,000
in capitation grants to training colleges,
due to a reduction in the numbers of
students in the colleges. This is in accordance with the policy which the Ministry
has always pursued of endeavouring only
to train the number of students necessary
to fill the vacancies which may be, expected to arise. Subhead A3 provides
for the salaries and other emoluments of
our public elementary school teachers.
and shows an increase. of some £7,000,
which is mainly attributable to the cost
of increments of salary.
At this stage I consider it appropriate
to mention for the information of the.
Committee that the number of children
enrolled in public elementary schools still
continues to fall slightly, the average
number on rolls during 1938 being
193,902 as compared with 196,839 in
1937-a decrease of nearly 3,000. Notwithstanding this decline in enrolment.
the total average attendance for 1938 was
only about 1,000 less than for 1937. This
shows that there was a slight improvement in the regularity of the, attendance
of children at school. I sincerely hope
that this very welcome improvement will
continue, and that we may in the near
future reach as high a standard in this
respect as already exists in Great Britain.
I wish it could be more fully realised
that parents who keep their children at
home without adequate cause are handicapping the education and, therefore, the
futures of these children. A little. more
foresight and co-operation on the parents'
part and a little less leniency on the part
of the attendance committees would undoubtedly result in an increased percentage of useful citizens.
As Hon. Members probably know.
schools are staffed on the basis of the
average attendance of pupils, and, therefore, it is a matter of very great importance to an assistant teacher that his
school shall maintain the figure of
average attendance required by the
regulations for the continuance of his
recognition. The gradual decline in
average attendance, which has been in
evidence for some years past, has, unfortunately, led to a number of assistants being in danger of losing their

During the past year, the special

In future, these subjects will be taught

Under Subhead A 5, hon. Members
will find that provision has been made

between the Government and that

ment.
The sum required in these Estimates
for secondary education-£209,150shows an increase of £7,010 over last
year. Most of this increase is due to the
necessary provision for greater capitation
and increment grants consequent upon
the continued expansion and development of secondary education. The numbers of pupils in attendance at secondary
schools last year was over 14,000, and
as there is no reason to believe that the
peak has yet been reached, provision has
been made for an increase of £4,000 in
the Estimate for the capitation grant
and of £2,750 in the increment grant
for teachers. The latter sum is necessitated partly by the normal increments
payable to teachers with increased ser-
Ministry of Education 1018
Estimates
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
vice, and partly because more teachers
are needed for the increase in the number of pupils.
It will interest the Committee, I
think, to look back upon the great
change and development that has taken
place in secondary education in this area.
since the Government of Northern Ireland was established. Sixteen years ago
there were less than 7,000 pupils in
attendance at the schools, to-day, as I
say, there are more than 14,000; sixteen years ago the State's contribution
to the finances of the secondary schools
was less than £70,000, to-day it is
This
almost three times as much.
remarkable expansion has taken place
not only in the big city schools, but
also, I am very glad to say, in the
secondary schools in the small towns
scattered throughout the Province.
And here I should like to take the
opportunity of acknowledging the part
played by the regional education committees in this expansion, for since the
Ministry were established they have
given the secondary schools outside Belfast
and Londonderry more than
£70,000 for the provision of new buildings and for the extension and repair
of existing buildings.
Coming now to the provision in the
Estimates for the examinations, hon.
Members will find a small increase of
£200, due to the fact that the numbers
of pupils who take these examinations
are also increasing steadily. As the
Committee are aware, the Ministry conducts a Junior Certificate Examination,
the purpose of which is to testify to the
conclusion of a well-balanced course of
general education extending as a rule
over three years at a secondary school,
and a Senior Certificate Examination
which is intended to mark the satisfactory completion of a course of higher
education suitable for pupils who leave
school at 17 or 18 years of age.
This
latter examination, of course, is the preliminary to the University, the Training College, and the various professions,
and is taken by all secondary pupils who
propose to continue their education in
one form or another beyond the
secondary school stage.
These two examinations, the Junior
and the Senior, are of the greatest
interest to secondary pupils and their
parents, and with your permission I
shall say a few words on certain points
which I think are of importance. First,
the Junior Certificate Examination concerns each year something less than
2,500 boys and girls, that is to say about
90 per cent. of the children who complete the Intermediate course and would
normally be ready to sit for the
examination. Further, the Senior
Certificate Examination is taken
annually by about 1,300 boys and girls.
who constitute about 80 per cent. of the
children who are completing a postintermediate course. Thus there is no
reluctance on the part of the schools to
take the examinations; they are recognised as the natural and proper
corollaries to the courses which the
pupils are undergoing, and when I say
that the percentage of passes is about
77 or 78 hon. Members will agree that the
two examinations provide clear testimony to the steady and efficient work
that is done year by year in the
secondary schools.
Now, there are two points which I
think are at present interesting parents
and teachers in connection with these
examinations. The first is the existing
system of exhibitions and prizes, and the
second is homework. With regard to
the exhibitions, if hon. Members look
at the Estimates they will find that a
sum of £1,650 is provided annually for
the award of exhibitions and prizes to
children who have shown outstanding
merit at these examinations, and some
teachers maintain that it is wrong at the
Junior Certificate stage that pupils of
15 or 16 should be encouraged to strive
for these awards, that they should be
unduly "crammed" and that the lure of
monetary prizes should force the
examination to become strictly competitive instead of a reasonable qualifying
examination for pupils who are halfway through their full secondary course.
There are many answers to this charge
and I hope to satisfy the Committee that
they are good answers. In the first
place, last year the 41 junior exhibitions
and prizes were awarded, and 2,490
pupils took the examinations that is.
there is generally about one award for
every 60 pupils. I do not believe for
a moment that any competent headmaster or headmistress will unduly force
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
20 APRIL 1939
or harass a class of ordinary pupils in
order to try and gain for them an award
which obviously is destined for the outstanding pupil who, if he is well taught
and has the merit, will win the prize
without any undue forcing. Besides, I
think the schools recognise that the
examination papers are very carefully
chosen with particular regard to the
capabilities of the normal pupil, and
that the ordinary well-taught pupil can
always score sufficient marks to pass, and
to pass with credit, without bothering
himself or herself with the odd question
at the end of the paper which is clearly
designed to catch the eye and awaken
the interest of the brilliant pupil. It
occurs to me that sometimes there is
a slight tendency in education to-day,
both here and elsewhere, rather to
neglect the pupil of outstanding merit,
and to concentrate rather much on the
average or the sub-average.
But there is another reason why the
Ministry is reluctant to abolish these
awards at the Junior Certificate Examination. Our system of scholarships here
in Northern Ireland is relatively young
and in this matter we are moving slowly
and with caution, as is our custom. Now,
while I do not wish to say a word which
might detract in one small particular
from the excellent work which education
committees are doing in this respect, yet
the fact is that an exhibition of £30,
awarded to a Junior Certificate candidate
of outstanding merit and devoted, as it
must be, to furthering the education of
the recipient, can be an enormous help
to the parents if he is one of that wide
class that just fails to come within the
means test of a scholarship scheme, and
yet finds it difficult to provide the money
necessary to give his children a full
secondary education. And I may say
that while naturally it is not possible to
give accurate statistics as to the financial
position of all parents whose children
gain exhibitions or prizes, there is pretty
clear evidence that many of these
awards go to scholarship holders and
many others to children whose parents
are not very well-to-do.
A few words more, if I may, about
homework in the secondary school. I
think there is a sort of vague impression
about nowadays that the secondary
school child is driven night and day by
a relentless administration and a body
of stony-hearted heads of schools. It is
a difficult problem to reduce to precise
terms, but I think nobody will deny that
a secondary school pupil must do a
certain amount of homework if he or she
is to gain proper benefit from a secondary
school, and I myself attach value to the
disciplinary effect of exercises performed
by the pupil alone the habit of independent thought and self-reliance is inculcated, and there is a real advance
made when the pupil learns to do well
by himself what he has to be prompted
and egged on to do in the classroom. On
the other side, it will be agreed that
outside interests attract the pupil-and
perhaps the parent-more and more as
years go by. The cinema and the radio
are distracting influences, and the local
Scouts and Guides and parochial
functions make their call.
I have two observation to make which
may perhaps be of interest. The recuirements of the Ministry with regard to
the Junior Certificate Examination are
that the candidate shall take at least six
subjects; English, a language other than
English, History or Geography, Arithmetic, Algebra or Geometry, and any
other subjects, and yet we find that the
average pupil takes 8, 9 or ten subjects.
I think that is a very interesting and
illuminating point. That is evidence, I
think, that the Ministry's requirements
are not too stringent, and it is evidence
also that in these days of high specialisation and intensive competition for
posts in after-life the parent and the
principal recognise that the child's
future career is as yet undetermined, and
that the best basis that can be laid for
coming years is the broad basis of a
sound general education.
The other observation I have to make
is that the questionnaire on homework
was recently issued to the 76 recognised
secondary schools in the area, and from
the replies which were received it was
apparent that at least 64 had in operation well thought out and carefuly
designed schedules prescribing maximum
periods of homework each night, and
that in most of the remaining 12, clear
precautions were taken to ensure that
the amount of unaided work done by the
pupil was well within his capacity.
I have, I fear, detained the Committee
rather long on secondary education, but
you will forgive me, for there are very

many matters of engrossing interest in

Two more I feel I must mention, and
I shall touch on them very briefly. In
the Senior Certificate Examination two
changes have been made which I think
have been welcomed by the schools. After
consultation with the Art Advisory
Council it has been decided that as from
1940 a
new subject will be introduced
which, very shortly, may be described
as art that is, design and the history
of art. Also, in the same examination,
we are lightening the burden on those
girls who have no aptitude for mathematics and are not likely to need the
subject in their future careers, for they
will be allowed to gain the Senior
Certificate by substituting domestic
economy, music or art instead of
mathematics as one of the necessary

Since I introduced the Estimates last
year the Committee of Scholarships which
sat under the chairmanship of the
Minister has completed its labours and
furnished its Report. The Report contained a number of recommendations of
far-reaching importance which demanded
a great deal of research and investigation, and as the Ministry has been passing through a period of unexampled
stress and work due to various causes, it
has not been possible to complete these
investigations in time for the issue of a
memorandum to education committees.
A great deal of work has, however, been
done on the matter, and the Ministry
hopes to be able to communicate its views
on the subject in good time to allow
education committees to consider the
amendment of their schemes for next
year.
I turn now to Technical Instruction.
The total Vote under this head is £86,110,
and is greater than last year's by £5,590.
The increase is almost all in respect of
the grants-in-aid payable for the
attendance of pupils and for increment
grants towards the salaries. Here again,
as in secondary education, I have to report a gratifying expansion. Apart
from a general all-round increase in
attendance, four new centres of technical
instruction have been established in districts which hitherto have been without
such provision.
Technical Instruction has from its inception less than 40 years ago made a
special appeal to the people of Northern
Ireland. From the first it was under
local control, and it was for many years
the only part of the educational system
which was aided by local rates. It may
be that to these conditions is due the
wide extent of the provisions, for at the
present time there is hardly a town of
any size which has not its Technical
School. In more recent years the most
notable development has been the organisation of the full-time day Junior Technical Schools. They are of three types,
one providing courses suitable for boys
who intend entering upon industrial
Occupations, such as in mechanical,
electrical or motor-car engineering, or in
building trades; another preparing boys
and girls for commercial occupations,
and the third affording courses for girls in
domestic science and household management.
These schools are, however, not
strictly vocational, for in each case the
curriculum is based upon the study of
subjects of general educational value,
English, mathematics, geography, etc...
and includes, in addition, the more
specialised subjects appropriate to the
aims of the students. The valuable part
which schools of these types play in the
preparation of young people for entry
upon life is now becoming more fully
realised. They are complementary to
the secondary schools, and afford what
are very suitable pre-vocational courses
for pupils who cannot spend more than
two or three years in full-time postelementary education.
The estimated grants to local education
authorities show an increase of £7,000
which is due to the anticipated increase
in the sum which will be expended by
these authorities, and will therefore
attract the appropriate grant payable
from Government Funds under the
Education Act of 1923.
Provision is made under Subhead G
for grants under the Physical Training
and Recreation Act, and the increased
sum of £22,000 is due to the fact that
last year's estimate was in respect of
a part-year only. In this connection I
would like to inform the Committee that
voluntary organisations are taking
advantage of the Act to a gratifying and
increasing extent. It would appear,
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
20 APRIL 1939
however, that, generally speaking, our
local authorities, which includes education authorities, have not yet realised the
possibilities of the opportunity afforded to
them under the Act of qualifying for
substantial grants towards the provision
of adequate facilities for physical training, and recreation within their
spective areas.
re-
I am glad, however, to be in a position.
to announce that a number of excellent
schemes from local authorities have
already been approved, and that other
schemes are in contemplation. I am
aware of the many calls on the resources
of these authorities, and of the very
natural and proper desire on their part
to restrict their expenditure in every way
consonant with the welfare of the communities whom they represent.
In view
of the wide consensus of opinion regarding
the benefits conferred on any community
by the possession of ample facilities for
physical training and recreation, however, I feel that I am justified in commending the Act still more fully to their
consideration.
I would also like to emphasise that,
where any scheme under the Act qualifies
as a public utility scheme, it is possible
for the local authority to receive an unemployment relief grant in addition to a
grant under the Physical Training Act.
The final capital cost to the authority
may therefore work out at only a
fraction of the gross cost of the scheme,
and, in such circumstances, a unique
opportunity is afforded for providing
physical training and recreation facilities on most advantageous terms.
There are many other activities of the
Ministry to which I would have been
glad to refer, but I feel that the Committee will appreciate my desire to confine my remarks to those aspects of our
educational system which have been most
in the public mind of late.
It is true that the sums with which
we are dealing are large, but it is difficult
to see in what direction the nation's
money could be spent to better advantage than in preparing and equipping its
future citizens to take up and carry on
the work when this generation lays it
down. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to express my regret at the illness of the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of
Education. At the moment I feel that
education in Northern Ireland is lacking
in something, and that that something is
the hand of the Permanent Secretary.
I represent the strongest teachers'
organisation, in numbers, both North
and South, and during our annual conference at Queen's University last week
there was throughout a note of regret
at the illness of Mr. Bonaparte Wyse,
who has for so long been connected with
education in Ireland as a whole, and for
many years past in Northern Ireland.
The Parliamentary Secretary has once
more explained very clearly education as
it is being carried on in the Six Counties,
and if we accepted her statement at its
face value we would be inclined to say
that everything in the garden is lovely.
In other words, there is not a ripple on
the educational waters. I am within the
circle that is best able to judge of that
matter, and unfortunately I know there
are various things that could be adjusted
if the right hon. Gentleman who faces
me (Mr. Andrews) would only be as
generous with the teachers as he has been
with other units of the community.
I know that he has the power to make
the rough waters calm, and I would ask
him to present the actuarial report on
the lump sum on retirement which I
have been awaiting for a long time. That
is causing a certain amount of anxiety
in the minds of the older teachers; they
are wondering if they are going to be
left out in the cold. It has always been
put forward that as they are loyal,
attached to this part of the world, and
subect to the control and authority of
the Northern Government, the least they
are entitled to is the benefit of the stepby-step policy, which would bring them
into line with the teachers in England
and Scotland. My organisation makes
the overture to the right hon. Gentleman,
the Minister of Finance, that this lump
sum payment should be made retrospective to the year 1922, and I say that that
is a reasonable request. I hope that in
the near future the Government will
grant that act of justice to the older
serving teachers, and thus make. the
rough waters smooth.
That is not the last request I have to
make. We still have broken promises
and broken agreements. When the
Imperial Exchequer considered the
position of Irish teachers in the year
Ministry of Education 1026
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
1920 there was a solemn agreement drawn
up, signed, sealed and delivered. That
agreement was binding on the Northern
Government in regard to salaries. That
agreement is known to teachers throughout the whole of Ireland, North and
South, as the 1920 salary agreement. We
are still waiting for the restoration of the
cut that was made in the salary scale,
and I have not given up hope of seeing
it restored at a very early date. At the
moment I am not pressing for it. But
those two items are outstanding, and I
believe that if the Minister cleared those
two grievances out of the way education
would be in very smooth waters.
I should like to refer to the Parliamentary Secretary's use of the word
"model" in regard to certain schools.
There are no such schools as Model
Schools; they do not exist. There are
now no class distinctions in primary
education. I hope the hon. Lady agrees
with me. I was rather disappointed
when she used the word model. That
title. passed away when the Act of 1923
was passed. That Measure gave equal
classification to the children of all the
primary schools. The Model Schools
were established under the old Irish
educational system, but it is wrong to
describe any existing elementary school
as a Model School. The term was used
by the Director of Education in Belfast.
I think we knocked that designation out
of existence, so far as Belfast is concerned, and I hope the hon. Lady will
not be led into using a description that
does not now apply.
Mr. ANDREWS: What is wrong with
it?
Mr.
BEATTIE: The right hon.
Gentleman asks what is wrong with it.
Under the 1923 Act it was decided to
provide every working-class child with
equal education facilities, and to give no
special privileges to any school. The
schools in Northern Ireland were erected
on the basis of justice. for all. The old
Model School was for the privileged few.
The teachers were of a special type, with
special qualifications. To-day all the
teachers have the same qualifications as
the teachers in the old Model Schools.
Therefore, there is no justification for the
description of any school in Northern
Ireland as a Model School.
Another point that I wish to bring
forward, is that the civil rights of
teachers in Northern Ireland have not
yet been conceded. This is the only part
of the world where the teachers have not
their civil rights. Why that is so I cannot understand. The teachers actually
thought they had civil rights for a period
of eight years, and they never did any
damage to education or to the educational
world. I hope that at an early date the
Government will concede civil rights to
all teachers in Northern Ireland.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE: It was startling and
annoying to see. in the Belfast newspapers
that the members of the Education Committee had advocated the suspension of
the raising of the school-leaving age for
one year owing to the lack of school
accommodation. It is the committee's
fault that there is not adequate accommodation for the children who will remain at school after they attain fourteen
years of age. If the committee did not
provide accommodation in the past they
are not likely to do so in the future. I
hope that the Parliamentary Secretary
will not accede to the request of the
Belfast Education Committee, and that
she will put the Act into operation in
July next.
On the question of school accommodation, I feel that we are not working on
the
proper lines.
We are building
palatial schools to accommodate anything
from 800 to 1,200 pupils. That is a
factor that is not doing education any
good; it is doing it harm. Those schools
will go out in twenty or twenty-five
years. I am standing for the erection of
smaller schools, cheaper schools with all
modern requirements, based on a life of
twenty-five years. I do not understand
why we spend so much money in the erection of palatial schools. In thirty years
some of those schools will be as antiquated
as some of the little schools in the backward areas of Northern Ireland. To day
all educationists agree that a school
should not accommodate more than 500
pupils. The school of that size should be
provided with all modern requirements,
and the cost should be based on a life of
twenty-five years. I hope that that view
will be put before the regional committees who are erecting very lavish
schools at the moment.
Ministry of Education 1028
Estimates-
20 APRIL 1939
The next point to which I wish to draw
attention is that of the falling averages.
The decline of the school population is
going to be a serious problem in our
area, and the matter has got to be
handled quickly. By a temporary
arrangement the two quarters have been
extended to six quarters, but that will
not meet the requirements of the future.
That is only a palliative for a transitional
period. The whole population is still on
the decline in this part of the country;
indeed, it is on the decline throughout
the whole of Ireland. That decline is
going to jeopardise the position of many
teachers, and the sooner the Government
bring in legislation to give the teachers.
the same standing as civil servants the
better. Security of tenure must be given
to the teachers, for if this decline in the
school population continues, not only will
it put teachers out of schools, but it
will injure education. The teachers will
be uncertain of their position, and they
will not be working in the normal
atmosphere which is necessary to the
efficient carrying on of their work.
We must, therefore, give the teachers
security of tenure, such as is enjoyed by
established civil servants.
It is very
difficult for me to speak while the Minister of Finance and the Minister of
Commerce are indulging in smiles and
laughter. To meet the conditions of
which I have been speaking, we have
again had to reduce the numbers in the
training colleges. As you know, there
are training colleges that are kept going
by capitation grants. If you go to
extreme lengths in cutting down the
numbers attending these colleges, you are.
going to pauperise the education of the
students. You may go to the point of
closing the colleges altogether. Stranmillis is in the happy position of being
State-aided, and the position is not so
serious from the point of view of that
college; but from the Catholic point of
view their colleges are maintained on
the basis of capitation grants-it would
be very dangerous to go too near the bone
in the cutting down of the numbers of
students. I agree that it is necessary
and essential to try to keep out of the
profession the numbers who are seeking
to enter it; that will save them from
what I may call educational suicide. It
will prevent their having to walk about
for three or four or five. years without
work.
I was present at the start of the Milk
Week campaign, and I have several remarks to make about the value of milk.
There is nothing so valuable in the life
of a child as milk. I think milk should
be used in the schools of Northern Ireland
more than it is at the moment. I understand there is a distributor of milk who
has little cartons of Grade A milk, and
who is prepared to supply many of the
schools in the Six Counties, but the
children attending the schools would not
have the money to pay for the cartons.
I understand he is prepared to serve
Grade. A milk to the schools at 1d per
carton. We have spent money in many
directions. We have given £150,000
towards the development of flax. Flax
is all-important, but is it more important
than the development of the future.
citizens of Ulster?
I claim on behalf of the poor children
attending our public elementary schools
that we
are entitled to have the milk
scheme subsidised so that every child at
school will have a supply of pure milk.
If that were done it would mean money
well spent. The under nourishment of
the children to-day is due to the failure
of the parents to purchase sufficient to
give them that standing in life which
they require in order to get a good
serviceable education. How can anyone
expect children to go to school on a little
bit of bread and butter and half a cup
of tea. Many of the children in the
poorer areas are underfed. They get a
cup of tea and half a slice of buttered
bread before going to school. On this
food they cannot survive the battle they
have to meet in after life, nor can they
be in a proper condition during the
school day to take sufficient interest in
the work of the teacher. The failure to
supply milk to the schools is a policy of
penny wise and pound foolish. I hope
the right hon. Gentleman will see that

Many women
teachers, principally
Presbyterians and Methodists, are
trained because they were afraid to go
to the Marlborough Street Training
College, Dublin, owing to the unsanitary conditions in the women's side of
that institution. Well, I never knew a
Presbyterian who was afraid of anything. Many young women who went
to Marlborough Street suffered in health
by so doing, and this deterred many
others from going. These teachers are
still untrained and find that they cannot
proceed higher than a salary of £199
per annum on efficient service, whilst
the trained teacher who is marked
efficient can rise to £280. If the untrained teacher is rated highly efficient
she can rise to £280. Thus she loses
ultimately £81 per annum if she does
not secure the highly efficient mark.
The trained teacher, if she is rated
highly efficient, rises to £307, so that if
she fails to get the higher rating her
loss is only £27 per annum. It would
be interesting to know the number of
untrained women teachers who have
been kept at £199 during the past ten
years through being denied the highly
efficient mark. It seems practically impossible for any of these untrained
teachers to get the highly efficient mark.
Why is this? Why are they stopped at
£199 when marked efficient? I might
comment on that, but I think it better
not to do so because as the representative of an organisation whose membership believe in all teachers being
trained the rate we claim is the trained
rate I might be subjected to very
severe criticism. Nevertheless it
seem to be an injustice to the untrained
teacher who is a Presbyterian or
Methodist that she can only rise to £199,
while the other teacher reaches £281.

Another question is in regard to lay
assistants in Convent schools. They had
no pensions before 1922. After that
time pension rights were granted and
they claim that they are entitled to have
service rendered prior to 1922 recognised. I see the justness of their claim.
If they were entitled to pension rights
from 1922 it should be remembered that
the same conditions of service and the
same qualifications applied previous to
that year. Why 1922 was taken as the
year I do not understand. On their
behalf I claim that they are entitled to
full pension rights for full service. I
hope this point will be favourably
considered.
I now come to the scholarship system,
which is not working out as well as
intended. It seems that the underlying
motive in the scholarship system was to
give an opportunity to poor children,
whose parents were not financially
strong. From the evidence I have
received from the Six County area the
system does not seem to be working out
in accordance with the ideas of its
framers. The means test is rarely
applied. The majority of the scholarships go to children whose parents are
quite well able to pay for their education. That is to the detriment of the
poorer children. These are points in
regard to the scholarship system which

I now wish to deal with the grant of
£10,000 for the school in May Street.
I do not think that that is a good site
on which to erect a school. In Beechfield Street school, which is in my
division,
have 14 teachers in 13
classrooms. It is a new school, and
there is not a hon. Member of this House
who has not heard the architect and the
Belfast Education Committee eulogised
in regard to it, yet there is a school
which has only 13 classrooms for 14
teachers. It is one of the latest schools
built in my division. That matter requires some attention. In my opinion
the organisation of schools is wrong.
We have what is called the junior and
senior schools and the all-in schools.
We have a school on the Beersbridge
Road known as Elmgrove, and it can
take infants and seniors. We have the
Avoniel Road school which only takes
in juniors, and it is lying half empty.
There are two lovely schools siting side
by side, and while one is allowed to take
in infants and seniors the other is confined to juniors. The teachers in the
Avoniel School-which, as I have stated,
is half empty-could get numbers of
children into the school provided they
could accept seniors.
This is what occurs in the senior and
infant schools When wee Johnny or
wee Mary wants to go to school there is
Bobby or Sarah to take them. The
seniors can take the younger children
along with them. And when a child gets
into a school it remains there until it
has finished its school life. That keeps
up the average at that school and this
other new school, a later addition than
that school, is sitting there on the Avoniel
Road half empty, and every teacher in
that school is suffering the loss of fees.
It cannot take in seniors. The moment
the child comes to the third standard it
must go out. I think that organisation
is wrong, and I would like to restore the
all-in schools where a boy or girl goes
in as an infant and the place is so well
equipped that he will be able to finish
his educational life within that building
in personal touch with the teacher. I
believe that is the best system of education. This separation, as I see it
operating, has not the results that the
older system with the personal touch
had.
a
We have these conditions not only in
my Division; the same thing operates
outside my Division, and you have
schools competing one with the other for
children. That competition is creating
disturbance within the educational
atmosphere. It may not be outward,
but I as an official know it is inward.
I say it is not fair to give preferential
treatment to any school, and the sooner
we go back to the old system of school
regulation in which I was brought up
the better. You went in as a baby and
came out as a man. There the teacher had
personal touch from babyhood to 15
years of age. You go out and can
regulate your educational life in the
various stages it takes you to advance
until you leave school. This thing of
going into a school and going out of that
school at a certain time, not knowing
who the principal of the school is, is
disturbing.
In some schools the children to-day
could not tell you the name of the
principal. I have one in mind at the
present moment, a junior school where
the child is sent away from the school
at the third standard and goes into a
senior school-a new school altogetherand leaves there at 14 years of age and
he does not know the teacher of the
next class. The personal touch being
absent is a menace to the good education of the child and the sooner it is
restored the better. These are the few
remarks I had to make. I wish to
thank the hon. Lady Member again for
the clearness with which she set out
the Educational Estimates. The increase is not of such a large amount that
any Member of the House should take
objection to it.

It is therefore recommended that

Mr. YOUNG: In the first place I
would like to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary on the way she introduced the Estimates, and I regret the
fact that the Permanent Secretary is
absent through illness. Although I congratulate the hon. Lady on her introduction of the Estimates, I disagree with
her on the subject of homework. She
said in the course of her remarks that
she was in favour of a certain amount of
homework. The question is what is a
certain amount of homework. You will
get parents in all classes of the community at the present time whose
children are getting as much as three
hours work at night.
That in my
opinion is due to two causes.
In the
first place each master in a subject seems
to think there is no other master or mistress in any subject. The result is that
the child gets four or five subjects for
homework, any one of which would do
alone. The hon. Lady said that by
having homework the child learned to
do work by himself. From the little I
know the child does not learn to do it
but his parents and relations all help
to do that homework.
I think the mistake is this, that all
this homework business is based on the
child that happens to be a genius, whereas the average child is not a genius.
The average child is a plodder. I
thoroughly sympathise with plodders,
because I was a plodder myself. I was
in an English Public School where they
set aside one and a half hours each night
for preparation which took the place of
what is called home lessons. I always took
about three-quarters of an hour extra as
well as the one and a half hours, and
often the other boy who did nothing but
make a fool of the master or make a
fool of his neighbour seemed to know
far more about the lessons than I did.
That type of boy got a double remove at
the end of the term and I was very
fortunate if I got one remove in the
year. I think if there had been such
a thing as superannuation at a public
school I would have been superannuated.
But as far as I can see I have got on
as well as most people.
As far as I understand a few months
ago a committee was set up by the
English and Welsh education authorities
in regard to this question of homework,
I could produce you dozens, if not
hundreds, of parents who would go into
the law courts and swear that it takes
their children over three hours at night
to do the homework. There is another
point I raised in this House. When I
was a child if you met a child in the
street going to school wearing spectacles
you turned round to look after him, but
look at the number wearing spectacles
now. In my opinion the reason of that
is the excessive amount of homework
done with poor artificial light. A public meeting of parents was held in the
Y.M.C.A. minor hall, Belfast, on 23rd
March this year and the parents gave
different instances. One was of a child
having to sit up to 2 a.m. to finish homework. The child remarked: "I must
do it or I dare not go to school." In
my opinion that was cruelty, and if it
was the only instance it justifies an
alteration. Even if one child in the
whole of Northern Ireland had to sit up
to 2 a.m. to do homework-I am not in
favour of strikes but if I were the parent
of that child I would go on strike and
refuse to send the child back to school.
Mr. HENDERSON: Are you preaching revolution?
Mr. YOUNG: Another parent gave
an example of the week's programme involving 25 subjects, 12 exercises, and 13
set pieces to learn. This I think was
the worst of the whole lot. A parent
gave this example of homework that a
child of nine years had to do. I will be
quite candid. When I was nine years
old I could not read, yet here is a child
of nine years who had this homework
for one night: Six sums, composition to
the extent of four pages, geography, two
verses to learn, and history. All I can
say is when I was nine years if I had had
to learn two verses my father would
have had to read the verses aloud
because I could not read them myself.

Again from the medical point of view
a doctor who was not a ashamed to give
his name Dr. J. Armstrong, M.D.,
F.R.C.S. writing to a Ballymena paper
in the course of a letter says:
in
From personal observation and experience I have no hesitation
saying that the present system of
education as a whole is in all cases conducive to a low standard of physical
health in the growing child and in a
measurable percentage of cases results
in permanent invalidism
or early
death.
This medical man with M.D. and
F.R.C.S. after his name goes on to say:
It is undoubtedly the excessive
homework with the consequent curtailment or total absence of the open
air and exercise necessary for the
health of the growing child that is the
chief offender. Homework therefore
should be abolished altogether or very
strictly limited according to the age
of the child.
Now I think I have made out a very
good case that this system of homework
under the Ministry of Education is
nothing short of cruelty to children.
Mr. BYRNE: I join with the other
Members in expressing regret at the illness of the permanent secretary of the
Ministry of Education and I hope he
will soon be restored to health again.
Every year when these Estimates come
up I consider that on behalf of the
people I represent I have a duty to perform, and that is to complain and complain very bitterly of the treatment
meted out to the Catholic community
with regard to our schools. I think it
is stated that £2,688,198 is spent on
education. I have no objection whatever
to this expenditure. I am sure the
money is well spent, but I think it is
most unfair that we who are the poorest
section of the community in this city
and who are endeavouring to build
schools and are in great want of schools
are refused an equal grant with those of
other denominations. At the same
time we, poor as we are, are heavy ratepayers and have to contribute our fair
share of the rates to erect these schools.
This appeal has been made in this
House year after year and we are told
by a prominent man here, the noble
Lord himself, if we had complaints to
make to come here and we would be
listened to. Others told us that if complaint was to be made this is the place
to make it and on behalf of the Catholic
community-and it is a very important
community-I make an appeal to the
Government to-day if they do not give
us at least the same treatment as others
they should consider giving us an increased grant for the erection of our
schools. There are several schools I
know myself and which I visited and
they are most unsanitary and the
children are suffering severely from illhealth. It is unfair to keep these
children huddled up in these unsanitary
schools, and not treat them the way
other people are treated. Every effort
has been made by both priests and
people to raise money in order to erect
schools. We are collecting money
weekly, monthly, and yearly, and yet
we are unable to raise sufficient funds
to build the schools we require. I say
it is most unfair to penalise our people
in the way we are penalised in this area.
I am told on good authority that the
local authorities in England give more
than 75 per cent. in grants to Catholic
and voluntary schools, and yet here
after a big effort all we are able to get
is 50 per cent. I think that is most
unfair. I hope that in the near future
there will be some concession given to
our people so that we may be able to
come near the condition of other schools.
I will be told to-day, perhaps, in reply
to my request, that all we have to do is
to hand over our schools to the public
authority. It has been repeated over
and over again by members of Our
Church, from the highest to the lowest,
that we cannot hand over our schools to
any public authority. We are most
anxious that our children be brought up
and taught in the religion to which they
belong, but we will not surrender to any
public authority the teaching of our
school children. The only condition that
our people will consent or ever submit
to, no matter what the penalty is, is
that our children must be taught by
Catholic teachers in a Catholic school and
under Catholic management. On that
point we cannot surrender.
As regards giving grants for special
subjects, some time ago this Government

gave a paltry grant of £1,500 a year for

That being so, why do the Government

As to the school leaving age, which has

I do not think there is anything more

to take these poor children out of the

Mr. CLARK: I wish first of all to congratulate the hon. Lady on the very
lucid explanation she gave in introducing

I support the hon. Member for Bann Side in

the use of spectacles, and quoted what

number of these children come from poor

They come home from school, and with

The question of homework was raised
by the hon. Member for Bann Side (Mr.
Young), ably supported by the hon.
Member for Dock (Mr. Clark). I hope

An additional half-hour's tuition at

I wish to associate myself with those

An hon. Member for the University the

started by the Milk Council, and what

a credit to the Government and to the

in which the children were being
educated. There are many schools in

described as the Black Hole of Calcutta.
Agriculture is the backbone of this
country, and the agricultural community
return 90 per cent. of the Members of
this House. If they did not do so there
would be no Parliament here, because
the intelligent people of Belfast would
not return them. What are the facts!
The subjects taught in the syllabus do
not include agriculture, which is one of
our staple industries. Agriculture should
be part of the curriculum, but it
is not, because the Minister of Education

and the Parliamentary Secretary are not
