Another matter of vital importance to
this State, a matter which in my opinion
has been sadly neglected notwithstanding
the repeated efforts of Members on this
side of the Committee, including myself,
is in regard to the art of swimming. We
have built palatial schools in all parts of
Northern Ireland, but is it not true to
say there is not a swimming pool
attached to any of them? When the
architects are sending in plans of new
schools the Government should see that
in addition to the ordinary room available for recreation and physical culture
there is a swimming pond and also proper
facilities for sport. The Ministry have
passed plans and given grants for schools
with no playgrounds attached to them. I
have always protested against that. The
only people who have power to prevent
that taking place are the Minister and
the Ministry, and they take no action at
all.
At the earliest possible moment the
hon. Lady should take up the question
of seeing that every child is given facilities for being taught swimming. I do
not know whether she, or any of the
Cabinet Ministers, has read that about 30
per cent. of the deaths that take place
during the summer months are due to
drowning accidents. That is a very
serious state of affairs. It is true to say
that even in small seaside towns there is
nothing done to teach the children to
swim.
Even seven or eight out of every
ten fishermen at the Ulster ports are
unable to swim. The hon. Lady should
take up this question, because swimming
is like everything else. When a child is
taught to swim it will never forget.
When a child is taught to walk it will
continue to walk, unless it is prevented
through illness, and the same thing
applies to swimming. It never forgets
it.
Those are some of the things that antiquated Cabinet Ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries forget about, but
they are important factors in the life of
the child. One would have thought in
view of the fact that the hon. Lady represents an agricultural constituency she
would have raised the question of agriculture being taught in the schools, but
it has been left to the Members of this
side of the Committee to draw attention
to the matter. However, I am quite
satisfied that she will see that the Miniscareful
ter gives the question his
attention.
Then there is the question of afflicted
children. The majority of the afflicted
children are in the homes of the workingclass people who cannot afford to bring
in private tutors. The result is that in
thousands of homes afflicted children are
receiving no teaching at all. It is true
that we have the Haypark School in
Belfast, but there are no other schools in
Northern Ireland carrying on similar
work.
Mrs. PARKER: There is plenty of
room at Haypark.
Mr. HENDERSON: But working
people who have afflicted children like to
keep them at home, and they would like
to be in a position to send those children
to a school within reach of their homes.
If I lived in the Dungiven mountains and
I had an afflicted child, do you think I
would be happy at night if I knew he
was in a school in Belfast. My thoughts
would be about him all the time, as they
are now about my own child who is
healthy and strong, a lot stronger than
his father, thank goodness. We should
have at least a dozen centres in various
parts of Northern Ireland where afflicted
children could be educated, because if
there is one section of the community
that deserves the. sympathy and consideration of the Government it is the
afflicted children. Up to now they have
had to be kept in their homes, and
to-day, apart from the Haypark School,
we are no better off in this respect than
we were forty or fifty years ago.
If I were responsible for the policy of
the Government I would give the parents

12s a week towards their keep, as well as
educate them. That is the spirit of the
Oxford Group. That is what they stand
for, and if we could induce the Minister
of Education and the Parliamentary

One, of the things I have always fought
for is civil rights for school teachers.
The teachers of this country have a right
to say who shall be their leaders.
If you
would give them that privilege it would
be a godsend, because in a good many
places, particularly agricultural areas, if
a teacher got up and made a speech on
behalf of a candidate he would be almost
sure to be returned. The pupils would
go home and tell their fathers that their
master was speaking at Tandragee on
behalf of Mr. Brown, and they would
say, "Our master is quite right, and we
want you to vote for Mr. Brown."
Would the Parliamentary Secretary like
her civil rights to be taken away? It
took hundreds of years to get the
franchise for the working people of this
country, and why should that franchise
be denied to the teachers of the Six
Counties. At present they are not
allowed to vote. I feel there is gross
extravagance in this Ministry. It is
costing more than would run not only
this country, but half Europe.

I am glad the right hon. Member for
Bann Side has drawn attention to the
neglect of the children's eyes. I came
across a child in a small seaside place,
and it could hardly see a scrap. I drew
the attention of the parents to the
trouble. There is not the same medical
inspection in the country that there is
in the city of Belfast, and the result is
that the eyesight of the children in rural
areas is being ruined. The right hon.
Member for Bann Side was quite right
when he attributed this state of affairs to
the amount of homework given to the
children. The children are compelled to
do their homework in badly ventilated
and poorly lighted rooms.
Unless some
action be taken, all the children will be
wearing glasses soon.
It is very seldom that medical inspection is properly carried out in some
of the rural areas. I made inquiries outside Donaghadee, and I found that very
little was done in this respect. If parents
who can afford to pay for glasses do not
provide the necessary treatment, then
the hon. Lady should see that they are
prosecuted. Where the parents are too

should step in and pay for them. I hope
that the hon. Lady will pay attention to
her duties during the coming year.
hope that she will visit some of these

Another point I

which the hon. Gentleman spoke. I
think if we go on pampering children to
such an extent as to take away home
lessons from them, in a few years' time
there will be a strong effort to prevent
their doing work even when they are
attending school. As a result we may
have a race of men and women who are
perhaps bodily stronger than their
ancestors, but who will know practically
nothing when they leave school.
In my opinion the homework which
young children have to do nowadays is
considerably easier than that of their
predecessors of a generation ago, and
very much more simple than their grandfathers had to do. I can remember my
father telling me that when he was a
boy at school he had to know the whole
of the Thirty-nine Articles. At the
present time if a child has to learn a
verse of a poem the mother throws up
her hands in horror. I do not say that
a child of nine or ten should have home
lessons that would occupy three or four
hours every night, but if home lessons
are taken away altogether, or even to
the extent suggested by some hon. Members. I think the child at the age of 14
or 15 will be considerably less fit for the
duties of life than the child of the
present day.
Mr. AGNEW: We all realise that the
education of youth is the very basis of
society. The moulding of their lives to
make them fit and capable as the men
and women of to-morrow is the duty
that is in the hands of the Department
of Education in Northern Ireland. I
always appreciate the spending of money
on education, because, after all, the
future of this country depends upon the
intelligence of the boys and girls who
will be the generation of the future.
We should not look upon education from
the class point of view. It should be
the privilege of every child who is
mentally fit to go from the elementary
school to the university. I feel that
education should be open to all classes.
Among the working classes there can be
found the very best brains if they were
only allowed to develop, but under the
present system their education is limited
by the age of fifteen, and the result is
they become part of the army of unemployed. The privileged classes take full
advantage of the education provided
from the elementary schools to the university, simply because education is the
privilege of those who have means.
The question of homework is a very
important one. If we really understand the conditions under which the
working classes live, we must realise that
there is no scope in the room for
children to learn anything after they
leave
school. There should be no
necessity for homework unless in a case

I think the matter which aroused more
interest than any other was this question
of home work. I was glad to know that
the hon. Member for Iveagh and the hon.
Member for Clifton did not altogether
agree with the hon. Member for Bann
Side and the other hon. Members who
spoke in this connection. I think that
perhaps the hon. Member for Bann Side
went rather far, as the hon. Member for
Iveagh pointed out, when he spoke about
the effect upon the child of an excessive
amount of home work. I had purposed
to say exactly what the hon. Member for
Iveagh said, that the number of spectacles
which one sees on children throughout the
country possibly means—I am almost sure
it means- -a much more efficient system of
medical inspection. The children's defects
are now attended to and the spectacles do
not necessarily mean that children are
being overworked and blinded at home.
In this connection with regard to home
work I would like to say-I do not think
I am very hard-hearted-that it is absolutely essential for children of a certain age
to do a certain amount of home work. It
does give them an opportunity of using
their brains and their personalities in a
way which they cannot do when learning
in class. It teaches them to do necessary
memorising and saves a certain amount of
valuable time.
I am absolutely opposed to excessive
home work and so, of course, is the
Ministry which I represent. I do not
believe it would be right-it would be
very wrong to put pressure on a child
which would be harmful to health and
interfere with his recreation and enjoyment. Speaking for the Ministry we are
of opinion that home work should not be
required from any pupil below the third
standard and that for pupils in the third
and higher standards one hour each evening ought to be sufficient.
If in any
specific instance the amount of home work
is found to press with undue severity
upon the child the matter should be
brought to the notice of the principal
teacher or the manager of the school. I
am not quite sure that the hon. Members
who have spoken rather violently with regard to home work are not exaggerating
about the feeling which is prevalent in the
country on this matter. The hon.
Member for Bann Side, perhaps, has forgotten that Ballymena Regional Education Committee recently held an inquiry
into this matter, and I believe a very
large percentage-I am not prepared to
give the exact figures-an almost overwhelming percentage of those who attended that inquiry were in favour of
home work. Anyhow hon. Members can
rest assured that the Ministry are keeping their mind open on the question and
that we will not allow any children in
Northern Ireland to suffer unduly because
of the amount of home work.
Then we come to a major question
which was raised and with which I regret
once more to be forced to deal. It is
a pity that the hon. Member for Falls
should again have raised this question,
and raised it in the wording which he
employed. I did not take an actual
note of what he said, but he spoke about
discrimination against the Catholic population.
Once again I must point out
to him that the Protestant voluntary
schools are subject to exactly the same
treatment as the voluntary schools under
Roman Catholic management.
Mr. BYRNE: They are a very small
number.
Mrs. PARKER: No, a very large
number of Protestant voluntary schools.
Therefore, this is not a matter of discrimination against the Catholic population. The hon. Member knows that with
the introduction of the 1923 Act we endeavoured to establish a system of
education, which instead of being under
the old managerial control would be under
democratic control, and this necessitated
a differentiation between the voluntary

the country would realise what a great

THE PIG INSURANCE CHARGE.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether it is a fact that
in future, through the action of the
Ministry's representatives on the Pig
Industry Council, the Wiltshire pig producer will have to pay 7d per pig insurance in place of the 4d charge hitherto applying; and whether the dissolved
Pigs Marketing Board over two years
consistently and successfully opposed this
change on the grounds of its inequity;
and whether it is a fact that the Ministry's representatives on the new Pigs
Marketing Board reduced the administrative levy by 4d only in order to pass
3d of this on to the Wiltshire curers at
the expense of the producers.
Its
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): It is a fact
that the Pig Industry Council has agreed
to an insurance deduction not exceeding
sevenpence per pig being made in future
in respect of every pig delivered under
direct contracts to curers, instead of
fourpence as at present. The purpose of
the deduction is to cover the loss to the
curer in respect of pigs or parts of pigs
condemned on account of disease or
injured in transit or otherwise.
amount depends entirely upon the incidence of disease and damage experienced
by pigs in transport and it may vary
upwards or downwards. Information
collected by the Ministry has shown that
the present deduction of fourpence per
pig is inadequate to cover these losses.
This fact has been recognised by the
Pigs Marketing Board of which the hon.
Gentleman was a member, since they
agreed to curers deducting sixpence per
pig in respect of insurance in the case
of pigs purchased from the Board under
its bulk contracts with Wiltshire curers.
There is no connection between the
levy for the administrative expenses of
the Pigs Marketing Board and this insurance deduction. The inference sought
to be conveyed in the last part of the
hon. Member's question is absolutely
incorrect.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of that
reply, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman whether he is aware that one of the
Wiltshire factories, in which the Pigs
Marketing Board have a major interest
show in their audited accounts that on
the present insurance charge of 4d
a pig that factory made a profit of
£272 15s 6d, and whether, in view of
this, he will say that the increase in the
insurance charge is justified?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have not got
that information, but the information
my Ministry has received from the
curers justifies the increase.

Evidence Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Black) (who was received with general
cheers): This is a short Bill on the lines
of the Act which was passed into law in
England last year, the Evidence Act,
1938, which made certain amendments
in the law of documentary evidence.
Now, it is, of course, highly desirable.
that the rules as to evidence should be
the same in the Northern Ireland courts
as they are in the English courts, but
quite apart from that consideration I
think the House will find that the
alterations in the law suggested in this
Bill are desirable and commonsense
alterations. The Bill, of course, will be
said by Members of the House to be a
technical legal document. I have to
confess that it is, but its purpose is
really to endeavour to get away from
certain dry technicalities of law which
have grown up with regard to documentary evidence and to get back more
into the regions of practical commonsense by which ordinary men regulate
their everyday lives.
I take it that nearly every Member of
this House has had occasion often to be
present in courts of law, either as a
litigant, a witness, a juryman, or at any
rate an interested onlooker.
I take it
that every Member who has been in
court has often noticed and been bewildered by the technicalities as to the
admission in evidence of documents and
of statements in documents, and by the
difficulties and objections which are
often made by advocates with regard to
the admission of documents in evidence
and
was
Let me give a simple case. Suppose
an action is brought against John Brown
for driving a motor car negligently a
Portrush on a certain date in last July.
John Brown says, "I was not at Portrush at all on that date. On that date
I was in the employment of the Transport Board and was driving a bus
between Newry
Warrenpoint."
That is Brown's defence. An employe
of the Transport Board is called to give
evidence. He says, "I am an employee
of the Transport Board. I
stationed in Newry on the date in ques
tion. It is my duty there to keep an
account of the time each bus leaves
Newry for Warrenpoint and the time
each bus comes back, and to enter into
a record the name of the driver and the
conductor of each bus." He comes up
with that book that he keeps.
He proposes to say that that book says that this
John Brown, alleged to be driving
negligently at Portrush on that date.
was in fact engaged in his business on
that day driving a bus between Newry
and Warrenpoint, and so could not have
been in Portrush.
If any Member of the House other
than a lawyer wanted to deal with the
matter. I should think the first thing he
would say would be, "Let me see that
book," and if he saw in that book that
John Brown was entered there as having
made several journeys between Newry
and Warrenpoint he would say that that
was pretty strong evidence that John
Brown could not have been in Portrush.
Curiously enough, according to the
present law of evidence that is not admissible, and furthermore, the court is
not allowed to look at the book. What
Evidence Bill-
Second Reading
25 APRIL 1939
would be allowed is this.
The man
who kept the book would be called to
give evidence. He would say, “I keep
that book," but he would not be allowed
to hand it in.
He would be allowed to look at the
book, and then he would be asked if
having looked at the book and refreshed
his memory from what he saw in it
could he say whether John Brown was
or was not engaged in these journeys on
the day in question. What he would do
would be to refresh his memory by the
book and say, "Yes." I think it will
be obvious to every Member of the
House that that really is second best.
What any ordinary layman carrying on
the ordinary business of life would prefer would be to have a look at the book
himself rather than merely to have a
man bringing up the book, looking at
it, and giving as his recollection that
such-and-such is the case.
or
Then there is this difficulty. Suppose
the man who kept the book is not
available, under present law the fact
cannot be put into evidence at all.
Suppose the one man who knew about
this was the man who kept the book,
and suppose he had gone across to England or Scotland, or even further away,
or had joined the Navy or the merchant
service, or had gone to America
Australia and could not be available to
give evidence, the result would be that
the fact recorded in that book could not
be proved in evidence and that a great
injustice might thereby be done.
purpose of this Bill is that where there is
a duty on a man to record various routine
matters in a book or where any man in
the course of his ordinary everyday
avocation records in answer to questions
these matters that document if produced
should be admissible in evidence. I
think that every Member of the House
will regard that as ordinary commonsense.

Or take another illustration. Suppose
two adjoining farmers fall out about a
right of way. Farmer Jones claims he
has a right of way over Farmer Robinson's field and says that up to five years
ago along the boundary there was a
clearly defined path, and SO he is
entitled to have a right of way there.
The defendant says, "That is nonsense,
there never was a path along that field
at any time during the past 30, or 40,

or 50 years. The issue is joined on that
point. It turns out that some years
before the Water Commissioners had
been running a conduit for their Mourne
water supply through those farms, and
had sent one of their engineers to survey the district. He had a survey of
the fields, but was not concerned with
whether there was a path there or not.
He made a map of the place which
showed the path clearly. That plan has
been preserved in the archives of the
Water Commissioners. If that surveyor
was still living he could be called as a
witness. He could bring up his plan
and say, "I was not concerned with the
path at all, but I made a map of the
place and I find there was a path which
is marked on the map."
it would be
Suppose that man is out of the employment of the Water Commissioners.
Suppose he is in Australia or Canada,
or suppose he is taken seriously ill-that
he had a stroke or that he is in a
mental home, or something of that
nature, there is no way of proving that
map at all. Yet to the ordinary man
strong evidence that a
person in no way concerned with the
dispute, in no way interested in the dispute, had made a map of that place and
had shown on that map a path which
one of the parties says existed and which
the other says did not exist would prove
very strong evidence indeed. It seems
to me that it is apt to work very considerable injustice that that document
which is in existence, which is on record,
which is in the files of a public body,
cannot be put in evidence simply because
the individual who made it does not
happen to be available.
Those are the general principles of
the law. Those Members of the House
who are members of the legal profession
will recollect there are some very curious
exceptions. There are two principal
exceptions. One exception is that any
entry made in a document by a person
who is now dead will be admissible in
evidence, but only on certain conditions.
The first condition is that the entry was
against the pecuniary or proprietary
advantage of the man who made the
entry. The other circumstance under
which such an entry may be admissible
in evidence is if it was made by a person
whose duty it was to make such entries.

Just let me illustrate that. There is
well-known
law books a
where a question arose as to whether a
man had attained the age of 21 years
when he carried through a certain
transaction with regard to property.
The transaction had been carried
through on a day in the middle of
April, and the real question was whether
his twenty-first birthday fell on 2nd
April or on 22nd April. A curious
piece of evidence was available. A book
was produced which gave a record of the
accoucheur's attendance on the boy and
his mother, and it showed the date of
the birth as 22nd April.
In
The book also recorded the fee that
was charged for the attendance of the
accoucheur. He had marked the
amount of the fee paid. The question
arose whether that was admissible in
evidence. Hon. Members would say
that would be very good evidence, that
there could be no better evidence. The
man attended at the time of the birth
and had made a record of his attendance
and of the date of that attendance.
that particular case that record was admitted in evidence, but on one ground
and one ground only, that he had
marked the fee paid, because it was said
that having marked the fee paid that
entry was an entry against his pecuniary
interests as he would not be able to sue
again or charge again that fee.
Accordingly on that ground the entry
was admitted and the case decided upon
that entry.
Let us just consider that. If that
fee had not been marked paid you might
have had the whole of that entry void.
the
The entry was only admitted on
ground that the fee was marked paid,
and if it had not been for that small word
"paid" it would not have been admissible in evidence at all. Again, if the
accoucheur had not been paid at that
time the book would not have been
admissible in evidence. His books had
been carefully kept, and would have
convinced any ordinary man outside a
law court, but technically it would not
have been admissible
in
evidence,
according to our present technical rules.
It was admitted for only two reasonsfirst, because the man who made it was
dead, and, secondly, because the entry
was against his pecuniary interest. That
was the exceptional reason for which
entries in documents might be admitted
in evidence.
Another case is that where entries are
made by a person who is now dead, provided they were made by him in the
course of his duty to make such entries.
There, again, you get extraordinary
anomalies. Take the employee of a firm
whose duty it is to enter accounts in
books. His book, ten or fifteen years
old, is produced. He is dead, but it was
his duty to make such entries, and
accordingly they are admissible in
evidence. But suppose the entries were
made by a man who had no business to
make such entries. We have in law the
case of a stockbroker who had bought a
certain number of shares for a client, and
entered them in a book. After the death
of the stockbroker those entries were not
admitted in evidence because he was not
under any duty to make such entries.
Therefore you will see that under present
circumstances there are a great number
of anomalies in the law regarding the
admission in evidence of entries made in
documents, and even in these exceptional
cases where entries are admitted in
evidence they are only admitted where
the man who made the entry is dead.
The primary design of this Bill is to
make documents more readily available
in evidence, to get rid of these technical
difficulties, and to let the judge and jury
look at documents. The Bill does not
say they are to give credence to any
documents, because it is expressly provided that though the judge may look
at documents he is still to weigh the
considerations which arise in order to
decide what weight is to be attached to
the evidence from the documents. The
real importance of the Bill is not to let
justice be defeated or be made more extechnicalities
pensive because of the
which preclude the court from looking at
documents. Anyone connected with the
courts will know that one client may
very often put another client to considerable expense by compelling him to
bring a witness a considerable distance
to prove the execution of a document
about which everyone knows there is no
doubt or question at all.
If hon. Members would be good
enough to turn to the Bill, there are
one or two points to which at the outset I should like to call attention. The
•

first is that it deals only with documentary evidence. It does not deal
with any evidence other than evidence
contained in documents. The second
point is that the principal Clauses of
the Bill, Clauses 1 and 2, are concerned
only with civil proceedings and not with
criminal proceedings, and it is not proposed to relax the stringent rules of
evidence which must be observed in
criminal proceedings. Members will find
that Clause 1 provides for what I have
substantially stated to the House. That
is, that where you have any statement in
a document it is to be admissible in evidence for what it is worth, though only
if the maker of the statement in the
document had some personal knowledge
of the matter. For instance, if he was
an employee of a firm he may have got
his statement from some person who had
himself personal
personal knowledge of the
matter. He might be a bookkeeper
making a record from notes brought in
by clerks or van drivers in his place of
business, and then it is provided that a
statement in a document is to be considered only if the maker of the document is called as a witness in the
proceedings. That is the primary and
normal circumstances in which a court
can look at such a document.
Then there is a provision which deals.
with cases where this is not possible.
There is the case where the person who
made the document is dead. Obviously
he cannot be called as a witness, and if
a person is dead, or if he is unfit to be
called by reason of his bodily or mental
condition-if he is in a mental hospital
or has had a stroke and cannot be produced, in those circumstances the document may be looked at by the court.
Similarly, if he is beyond the seas, or
if it is not reasonably practicable to
secure his attendance, and if all reasonable efforts have been made to secure his
attendance, the statement in the document may be admitted in evidence. But
the ordinary normal cases will be where
the man who made the document is himself available and can be cross-examined,
but in order to do justice it is necessary
to make provision for cases where the
person who made the document is dead
or is not available.
There is a further provision that, in
exceptional cases, where hardship would
be caused by insisting on the strict rule,
a document may be looked at notwithstanding that the man can be called as
a witness. For instance, it may be
necessary to prove formally documents
which are in the archives of the City
of London. The court may say, "Here
is a document sent over from London,
and it would be improper to incur the
expense of bringing over someone from
London to prove any of the statements
contained in the document." In subclause (3) of this Clause there is a provision which is a very strong safeguard,
because it will be strictly enforced by
the court. That is that nothing in the
Clause is to render admissible as evidence any statement made by a person
interested at a time when proceedings were
pending or anticipated involving a dispute as to any fact which the statement
might tend to establish. One might use
the phrase that for any statement to be
admissible in evidence it must be made
ante litem motam. That is manifestly
essential if justice is to be done.
Clause 2 provides that the court,
having looked at the document, has to
estimate the weight of the evidence, and
to take into account the inference that
may be drawn from the document. This
particular Clause provides that one consideration which the court shall take into
account is whether the statement in the
document was made contemporaneously
with the occurrence or existence of the
facts stated. If the man made the record
at the time the event happened it will
naturally carry more weight than a
document made days, months, or years
after the event happened. The court is
also to take into account whether or not
the maker of the statement had any incentive to conceal or misrepresent the
facts. Those are matters which the
court would naturally take into account,
but it is better that they should be set
out in black and white in the enactment.
In sub-clause (2) of Clause 2 there is
a provision that where there is any rule
of law or practice regarding corroboration, the mere fact that a person has
made a statement in document is not
to be taken as amounting in law to corroboration of that evidence. Take a
breach of promise action. As Members
will recollect, it is necessary in a breach
of promise action that evidence of the
promise should be corroborated by some
Evidence Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
second witness. Suppose the lady herself had written a letter at the time of
the promise saying, "Tom asked me to
marry him last night, and I promised,"
that would probably be admissible in
evidence, but there must still be corroboration apart from the statement
made by the lady herself. It is well to
have provision in the Bill that notwithstanding this admission of documentary
evidence, it is still necessary to have the
old corroboration we always had, and a
statement made in a document is not to
be regarded as corroboration of the evidence of the person making it.
In the next two Clauses two minor
matters are dealt with. The third
Clause deals with instruments to which
attestation is necessary. There are
certain documents which the law requires
to be attested by a witness. Perhaps
the best known is an absolute Bill of
Sale, which is required to be attested by
a witness, and there are certain others.
Hitherto the law has required that when
you came to court and endeavoured to
prove that document you must call the
attesting witness to prove it, if he is
alive. Take, for instance, an absolute
Bill of Sale executed in the presence of
John Jones, who acts as attesting witness. It was not sufficient to call the
witness who was present when it was
executed, or other people who saw it
signed. You must call John Jones himself. This is a provision that documents
which need attestation are to be treated
the same as other documents, and any
person who can prove the signature is
entitled to do so. There is an exception
in the case of wills or other testamentary
documents, which must be proved in the
same way as before, by calling the witness to the document.
Clause 4 is not of very great effect.
Hitherto when a deed or document was
produced out of the proper custody, if
it was thirty years old it was said to
prove itself. If it was necessary that a
deed should be produced in a
case in
court and it turned out to be thirty
years old it was not necessary to prove
the actual execution of the deed. It
was only necessary to produce the deed
itself. About one hundred years ago,
the rule was that it must be forty years
old in order to have that privilege. The
time was afterwards shortened to thirty
years, and now, under this Bill, it is proposed to still further shorten the period
to twenty years. When the document
appears to be in the proper custody, and
to be correct on the face of it, it will not
be necessary to prove it by a witness; it
be sufficient to lay down the
document.
will
That is shortly the object of this Bill.
It was introduced in the House of Lords
by Lord Maugham, who was not then
Lord Chancellor, and it was supported by
men like Lord Atkin and the Lord
Chancellor of the time. Viscount
Hailsham. It had, therefore, the support of the highest legal authorities.
Before it reached the stage of a Bill it
had been carefully considered by a strong
committee of English judges, consisting
of men like Lord Justice Greer, Mr.
Justice Avory, Mr. Justice Roche, and
Mr. Justice Langton. It had also the
express approval of the late Lord Tomlin. ⠀
The House will see that before this
became the law of England it was most
carefully considered by the highest legal
authorities. It was thought to be a
proper Bill, which would bring the law
more. in accord with commonsense and
prevent possible injustices, and certainly
prevent a considerable accumulation of
expense in some cases. We feel that it
would be proper to follow the. English
Parliament in this matter, and to introduce the Bill here. Accordingly, I beg
to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

regarding proceedings before a jury

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: Two
points have been raised to which I wish
refer. The first is by the hon. Member for South Down with regard to subclause 1 of Clause 1, where only the
the
masculine is mentioned and not

draftsmanship of Acts of Parliaments
that the masculine is considered feminine. It is expressly provided for by
the Interpretation Act of 1889.
I think the proceedings mentioned by
the hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr.
Nixon) refer to the Summons Court.
This Bill relates to civil proceedings.
In regard to medical certificates where
a juryman wishes to be excused or where
the parent of a child is summoned for
non-attendance of that child at school, in
999 cases out of 1,000 the doctor's certificate is accepted. Unless there is
something exceptional about the matter
no trouble arises. I do not know the
particular case to which the hon. Member referred, but I think it will be found
that the practice in all courts on matters
like that is based on ordinary commonsense.

I am just as conscious of that as is the

in Ireland and in England.
and
I can state without hesitation,
with complete positiveness, that the
Ministry of Home Affairs in Northern
Ireland has invariably pursued the line
that they should treat the reports of
Inspectors of the Ministry of Home
Affairs as confidential documents for the
Minister's own use. The one exception.
which is only an apparent and not a real
exception, is the case of the Belfast
Housing inquiry where the Ministry
delegated its function to a distinguished
lawyer, gave him certain powers in
regard to evidence, and appointed him
for the purpose of making a public report. Save on that occasion I think I
am right in saying that none of these
reports have ever been published. I
have access to a wealth of experience of
the old Local Government Board in Ireland, and I have satisfied myself that
that custom prevailed there. I knew it
was not possible for me to get into direct
contact with the practice in Great
Britain, but, thanks to the assistance of
the learned Attorney-General, I have
been able to get the most positive and
definite statement upon this matter. I
am going to quote the exact words
of Sir John Simon, who was then
Attorney-General, when he stated in the
House of Lords: :-
The holding of local inquiries by
the Local Government Board is
directed by many Statutes, and it has
always been the practice of the Board
to treat the Reports of their Inspectors as confidential documents for
their own use.
The hon. Member for Woodvale suggested we were adopting an obstinate
course. I hope I shall never get the
reputation of being obstinate. He also
suggested I had given a smart answer.
I would like to be acquitted
both of giving a smart answer to

a Parliamentary question, and of pursuing an obstinate course. In the
course we have adopted we have

a line of conduct which has been going
on for at least fifty years in England,
and since 1898 in this country. However, the argument of precedent only
goes as far as this; that if a custom has

in Northern Ireland without being

Government administration in this

of men of the very highest standing,
statements on this very question by
three eminent Members of the House of
Lords, the highest tribunal in the land.
I am going to quote their exact words on
this very question to show to the public
the mischief that would be effected if
these reports were to be published.
They are confidential decuments which
must be available to the Minister if
they are to be of any value, but if they
are to be published to the world they
must lose that element of frankness
which is the one great value they have.
That is the reason and the basis behind
this custom, which has prevailed for
about fifty years.
The question that is raised here today was raised very definitely in the
House of Lords in 1915. On that
occasion Lord Moulton, sitting in the
House of Lords in his judicial capacity,
said:-
Like any administrative body the
Local Government Board must derive
its knowledge from its agents, and I
am unable to see any reason why the
reports which they make to the
Department should be made public.
It would in my opinion curb the usefulness of these inquiries. Such a
practice would, in my opinion, be
decidely mischievous.
Lord Shaw, of Dunfermline, said:-
If it were laid down that such disclosures could be compelled a serious
impediment might be placed on the
frankness which ought to obtain.
Lord Sumner said:-
If the local authority are ultimately to see it the Inspector might
hesitate to express himself in his report as frankly as might be desirable
for the guidance of the Board.
Frankness is the real essence of the
matter. That is the gist of the matter,
and if the practice of publishing the
Inspectors' reports is to prevail—and if
they are to be published in this particular case they must be published in all
cases the whole or a very great part of
the value of the Inspectors' reports is
gone, and I tell the House without
hesitation that it will seriously interfere
with the due administration of Local
Government. As I said a moment ago,
the Minister must have available to him
all the information which he can
properly get. A great deal of it could
not be supported as legal evidence.
When a local council is undertaking
the sewering of a street everything seems
to be in its favour, but when an Inspector makes inquiries he finds that a local
councillor owns the land fronting the
street. The Inspector has his own very
definite private opinion, but there is no
privilege in his report, and he might
quite well find himself involved in a libel
action. At the same time, no one would
suggest that the Minister should not
have that information, but if that report is going to be published to the
world that information would not be
contained in it. That is only one
instance that occurred to me on the spur
of the moment. I could enumerate a
hundred cases where it is absolutely
essential that information should be in
the possession of the Minister which the
Inspector could not possibly put on
paper if it were to be given out to the
world.

Question of Privilege.
Mr. SPEAKER: In accordance with
an undertaking given by me on Thursday
last to the hon. Member for Pottinger, I
have now carefully considered the information handed to me yesterday afternoon
a few minutes before the sitting of the
House. Two of the complaints relate
back to the last Session of Parliament in
October, 1938, and of course the matter
in respect to those complaints should have
been raised then. The third complaint
arose out of a comment made by the Parliamentary correspondent of the "Belfast
Telegraph" on April 21, 1939. In respect of this complaint I can find nothing
to establish a prima facie case to go before
the Committee of Privileges.
On the general question it must be
recognised that the Press, taken as a
whole, sometimes use allegorical phrases
which need not be taken too seriously
and employ language which from time to
time might be considered rather too personal, but, in my judgment, those comments which I have carefully examined
do not impute improper motives or corrupt conduct of any kind to Members of
this House. If they had done that, it
would have been my duty to take
appropriate action.
In weighing up all these considerations
I feel that it is vital to every democratic
country to preserve most carefully freedom of speech and the freedom of the
Press. This, of course implies the right
to criticise, and criticism is the breath
of public life.
Right hon. and and hon. Members can
rest assured that should this freedom at
any time degenerate into licence, affecting
the character or reputation of any right
hon. or hon. Member of this House I
will immediately advise the House what
action shall be taken.
At present I rule that there is no
prima facie case to go before the Committee of Privileges for consideration.
As regards Press permits, each Belfast
paper has two and each Dublin paper
one.
Mr. BEATTIE: Have we a right to
place the case as I see it now on review,
after its presentation by you as the
custodian of the rights and privileges of
Members of this House?
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps the hon.
Member will allow me to explain. This
is a considered ruling which, of course,
rests on my judgment, and no debate
can take place on that ruling. If the
hon. Member who raised this particular
subject wishes to ask a question to elucidate any point in the ruling I shall be
glad to answer it.
Mr. NIXON: I am not going to criticise your ruling--
Mr. SPEAKER: I cannot allow any
hon. Member in this House to intervene
except the hon. Member who raised the
question. He is entitled to ask a question.
Mr. NIXON: Mr. Sayers should write
jokes about his mammy, I am not going
to have this at all.
Mr. SPEAKER: Will the hon. Member resume his seat?
Mr. NIXON: I have resumed my seat.
Mr. BEATTIE: As you are aware, it
was not my intention to have any vote
of censure put on any journalist who
comes to this Parliament to write a fair
comment on the proceedings.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before the hon.
Member proceeds any further I want to
make it quite clear that he cannot debate
this subject. He can ask any question.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): There is an increase of £27,807 in this Vote, due to
increased provision for New Works, offset to some extent by increased
Appropriations-in-Aid. Before referring
to the details of the Estimate, I should
perhaps point out that a slight change
has been made in Subhead A. Comparison with the previous year is maintained,
but the practice of showing the details
of the previous year's works where the
works have been completed has now been
dropped, and all amounts voted in 1938-
39 for works completed during that year
have been bulked under one heading with
the result that the subhead presents a
much more compact appearance without
in any way restricting the available information.
Turning to the actual subheads. Subhead A shows a substantial increase due
to a provisional estimate of £26,000 for
the protection of the occupants of Government buildings against air raids and
a proposed store for general A.R.P.
equipment, together with the provision of
approximately £14,000 under the heading
"Furniture and Fittings" for obscuring
lights in Government buildings and so
forth. In fact, if these provisional items
had not been included there would have
been a decrease of £40,000 in this Vote.
The provision of £3,850 for accommodation at the Royal Ulster Constabulary

structing portion of the premises occupied

and landings and certain rooms in

and the wear and tear is considerable.
The provision of linoleum should lead to
economy in maintenance and greater

There is provision of £2,975, of which
£500 is a revote for the erection and improvement of cottages at various forestry
centres. The number of areas in which
lands are being acquired by the Government for afforestation is increasing year
by year, and accommodation is necessary
to house the staff required for supervision.
Where buildings do not exist new cottages
have to be provided. The amount required for this work in the coming
financial year covers the cost of erecting

places.
The provision of £580 for the erection
of a new gate. lodge at Stranmillis Training College is necessitated by the fact
that the present gate lodge at the Stranmillis Road entrance to the college has
been condemned. As the building does

weights and
administration.
The rise in fuel costs is due to the installation of central heating systems in employment exchanges and in the larger

measures
The contract work under the Bann
drainage scheme has now been completed,
but direct labour works by the Ministry's
own plant are being undertaken above
The Cutts sluices in order to provide a
better approach channel for the flood
waters to sluices and to reduce the flood
levels in the Agivey River district. The
money provision for this work is being
met from borrowings, but Subhead F of
the Estimate contains the annuity provision for repayment of the loan. The
Public Works and Buildings 1128
Estimates-
26 APRIL 1939
Committee is also informed in the same
subhead of the cost of the running of the
Government dredging craft engaged on
the work.
So far as the practical results of the
drainage scheme are concerned, the daily
records of lough and river levels, which
have, been kept since 1859, have enabled
the Ministry's engineers to compare
winter weather conditions over the
catchment area for each season during
the past eighty years. As a result of
careful examination of these records it
has been found that the winter rainfall
in 1938-39 very nearly equalled the
highest recorded winter rainfall, viz.,
that of the winter of 1876-7-in fact,
from October 1 to January 27 it was
even worse. One can, therefore, presume that the conditions experienced
during this last winter may be expected
to occur only on a few occasions in each
century. Despite these. abnormally unfavourable conditions, the highest level
attained in Lough Neagh this winter
was 8 inches below the level at which
flooding commences.
If the scheme which is now nearing
completion had not been executed-and
this is important-calculations show that
under similar weather conditions in precontract days Lough Neagh would have
attained flood level by the middle of
October last and would have remained
above that level consistently up to March
11, that is to say, during practically the
whole of the past five months many
thousands of acres surrounding Lough
Neagh would have been flooded, some to
a depth of nearly three feet.
A small amount of marginal flooding
along the banks of the Lower Bann River
has occurred in the Agivey River district,
but such flooding as has occurred was
approximately 3 feet 6 inches lower than
it would have been in pre-contract years
given similar weather conditions, and this
flooding has been due to the fact that the
intended channel improvements in
Loughans Island east channel have not
yet been completed.
The provision for the afforestation
scheme on the River Bann shows a small
reduction. Four hundred and sixty
acres between The Cutts (Coleraine) and
Toome have been planted. A further
200 acres remains to be planted, and it is
hoped to complete the work by the year
1941. I have now covered the main
items in this Vote, but there are a
number of details in connection with the
maintenance and construction of public
works and buildings, and it is not possible
for anyone to carry them in his head. If
the Committee. require any further information I will do my best to supply it.
I beg to move.

every Government likes a bit of fair play.

What is the cause of it? We will get

It is unfair and not proper that a

A policeman has a permanent job, and

think it would be advisable that you

Prime Minister has at his command other
police services while he is moving about.
I say, replace this policeman by a private
driver, one of the unemployed. I recommend that that procedure should be
adopted in all cases, and especially in the
case of the leading light of the Unionist
Party in Northern Ireland. I am sure
it will appeal to him.
There is another item in this Vote under

CATHOLIC APPLICANTS FOR
POOR LAW NURSING.
1. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he can state what consideration, if any, the Commissioners of
the Belfast Poor Law Board are giving
to Catholic applicants for nursing and
other appointments under their juris
diction.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Warnock): For
my right hon. Friend. Applications for
nursing and other appointments in the
Belfast Union are considered by the
Commissioners on their merits and without reference to the religious persuasion
of the applicants.
Mr. BYRNE: Is the Parliamentary
Secretary aware that under the elected
Board a poor percentage of these appointments were allotted to Catholic applicants?
APPLICATIONS FOR RELIEF IN
BELFAST.
2. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state how
many applications for relief, able-bodied
and ordinary, have been dealt with by
the Commissioners of Poor Law in the
Belfast Union: the number refused, and
the grounds for refusal.
Mr. WARNOCK: The number of
applications for able-bodied relief dealt
with by the Commissioners up to the
25th April is 201, of which 44 were
refused, while the number of applications
for ordinary relief is 230, of which 27
were refused. It is not possible to obtain
at short notice particulars of the reasons
for the refusal of relief in each case,
but I am informed that each case has
been dealt with on its merits. If the
hon. Member wishes to make representations to me with regard to any particular case I shall be pleased to have
the matter looked into.

4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of

an application of the London Passenger

organisations; whether there is any similar machinery in Northern Ireland, and,
if so, whether such sanction was obtained
by the Northern Ireland Road Transport
Board for the recent all-round increase in
their passenger fares, and, if not,
whether he will consider the setting up
of such machinery; whether the passenger end of the Northern Ireland Road
Transport Board continues to show a
substantial profit up to the time these increased fares were announced and that
the heavy losses of the Board are confined to the freight end of the undertaking; whether the bus passengers have to
shoulder the losses of the goods department of the concern; whether these increased fares may result in increasing
the Board's losses in view of the fact
that the bus fares are now in many cases
SO much higher than railway fares;
whether in the case of short single
journeys of school children, who go to
school by bus in the morning and walk
home in the afternoon, the increased bus
fares work out at one hundred per cent.;
whether the increased bus fares in
general will militate against the success
of
the tourist traffic industry and
whether in all the circumstances he is
prepared to prevent any further anticipation of the report of the Joint Select
Committee of this House and the Senate
now considering the whole transport
problem.
Mr. WARNOCK: As this question is
long and involves a large number of
questions the answer is very lengthy, and
with the consent of the hon. Member I
will circulate it in the Official Report.
The following is the answer: —
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
I understand that the Railway Rates
Tribunal in London is considering a proposal to increase railway fares within the
London area.
In the year 1937 that tribunal required
the four main line railways to increase
their charges by 5 per cent. or thereabouts. London was excluded from that
direction because of a complicated legal
position which arose out of the creation
of the London Passenger Transport
Board.
The proposal before the tribunal at
present is intended solely to bring
London railway fares into line with those
for the rest of the country. It relates
entirely to railway fares and is not concerned with fares for omnibuses, trolley
vehicles or tramways.
The London
Passenger Transport
Board is free to determine the fares to
be charged on most of its omnibus services-that is those operated within the
area of the Metropolitan Traffic Commissioners. In connection with its remaining omnibus services conditions may
be attached by the licensing authority to
secure that the fares charged are not unreasonable. All fares are, however, subject to review by the Rates Tribunal on
appeal.
The position of the Northern Ireland
Road Transport is similar to that of the
London Board. It also has freedom to
determine the fares to be charged but
that determination is subject to the
statutory requirement that the fares shall
be reasonable. It was not, therefore,
necessary that the Board should obtain
the prior approval of any body to the
increases which it has made.
A Transport Appeal Tribunal has
already been established in Northern
Ireland and any local authority, or any
association or body of persons representative of the interests of the passengers
concerned, has a statutory right to appeal
to that tribunal for the revision of any
fares chargeable by the Board.
I understand that the passenger services of the Board continue to show a
profit which, however, is not sufficient to
meet the Board's obligations on its
capital outlay in respect of these services.
an
The recent increases were imposed in
endeavour to enable the Board to
obtain sufficient revenue to meet the
obligations I have mentioned, and it is
entirely wrong to assume that the passengers carried in the Board's omnibuses
shoulder any
being required to shoulder
portion of the losses on the freight services.
are
I am not aware of any reason why it
should be assumed that the increased
fares may result in a loss to the Board,
and I have no information as to what
effect they have had as regards the
school children to whom the hon. Member refers. I understand that it would
not be possible to obtain any information regarding this particular consequence.
The increases cannot militate in any
way against the success of the tourist
traffic as the rates for tours and private
hire work have not been altered.
As the Board in increasing fares has
merely exercised a power already conferred upon it by Parliament with the
object of fulfilling the statutory obligation imposed upon it of fixing such fares,
rates and charges as shall secure revenue
sufficient to defray all charges imposed
upon it, I am sure the hon. Member will
agree that the Board has not in any way
anticipated the report of the Joint Select
Committee.

Question of Privilege.
A PERSONAL EXPLANATION.
The PRIME MINISTER: With your
permission, Mr. Speaker, and that of the
House, I would like to refer to an
incident which occurred yesterday, and
in doing so I am sure I have the full
acquiescence of Members on both sides. I
am speaking not as Prime Minister, but
as Leader of House. Members will
realise that part of my duty is quite
impartially to do what is possible to
maintain the highest traditions of Parliamentary life, the dignity of the Chair,
and to see that all our business is transacted in an orderly manner. I have a
feeling, having regard to the fact that
there may have been a little heat yesterday with perhaps judgments temporarily
upset, that the hon. Member for Pottinger may care to make a statement.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to make

n England and the present position in

niddle of the 17th century there were in

courts, which exercised jurisdiction in

the only decrees of divorce which these

only amounted to what is now called in

century special Acts of Parliament dissolving marriage became quite a recognised form of legislation, both in England and in Ireland.
May I quote a few words from the

They refer to this method of obtaining

they say:-
By this means the right to obtain
divorce a vinculo matrimonii was
definitely established. It was established, however, in the rudest and
most inconvenient manner, for the
procedure was a judicial one by legislative process and much inconvenience
was the necessary result of the discussion of such questions in a mixed and
popular assembly.
The procedure was a procedure
obviously ill-suited for the purpose, and
it was a procedure which as well as being
cumbersome bore on its face marks of
great injustice, for it was exceedingly
costly and available to the rich and wellto-do, and entirely closed to men and
women of moderate or humble means.
Notwithstanding all these objections it
remained the procedure in England up
to the year 1857, and it remains the
procedure in Northern Ireland to this
present day. But in the year 1857 a
great reform was effected in England.
The Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857 was
a great landmark in the history of
divorce procedure. By that Act of 1857
it was provided for the future that so
far as England was concerned the jurisdiction to grant a decree of divorce
a vinculo matrimonii, that is, complete
divorce, should no longer remain a legislative jurisdiction. It should no longer
be necessary to promote a special Act of
Parliament, but that in England for the
future jurisdiction to grant divorce
should be entrusted to the courts. A
court was set up under that Act called
the Court of Divorce and Matrimonial
Causes, and of course hon. Members are
aware that since the Judicature Acts this
jurisdiction in England of the Court of
Divorce and Matrimonial Causes has
been transferred and is now exercised

by His Majesty's High Court of Justice
and the Divorce Division of that court.
So much for England.
What is the position in regard to Northern Ireland? In Ireland prior to the
coming into operation of the Irish
Church Act of 1869 which disestablished
the Church of Ireland there was in
existence Ecclesiastical Courts to deal with
matrimonial causes just in the same way
as the Ecclesiastical Courts in England
had been before the passing of the Act
of 1857. After the passing of the Irish
Church Act and the disestablishment of
the Irish Church it became necessary to
make provision for the jurisdiction which
had been exercised by the Ecclesiastical
Courts, and by the Act of 1870 the
jurisdiction which had been exercised by
the Ecclesiastical Courts in Ireland in
matrimonial cases was transferred to a
new
court-a court for matrimonial
causes and matters. This court was
absorbed in the new Supreme Court and
its jurisdiction is still exercised by the
High Courts of Justice. But the unfortunate part, SO far as Ireland is
concerned, is that there was no reform
here similar to that effected in England
by the Act of 1857. There was no reform in Ireland making the granting of
a full divorce a judicial act. All that
was transferred to His Majesty's Courts
by the Act of 1870 was the old jurisdiction of the Ecclesiastical Courts. It
was expressly enacted by the Act of 1870
that the new matrimonial court could
proceed to give relief on principles and
rules which shall be as nearly as possible
conformable to the principles and rules
on which the Ecclesiastical Courts acted
and gave relief.
Hon. Members will see from this that
our High Court now has not the jurisdiction which the High Court in England
has in regard to divorces, and that it has
only got the jurisdiction that the old
Ecclesiastical Court exercised in Ireland.
In an action for a divorce a mensa et
thoro the court has no power to exercise
the jurisdiction which has been exercised
in England by the court since 1857, that
is, to dissolve a marriage. Before a man
or woman can secure a dissolution of
marriage here they have to promote and
secure the passage into law of a private
Act of Parliament. I think I may say
that it was recognised at the very outset
that it was somewhat of an absurdity
that the position should be left in this
way. The difference in this respect
between England and Ireland is that in
England you can get a divorce from the
court, but in Ireland you had to get a
private Bill passed in order to secure the
divorce. When the Act of 1857 was
before the Legislature in England Lord
Cranworth, the then Lord Chancellor,
expressly stated that after they had
disposed of the matter in England and
had passed into law the Bill which was
then before the House-the Bill to confer on the courts jurisdiction to grant
divorce-it was intended to introduce a
similar Measure for Ireland. But that
was, unfortunately, not done...
Up to the year 1920 the position in
Ireland still remained as it was before
1857. In England to get a full divorce
you had to get a private Act of Parliament. Up to 1920 a person who wished
to get a full divorce had to go through
this procedure. He had first of all to
come to the courts in Ireland and petition
for a divorce a mensa et thoro. After
the case had been tried, all the witnesses
heard and the matter fully discussed the
court acted on the petition. If the
person seeking the divorce was a husband
he had, in addition to bringing the
petition, to secure a divorce a mensa et
thoro, also to bring a common law action
against the adulterer claiming damages
for what lawyers call criminal conversation. So that before promoting the
Bill the case was litigated fully once, and
possibly twice, in the ordinary courts in
Ireland. The matter having been
litigated a Bill had to be promoted in
the Imperial Parliament, and the practice
there was that the. Bill was introduced
in the House of Lords. The Second
Reading of the Bill in the House of
Lords was essentially the trial of the
case. The parties to the Bill-the
petitioner and the respondent, if the respondent appeared-appeared by counsel
at the Bar of the House, and the House
of Lords in modern times for such purpose was, of course, constituted by the
law lords, that is those Members of the
Upper Chamber who sat there by virtue
of holding or having held high judicial
office. The House of Lords heard the
arguments, heard again the evidence of
the witnesses, and they decided on what
they had heard before them whether the
Bill should be passed.

If the Bill was passed by the House
of Lords it had to come formally before
the House of Commons and be passed
before it was eventually enacted into law.
Hon. Members will see that under this
procedure what had been fully gone into
and discussed in evidence and argued in
the courts in Ireland once, and possibly
twice, had to be gone all over again
before the House of Lords. In all cases
in which the wife was the petitioner
there had to be two hearings. If the
petitioner was the husband there, would
be three hearings, and the same subject
matter had to be gone into fully three
times. It will occur to anyone who gives
the slightest thought to the matter that
as a mode of securing something which
ought to be decided judicially this was
really a grotesque procedure, and it
certainly was a most expensive procedure.
no
Such was the position in Ireland up
to 1920. After the Act of 1920 was
passed it became necessary for our Parliament to consider what procedure they
should adopt in relation to divorce Bills.
Our Parliament, of course, has
judicial Members corresponding to the
judicial Members who sit in the House
of Lords. Hon. Members are aware that
the matter was discussed, and it was
inally determined in 1925 that divorce
Bills should be heard by a Joint Committee of both Houses. It is interesting
to remember that when these Standing
Orders were being discussed and formed
in 1925 it was apparently recognised that
they were only to exist for a comparatively short time, and be of temporary
nature, and that some Measure such
as this to-day would ultimately be
brought in. If hon. Members will
turn to the debates in the Senate
on the Standing Orders in 1925 they will
find that several Members of the Senate
most clearly and expressly referred to the
fact that this was really only a temporary
Measure, and it was contemplated that
before long the system here would be
put on the same basis as in England,
under which divorces in Northern Ireland
would be granted by courts of law, and
there would be no necessity to introduce
a special Bill and pass it into law.
Accordingly the Bill for this purpose
is the Bill before the House to-day. The
primary purpose, as I have said, is to
ransfer the right to grant divorces from
the legislature to the courts of law, and
to make the granting of divorces a
judicial and not a legislative act. So
far as this aspect of the Bill is concerned
I think it will not arouse controversy
amongst hon. Members. It is not a
question of whether there should or
should not be divorce at all. One
can quite understand the views of
those who on religious grounds consider
that there should be no divorce at all,
but that is not the position here. At
the present time we have a method of
securing divorce which can be freely
exercised. It is clear and open to those
who can fulfil two conditions. In the
first place they have to give evidence
before the Joint Committee of the Senate
and House. of Commons that they have
good ground for a divorce, and in the
second place, that they are in a position
to lay down sufficient money for the
presentation of a Bill before Parliament.
As I say, the question is not whether
there, should or should not be a divorce.
The question is whether the present
system should continue or whether the
jurisdiction should be assimilated to the
system which obtains in England, and
that the granting of a divorce should be.
entrusted henceforth to the court. I
say that there will not be controversy on
this Bill. This system I have outlined—
the bringing of an action for criminal
conversation, the presentation of a
petition to the court, and then, subsequently, the presenting of a Bill to
Parliament is a procedure which is hard
to defend in any logical way. If it is
hard to defend on logical grounds it is
impossible, I think, to defend at all when
one considers the matter of expense. It
is not a credit, I think, to our system
of administration of justice to think
in a matter such as divorce that it is
open readily to the man or woman who
has considerable means at his or her command, while for all practical purposes
it is closed entirely to the humbler man,
the man with slender resources who finds
it impossible to adopt that procedure
which is so expensive.
I think that any lawyer will tell you
that he has been approached time, and
again on behalf of some possible client
and asked this question, "How much will
it cost me to get a divorce in the courts
and promote a Bill." When he replies

If hon. Members will turn to the Bill

I have spoken of. Clause I proposes to

5, sub-clause 2 of which proposes
enact that if the court is satisfied on the

but if the court is not satisfied it shall

other words, Clause 8 sets out the
essential object of
of judicial divorce,
namely, to place the parties in the same

If I may turn now to Clause 18, that
Clause provides for a husband's divorce.
As I have said, under the existing law
he has to bring a separate action for
criminal conversation in the common
courts claiming damages against the
adulterer. Clause 18 provides that this
necessity for a separate action for
criminal conversation shall be done away

which the divorce is sought by the

proceedings, and so instead of having

case litigated. By those proceedings at
that one hearing as well as obtaining
a decree of divorce against the wife the
husband may be entitled to obtain an
award of damages against the adulterer
who was the author of the matrimonial
offence.
Assuming that the House is so far
with me, and that it decides that divorce
should henceforth be a matter for the
courts, the question then arises of what
principles the court should proceed upon
when deciding whether a divorce ought
to be granted or not. When the granting of a divorce is a matter for the
legislature, as it is now in Northern Ireland, the Parliament which passes such
legislation is, of
is, of course, theoretically
entitled to pass an Act granting divorce
on any grounds it pleases; in fact, it is
entitled to pass an Act granting divorce

certain well-recognised grounds.
grounds. Still
from the very nature of the case and
the wide jurisdiction and discretion of
Parliament as to the grounds on which

and cannot be affected by any rule of

When you are taking away from the
legislature the granting of divorce, or.
I should say, entrusting to the courts
the granting of divorce, you cannot leave

whatever principles they think fit. You
must prescribe some rule of the

proceed. When you are entrusting the
granting of divorce to a judicial tribunal

Before coming to what we propose to
enact in the Bill I think it might be
useful to recollect for a moment how the
practice of the legislature stands at
present. So far as the House of Lords
were concerned-that is, before our
Parliament was set up they dealt with
Irish Divorce Bills the principles upon
which they would pass a Divorce Bill for
Ireland were fully considered by a strong
House of Lords in a case which is reported in our law books and which is
recognised as the leading authority on
the subject. It was a case heard in the
year 1886 by the House of Lords consisting of Lord Herschell, Lord Blackburne, Lord Watson, Lord FitzGerald,
Lord Halsbury, and Lord Ashbourne,
and it was laid down definitely in that
case that the rule upon which the
House of Lords would act in considering
whether it would pass into law an Irish
Divorce Bill was that they would pass
into law a Bill granting a divorce in
Ireland
upon any ground which would
have been a sufficient ground for the
granting of a divorce by the courts in
England.
Hon. Members will remember that in
1886 thirty years almost had passed
since the Act of 1857 and it was not
necessary to bring English cases before
the House of Lords, but in dealing with
Irish cases the principle laid down by the
House of Lords was this, "If we find
there are in this case grounds upon which
the courts in England would grant a
divorce we will sanction a Bill from Ireland granting a divorce upon the same
grounds." That was a simple principle
the House of Lords continued to act
upon up to 1920, and this, I take it,
was the principle of practice which our
Parliament would take over when it was
set up here and when it appointed its.
Joint Committee to deal with divorce
legislation.
But some years ago a very nice point
as to this matter arose before our Joint
Committee on divorce legislation. Hon.
Members will remember that the rule of
law in England used to be this, that while
the husband could obtain a divorce on
the ground of the adultery of his wife,
and needed no other ground to entitle
him to a divorce, the wife on the
other hand could not obtain a full
divorce against her husband on the
ground of adultery alone, but could only
obtain such a decree if in addition to
adultery she was able to prove some other
matrimonial offence such as cruelty.
This remained the rule of law in England
up to 1920, and so was the rule of law
when our Parliament took over here.
This rule was altered in England by
an Act in the British Parliament in
1923. By that Measure it was enacted
that in England a wife could thereafter
obtain a divorce on the ground of
adultery alone, and that it was no longer
necessary for her to prove in addition a
matrimonial offence, such as cruelty.
The question then arose whether the
Joint Committee of our two Houses here
would follow this alteration in the
English law and would consider that
they were entitled to grant a divorce to
a wife on the ground of the adultery
of the husband alone without any other
matrimonial offence.
There were two schools of thought on
that. Some persons considered that any
alteration
on
of the ground
which
divorce could be granted here in Northern Ireland ought only to be made by
a general Act of Parliament. Persons of
this school of thought considered that
the absolute discretion of the legislature
was an essence of any system of legislation in force, and that it would be
legally possible for the alteration in the

entitled to follow the English law without having a general Act of the Parliament of Northern Ireland passed to
enable them to do so. They followed
the English law, and in that particular
case granted the wife a divorce on the

Why I mention that is this. There

1937. It is an Act which will be associated with the name of Mr. A. P.

England. In framing that Act the

reported in 1912. It sat under the
chairmanship of Lord Gorell who, as Sir
Gorell Barnes, for many years was
President of the Divorce Division. That
Report is really a great historic document. It is of very great value and of
absolutely first-class importance to the
study of divorce and of divorce law.
The Act of 1937 is really framed on the
basis of the conclusions and recommendations made in the Report of that
1912 Commission.

Those are questions of detail, but the
main feature of the Bill is twofold-first
to see that in future in Northern Ireland instead of a divorce being given by
the legislature it shall be given by the

learned
has

an educated woman the daughter of
respectable parents, married for a number of years, enduring the trials and
tribulations of domestic life. Her
reason goes and she is taken away to a

culpability; she has done no wrong, committed no offence. She may recover her
reason later, and what is her position?
She is divorced, her home life gone, the
right to the respect of her children gone.
I say it is a cruel thing to introduce into
this House a Clause of this kind at all.
I read long ago one of the most beautiful poems of Tennyson. It deals with a
case of leprosy. In those days, called
the middle ages, lepers were segregated
from the rest of the community. For
reasons of health they lived apart. They
lived in little hovels or huts of their
own.
The question arose if a man

This Bill will degrade the law in the Six

has existed in England since 1857. The

any
time-no Minister in that Parliament

to name even one body that is clamouring for this measure. To vast numbers
this Measure will be abhorrent. In the
rest of Ireland there is no divorce law:
there is no divorce court. I think that
is one of the peculiar glories of the Eire
part of Ireland. It was the same
throughout Christendom down to the sixteenth century. There was no divorce

there was no divorce court. Then came
the Reformation and things changed.
I know of no nation of the globe
where family purity is more prized than
it is among the Irish and it is a bitter
and evil fruit of partition that this Bill
should be brought in here applying this
system of divorce in any part of Irish
territory. Burke said that it was the
wisdom of every legislature to add every
possible safeguard that could be devised
to maintain the stable structure of
marriage. This loosens that structure.
That was Burke's idea, a statesman of
incomparable wisdom whose name grows
larger and larger as years pass by. Of
course there has been degeneracy on an
increasing scale since Burke's day. I
say facilities for divorce such as this Bill
gives add a distinct danger, a dreadful
danger to the greatest happiness that
can follow married life, and that is pure
conjugal love, loyal and true to the end.
The landmarks and precedents of history
prove that where facilities for divorce
are given there is a lowering of the
general standard of morality in whatever
community these facilities are provided.
That is a lesson which anyone who reads
history knows to be incapable of
challenge.
And these divorce facilities are but
stages and steps along the road which
leads one back to the conditions in which
Christianity found heathenism. To the
Christian the idea of divorce is
anathema. It was Christianity that
changed the whole moral aspect of life.
It breathed a free pure breath into the decaying civilisation of 20 centuries ago. Do
these divorce legislators ever think what
a curse it is rampant in the States and

children? Their welfare is disregarded.

life means, lost and denied them. I
remember some little time ago reading

Such smiling rogues as these

they will have nothing to do with the

He, apparently, complains that the

to the Press. I do not think the House
