As well as those objections on principle
there are one or two matters of detail
which are primarily matters for the Committee stage. It is, however, proper
that one or two of them should be
referred to now. The first was the point
raised by the hon. Member for Woodvale
(Mr. Nixon). His objection was to the
Clause which proposes to permit divorce
on the grounds of incurable insanity, and
if the respondent has been an inmate of
an asylum or under care for a period of
five years. He objects to that Clause as
though it were imposing something in the
way of a penalty on the unfortunate inmate of the asylum. I should like the
hon. Member to look at the case from
another aspect. The purpose of divorce
jurisdiction is not to impose a penalty on
anybody; it is to give relief to the applicant from a misfortune from which he
suffers. The purpose is not that of imposing anything in the nature of punishment on the respondent, but to relieve
the applicant from an intolerable
misfortune.
I think the hon. Member for Woodvale will find it very easy to visualise
cases where there might be such an
intolerable misfortune which would be
met by this proposal. Take the case of
a
young wife married to a young
husband. The young husband becomes
afflicted by some incurable mental disease and he is carried away to an asylum.
He becomes quite incurable and has no
knowledge of his wife or her existence,
or the existence of his children; in fact,
if one may say so, he is practically dead
to the world. He lives on in the asylum
for 20 or 30 years, and his young wife,
left in the world with one or two
children, may, perhaps, meet a man who
could give her the greatest happiness.
Does not it seem to be a misfortune that
she should continue to be tied to a man
who, to all intents and purposes, is dead.
He can never be with her. A case like
that is one which I suggest deserves to
be considered sympathetically. I quite
agree that there will not be many cases
of the kind brought into the Courts. In
a great number of cases the wives will
prefer to go on and live alone and will
not divorce their husbands. However,
there are cases of hardship and individual cases which this provision will meet.

It might suggest that there is something

hon. Member would not like anything
of that nature to go forth.
In framing this Bill the Government
have given consideration to the point,
and they thought on the whole it was
better to leave the matter to the discretion of the court. It must be remembered that some of the grossest and most
outrageous matrimonial affairs, the most
shocking to mention, are often only discovered in the very early months of
matrimony. It would be
would be a shocking
thing if, in a matter of that kind, one
had to wait three or five years and could
not get relief at once. The provision in
the English Act is, after all, a compromise. A five-year period was suggested
on the one hand, while on the other hand

particularly the legal Members, suggested

three years were reached as a compromise. I suggest to the hon. Member for
the University that on consideration he
will see that there are reasons, and
reasons of weight, why this three-year
bar should not be inserted in the Bill,
and why it should be left to the good
sense and discretion of the Courts as to
whether, within the early period after
marriage, it should be possible to give a
divorce or not.
Question, "That the Bill be now read
a Second time," put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Warnock):
Before I say anything on the Estimates
to-day I am sure every person in the
House will regret the circumstance which
leads me to present these Estimates. I
am glad to say that the Minister of Home
Affairs is progressing well, and I am sure
the whole House, in whatever quarter
Members may sit, will look forward to
his return in the near future to preside once again over his own Department. With the permission of the House,
I propose to adopt what I understand is
the usual custom and speak generally on
the Estimate in introducing this Vote.
On looking at the figures for the service of the Ministry during the year, the
first matter which attracts attention is
the fact that the Vote is up as compared
with the previous year to the extent of
£206,000. That would be a figure which
would demand very careful consideration
in ordinary circumstances, but the increase for the present year is attributable
entirely to three particular items. There
is an increase of £107,000 in the cost of
the "B" Special Constabulary; an increase of £69,000 in respect of air raid
precautions service, and an increase of
£27,000 in respect of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. Those three figures together amount to £203,000, and as the
increase over the whole Estimate is only
£206,000 it will be seen that on a Vote
of over 2 millions the actual increase,
if we ignore these three items, amounts
to £3,000, so that speaking of the Estimate generally it may be said to be
fairly constant.
The first item is that of the Special
Constabulary, £107,000. It will be
fresh in everyone's memory that events
which occurred in December of last year
led the Government to the decision to
put the "B" Special Constabulary in the
patrol category. There are about 12,000
members in the Force and they receive a
bounty at the rate of £10 per annum,
but the actual increase in the Estimate is
a little lower than that, £107,000. The
Royal Ulster Constabulary Estimate
itself is up by £27,000. Of that sum
approximately £8,000 is due to an increase in the personnel. The personnel
of the Force at the date of the presentation of this Estimate is about 39 or 40
higher than it was at the corresponding
date last year. If you take an average
payment of £4 a week, which is only a

Estimates--

[Mr. Warnock]
round figure, it is approximately £8,000
increase. Five thousand pounds of the
increase is attributable to the service of
the loans in respect of the scheme of
barrack reconstruction in pursuance of
the Exchequer and Financial Provisions
Act of 1924. The service of the loans is
put at about £5,000 consequent on the
expenditure which was made on police.
barracks in pursuance of the major
scheme.
Two thousand five hundred pounds, a
figure estimated at £50, is due to the
provision for the first time since 1924 of
certain bedding, linen sheeting I am glad
to say, in the main, in connection with
the provision of new bedding for the
Force.
The pensions figure is up about
£1,300. The actual deficit of £27,000 is
also attributable to the fact that the
receipts in aid are down by about £9,000
in connection with the rebate which was
got from the Customs for customs duty
performed as compared with last year.
I am glad to say that the efficiency of
both the Royal Ulster Constabulary and
the Special Constabulary has been well
maintained throughout the year. The
building up of the Police Force, which I
still hope enjoys the confidence of all
sections of the community, has been one
of the major
major undertakings of the
Government.
I do not want to trouble the Committee unnecessarily with figures, but just
as one example of the efficiency of the
Force I would like to give four very
simple figures. In the year 1935 the
number of outrages specially reported was
2,696, and the number of cases in which
persons were made amenable was 1,290,
the percentage being 45.6. In the
following year (1936) the. figures were
2,122 and 1,267, percentage 59.7; in
1937, 2,165 and 1,453, percentage 67.1;
in 1938, 2,179 and 1,651, percentage
75.8. The lesson to be drawn from that
is that the persons made amenable in
45 per cent. of specially reported cases
rose to 59 per cent. in the following year,
to 67 per cent. in the next year, and to
75 per cent. in 1938. Those figures are
very remarkable, and I think they are
a very fair tribute to the general efficiency
of the Force so far as the prevention and
detection of crime are concerned.
The next increase is that in relation to
air raid precaution services. The Estimate is up by about £69,000. I would
have had a good deal to say on this question of air raid precautions to-day but
for the fact that the, hon. Member for
Pottinger has on the Order Paper for
next Tuesday a Motion which I understand is going to be taken on that day.
Having regard to that I thought it would
be inadvisable for me to go into any
lengthy or detailed explanation of the
proposals of the Government in respect of
air raid precautions. I think and I
believe the Committee will agree with me
-that the matter will be the subject of
a full-dress debate on Tuesday. The
whole matter will be ventilated, and the
programme and policy of the Government
can be stated better on that occasion
than by myself when merely introducing
the Estimates. The air raid precautions
estimate for this year must necessarily be
in the nature of a token estimate.
beyond the power of any person to say
in the changing situation of to-day what
our expenditure for air raid precautions
will be. We have an increase of £33,000
in respect of general equipment, an
increase of £29,000 in respect of firefighting equipment, and an increase of
£5,000 in respect of grants to local
authorities. These figures are minimum
figures. I have little doubt, unless the
international situation improves beyond
all recognition, that our expenditure on
these vital services will probably be very
much higher, and that supplementary
estimates will probably be necessary.
It is
Those are the three items which account
for the increase in the Estimates of this
Department. I would like to pass
rapidly over one or two matters in connection with the work of the Department
which seem to call for special mention.
The local government services of the
Ministry are, of course, tremendously
important, as they bring us in contact
with local bodies. The system of local
government through the country has
worked normally and smoothly as a whole.
We have had one matter which aroused a
good deal of attention in connection with
the Belfast Board of Guardians, but save
for that the local government services
throughout the year have not been the
subject of any violent controversy, and
I think on the whole these services have
been successfully and adequately performed.
Ministry of Home Affairs 1276
Estimates
3 MAY 1939
One other matter which does not
appear very clearly on the Estimate, but
which is worthy of comment, is the increased attention which is being paid by
local authorities to better water and
sewerage facilities. During the year the
Ministry have sanctioned loans amounting to £116,000 in respect of these
services. They are not spectacular; they
do not receive much publicity, but they
do make a very important contribution to
the public health of the country. Unemployment relief grants from the Ministry
of Labour covered 85 per cent. of the
labour costs of these schemes, and the
Ministry will be glad to see local authorities take the fullest possible advantage
of the facilities they are offering in this
direction.
The question of housing has been dealt
with too recently here to occupy the Committee in relation to it. I will only say
that the recrudescence of activity in
connection with the Labourers Acts will
result in the near future in the provision
of approximately 4,500 new labourers'
cottages. I am glad to say that every
rural district council, with the exception
of two, have promulgated schemes in connection with the provision of labourers'
cottages.
There is one other matter to which I
want to refer. I am in the happy
position of being able to give some very
striking figures in connection with the
public health services in relation to
tuberculosis. This disease has always
been spoken of and treated as a great
Scourge in this country. I am glad to
say that tremendous advances have been
made during the past 16 or 17 years. In
1922 the number of people who died from
tuberculosis in Northern Ireland was
2,107; in 1927, 1,767; in 1932, 1,415;
in 1935, 1,350; in 1936, 1,315, and in
1937, 1,251. Although I have not got
the exact figure I am in a position to say
that for 1938 the figure will be the lowest
ever recorded. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) To reduce the number of deaths
from one, particular source from 2,107 in
1922 to 1,251 in 1937 represents a very
remarkable achievement. We hope in
the near future to see a further advance
in these figures.
As everybody knows, the Belfast Corporation have had in contemplation for a
good while a major scheme for the treatment of this disease. For some considerable time past the best medical opinions,
or what we consider the best, have taken
the view that this disease was best treated
in one, central institution which would
serve not only the city of Belfast but, if
possible, the whole of the Six Counties,
and if not that at least the three adjoining counties. The Ministry having been
advised along these lines did their best
to attract the minds and activities of
local authorities to the matter. Conversations have taken place frequently
between the technical officers of the
Ministry and the Ministers and the local
authorities, and early this year a conference was held which was attended by
representatives of the Belfast Corporation and each of the counties in Northern
Ireland. The possibility of a central
institution was explored. I am very
sorry to say that the administrative, and
financial difficulties which were quite
obvious, but which we hoped might have
been overcome, have proved insuperable,
and we have had to come to the conclusion that that scheme at the moment
at all events is not practicable.
Having come to that decision, and the
Belfast Corporation being anxious to go
on with their own scheme, the Ministry
have now given sanction to one of the
sites which was put forward by the
Belfast Corporation. I think when that
scheme comes into operation we shall find
that the tuberculosis figures which I have
given will show a very marked improvement. We wish the Corporation well
with their scheme. I am sure it will
be a good scheme. As I say, we would
have preferred a big central scheme,
where medical and surgical attention and
all the best specialists could have concentrated. But no blame to anybody.
The difficulties have been insurmountable.
The matter was approached with goodwill on both sides. I do hope that the
Belfast Corporation in their new scheme
will be so successful as to make a very
great improvement in the figures I have
given.
I have been able to speak hopefully
with regard to tuberculosis. There is one
other matter, that is, the, service in connection with maternity and child welfare,
with which the Ministry is far from
satisfied. A departmental committee has
been sitting for some considerable time
and a report is expected at a very early

date. There are far too many children
dying in infancy in this country and too
The.
many mothers die in childbirth.
reception of the report of that committee will be made the opportunity by

That is the stuff.

Another boy writes to say that Mr. Watson, the Governor, had given him help
that he had never received from any

I do not think I can usefully add anything in connection with the Estimates,
but may I be permitted as representing
the Ministry to-day to bid an affectionate
farewell to Mr. Walter Magill? Every
member of the Committee knew Mr.
Walter Magill. His loss to the Ministry
is great. He was one of the wisest men
I have come across. I personally owe
him a deep debt of gratitude because
when I came into the Ministry completely inexperienced he guided me and
kept me from making many major
blunders. Everybody in the Ministry
regrets his departure, and I am sure the

his very best to the Government of Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like before
casting my mind back to the Estimates

Minister will soon be restored to health

Having said that, I feel it is my

an
I was very pleased to hear the letters

There is in Great Britain to-day a training scheme to teach intelligent boys how

I come now to prisons. I am still
firmly convinced that our prison system
is wrong. It is wrong in its make-up
because in the first instance the prison
on the Crumlin Road was built for shortterm prisoners. When the Government
of Northern Ireland took over control
the powers that be in Britain realised
that our prison system could not be
adapted for long-term prisoners, and they
made a grant towards the establishment
of a prison in Northern Ireland to meet
the case of the long-term or life prisoner.
Instead of that grant being utilised to
provide a building or settlement suitable
for that type of prisoner it was applied
in other directions. No matter how we
may spend money on the Crumlin Road
Prison we cannot give justice to the men
imprisoned there for long terms of years
or for life. This is one of the crying-out
scandals of our prison system in Northern Ireland. No other country in the
world would keep a life prisoner in a
short-term prison because the population
would cry out against that kind of
punishment. I feel that sooner or later
we will have to apply ourselves to the
reconstruction of the prison system in
Northern Ireland.
I pass on to the question of buildings.
We have been applying ourselves to the
question of housing for police, for
warders, and for others serving under
this Ministry, and I am pleased to know
that we have met with a very large
amount of success, but there is the question of the price paid. Taking the police
force as an example I am rather inclined
to think that if we were to house the
police in silver huts those in authority
would ask for gold ones. No one can
leave the charge at my door that I fail
to appreciate decent housing conditions.
I always agree that good housing conditions should exist, but I fail to agree
with the amount being expended on
police barracks. I think after reviewing
the situation in Northern Ireland that
we should call a halt to this expenditure.
I am told there are certain districts
yet to be accommodated with police
barracks. I would say, erect barracks in
those districts that require them, but

erect them in a manner that is likely to

I understand there is an increase on

You can go hungry and be without

That should have been done years ago.

Initiative than the supervisors of the

I refer to the matter now because of

we all know, the mortality figures in

on medical skill, but on competent nursing. Recognising that, the Government,
as in Great Britain, has increased the

until now, in the ordinary course, it extends over two years. But the class from

which these pupils are trained are

Britain, as I understand the situation,

eventually-and the matter is coming to
a head I understand speedily—a lack of
competent nurses, and that is not the
way to improve the mortality figures.
But it goes further than that. While
these pupils are in residence they do as
part consideration for the training a very
considerable amount of work, and if they
leave Northern Ireland it means that
the hospitals concerned will have to find
extra labour to perform these duties.
And so hospitals such as
as the Royal
Maternity Hospital are faced not only
with a lack of pupils, with a resulting
reduction of revenue due to fees, but
with the probability that they will have
to expend more in obtaining labour in
substitution for that of the pupils who
might otherwise have attended for instruction.
This is a matter which should be
remedied at once. I understand the
money necessary to put matters on a parity
with Great Britain is not large, but
unless the matter is taken in hands soon
the situation will become a very difficult
one, and instead of getting conditions
improved they will tend to get worse.
I suggest to the Parliamentary Secretary
and his Ministry that this matter should
not be allowed to drift along until the
results of an inquiry come in. It is

Another matter I would like to
mention is tuberculosis. I am not competent to offer any opinion as to the
virtues of a centralised system. We have
heard expert opinion that it is the best
system, but we all know that expert
opinion in these matters tends to run in
circles. However that may be, there is
one thing of vital importance, if the
improved figures are to be still further
improved, and that is that those who are
in the early stages of the dread disease
should be encouraged to seek skilled
treatment at once. There is no use
spending large sums of money on up-todate hospitals if patients come too late.
Therefore I think it would be well for
everything that can be done to encourage
those who are stricken to seek treatment
in the very early stages.

names over the door

to indicate the character of the work that

I have never demanded that the Government should attempt to prohibit betting

That

And he was a man who spoke from experience. As I say, I blow hot and I
blow cold when I talk about the activities
of this Ministry, but at the same time I
appreciate the difficulties. That is all I
have to say along those lines.
To turn now to other matters where I
am in full agreement with the Ministry, I
would like to say that everyone in Northern Ireland approves of the ability and
the, courage with which they have maintained law and order in our districts, and
it has required a good deal of courage.
The Government have a number of critics,
particularly in the English Press, in regard to this matter. It is a delicate
matter, and one, perhaps, that I should
not have broached at all, but I would
like to say that the critics of the Government forget that the Government are
confronted with two very different types
of law breakers. On the one hand there
are the ordinary criminals-burglars,
shop-lifters, drunken brawlers-acting
alone and from selfish motives, and who
usually have a bad conscience.
They
have no organisation behind them. The
ordinary practices of the Government are
quite adequate to deal with law-breakers
of that type.
In addition, our Government are confronted with law breakers of a very
different type, who believe their motives
are quite justifiable. I need not
elaborate on the point, but when people
claim the rights of war and the right to
burn and shoot at will, and to do it with
a good conscience, and animated by high
ideals, though very mistaken, and who
have all the paraphernalia of organisation
behind them to give them material and
moral support, I would ask these critics
of the Government to remember that law
breakers of that sort require to be dealt
with in a very different way. They cannot have it both ways. If these people
are ordinary citizens they will be treated
as ordinary citizens, but if they claim to
be, at war and to have the rights of war
they need not complain if they are dealt
with in other ways.
There is just one other matter I want
to refer to, and that is, the administration of the poor law in Northern Ireland.
This presents great difficulties to the
Ministry in view of the fact that we
have tremendous unemployment. There
are a number of middle-aged and elderly
people who have. lost their way, who are
semi-derelicts, who are under-fed and who

rooms is not a very satisfactory or
economical way for these men, they would
rather be. in lodging-houses or other
respectable places; but it would appear.
according to the interpretation of the law,
in those circumstances they have no right
to anything. I know the Government
looks on this matter sympathetically, but
it is a considerable and pressing problem
on the conscience. of a number of people.
May I say that it is twelve years
since the Commission on Local Government issued their report. In that report
they recommended that the workhouses
should undergo a complete overhauling,

there. Decent, elderly people should have

this report. We have now a very able
and energetic Parliamentary Secretary.
and he might refresh his memory upon

COMPULSORY TRAINING.
Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice)
asked the Prime Minister whether he is
prepared to make a full statement to
the House of the conversations that took
place between himself and the Prime
Minister of Great Britain on the question
of the Compulsory Military Training Bill
as it will apply to Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: I welcome
the opportunity of making a statement
in this House on the representations
which I made on behalf of the Government of Northern Ireland to Mr. Chamberlain with regard to the application
of the Military Training Bill to Northern Ireland. Hon. Members will appreciate that the military defence of the
United Kingdom of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland is a matter reserved
exclusively to the Imperial Government,
but my colleagues and I are grateful to
Mr. Chamberlain for his invitation and
for the opportunity which he gave me.
to lay before him personally the feelings
of the people of Ulster.
In order to give a clear picture of the
events which have taken place I should
first remind you that, following the
announcement by the Imperial Government of their intention to introduce into
the Parliament at Westminster the Mili-
Compulsory Training 1318
Oral Answer-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
tary Training Bill, I communicated at
once with the Imperial Government informing them that Northern Ireland
would deplore any differentiation between different parts of the United
Kingdom and, as a most loyal part of
the Kingdom, would deeply resent any
suggestion that she should not be included within the Measure. Hon. Members are aware that I also issued a
statement to that effect to the Press.
In my conversations with Mr. Chamberlain I again emphasised the desire of
the people of Northern Ireland to be
called upon to bear the same obligations.
as their fellow-citizens in the rest of the
Kingdom and recognising that the responsibility rested with the United
Kingdom Government for deciding in
what way Northern Ireland's contribution could best be utilised, I assured
Mr. Chamberlain that the entire
resources of Northern Ireland were at
the disposal of the Imperial Government
and said that our people awaited his
decision as to how
we could most
effectively assist.
I understand that Mr. Chamberlain
will, in the course of his Second Reading
speech on the Bill to-day at Westminster,
deal with the position of Northern Ireland, and I hope he will be able to
announce in what further manner the
people of our Province may contribute
to the defence of the Mother Country.
Let me just remind you what we are
doing already in that respect. We have
our three infantry regiments-the Royal
Ulster Rifles, the Royal Inniskillings and
the Royal Irish Fusiliers; we make our
contribution to the regular forces of the
Royal Navy and the Royal Air Force;
we have our Royal Naval Volunteer
Reserve unit, and more recently other
reserve formations have been added, the
Coast Defence Territorial Artillery, a
whole Anti-Aircraft Brigade of the
Supplementary Reserve and reserve units
of the Royal Air Force; and we are not
yet at an end of these additional formations.
I would like to emphasise that the
loyal desires of the people of Northern
Ireland to bear such obligations as the
Imperial Government may decide to
impose on them have been fully recognised and appreciated. In my judgment.
the British public would have every
reason for resentment if the slightest
embarrassment were
caused to His
Majesty's Government at this critical
time. Loyalty, as we understand it in
Ulster, if it is to be fully expressed,
means supporting the Government of the
United Kingdom in the heroic task they
are undertaking; if we did otherwise, the
high esteem in which we are held in
Great Britain and the Empire might be
vitally prejudiced. The unconditional
offer of the whole of our resources should
consequently contain no reservations
whatever. As in the past, our loyalty is
not conditional in any way and our
people can best contribute in these difficult times to assist the Mother Country
by an unquestioning acceptance of whatever decisions the Imperial Government
may find it necessary to take.
I may add that the conversations which
took place in no way affect the constitutional position of Northern Ireland as
clearly and repeatedly defined by Mr.
Chamberlain speaking on behalf of His
Majeusty's Government.

PERSONAL EXPLANATION BY
MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): By leave of
the House I wish to make a personal explanation concerning my replies to the
supplementary questions put to me. by
the hon. Member for Woodvale last
Thursday regarding the two members of
the old Pigs Marketing Board who are
serving as producers' representatives on
the new Board.
I think I inadvertently conveyed to
the hon. Member and to the House the
impression that these. two gentlemen did
not cease to be members of the Board
when the scheme was amended, putting
the old Board out of office. This is
rather a misleading account of what
happened, and I would like to explain
more accurately, and with more detail
than was possible at the time, what the
facts of the situation are.
The two members of the. Board in
question, Mr. Crowe, of Fermanagh, and
Mr. Graham, of Armagh, were not in
agreement with their colleagues on the
old Board. The new scheme which, as
I have said before, is a temporary oneprovided for the dismissal of the old
Board and for the elected representatives
of the old Board meeting and choosing
two of their number to serve on the new
temporary Board. With the exception
of Mr. Crowe and Mr. Graham, the
members of the old Board intimated
through their solicitor that they did not
propose to attend the meeting called for
the purpose of electing two members to
represent them on the new Board; but
both Mr. Crowe and Mr. Graham
intimated to me their willingness to
serve, being anxious, as elected producers'
representatives, to bear their share in
straightening matters out. Of this
willingness I was very glad to take
advantage, and Mr. Crowe and Mr.
Graham were accordingly elected to the
new Board. I trust this explanation.
will make the matter clear to the hon.
Member and to the House, and I must
express my regret that my original
replies should require. this additional
elucidation.
Mr. ELLIOTT rose.

my information is that only one of the
members did disagree, and that was Mr.
Crowe. Mr. Graham prior to that expressed no disagreement, as shown by the

is my information.

£40,000 was entirely due to air raid precautions, so that if the £33,000 is deducted there would actually be a decrease
of £7,000 as compared with last year.
If a comparison is made on a fair basis,
leaving out air raid precautions, it will
be found that there is a decrease instead
of an increase.
The hon. Member for Pottinger also
raised the question of furniture in this
House. The item of £13,000 is a provisional estimate for air raid precautions
only. It depends exactly on what steps
are taken for the blinding of the Parliament Buildings and first aid equipment. As to the normal furniture for
the whole of the Government buildings,
this is reviewed periodically by the Ministry. The total renewals come to £5,600,
so that there is a reduction of £300 this
year. I can assure the hon. Member
that this is a question which the Ministry have under review and will keep
under review. With reference to the
question of printing, the hon. Member
seems to think that it should be done
in a centralised department. I am
afraid I cannot agree with him that we
should set up a Government printing
works. It would be a wrong thing to
do. Competition is the life of trade.
The Government printing is put out to
tender, and there are at least ten firms
amongst whom the printing is divided.
Competition brings the price down.
Mr. BEATTIE: What competition is
there for the printing of Hansard?
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I do not
know exactly. I cannot answer that.
The general Government printing is put
out to tender. The ten firms are on the
tender list and get contracts for the
printing. This competition keeps the
price down and saves the State money.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is not the point.
What competition is there for the Hansard printing?
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I am not
able to answer that. I understand that
Hansard is under the control of Mr.
Speaker. As regards the question
raised by the Member for Shankill about
the paper mills, these paper mills are on
the list for tendering here and in the
United Kingdom. When the price is
within bounds they are given contracts
the same
as anybody else. The hon.
Member for South Down referred to
things coming under the Ministry of
Agriculture and outside my province. It
would be wrong for me to refer to them,
otherwise I might get bees in my bonnet.
The hon. Member for Woodvale raised
the question of Civil Service examinations held in England. While he is
right in saying that the competition.
there is not open-
Mr. NIXON: I did not say the competition was not open.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: While the
examinations are open to people in
South Africa and Australia, the examinations do not cover entry to the services
in the Dominions. If we were to set up
a Civil Service examination solely for
Northern Ireland, I am afraid in the words
of a former Vice-Chancellor of Queen's
University, a great disservice would be
done to those who wished to enter the
service. They would have to face two
examinations if solely for Northern Ireland. If they wish to compete for a
Colonial service or diplomatic service
they would have to go in for another
examination. That would restrict
entrants and do a great deal of harm.
What we want to do is to attract the
best people to Northern Ireland no
matter where they come from. I wish
to correct a statement made by the hon.
Member for Woodvale as to the Whip's
office. The hon. Member said the Chief
Whip had his salary voted on this Estimate, plus £450, which went to his
salary. That £450 is for the upkeep of
the Whip's office on the Lobby outside.
Every Member will agree with me that
it fulfils a most useful service. Ever
since I have been a Member it has been
borne on the Estimate. It is not correct
to sav that the £450 is an addition to
the Whip's salary.
Estimates-
Ministry of Finance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
The hon. Member for Shankill referred to the increase in the County
Courts and Resident Magistrates Vote..
In this connection I would like to point
out that this increase is entirely due to
the retirement of the Clerk of the Crown
and Peace for Fermanagh and to the
lamented death of the Clerk of the
Crown and Peace for County Armagh.
These salaries were borne on the Imperial
Votes, but now that one, has retired and
the other is dead the salaries of the new
holders of the offices are borne on the
Votes of Northern Ireland. The sum
total is the same, but the salaries of those
two officials are borne on our Votes
instead of on the Imperial Votes and recovered from the Imperial Contribution.
I think I have covered most of the points
raised by hon. Members, and I would
like to thank them for the way in which
these Estimates have been received.
Mr. NIXON: The Financial Secretary
was unfair in the latter part of his remarks about the £450. I did say, and
I still say, that £1,000 and £450 are paid

Secretary referred to that office out there.
That office, like the rest of this building,
is carried on the general Vote. No rent
is paid for it. It is a room placed at the

is quite right; I do not object to that
at all. The Chief Whip could not spend
£450 on it, or even fifty pence. Everything is paid out of the general Vote for
the upkeep of the building. I am quite
right in what I say. During all the
time Parliament has met the Government
have had no expense for that office, nor
has the Chief Whip, unless he keeps some
refreshment in it that I never saw.
know there is a refreshment place in this
House.

It may be, and possibly is, a fact that
he pays that £450 to his private secretary, who is purely a political agent, and
I am not reflecting on him when I say
that. Every party has a political agent.
I am quite right when I say the money
is paid to the Chief Whip, and that
room, called his office, does not cost fifty
pence, or five pence. What he does with
the money after he gets it is nothing at

income tax.

Mr. BROWN: There is a matter of
which I have given notice to the Minister of Agriculture. It formed the subject of a question to the noble Lord, the
Prime Minister. For many weeks past
I have been pleading for a "produce
more food" campaign in connection with
our preparedness for war. I was glad
to see in the papers to-day an announcement to the effect that a grant of £2
per acre will be given in respect of all
land tilled after a certain period. Northern Ireland, I am glad to say, is
included. We are anxious to produce all
the food we possibly can, both for the
people of Northern Ireland and for our
friends in Great Britain. It is of extreme importance that there should be
an ample food supply, both for ourselves and those across the Channel. We
Tillage of Grass Land-
Adjournment-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Brown]
all know that in the last war we were
faced with starvation. Twenty years
have elapsed since then. We have now
more mouths to feed, and we have fewer
ships in which to carry food. It is,
therefore, of vital importance that we
should take this matter up.
The only snag in regard to the grant,
so far as Northern Ireland is concerned,
is that the £2 per acre will not apply
except to land which has been under grass
for seven years. In other words, only land
that has not been tilled for seven years
will qualify for a grant. That is one
point. The second point is that it will
not apply to less than two acres of land.
We should make representations to the
Imperial authorities to see if we can
receive special consideration in this
matter. On my recent visit to Yorkshire I saw thousands of acres of
absolutely waste land. If any person
came along and said he would pay the
taxes he would get it. The amount of
land going to waste in England far exreeds, in proportion to the size of the
country, what is wasted in Northern
Ireland. Therefore this restriction of
seven years hits us much more seriously
than the people on the other side of the
Channel. We should suggest to the
British authorities that in their own
interests-we want to help them as well
as we want to help ourselves in regard
to providing food-the seven years restriction should be omitted so far as
Northern Ireland is concerned.
Another point is that the holdings in
Northern Ireland are considerably
smaller than the holdings in England.
Over there it is common for people to
have 100 or 150-acre farms, whereas in
Northern Ireland the holdings sometimes
consist of two or three acres. This grant
will not be paid in respect of any land
under two acres. Therefore it will be
seen that we have a very good case for
asking the restriction to be removed so
far as we are concerned.

This is another reminder that legislation does not work out as fairly as one
might expect. Take two instances.
regard to the subsidy for sugar beetit amounted to £40,000,000—we did not
get a penny during the past fifteen
years. We should get an expert to come
over here and find out once and for all
whether or not we can grow sugar beet.
If we cannot we should ask for a subsidy in lieu of our share of the
£40,000,000. We should also ask for a
subsidy in lieu of the £900,000 overpaid
in respect of the wheat subsidy. We
paid £900,000 more than we received
since the Act came into force. I am
perfectly certain the Minister is as much
alive to this point as I am. I do not
suggest he is not, but I should like him
to give us an assurance that the matter
will be looked into and, if possible, something done.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The hon.

he will be good enough to put down a

raised.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Bacon Industry Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Bacon
Industry Bill has been in the hands of
members for a considerable time. The
memorandum deals with various matters,
the most important of which is a
rationalisation scheme under which a
number of the smaller roll and ham
factories will be closed down and com-
1363 Bacon Industry Bill-

9 MAY 1939
Second Reading
pensation paid to the owners; a simple
form of contract for the sale of pigs by
producers to curers but with exemption
in the case of the small producer, for
whom a special registration system has
been devised. The present exemption.
limit in the Bill is 20 pigs per annum,
but I am prepared later on in the course
of this Bill through the House to in
crease this limit to 30 pigs. Finally,
there is the provision for financial
assistance to producers and curers by
means of a guaranteed price for a
standard pig of the Wiltshire type when
the cost of feeding stuffs ration is 8s 6d
per cwt. This guaranteed price is 70s
per cwt. to start with and is reduced
slightly in the second and third years.
As Members are aware, these are the
outstanding provisions of the Bill and I
need not elaborate them further.
When the British Bacon Industry
Act was introduced in the Imperial
Parliament over a year ago I was pressed
for a similar measure of assistance here.
At that time the position was much
more attractive than is the case at the
present time. Then feeding stuffs were
10s 4d per cwt., and consequently the
price paid to producers was 78s 9d per
ewt. for a standard pig of the Wiltshire
type. Since that date feeding stuffs are
3s 3d per cwt., and the price of the
standard pig under the Act has declined
to 68s 10d per cwt. The financial
attraction of the producer is that he is
to have no trading levy. Some producers may take the short view that the
Bill is not really giving the industry
material advantage, whilst he is
called upon to undertake greater responsibilities, and I have been likened to
the Workhouse Master in "Oliver
Twist-refusing the request of the
farmer for more.
any
But the long view and that is the
most important one is that the producer
is guaranteed a definite price for his
pigs and by this Bill we will have established a price insurance.
The producer is absolutely free from
all risks due to fluctuations in feeding
stuff prices or in the price of bacon, and
can concentrate on producing pigs,
knowing that he is assured by the Government of a price which will at least mean
a reasonable profit for the efficient producer. This position has not been
achieved without very considerable difficulty. When the British authorities were
first approached with regard to the introduction of this Bacon Industry Bill in
Northern Ireland they took the view that
there was no necessity for its introduction here. They argued that conditions
in Great Britain, where the pigs marketing scheme had broken down, were
different from conditions in Northern
Ireland, and that there was no reason
for the introduction of a similar Measure
in Northern Ireland, simply because the
Bacon Industry Act in Great Britain was
introduced there and provided for certain
Government assistance.
I have had the very greatest difficulty
in overcoming the objections raised by
British Departments to the introduction
of this Bill for Northern Ireland. The
reason why, in face of the opposition
which I encountered, I persisted in the
demand that we should be allowed to
introduce this Measure in Northern
Ireland has simply been this-the keystone of my policy as Minister of Agriculture has been to secure for producers
in Northern Ireland a degree of assistance
strictly similar to that which is extended
by the Imperial Government to producers
in Great Britain. I have not, I think,
been unsuccessful in securing this
princple in the past. The beef subsidy
extends to the whole of the United Kingdom; the oats and barley subsidy, under
which a payment of 13s 2d per acre of
oats will be made immediately and a
further payment later in the year, again
extends to Northern Ireland as well as
to Great Britain. The same is true of
the land fertility scheme.
At the present moment, in connection
with the Imperial Government's policy of
price insurance for agricultural products,
considerable further assistance to the
industry is under consideration, and I
have every reason to anticipate that this
assistance will be extended to our producers in Northern Ireland also. That is
why I attach the very greatest importance to us in Northern Ireland introducing a Bacon Industry Bill which,
subject to certain changes to meet Northern Ireland conditions, is based upon the
same principles as the Bacon Industry
Act in Great Britain. That I have
achieved, and whatever criticisms or
objections may be raised to the Bill I
personally cannot take the responsibility
Bacon Industry Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
of failing to go on with it, because I do
consider that this Bill is of crucial importance to Northern Ireland agriculture
in establishing the principle that agriculture in Northern Ireland is entitled
to the same
measure of assistance as
agriculture in Great Britain. It is only
necessary to point out that the pig
industry in this country is by far and
away the most important side of our
activities, and if we refuse a price insurance scheme for pigs it will be quite impossible to argue in the future that we
participate in a price insurance scheme.
for other commodities.
Since the Bill was published I have
discussed it with every county committee
of agriculture in Northern Ireland twice,
and have also had frequent discussions
with representatives of curers and producers. The Bill does not give all that
either producers or curers want or would
like, but from no quarter have I received
the suggestion that the Bill should be
rejected. I have been asked to amend
the Bill in this way or that. Invariably
each representative body has asked for
more assistance in their own particular
way. That is natural.
It may be said that the. scheme in
Great Britain is not working. It is, of
course, not the fact. Unfortunately the
pig population in Great Britain has
declined and the numbers of pigs contracted for delivery to bacon curers this
year are not as great as the numbers of
pigs contracted three years ago in the last
year of the old scheme. That, however,
is because, as I say, the pig population
in Great Britain has declined, and it is
true to say that practically all the pigs
available for bacon production in Great
Britain are being offered to curers under
contract in accordance with the provisions
of their Bacon Industry Act. The noncontract pigs are only those sufficient to
supply the needs of the fresh pork market
in Great Britain, which normally absorbs
one-half to two-thirds of the pigs produced in that country. This is evidenced
by the fact that although curers in Great
Britain have been allowed to purchase.
non-contract pigs the numbers obtained
have been only 10 per cent. of the total
supply during the first three months of
the scheme.
Those, responsible for the running of
the scheme would like to see an increased
number of pigs delivered to curers under
the provision of the Bacon Industry Act
there. With a view to bringing about
this object the suggestion has been made
by producers in Great Britain that the
terms of the Government's financial
assistance should be improved, and representations are being made to the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries with this
object in view. I do not know whether
those representations will be successful or
not.
If they are, and if a modification
in the Bacon Industry Act in Great
Britain is made, Northern Ireland will
naturally obtain the same benefits if the
present Bill is passed here, and the
financial attractiveness of the Measure to
producers would be enhanced. If, however, we do not proceed with the Bill
in Northern Ireland, then so far as pigs
are concerned we shall be striking out on
our own, and producers and curers must
face the consequences of carrying on in
Northern Ireland without the Government assistance which is being given to
the industry both now and in the future
in Great Britain.
It is common knowledge that the
British Government has under contemplation a price. insurance policy for those
agricultural products which can be truly
considered as fundamental to the fertility
of the land, and it is, of course, essential
that Northern Ireland should be included.
The British scheme for bacon, of which
this Measure is the. Northern Ireland
counterpart, is essentially a price insurance scheme, and if we were to take the
line on this product, which constitutes a
much more important part of our agricultural output than in the case. of Great
Britain, that price insurance was not
necessary it would, I fear, make it difficult, if not impossible, for us to argue
that it was necessary in other products
such as sheep.
There is, moreover, the important consideration that this Bill for the first time
puts our pig producers in a position of
absolute equality with English and
Scottish producers with regard to price.
They will be, with regard to their prices.
in exactly the same position as if our Six
Counties were situated in England or in
Scotland, but with the advantage that
they will not be subject to the more
onerous aspects of the contract system.
It will, I know, be argued again that
we are introducing a contract system in
Bacon Industry Bill-

Northern Ireland which has proved unworkable in Great Britain. That, of
course, is not the case. The circumstances here are entirely different from
those in Great Britain simply because in
Great Britain the pork market affords a
counter-attraction to the bacon market,
and producers have at times refrained
from entering into contracts for the
delivery of bacon pigs, because they considered that the prices on the pork market
would be more attractive. That complication does not exist in Northern Ireland,
and the entire output of our pig producers is absorbed by the bacon curing
factories.
The reason for the temporary breakdown of the contract system in Great
Britain two and a half years ago was
indeed owing to the existence of the pork
market there, a circumstance which does
not affect Northern Ireland directly.
Special provisions have been made, to deal
with the case of the small producer in
Northern Ireland through the registration system. I have no doubt that, given
goodwill, the system of pig supply provided in the Bill can be introduced in
Northern Ireland without difficulty. As
Members are aware, during the last few
years, while the scheme has broken down
in England here it has not broken down.
The structure was
sound one and,
therefore, it worked. I am quite, confident that it is administratively possible
for us to carry out the provisions of the
Bacon Industry Bill in Northern Ireland
without difficulty, and I would ask you
to accept that assurance.
a
So far I have spoken with regard to the
position of the producer. There is also
the position with regard to the curers.
I have had numerous conversations with
representatives of curers regarding the
provisions of the Bill and they have not
been able to accept the Bill for reasons I
will explain. The Act in Great Britain
provided a definite margin to the curer
for curing pigs. The Bill in Northern
Ireland provides that the assistance to the
curer in Northern Ireland will be
identical with the assistance to the curer
in Great Britain. I cannot ask for more
in the same way that I cannot ask for a
higher price to the producer here. I do
not believe that there is any inherent
reason why the curer in Northern Ireland
should not be able to operate on the same
curing margin as the curer in every part
of Great Britain, for it must be remembered that the British Act extends all
over the country from Cornwall in the
South to Sutherland in the North of
Scotland. I cannot think that the drawback of distance from markets is any
greater in the case of the curer in Northern Ireland than it is in the case of the
curer in remote parts of Great Britain.
In any event, the only way in which the
position of the curer in Northern Ireland
could be improved would be directly at
the expense of the producer in Northern
Ireland.
not

Everything will depend upon the course

I turn now to the provisions of the
Bill relating to the rationalisation of the
I think hon. Members
curing trade.
will agree that when assistance is given
by the Government to any industry or
product it is right that the Government
should ask the industry to take whatever steps are practical to increase its
efficiency. In the case of the producer
this is being done by asking him to undertake a definite responsibility in connection with the supply of pigs for a stated
period, so as to give the industry greater
assurance regarding pig supplies. In the
case of the curing trade the position is
that, other things being equal, one important factor in curing costs is the size
or output of the factory. Hon. Members will all appreciate that when overhead costs can be spread over a large
output costs can be reduced to a much
lower figure than when the output is
small. This is very definitely the case in
the curing trade, and in consequence the
Bill provides that a factory rationalisation scheme may be prepared under which
certain factories will be closed down on
payment of compensation. A scheme will
be worked out by my Ministry in consultation with the curers, but before any
scheme can be put into operation it must
be submitted to and approved by each
House of Parliament. Whatever scheme,
therefore, is brought in will be submitted
to the House for its approval, and it will
come into force when it is approved of.
Finally, I should like to say a few
words regarding the effect of the Bill
on the Pigs Marketing Scheme. Broadly
speaking, the effect of the Bill is simply
to modify the powers of the Pigs Marketing Board, so as to enable the contract
or registration system to be introduced.
At present the Pigs Board can require all
pigs to be sold only to the Board. This
power is removed under the Bill.
Actually, however, the Board has never
required dead pigs to be sold to it, nor
live pigs sold to curers on contract, and
the Board has only exercised its power
by requiring live pigs, other than those
sold on contract, to be sold to it. These
pigs have then been either resold to
Wiltshire curers or shipped to Great
Britain. Since under the Bill all pigs
sold to curers in Northern Ireland will
in future be sold under contract, or under
registered agreements in the case of the
man producing less than 30 pigs per
year, the only pigs which will in future
be purchased by the Board will be surplus pigs which are sold to the Board
for shipping to Great Britain, and it
is intended that the Board should continue to have, a monopoly of the shipping
trade.
The power of the Board to regulate
sales of pigs by determining the descriptions of pigs which may be sold and the
persons to, or through the agency of
whom, pigs of any description may be
sold, is also removed. Actually, however, the Board has never exercised its
powers under this provision and, consequently, this does not in any way affect
the actual operations of the scheme.
Similarly, a power under the scheme for
the Board to limit the number of pigs
which any individual producer could sell
has been removed. This again, however,
was a power which was never exercised.
The Bill leaves untouched the powers of
the Board in connection with buying and
selling pigs, its investments in curing
slaughter-houses, and to sell, pack, store,
adapt for sale, advertise. and transport
any pigs bought or commodities produced
by the Board. These powers retained by
the Pigs Board are set out in Clause 16.
Moreover, I anticipate that the organisation built up by the. Board for the collection of live pigs will continue to be of
the greatest service to producers even
after the contract or registration system
has come into force, and that these. collecting arrangements will continue to be
utilised.
I should also like to say that, as I
have already informed the House, the
present Board is only a temporary
Board and shall only continue in office
until the whole pig position has been

placed, as I think he ought to be placed,
in a rather privileged position.

I gather that it is the intention

We are, I think, accustomed in this
House to hear rather terrifying accounts
of what is going to happen in the case of
practically every proposal which the
Minister of Agriculture brings forward.
The whole industry was not only going
to be ruined, but our country markets
also. Now, what has actually happened?
The Minister of Agriculture introduced
a scheme which stood up to every shock.
It not only survived, but went on and
succeeded when the scheme in England
collapsed. Did the prophets over here
not exclaim when the English scheme
broke down that the same fate awaited
us? That prophecy was wrong.
What I beg this House to realise
above everything else is this simple yet
glaring fact, that the Minister of Agriculture gave Northern Ireland a scheme
which enabled us to increase our output
from 280,000 pigs a year to 750,000 a
year in the incredibly short period of
five years.
Not only that, we are now
producing one-third of the United
Kingdom output of bacon and hams.
That to me is the acid test. Anybody
who has eyes in his head and who goes
through our Province can see at a glance
the enormous development that has
taken place in pig production. This
Bill makes provision for still greater
expansion of our output. and for the
curing of all these pigs in our own
factories, and, being satisfied that the
Minister has not only given a square deal
to the small farmer but placed him in a
favourable position, I am going to
support the Second Reading, and I
sincerely hope the House will pass the
Bill without a Division.

The conditions are somewhat different

and what is happening to-day in Great

The Act was introduced in Great

informed, it has neither stimulated nor

Looking at the Bill from the curers'
standpoint, there are many factories in
Great Britain, and the reason for the
introduction of the Bill there was the
necessity for a rationalisation scheme as

there were too many factories. Some of

cent. of their quota, and in order to

There we find-and I speak with some

curers are not getting the percentage
they hoped to get, and are still operating under a very inefficient quota. The
same question does not arise in Northern Ireland. I am glad to say that
nearly every factory in Northern Ireland is operating up to its full quota.
There may be some factories which are
perhaps a little below that, but, taking
it all through, I think we are in the
happy position of having sufficient pigs
to give every factory every pig the

Therefore the same necessity for a
rationalisation scheme does not exist in

There would be no necessity here for

be very difficult for either the small producer or the large producer to contract

Ministry of Agriculture on the Exchequer
was getting too heavy the Minister of
Agriculture would go to the Minister of
Finance or vice versa, and say, "We. cannot allow this to go on any longer. We
will bring in this Order."
It being half-past Four of the Clock
further proceeding was postponed pursuant to Standing Order No. 2.
Air Raid Precautions.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move, "That
this House regrets the unsatisfactory
position that the citizens of Northern
Ireland are placed under due to the
failure of the Government in not applying an adequate scheme for air raid
precautions."
To some, I presume, this Motion may
seem delayed. Nevertheless, my reason
for adjourning it so often was the
absence through illness of the Minister
of Home Affairs. I understand to-day
that the Prime Minister is going to take
on himself the position of explaining to
the House that progress that has been
made in regard to the question contained
in the Motion. I feel that certain
positions have been created in Northern
Ireland likely to lead the people to have
a fear that nothing is being done, and
I would ask the noble Lord to pay
strict attention to the points which I
shall endeavour to make in regard to
this Motion. I have "The Protection
of Your Home Against Air Raids," by
Sir Samuel Hoare. I have also got
several schemes operating in cities such
as Belfast, and I am inclined to think
that Belfast is not making the headway
which I would like it to make.
The defence of the population from
aerial attack is not solely a problem for
governments; it is a problem that affects
every aspect of our national life. It survives the shifting fortunes of Cabinets.
and Ministers. This is, moreover, a
technical question and a technical
question of some complexity. It cannot be
solved by haphazard and unco-ordinated
measures. Only a body of scientific
workers and technicians is capable of
formulating proposals that will satisfactorily meet all the difficulties we are
likely to encounter.
Let us consider the nature of these
difficulties. We have to evacuate a proportion of the public from the vulnerable centres and we have to provide the
rest with protection that will guarantee
them relative immunity. In addition,
we have to prepare for possible casualties, for supplies of food and other
necessities, and for
for carrying on the
essential services. But to achieve all
this we require the systematised help of
a whole array of statisticians, surveyors,
architects, town planners, engineers,
chemists, hospital authorities, physiologists, and so forth. Each part of the
complicated scheme must be adjusted to
every other part; the whole plan must be
so carefully arranged that at the outbreak
of hostilities the public would change the
pattern of its daily life with the minimum of friction, delay and perturbation.
There can in the nature of things be
only one scientifically "best" method of
solving this social problem. I call this.
a
social problem. Have we yet discovered and applied this scientific
method? The trouble of all ill-considered
and improvised schemes is that their
hasty application retards and even prevents the maturing of more satisfactory
measures of protection. Money is spent
on the wrong objects; the public mind
grows confused; the authorities are pre-
Motion-
Air Raid Precautions
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
sented with overlapping and contradictory recommendations. Yet the
problem is an urgent one. If it is not
well solved in the near future it will
be badly solved, and we shall find ourselves embarked on a war for which we
are ill-prepared.
An attempt is being made to draw
together in a systematic form all that
has so far been established scientifically
and technically about the subject of air
raid protection. There are very few of
those competent to judge who will not
agree with all its main conclusions; and
there are many hundreds of experts in
diverse fields of science and technology
who will welcome its publication. Now
I claim that the points I am putting
before you will be welcomed by the
public at any rate. Until we start to
apply our theories no one can say that
we have reached our final conclusions.
The principles and theories enunciated
herein can be and must be indefinitely
studied and expanded so long as we have
the leisure to discuss these vital problems
before putting our ideas into practice.
I have read this little handbook
known as "The Protection of Your Home
Against Air Raids," by Sir Samuel
Hoare. I understood the Prime Minister was going to take this question and
I would like his attention to the words
of warning by Sir Samuel Hoare:-
"If this country were ever at war
the target of the enemy's bombers
would be the staunchness of the people
at home. We all hope and work to
prevent war, but while there is a risk
of it we cannot afford to neglect the
duty of preparing ourselves and the
country for such an emergency. This
book is being sent out to help householders to realise what they can do if
the need arises to make their home and
household more safe against air attack.
The Home Office is working with the
local authorities in preparing schemes
for the protection of the civil population during an attack.
But it is impossible to devise a
scheme that will cover everybody unless each home and family play their
part in doing what they can for
themselves. In this duty to themselves
they must count upon the help and
advice of those who have undertaken
the duty of advice and instruction. If
the emergency comes the country will
look for her safety not only to her
sailors and soldiers and airmen, but
also to the organised courage and foresight of every household. It is for
the volunteers in the air raid precautions services to help every household for this purpose and in sending
out this book I ask for their help."
I want to say that that help will be
forthcoming and in no place will it come
more quickly than in Northern Ireland.
The volunteers who came forward for the
purpose of serving were in such great
numbers that their enthusiasm after a
few weeks was damped because of the
failure of the Government and of those
responsible to give attention to the needs.
and requirements of these volunteers as
they should have done. The result today is this, that large numbers of
very enthusiastic volunteers have been
disappointed and have eased off from the
duties which they thought they were entitled to perform on behalf of those other
citizens of Northern Ireland. I put that
damping of the squib down to the door
of the Government. They have really
been the damper of the enthusiasm
in regard to A.R.P. in Northern Ireland. They have refused to recognise
that this question of money should not
be a factor or obstacle in the progress
that should be made at the earliest
opportunity for the protection of its
people, and the factor of money was the
deterrent obstacle in this question of
carrying out the arrangements necessary
to protect the citizens of the Six
Counties.
Having said that, I would ask what
the Government have done to justify the
argument against my charge of failure.
They have quite truly been responsible
for the bringing in of a number of gas
masks, but have they along with the
local authorities started first and foremost at the bottom rung of the ladder?
Have they had a central organisation to
control the needs and requirements of
the voluntary services they had at their
disposal? I say they have not.
have allowed every unit to go shillyshallying in their own way in regard to
this very important social question which
will affect the lives and homes of the
people of Northern Ireland. They have,
and I give them credit for it, got a num-
Thev

ber of gas masks distributed through the
city of Belfast. How serviceable those
masks may be in a few months' time or
years' time, I am not going to judge; I
am rather inclined to think that the
business has been badly managed.
It is not the most important part of
the protection that I am asking the Government to take in hand. There is
great danger from gas, different kinds
of gas, but there is a bigger danger from
incendiary bombs. There is a danger
that we might all within a few hours be
in contact with a very big fire. Is there
any organisation to meet conditions such
as might arise by the dropping of these
bombs known to be capable of destroying
towns twice the size of the city of Belfast
inside a period of one and a half hours.
What have the Government done in
regard to that matter? They may tell
me they have ordered a fleet of firefighting engines for the purpose of
putting out or subduing fires. The
engines require the volunteers, who will
have to be many and varied. The
appliances for the volunteers will not
need to be handed to them on the day
the fire takes place. The people going
to work the fire engines and appliances
will have to be thoroughly instructed in
how to get to the nearest point so as to
be able to deal with the damage done
in any particular area by incendiary
bombs which may be dropped. That is
a more important point than gas masks.
But we have another type of bomb
which is likely to destroy homes and the
human elements of the community without resorting to fire. Have we done anything in regard to that genius of science.
who has been responsible for bringing
into this world bombs that can destroy
life within a radius of 440 yards? Hon.
Members on the Government side do not
seem to be interested. There are not
many of them.
Mr. GRANT: There are not many on
the other side.
Mr. BEATTIE: There never are
many.
The Nationalists do not seem to
care whether bombs drop or not. They
claim to be prepared at every hour of
the day.
Mr. GRANT: Bomb proof.
Mr. BEATTIE: My hon. Friend
(Mr. Agnew) and I are the authors of
this Motion. I believe this is a question
where it makes no difference whether
you are a Tory or Liberal, Nationalist,
Socialist, or Communist.
Mr. GORDON: Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE: The bomb will pick
you out no matter what class, creed or
religion you belong to. We are not
taking this on as a political issue at all.
This issue is one where we can all try to
tackle it in the most efficient manner
possible. That being so I am now
giving my opinion with helpful thought
not critical thought behind it. Hon.
Members on the other side who have
been runners in their day know how
long it takes to cover 440 yards and
they know they would be caught in the
upheaval caused by the explosive bombs
I have referred to. Again I want to
know have the Government yet made
any effort to equal at least the protection carried out in that direction in
Great Britain?
I do not agree that steel shelters are
the most serviceable things for protection. The British Home Office have
agreed to these shelters which are to be
so many feet underground and so many
above the ground and covered with
earth. According to Sir John Anderson they have found them highly
efficient. I would be rather doubtful of
my life if I were to depend on one of
the steel shelters saving me from the
dangers of the air and the type of
bombs I have read of being manufactured for the purposes of destruction. I am not too delighted with that
form of protection. Nevertheless it is
an effort which has been made in Great
Britain and no effort in that direction
has been made in Northern Ireland. Is
it a case that Northern Ireland feels
that these shelters are of no service
or is it they are thinking out some
other scheme of deep underground
trenches-the only suitable, serviceable
and efficient way of protecting the lives
of the citizens. I am not the authority
that gives you that. I have the
authority of the higher élite and old
school-tie class. Take Eton College for
instance. Let us see how Eton has prepared itself for aerial attack. It has

to follow in giving protection which, in

It is dealt with by Mr. Haldane in his

In lieu of that underground shelter
which we have not made provision for
here we were told to dig trenches in our

hedges or

people who are living back to back in
the district I represent, where there is

houses, put up a steel shelter or brick
shelter or any other type of shelter? A
bomb which would be likely to drop somewhere in four streets of that area would
affect the whole people in the district. We
must admit that the houses in some parts
of the city, the east end in particular, were
built in a hurried fashion over fifty
years ago. That district was all in
fields, but owing to the development of
shipbuilding the jerry builders came
along and erected houses in thousands.
The supervision of building at that time
was carried out by the Corporation. The
history of the Belfast Corporation and
their supervision of building at that
early period is something I do not like.
to read about. There was hardly any
supervision over building. The houses
were required to be erected and they
were erected. Those houses exist today, and the inhabitants are asked to
protect themselves from aerial attack by
putting up steel shelters or brick shelters,
the latter being a new idea brought up by
our friend, Sir John Anderson, who at
one time was in Dublin Castle. I am sorry
that I broke my word to the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Warnock). I
would not have raised this matter until
the responsible Minister was here, but I
was encouraged by the Prime Minister
to put the Motion on the Order Paper
thinking he was the Minister responsible.
Mr. WARNOCK: I have no complaint to make.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is very good.
It is not due to any haste or hurry I
raise this matter. Sir John Anderson has
issued another pamphlet, and in it he is
offering the public a new line in A.R.P.
kennels. It is called "Directions for
the erection of domestic surface
shelters." The new line is supposed to
meet the needs of those who have no
suitable site for the little steel shelters
(the "Anderson Alibis') and no basement suitable for strengthening. We
have no suitable place for steel shelters.
The gardens in the area I represent are
on the window sills of the houses. You
will see the flower boxes in the windows.
Here is the alternative to the steel
shelters. As I said the new line is
supposed to meet the needs of those who
have no suitable site for the little steel
shelters (the "Anderson Alibis'), and
no basement suitable for "strengthening." This includes practically everyone living in any crowded area in any
city in any danger area. The steel
kennels are not merely of very little
value in themselves, but cannot be
erected in crowded areas. The direc
tions indicate that it is even more of an
insult to the public intelligence than the
steel kennels. The "alternative"
shelters are to be made of brick or concrete with reinforced concrete roofs, and
with a concrete floor in places where the
site conditions make this necessary.
The single shelter will have a minimum
internal floor space measuring 6 ft. 6 in.
by 4 ft. 6 in. "It will"-the pamphlet
declares "hold six persons, but the
internal dimensions can be increased so
as to take eight, ten and twelve
persons."
Again I say that would be futile and
useless for the type of building in most
of the areas of Belfast. The very
foundations on which some of the houses
are built would not stand the strain
without pressed piling, and the Government are not likely to do that pressed
piling for the sake of allowing such
shelters to be erected. The idea is not
suitable for Belfast. The Government
will have to think out some scheme
whereby the area which they represent
will have sufficient shelters in order to

provide for the requirements of the

The next matter I want to refer to is
evacuation. What have the Government done in regard to that question?
It is true that they have sent out letters
to districts outside Belfast asking the
residents in those areas the number of
children that could be accommodated in
the case of evacuation from the city.
This haphazard way of dealing with
evacuation is going to lead us nowhere.
Evacuation must be done on a scale
never thought of by any member of the
Government up to the moment, and the
proof of that statement lies in the
instructions sent out by a department
operated by the Government. To ask
responsible parties outside how many
children or old people they are prepared
to take in case of air raids is ridiculous.
You have to start a scheme suitable for
the evacuation of the population, and
for the elements that remain you have to
provide sufficient protection. We cannot in case of war evacuate the whole
population. That is an impossibility.
There is no provision made for the units
who are compelled by circumstances to
remain shipwrights, engineers and
other classes who will have to stay in the
city during air raids. It is all right to
evacuate the children, the aged, the
lame. the sick, and that type of people,
but you cannot evacuate them without
making arrangements in the outside
areas, and the houshold accommodation
in the outside areas would not be
sufficient to meet the requirements of
those evacuated.

order to provide for evacuation it is

Again, you will have to erect shelters

the school children in the way suggested

I may
say it was a twopence-halfpenny thing that

Then in regard to evacuation, I believe
that if this shelter accommodation for the

of pounds that would be spent would be

should be erected. I know of large

anything happened at the moment there
would be hardly one employee safe. No

I challenged a gentleman who runs an
industry as to what provision he has made
for his workers. He said, "If you can
tell me what provision the Government
is making to help me to give the necessary
protection for the workers I will tell you
what I am prepared to do." The onus
of responsibility rests on the Govern-

ment. The example set by the Government is being copied by other classes in
the community who make the lame
excuse, "What is the Government doing

or women in their respective factories.
In my opinion the Government should
set up a Department under the control of
a Minister. I do not say that the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary are
not capable of carrying on the work, but
they have so many units of service in

In regard to the officers who are working this scheme at the moment, I want
to say quite openly that I have every
respect for their work. Under the conditions in which they are labouring they
are doing the best they can, but their
best is imited. We have large numbers

There is another aspect which I want
to raise, and that is the question of the
services given at the moment. It is
rather hard to go down to a school and

the distribution of gas masks. I have
not very much faith in them, but nevertheless the scheme has to be carried out.
In one school in particular one man was

necessary. Is one man sufficient for the

masks each evening? If the hon. and
learned Gentleman has not visited any

It is a
scandal that people should be asked to
wait three hours to get masks fitted. It
is then recorded that their masks have
been served.
I will now come to a conclusion in
order to give ample time to the Parliamentary Secretary to reply. The Parliamentary Secretary and those. working
with him may believe they are doing their
utmost, but the general public and those
taking an interest in this work do not
think so. They believe there is no encouragement being given by the Government. They hold the view that
encouragement is being withheld because
of the limited financial assistance A.R.P.
is getting, and until the Government relax the purse strings the outside. public
will gradually withdraw their sympathy,
and we will find ourselves in a very
awkward position if the peace of the
world is not maintained.
We will find ourselves in a very difficult position as compared with some of
the cities in England, Wales and Scotland. Therefore, I make an appeal to
the Parliamentary Secretary in the hope
that he will show that something of a
beneficial nature is being done in regard

That scheme should be in charge of a
Minister responsible to this House in
order to bring security and confidence
to the people in this area. If that is

A.R.P., because air raid precautions are
