terms of the Motion related only to
A.R.P., and since that was a matter
entirely under the control of the Ministry of Home Affairs, I was asked to
reply for the Government.
are
In attacking this problem we
breaking entirely new ground. We have
no standard against which to measure
our risk. For instance, we do not know
whether or not Northern Ireland will be
the object of attack at all. We do not
know whether, if enemy planes come,
they will
come as single spies or in
battalions. We do not know whether
we will be attacked by gas or high explosives, or by incendiary bombs or
otherwise. One of the duties of the Department is to make provision for the
treatment of casualties. No person can
tell me whether we have to make
arrangements for 5, 50, 500, or 5,000
casualties, and no matter from what
point you approach this problem the
risk is incalculable. That is the great
difficulty that presents itself to the Government. You have no yard-stick with
which to measure your risk. You do not
know in fact what you have got to guard
against, and the best you can do is, from
the most instructed information you
can obtain, to form an estimate of the
danger and try to take precautions
accordingly.
There are certain factors which
operate very greatly in our favour,
factors which lead to the hope, if not the
belief, that we may either escape entirely or at least be relatively immume
from the visits of enemy aircraft. It
is a fact that we are the most remote
large city of the United Kingdom from
any possible enemy base. It is approximately 550 miles from the nearest point
of any possible enemy base to this city,
and to visit us by the shortest route
involves a flight of 550 miles. It also
involves crossing the active defences of
Great Britain, and if the enemy wished
to avoid passing through the active
defences of Great Britain his journey is
increased by probably 200 miles.
In the course of his journey many
targets, presumably even more attractive
than that of Belfast or Northern Ireland, present themselves to the aviator
en route. But although these factors
operate very strongly in our favour I
have not found any support for the view
that Northern Ireland can hope to
escape from air attack. On the contrary,
the best opinion which we
can obtain
goes to show that a triangle which lies
between the three points, Donaghadee,
Belfast, Larne, must be treated as the
part of very real danger, with the city
and port of Belfast as the focal point of
attack.
Since the best information we could
get proceeded along these lines, the
question was as to the extent of our precautionary measures. When the Air

When, in 1938, the Air Raid Precautions Bill was introduced, we
were
in the unhappy position that nothing
was available. I remember an occasion,
a good many years ago, when I took the
stage in a play called "The Importance
of Being Earnest." I played the part
of the butler. My master came in and
asked me why there were no cucumbers.
I had to say "There were no cucumbers
in the market this morning"-he looked
at me very hard-"not even for ready
money." That was the position in
regard to equipment in the month of
September last; it was not available.
even for ready money. All we could do
at that time was to provide the nucleus
of a trained organisation, and that
trained organisation is now in existence
over a good part of the country, and
certainly in all the areas which can be
classed as the most vulnerable.
The situation has now changed very
rapidly in our favour. Production is
flowing very fast in Great Britain. The
hon. Member spoke of the question of
fire. One of the great dangers that we
visualise is the possibility of attack by

incendiary bombs, and any person who
has seen any of the demonstrations of
the thermite bomb must realise its

have arrived, ten more will be on the

number are on order, and will be

to a very considerable extent has already

in Belfast, the personnel has
has been

there will be more next week. The
particular type of pump which we have

and for immediate despatch to any place
in which a fire may break out. There
will be a very considerable number of
them in Belfast, with auxiliary personnel capable of working them. The
smaller type of pump is one which deals

The next question to which we had
to direct attention was the question of
evacuation. In the memorandum which
the hon. Member for Pottinger presented to the House on that occasion, he
proposed the evacuation of about
210,000 people. The Government have
not thought at present it was pressing to
make arrangements for extensive evacuation, for the reasons which I have
indicated-the distance and the
probability that if we are attacked we
shall be more likely to be attacked
sporadically than continuously. There
are approximately 65,000 school children
on the rolls of the public elementary
schools in Belfast, and of children below
the school age there are probably
another 35,000. That accounts for
about 100,000 children. A very considerable number of parents will not be
prepared to be separated from their
children. A very considerable number
have already made their own arrangements for the evacuation of their
children to friends in the country.
We have made plans for the evacuation of 50.000 children. We are making
a survey of the available accommodation
in the areas which we consider, from the
best information we have got, to be
relatively safe. That survey is at
present being made, and I hope to have
the results probably within a week. I
should like here to pay a tribute to the
prompt acceptance of obligations on the
part of the local authorities, quite unofficially, and for assistance given us,
in this conection, when we told them
that we were anxious to get this survey
made quickly. We called the clerks of
the local authorities together, and they
were extraordinarily good in making
arrangements to help.
This question of evacuation is a very
big problem in Belfast. The more you
look into it, the more difficulties present
themselves. We try to deal with them
as they arise. It is necessary to have a
band of people to accompany the
children to the country; it is necessary
to have reception committees in the
country. When they have got there, if
they are going to stay for a length of
time, arrangements will have to be made
for continuity of education, if that be
possible, or for adults to keep the
children occupied. You cannot leave
50,000 children in the country without
keeping them occupied. There are a
great many problems which have arisen,
and they are under consideration by the
staff of the Ministry who are working
at full pressure upon these questions.
and I hope that in the near future we
will be able to produce a workable
scheme.
No scheme will ever work without a
certain amount of confusion. A mother
will not be prepared for little Johnny
to go to Kilrea because it will be too
hard for her to visit him. All sorts of
human difficulties are bound to arise.
We are visualising them, and if an
emergency arises we shall be able very
promptly to clear out of this city
approximately 50,000 school children.
If we do that, I think we will have made
a very substantial contribution to
safety, and, where certain inconveniences occur, people will just have to
remember it is war.
The next problem which presented
itself was that of warning. Having
regard to all the information we have
received, it seems very doubtful whether
on every occasion we shall receive warning at all, because, in Spain at all

events, what is known as the technique
of the silent approach was developed by
the bombing planes. The plane attains
a great height, the engine is shut off,
and the machine volplanes down towards

hand, we may get warning once a plane
crosses a certain line in England heading in a certain direction. A system of
warnings which comes through from
Great Britain is in operation; it has
been tested and has proved satisfactory.
During the past few days the A.R.P.
Officer of Belfast Corporation has tested
the siren system which we propose to
adopt in this country, and from the date
of the outbreak of war it will not be
permissible to use a siren for any purpose other than as an air raid warning.
Then we come to the question of
shelters. Here, as everywhere else, we
are up against a most real difficulty.
The policy of deep bomb-proof shelters
which was advocated by the hon. Member for Pottinger, when the A.R.P. Bill
was before the House, has not found
favour with any authority. Generally
speaking, that policy has not been
accepted, and I think we may take it
that it has received very careful con-
If it is not necessary to
sideration.
have deep bomb-proof shelters in a place.
like London, I do not see how we in
the North of Ireland can possibly justify
their erection. If, in fact, we are not
going to get warning of air raids, our
air raid shelters are useless. But, in
addition to the other arguments which
may be presented against deep bombproof shelters for communal use in Great
Britain, there is one other objection in
this country, and that is that in those
areas where the density of population is
such as to render deep bomb-proof
shelters useful at all, the sub-soil is quite
unsuitable for their erection.
The policy in Great Britain has been
based mainly upon the Anderson Steel
Shelter. Its value. of course, lies in
the fact not that it will stop anything in.
the nature of a direct hit, but that by
reason of the angle of descent of the
bomb the house, generally speaking, will
stand between the bomb and the shelter,
and the shelter, although not proof
against a direct hit, is strong enough to
withstand the fall of masonry.
Basements is another policy in England,
but Belfast is not a city of basements. A
difficulty which the hon. Member for
Pottinger spoke of is that the houses we
have in Belfast, and, indeed, in all large
cities, are back to back, with only a small
yard and a four-foot passage. That is a
problem which is extremely difficult of
solution. I admit at once no really
satisfactory solution has been propounded, but the Anderson steel shelters.
hold the field at the moment. They are
not, unfortunately, yet available for
Northern Ireland. We have available
for what they are worth sandbags to the
extent of about two million. They will
be useful in certain events. A great deal
of merriment was caused by the sandbag
erection at the City Hall on the last
occasion. As an old soldier I agree it
was not satisfactory, but we will do
better next time.
The other matter which the Ministry
has under consideration is that of
hospital arrangements and casualty service. There, as I said a few moments
ago, arises the difficulty of measuring the
danger. Are we to provide for 500 or
5,000 casualties? We are not so badly
off as a matter of fact because we have
available at very short notice, almost instantaneously, approximately 1,300 beds
and 10,000 blankets. We will be able to
put our hands on these at short notice.
More than 3,000 persons have volunteered
under the National Service Scheme for
the nursing services. My Department is
in personal touch with the Joint Committee of the Order of St. John and the
British Red Cross.
All over Belfast, as anyone in touch
with the National Service movement is
aware, classes are going on continuously.
The nurses in the hospitals are going to
help us by giving our first-aid people
further training in actual nursing services. The hon. and gallant Member for
the University (Lieut-Colonel Mitchell),
the senior medical Member, has been
speaking to me on that subject, and has
made an offer on behalf of the Royal
Victoria Hospital, which we gratefully
accept. Whenever any emergency arises
the medical profession come out with the
most amazing generosity. I should like
to pay a tribute to the public spirit
shown by the medical profession throughout the whole of the negotiations in regard
to hospital arrangements and casualties.

In every way they are giving of their

Another matter which we are dealing

in the interest of the safety of the public

in regard to lighting. In the near future

blackout. I think the
will be
Bangor. We will have the co-operation

area
experiment. The season of the year

I have tried to outline to the House.
the lines along which the Ministry is
working. I have spoken early in this
debate for that reason. We want to get
from each Member of the House, all the
criticism and all the advice he can give
us. This, fortunately, is a question upon

everyone has the same aim in view. Every
person can make some contribution to
the safety of the public. I can promise,
on behalf of my Department, that any
suggestion which is made shall receive
the most careful consideration.
We are
working at very full pressure at the

defence. We are conscious, I was going

the great difficulties, but we shall be

Mr. BEATTIE: There is nothing in
the Parliamentary Secretary's reply to
which I wish to refer except one item
with which I disagree. He stated that
there is no proof of any authority
approving of the deep trench protection.
I gave that as a most perfect scheme of
protection. After examining the protective measures taken in Spain during
recent bombardments the present airraid protections in the city of Paris and
the Finsbury scheme, I feel that the only
authorities on A.R.P. are those who have
taken upon themselves the construction
of those deep shelters. Every one of the
areas I have mentioned has these shelters
and experts have expressed the opinion-
I have the names of the experts that
they are the only safe way of protecting
the citizens against all forms of air raids.
That is the only point to which I wish to
reply. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary accepts the opinion of the experts.

Mr. BAILEY: There are
matters of importance which I wish to
draw the attention of the Minister to and
which he did not refer to during his
Second Reading speech, and on these I
want to get an assurance from him. I
also wish to say that the statements which
are being made up and down the country
that the English scheme has broken down
and that the breakdown is due to the
contract system, are both untrue. I do
not know whether those who make those
statements are ignorant of the true facts
or whether they are trying to mislead
our producers. I am almost sure they
are trying to mislead. The contract system in England has not broken down and
it is significant that despite all the
difficulties which have been experienced
in England and in spite of the breakdown of the English scheme two years
ago, the English farmers asked for the
contract system to be re-established, and
that system in England has been and is
now a success.
The difficulties arose in England because more than half the pigs produced
go into the fresh meat market and are
outside the scheme altogether. In other
words, one farmer will take on a contract while his neighbour supplies the
fresh meat market. If there is a good
demand for the fresh meat the price
might go up by 5s or 10s a cwt., while
the man with the contract has to keep
on supplying at the contract or standard
price. He, of course, would be dissatisfied, and would resolve not to take on
another contract, with the result that
there were not enough pigs for the curer.
Another source of dissatisfaction is that
pigs have to be sent to the curers a very
long distance. That is one of the greatest
sources of complaint. They cannot get
enough for these particular curers because
when one man puts his on the fresh meat
market and gets a higher price his neighbours become dissatisfied.
None of these conditions apply here.
For all practical purposes we have only
one outlet, the bacon factory, and there
are at present more pigs than the factory
has been able to take. As I read this
Bill the Minister has devised the scheme
in such a way that the smallest producer
in the country can take advantage of it
just the same as the larger producer. By
the system of registration, under which
I understand the small man can register
and supply from one up to 30 pigs, the
Minister has robbed the contract system
of most of the worry as far as the small
producer is concerned. A point which I

The hon. Member for Antrim raised
the point that he feared some of the
producers would be scared of the contract system. I must admit that none
of us is very keen about the contract
system, because we realise that farmers
in the backward parts of this country

simple indeed. He would have preferred that contracts were to be made

difficulty that arises is that the curers
quite definitely object to the fact that
the Board, being curers themselves,

pigs. I do not think the hon. Gentleman need fear that the position will be
SO altered that it may upset the
producer.
The producer is in this position-he
can either make a direct contract with
a curer, or, if he feels that that is going
to tie him too much, he can make an
open contract through the Board.
He
simply says to the Board, "I am prepared to enter into a contract. Will the
pigs be distributed?" I do not think
there is anything very terrible about
that. Coming to the registered man,
producing up to 30 pigs, I wish to point
out that in the normal course of events,
as he does at present, he will say to the
curer, "I have so many pigs." Except
for the actual signing of the contract,
and the obligation that it has to be
within certain limits, there is really no
very great change. I think the great
fear of the contract system which exists
in this country is really imaginary.
The hon. Member for West Down
raised a point about the position of the
pedigree breeders who sell a number of
their pedigree pigs for breeding purposes, the number depending on the
condition of the market. I would point
out to him that a substantial amount of
protection exists in the contract.
Secondly, and most important of all, it
is necessary to remember that such
sales of pedigree stock only take place
because the price is much higher than
the commercial value. If a producer is
likely to be short of his contract, he
can always buy pigs to make up either
from the Board or from other producers.
I should like to deal with the points
which have been raised by the hon.
Member who moved the rejection of the
Bill, and the two hon. Gentlemen who
supported him. The story of price control in the past is this. The price was
controlled because the British Government limited the imports of bacon into
this country. Now the British Government, in view of possible future trade.
arrangements, have made up their minds
that they may wish to allow a greater
quantity of bacon into this country, and
consequently the price would crash or
be considerably lower than it is at
present. That would answer the hon.
Member for Pottinger. The actual
price which is paid to the producer,
which the curer has guaranteed, will
not affect the actual price of bacon.
because there will probably be larger
amounts of bacon allowed into this
country than there were before. The
consumer will not be affected in any way
by the Bill; but, if there is any anxiety
about this, I will certainly consider any
representations that the hon. Gentleman
may make to me.
I am just as anxious
as he is to see that the consumers get
fair crack of the whip and are not imposed upon.
If this Bill is rejected, the producers
in this country will be at the mercy of
perhaps a flood of imports of bacon. I
cannot say how much it will be or how
little; but in view of the British Government arrangement, the Treasury assistance, and their desire to make trade
agreements with other countries, there
is every probability, to say the least of
it, that bacon will be allowed in, anyhow in sufficient quantities, to reduce
the present price of bacon. What is the
answer that the hon. Member for North
Derry is going to give to the farmers if
their prices go down? Is he going to

I cannot see how it is possible to have a
half-way house, when the Minister is
finally responsible to this House. The
only alternative is to have these Boards
entirely away from all Government control. Then, of course, the Minister is
not responsible. I cannot see the House
giving that control. I cannot see any
Minister bringing forward a Bill which
would suggest it, and, therefore, as I
said, the dislike to losing producercontrol is answered-the nigger in the
woodpile. It is not a question of the
value of the Bill or whether it is going
to assist the farmers. The hon. Member for North Derry said that perhaps he
had a bee in his bonnet about producercontrol. Surely the important thing is
not producer-control, but how we can
help the farmers. In this Bill we have
something which is going to give a price
insurance. If you do not pass the Bill then
there is no insurance, but the possibility
of serious loss to the farmers. We are
not, for financial reasons, in a position
to go outside the four walls of the
English Bill. It is agreed by the
English Treasury that this Measure ist
within the four walls, but I am not in
a position to explain the position as well
as my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance. If we remain within those
four walls, then we are in a position to
deduct from the moneys normally paid
into England £400,000 in any one year.
I think that is correct.
Hon. Members say why not have a
subsidy here. They are suggesting something impossible, something which would
compel my right hon. Friend to put on
further taxation to cover the expense.
I am hoping these gentlemen will realise
the danger of suggesting that other
schemes should come into force. I cannot introduce any scheme which will
benefit the farmers as much as this one
will. As I pointed out in my speech
introducing the Bill, if a price insurance
is brought into force in England, and if-
I admit there are "ifs," but we are living
in hope the assistance is greater than it
is at the present time, Northern Ireland
will benefit to the same extent. If we do
not go on with this scheme we would not
have any argument to put forward for
asking the British Government to allow
Northern Ireland farmers to have the
same assistance as the farmers on the
other side. If that happened I would
have no argument to put forward in the
event of a price insurance scheme being
introduced for other commodities.
I hope the House will realise that
something of real worth has been introduced, that we have made it a simpler
and easier Bill to work than the English
one, and that in the end, contrary to the
expectations of the Jeremiahs I repeat
that word-we shall be successful and do
something which will be of real assistance
to the agriculturists of this country.

11 MAY 1939
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In introducing the Estimates.
for the current financial year I propose
to deal mainly with those new developments which the Department has been
carrying out during the past twelve
months.
Last year I gave a comprehensive
review of the various activities of the
Department of the Ministry of Labour
and I feel hon. Members will not expect me to go minutely into every detail
of the work, but I shall be glad to give
every information possible to the members with reference to those Departments
of the Ministry that I have not dealt
with in the course of my statement to
the House here this evening.
The total net Estimates of the Ministry
of Labour for the current financial year
amount in round figures to six and a
quarter million pounds. Ten years ago
the total was just under there millions.
In ten years, therefore, the Exchequer
provision for the services administered
by the Ministry of Labour has more than
doubled. If we look at the year 1922-23,
the first full financial year of the operation of the Ministry, and include the
cost of old age pensions, which was then
carried on the Vote of the Ministry of
Finance, we find that the Exchequer provision was £1,691,000, so that hon.
Members will observe that the Ministry
of Labour services have grown almost
four-fold, and their proportion of the
total net Estimates for all Northern Ire
land services has increased from under
one-quarter to just over one-half.
We entered the financial year that has
just closed with the register of unemployment at the high figure of over 94,000.
At the end of the financial year it had
fallen by 7,300 to a figure of 87,000.
throughout the year, until the usual
The numbers diminished fairly regularly
seasonal rise in outdoor occupations
began in November. During the three
months of mid-winter, the register began
to show its usual seasonal rise. This, of
course, is accentuated since our figures
began to include agricultural workers.
The peak was reached in January, but it
was lower by 4,600 than in January of
the year before. Since then, I am glad
to report to the Committee, that there
has been a steady fall in the register,
the total decrease being 13,000. Unemployment in the shipbuilding and ship-

repairing group fell by nine points between April 1938, and April, 1939, the
linen group by seven and a half points,
and the making-up group by three and
a half points.
The
Unfortunately, I am sorry to say, the
position in agriculture is not so good, as
farming operations were retarded by the
weather in the early spring of this year.
The question of unemployment is a
grave one and it has always given the
Government serious concern. I have
already spoken in this strain in the House
on a previous occasion, but I should like
to emphasise once again that the monthly
unemployment figures do not by any
means represent a standing body of
persons permanently out of work.
composition of the register is constantly
changing; numbers going off into employment and others coming on week by
week according as spells of work begin
and end. For example, when the count
was taken last month of those on the
register who were applying for insurance
benefit or unemployment allowances,
almost one-quarter of the applicants had
been out of work for less than four weeks,
and little more than half of the unemployed persons had been out of work for
more than three months.
We are anxious about the position, and
we are doing our utmost to stimulate
industry and agriculture and so increase
the volume of work for our unemployed
people. Since 1922 the Ministry has
consistently encouraged local authorities
and public bodies to carry out employment schemes by offering very liberal
grants. The rate of grant was raised in
March, 1938, to 85 per cent. of the wages
cost, and during the last financial year I
am glad to say 87 schemes were
sanctioned at a total estimated labour
cost of £330,000, providing employment
for some 5,000 men.
Last year I mentioned that we were
looking forward to promoting a new
Factories Act. This Act has now been
passed, and it comes into general effect on
the 1st July. It has been, if I may say
so, an outstanding and far-reaching event
in industrial legislation. The important
changes in the Factory Code which it
effects has made necessary a large amount
of preparatory work. Much of this has
been of an intructional nature-advising
factory occupiers on their new responsibilities and on such changes as will be
Ministry of Labour 146
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
necessary in the running of their undertakings.
Hon. Members will remember that the
Holidays With Pay Act came into operation on the 24th November, 1938. Under
this Act trade boards are empowered to
arrange for holidays with pay up to a
maximum of one week for workers for
whom a minimum rate of wages or remuneration has been or is being fixed.
Action in this direction has already been
taken by five trade boards, and in seven
other boards notice of motion to apply
the provisions of the Act has been given.
The Act also empowers the Ministry to
facilitate voluntary agreements for
holidays with pay in trades not already
covered by the Trade Boards Act, and
I can
assure the Committee that the
Department will give every assistance to
the industries concerned to arrive. at
agreements which I hope will prove
acceptable to all parties concerned in
industry.
I am glad to say we in Northern
Ireland continue to enjoy a freedom from
stoppages of work due to trade disputes.
In all cases it has been the aim of the
Department to incorporate, in settlements, provisions for the avoidance. of
disputes and the proper negotiation of
future differences. Attention has also
been given to setting up standing voluntary machinery for negotiating agreements for wages and conditions of work
in the various industries.
The latest developments cover the electricity supply industry, the cinema trade,
the wholesale. and retail drapery trade,
and the wholesale boot and shoe and
leather trade. A Joint Industrial
Council was also recently formed in the
provender milling industry. The trade
agreement, I always feel, is the treaty
of peace in industry, and experience with
such compacts warrants the conclusion
that they constitute the most effective
agency for the promotion of industrial
goodwill.
Hon. Members will be interested to
hear that the special voluntary insurance
scheme which came into operation in
January, 1938, has been more successful
than we at first anticipated. During the
first three months of its operation
approximately 6,000 persons applied to
join the scheme. From the end of
October there was a marked increase as a
result of steps taken to remind the publie
of the special terms for those who applied
to become members during the initial
year. Between November and the close
of the initial year over 15,000 applica
tions were received, and we expect that
the number ultimately admitted on the
special terms will be about 18,000.
I would like to refer to the arrange
ments we have made with the Ministry
of Labour in Great Britain for the training of unemployed young men. We are
specially interested in the young me
who have never had an opportunity of
embarking on an industrial career, and
we were anxious that these young mer
should get an opportunity of learning
some new occupation that would fit ther
to take their place as citizens of this
country. Consequently we
arrangement with the Ministry of Labour
in Great Britain to train a number cí
young men who, through instructional
centres in Great Britain obtain intensive
instruction in trades where prospects of
employment are good. Every care
taken to choose, the most suitable persons
and strict regard is paid to the prospect
of employment at the end of ther
training.
came to an
The majority of the trainees have been
placed in the engineering trades, wher
there is the greatest demand for workers
Over 300 have undergone training, and
those who have completed their courses
have been placed in employment in Great
Britain. We also provide training &
Gravesend Sea School for boys who wish
to go to sea, and I am glad to say a
number have. availed themselves of this
opportunity.

Early in January we undertook, in cooperation with the Ministry of Labour
in Great Britain, to help in furthering

ment for National Service continues to

And now, I come to the figures in
the Estimates themselves. Of the seven
Votes that I am presenting to-day four
show increases, and three show decreases
I shall deal first with the four showing
increases. Vote 1 for the expenses of
the Ministry shows a net increase of
just over £19,000. Actually, however,
only £4,000 of this represents increased
gross expenditure. The Committee will
remember that last year it was decided
to abolish the deduction from the
remuneration of dispensary medical
officers under the Medical Benefit
Scheme. Accordingly, that source of
income is no longer available to the
Ministry as an appropriation-in-aid.
So far, therefore, as net expenditure
under this Vote is concerned, the
position is that over £15.000 of the
apparent increase is due to a falling off
in appropriations - in - aid and only
slightly over £4,000 to increased
expenditure. This increase of £4,000
is due, in part, to additional staff required for the administration of the new
Factories Act and for the better control
of unemployment benefit, and in part
to the normal increments in salary.
As regards Vote 3, I am estimating
for a net increase of £75,000. This increase is not due, however, to any estimated increase in the live register of
unemploved, which, indeed, we assume
will be lower than the average for last
financial year. There will be a consequent increase in the income of the
Fund by way of stamp sales with an
expected addition of £8,000 in the Exchequer grant provided in Sub-head A.
We have, however, an obligation
under the Reinsurance Agreement to

keep our Fund in parity with the Unemployment Fund in Great Britain. I

The increase of £56,000 in Vote 5 is due

Contributors Act. The
Act. The Exchequer is

About 18,000 persons are concerned and

As regards Vote 7, I have already
mentioned that we expect unemployment to be less during the current
financial year than during the
just ended. We do not, however, expect that the reduction will be reflected
in the payments to be made by way of
unemployment allowances. I am advised that the saving is more likely to
accrue in unemployment benefit, and
that there may be a small increase in
the amount paid in assistance. I have,
accordingly, provided in the Estimates
for a slight increase in the numbers of
staff required to administer the scheme,
and this, together with normal increments of salary, is responsible for the
increase of about £2,000 in the Vote.
I shall now deal with the three Votes
that show decreases. Vote 2 is the
provision that Parliament is asked to
make for State grant to the National
Health Insurance Scheme. On the advice of the Government actuary, we are
asking for about £3,400 less during
1939-40, based on our experience of the

Services.

The main items in this Vote
are, the Exchequer grants to local authorities for employment schemes under subhead A, and the cost of the various
training and instruction activities of the
Department. Hon. Members will notice
that the estimated total gross expenditure is almost unchanged, as compared
with last year, at about £167,000. But
there are substantial variations in the
first three sub-heads. Taking into
account our existing commitments, and
making a provision for new schemes that
we expect to approve, we are asking for
£130,000 for grants to local authorities
for schemes of employment. This is
£17,000 less than last year. Expenditure
under this sub-head is dependent on the
progress made by local authorities in
carrying out
out works that have been
approved. Should it be found necessary
to spend more money a Supplementary
Estimate, will be presented.
Sub-heads B and C deal with the provision for juvenile instruction. Since
last year's Estimates were presented I
have received the report of the committee appointed by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, while he
presided over the destinies of the Ministry of Labour, to advise. the Department
on this subject. We have decided to
accept the report of that committee,
which, as hon. Members will remember,
was presided over by Mr. F. W. Ogilvie,
former Vice-Chancellor of Queen's
University. The scheme of instruction
which we contemplate will necessarily
take some time to put into operation, as
arrangements and details have to be discussed with education authorities. I
hope, however, that the classes will be in
being at a number of centres by 1st
October, 1939.
Accordingly, I am asking Parliament
to make provision for an Exchequer grant
appropriate to the part of the financial
year during which we hope the scheme
will operate. The arrangement is that
the courses will be organised by education
authorities, and that, on average, 75
per cent. of the cost will be met by the
State. Although the gross expenditure
on this Vote remains at approximately
the same as for last year, the net expenditure is estimated at almost £19,000
less. The reason is that larger appropriations come from the Unemployment

and Assistance Funds, due to increased
expenditure on training and instruction,
of which the cost can be recovered by

Vote. 6 makes provision for the cost of
"over 70" old age pensions. We are asking for £4,000 less than last year. The
reason for the decrease is, not that we
shall have fewer pensioners, but that
during 1939-40 there will be only 52
pay days as against 53 in 1938-39.
That completes my survey of the Estimates which I submit to the Committee
this afternoon, but as this is the first
time I have. had the honour of submitting
the Votes as Minister of Labour-I have,
of course, presented them in former years
as Parliamentary Secretary-I am sure
the Committee will forgive me if I take
this opportunity of paying a tribute to
the way the staff of the Department, at
headquarters, in the employment
exchanges, and in the outdoor inspectorate, have carried out their duties.
The Ministry of Labour comes more
closely into touch with the lives and the
feelings of the people than any other
Department of our Government, and it
is a source of great gratification to me
constantly to hear of the unfailing
courtesy and helpfulness shown by the
officers of the Department in their manifold dealings with the public. I should
also like to take this opportunity of expressing my warm and sincere appreciation of the help I have had from every
officer of the senior grade since my
appointment as Minister.
Then there is a great body of publicspirited persons in the community who
act on the numerous committees which
are associated with the activities of the
Department, and who give their services.
quite voluntarily, and are of great assistance in securing proper administration.
They have done much to smooth the difficulties that confront the Department,
and I should like to offer them the
warmest thanks of the Government for
all their services. I think it is but
fitting that I should specially mention.
the great help I have received from my
friend, the Parliamentary Secretary.
especially in carrying out the National
Service campaign. The continued success
of the scheme is largely due to his cooperation, and no words of mine could
adequately express my appreciation of his
work. I beg to move.

I want to refer to the question of old

It is a terrible tragedy to see the people
up in years trying to keep the little
home together, and trying to exist on
10s a week. I do not know how it is

poor.
The chief matter referred to in these
Estimates and the subject of the principal
allocation of the finances is the question
of unemployment. The hon. Member for
Windsor (Mr. Dowling), who sits opposite
to me, made a remarkable speech on this
question of unemployment some months
ago, and it would be of very great
assistance. to this Committee in reaching
some decision as to how to tackle this
problem if the Member for Windsor
would give us the benefit and privilege of
the facts and figures he set out in that

about unemployment. I do not care how
much of a bore I become-it is quite
immaterial to me whether other Members
think me a bore or not-I am going to
keep on reiterating that we have to do
something about the unemployment question. I do not care how I bore certain
Members here, I am going on reiterating
that until I get something done. Something must be, done. We cannot go on
accepting as a permanent basis of our
existence the presence of almost 100,000
unemployed. We have no right to sit
here as legislators if we are not going to
do something about it. I am very glad
to see that the figures were substantially
reduced lately, and I believe they could
be further reduced in various ways.
I am going to repeat the suggestion
that we should set up a Select Committee, representative of every party in
this House, to hear evidence from every
part of the Province and from every interest in the Province as to how this great
evil of unemployment could be definitely
cured. I still refuse to believe that there
is no cure for it. I am optimistic enough
to believe that if we cannot cure it entirely we can very substantially reduce it.
One of the schemes put forward by the
Government for the reduction of unemployment and for providing additional
employment in rural areas took the form
of grants for drainage works. Unfortunately the grants were restricted to
holdings of a certain poor-law valuation. I
think it would be a good step for us to
take it would be a small one, but it
would still help-if we removed entirely
any restrictions on the grants.

15s per week for a period, and after

Is that justice? It is not, and I demand

to me.

than three months out of employment.
The hon. Member said he could not

many of the same faces day after day.
There may be many reasons for that.
Might I suggest to him, not very
seriously, that as he is a constant visitor

there could, if they had an opportunity

31,000 men, which makes a total of 36,000

There are hundreds and thousands of

the matter. I know from previous experience that the hon. Member for Pottinger has no love for the Unemployment

The
to come before everything else.
Minister being a loyal Minister of the

he possibly could to this question of
National Service.
The hon. and gallant Member for
Cromac (Major Sinclair) raised the question of the administrative costs of unemployment assistance and said it looked as
if the expenditure under this head was
very heavy. It is true that the cost of
unemployment assistance is much greater
than that of unemployment insurance.
That is natural because in unemployment
insurance the person has simply to walk
down to the exchange and make his claim.
When it is investigated if he has sufficient
stamps and meets the statutory requirements he is entitled to benefit. Unemployment assistance is a different matter
altogether. The means test applies, and
investigations have to be made to find out
the income going into the home. You do
not always get the correct information
when you make your investigations, and
many sources have to be tapped before
this matter is definitely fixed up.
Therefore it does cost much more to
administer unemployment assistance
than unemployment insurance. I would
like to point out that unemployment
assistance in Northern Ireland is administered much more cheaply than in Great
Britain, and, of course, there it is higher
than unemployment insurance. I appreciate the point that the hon. and gallant
member put forward. In regard to the
cost, he will realise from the. facts that
I have put before him that it is very
necessary that the taxpayers' money
should be administered very wisely, and
that every precaution should be taken
to see that there is no abuse of the scheme.
The hon. Member for South Down
(Mr. Brown) said quite a lot of things
that I am in entire agreement with, but
in regard to other things I am not in
agreement. I would like to point out to
him that there has been a considerable
amount of Government work in con-

Mr. MacDERMOTT: I have been
instructed by the Joint Select Committee
on Transport to draw your attention to
an article in yesterday's issue of the
"Daily Mail," as published in Belfast,
which appears to the Committee to raise
a question of Parliamentary privilege.
Before referring you to the article I have
mentioned, it should be stated that,
following the usual practice of this Parliament, the Committee has conducted its
business in private, and that on Saturday, 6th May, there was circulated to
Members of the Committee for their
perusal and consideration a draft report.
This was a confidential document, and
was clearly so marked. The article referred to is entitled, "Transport Problem in Ulster Budget." After a reference to the problems confronting the
Minister of Finance the article proceeds
as follows:
M.P.'s, especially those who have
been sitting on the. Select Committee to
consider transport, await the Budget
with exceptional interest, for they have
had the position summarised to them in
these words:
And then there. is a quotation:
"The transport experiment will cost
the Government more than £4,000,000,
of which a good half will probably
never show any return."
That
That is the end of the quotation.
quotation, with the exception of one or
two transposed words, is taken verbatim
from the draft report to which I have referred. Then follows the paragraph,
which reads:
They have also been reminded that
whatever proportion this loss may
assume elsewhere it is, for a country of
the size and resources of Northern
Ireland, a most serious embarrassment
which cannot be repeated without grave
consequences to the community.
That also, except for the two or three
opening words, is taken verbatim from
the draft report. They are not within
quotation marks. I do not wish to be
taken as suggesting that the quotations
from the draft report which have thus
been published are in themselves of vital
importance. But it seems to the Committee that deliberate quotation from a
confidential document raises a question of
principle, which, if ignored, may result
in the continuation and development of
what is now complained of.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that a
copy of the draft report has been for a
whole afternoon on the table of the Chief
Whip's office out there?

THE BUDGET.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Financial Statement, 1939-40.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): I propose again to follow the
usual practice. of reviewing briefly the
general industrial position in the year
that has gone, and of referring to the
prospects of the future, before entering
on my main task-that of accounting for
my stewardship during the past year and
of revealing my proposals for the current
one. Hon. Members know that the prosperity of every country, and especially of
an exporting one such as ours, depends
largely upon the state of world trade.
The great extent to which the industries
of Northern Ireland rely on export
markets was brought out very strikingly
by my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Commerce, when he introduced the
Estimates of his Department a few weeks
ago.
It is inevitable, therefore, that the
volume of our industrial activity has been
and is still being affected by the insecurity
caused by what is happening, unfortunately, in the Far East, in Spain,
and, above all, in Central Europe. Over
these unhappy events the Government
has no control. And yet, in their
economic aspects, as well as in other ways,
they injure, our export trade gravely and,
of course, create unemployment, for they
undermine that confidence and security
without which industry cannot thrive.
Considering the acuteness of the international tension and the widespread disturbances in our world markets, it is
remarkable how well our economic and
industrial life has stood the strain
The future, of world affairs is still uncertain. We have ground for hope, however, that, as the defensive strength of
the Empire grows and the community of
nations prepared to resist armed
aggression becomes more closely knit, the
awful catastrophe of war that threatens
civilisation will recede, and give place to
an enduring peace. The time must
surely come when the people of the world
will realise that war settles nothing, and
that force as a principle of policy in
international relations must give way to
reason and justice.. The test of prosperity
in every State is-how do the masses
live? What measure of life in its fullest
sense is enjoyed by all within its borders?
On this occasion I can deal only with
financial and economic aspects.
I have already said that we should be
encouraged by the strength which
industries have shown, even in face of
the abnormal strains to which they have
been subject for several years. Those
engaged in our linen industry have shown
courage and perseverance in very difficult
Minister's Financial Statement 1512
The Budget-
16 MAY 1939
times, and the new Trade Agreement
between the United Kingdom and the
United States of America should ultimately prove of considerable value to all
who are engaged in our historic industry.
So far as shipbuilding is concerned,
the prospects of this industry have improved during the last few weeks. Our
shipbuilding yard has recently received
contracts for two important ships for
His Majesty's Navy, and our loans
guarantee facilities, together with the
British Government's scheme for the
assistance of shipping and shipbuilding,
have resulted in orders being placed
locally for a considerable number of cargo
vessels, particulars of which will be
announced in due course.
The building and allied industries will
be helped by our housing measures,
which should not only give useful employment, but should improve greatly the
housing conditions in Northern Ireland.
An extensive programme of building and
public works is also being put in hand
here by the United Kingdom Government under the Defence Scheme, as well
as by our own Government and by our
local authorities and public bodies.
The capacity of our manufacturers is
proved by the number and variety of very
substantial contracts that have been entrusted to them under the rearmament
programme, and the establishment of the
important aeroplane. industry in our
midst proves how adaptable our workpeople are to new processes of manufacture.
The legislation that this Parliament
has passed to broaden the base of our
industrial activities is being justified.
We are making steady progress towards
this end, progress which is all the more
satisfactory because we are aiming at
"long term" results. During the past
financial year the Government has undertaken to advance to firms qualified for
assistance under the New Industries Acts,
loan assistance totalling approximately
£270,000 of which £72,000 has been
issued to date and annual rental grants
amounting approximately to an aggregate sum of £3,000; in addition, contributions towards the income tax payable
by twenty-four firms have been agreed
upon.
Our London Office already performs a
useful service in this respect, not only
in attracting new customers and industries to this part of the Kingdom, but
also in assisting our industrialists to make
their products still better known in Great
Britain and elsewhere.
Agriculture, our chief industry, has
greatly benefited by the efforts of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture,
and in consequence of our position within
the United Kingdom we are reaping the
full advantages of the increasing assistance which the Government at Westminster is giving to the development of
an industry which is of such vital importance to the. Kingdom.
May I say, however, that I believe we
should guard against the growing
tendency to consider that it is the duty
of the Government to give more and more
help from public funds to everyone in
the community, and to expect the State to
take an excessive part in the development
of industry and the promotion of trade.
If this were carried out beyond reasonable limits it would be altogether inconsistent with that private enterprise,
personal initiative and responsibility, to
which Ulster has owed so much in the
past. Even some of our local authorities and public bodies appear to imagine
that the funds at my disposal are inexhaustible. They forget that our
financial relations with the Exchequer of
the United Kingdom are based upon
equality throughout the Kingdom, and
that the happy and helpful relations that
exist between the British Treasury and
my Ministry are due to mutual confidence
and to a realisation of the fact that we
here desire only a fair deal as co-partners
in the Kingdom's welfare.
Whatever concessions I feel
can be
afforded I willingly give, but I admit
that I am slow to enter into "long term"
financial engagements. I have always to
remember that taxation is abnormally
high as compared with the past, owing
to the necessities of defence. If it comes
to be reduced, as the international situation, we trust, ceases to be so menacing,
our revenues will diminish. It is then
that our financial position will be strained
unless expenditure can be brought down
to at least a similar degree.
Expenditure, 1938-39.
I shall now follow the normal practice
of reviewing the figures of the past year
before considering the problems of the
future.

CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
Dealing first of all with the expenditure, we find that Consolidated Fund
Services, apart from the Road Fund and
the self-balancing item of the Milk Industry Assistance Grant, accounted for
£665,570, or £194,570 above the Estimate. This large increase in expenditure
over the Estimate is due to the fact that,
owing to the satisfactory state of our
revenues at the end of the financial year,
I was able to allocate a sum of approximately £196,000, not provided for in
last year's Budget, in repayment of sums.
borrowed in previous years for meeting
instalments of principal falling due in
respect of loans guaranteed under the
Loans Guarantee Acts, and so to clear
these borrowings off our books.
ROAD FUND.
The Road Fund payment of £635,549
is £35,451 less than the Budget Estimate.
The actual receipts from the duties on
private cars were approximately £8,000
less than the Estimate, which was due to
a decrease in the number of new registrations. The balance of the decrease is
largely attributed to the fact that the
revenue from goods vehicles in 1937-38
was inflated by the inclusion of a large
number of vehicles acquired by the.
Transport Board which were taxed when
acquired, but which were subsequently
taken off the road by the Board. This
applies to as many as 600 vehicles.
INTEREST ON BORROWINGS.
The Committee will observe that the
Exchequer issues in respect of interest on
temporary borrowings were about £1,800
under the Estimate, which is a very
satisfactory index of the financial
stability of
our Government, having
regard to the financial repercussions of
the past eventful year. The average rate
of discount for bills accepted by tender
from the money market was only 11s 6d
per cent. per annum for 1938-39.
MILK GRANT.
The expenditure out of the grant from
the Imperial Government in aid of our
creamery industry was £2,038.
SUPPLY SERVICES.
The Budget Estimate for Supply
Services was £11,048,666; to this must

the new service of air raid precautions,

The actual expenditure for the year
was £11,470,091; a gross saving of
£324,710.

been realised. Stamp duties also show a

for the current year. The

CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
In the item of £91,000 for interest on
borrowings, the sum of £21,000 is
included for interest on Treasury bills.
Last September the clearing banks placed
a ban on the acceptance of bills that were
not eligible for rediscount at the Bank of
England. Northern Ireland Treasury
Bills, in common with those of local
authorities in Great Britain, were not at
that time rediscountable at the Bank of
England. This ban would undoubtedly
have increased very substantially the cost
of our Treasury bills. Representations.
were accordingly made by my Department to the Treasury, and satisfactory
arrangements were concluded, which
have resulted in our bills being accepted
by all banks on the same footing as
British Treasury bills. In view, however, of the general rise in interest rates
due to the state of the money market, I
have made an increased provision for this
item for 1939-40.

in Table II) representing the annual payment to the Imperial Government of the
"new" land purchase annuities (estimated at £300,000) and the loans made
to local authorities in Northern Ireland
prior to the transfer of services to this
Government (estimated at £50,000).
These two sums, therefore, which are
balanced by a corresponding receipt,
account for a total of £350,000.
Finally, I have provided as a charge
on the revenues of this year a sum representing a payment that will fall to be
made to the United Kingdom Government during the year as an adjustment
of the Northern Ireland residuary share
of reserved taxes in respect of an overpayment for the year 1937-38. Hon.
Members are aware that the payments
made to our Government in respect of
reserved taxes in any year are provisional
payments, which are based on estimates
made at the beginning of the year of the
expected yield of reserved taxes in Northern Ireland. The actual outurn of the
year is not known until some twelve
months after the end of the financial year.
owing to the necessity of applying a process of attribution to various items of
revenue which, although collected in
Great Britain, are properly due to the
Northern Ireland Exchequer, and vice
versa.
An adjustment of this nature
between the two Exchequers has, therefore, to be made two years later and falls
to be met from the revenue of that year.
I anticipate that in 1939-40 an adjusting payment from our Exchequer to the
United Kingdom Exchequer will be due
in respect of the year 1937-38, and I
have provided for this purpose a sum of
£123,000.
SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES.
I have now to consider what margin
should be allowed for Supplementary
Estimates for charges likely to arise
during the present year, and for which no
provision has been made in the Estimates
already presented to Parliament. Hon.
Members know that a Civil Defence Bill
has recently been before the British.
House of Commons, and that substantial
expenditure on civil defence and air raid
precautions in Great Britain is anticipated during the current year. A sum
of £188,000 has been included in the Air
Raid Precautions Estimates that have
been presented to this House for similar
services in Northern Ireland. I anticipate, however, that before the end of the
financial year a further substantial sum
will be needed for air raid precautions
and civil defence.
Secondly, there is the cost of the
arrangement arrived at with the Belfast
Harbour Commissioners, in which the
Government has undertaken to make a
grant of 25s for every 20s contributed
to the dredging scheme to be undertaken
by the Commissioners to enable ships of
the largest type to be launched from our
Minister's Financial Statement1520
The Budget-
16 MAY 1939
shipyard. I understand from the
Harbour Commissioners that this work
has already begun, and a charge will,
therefore, fall upon the Exchequer for
the Government's proportion of the cost.
of this work. I am, therefore, providing
a sum of £200,000 as provision for a
Supplementary Estimate for the two
services of Civil Defence and the grant
to the Belfast Harbour.
The total estimated expenditure for the
year (including possible Supplementary
Estimates) is, therefore, £16,192,000.

Before arriving at the amount available for the Imperial contribution I have
to consider, first, whether any changes
in our
revenue should be made, and,
secondly, whether there are any further
items of expenditure likely to emerge
during the coming year for which I have
not made provision, and which would
have to be met from this margin.
I have mentioned that in his recent
Budget the British Chancellor of the
Exchequer has increased certain taxes in
order to meet the additional defence expenditure. These increases will have the
effect of spreading the additional burden
over all classes of the community. The
increase in sur-tax has affected the
wealthy, the increases in sugar and
tobacco duties all classes, and as these
are reserved taxes they are. automatically
applied to Northern Ireland, and our
citizens will bear their full share.
Another change in taxation is the
increase in the duties on private, motorcars, and it will be remembered that the
Chancellor proposed this increase as a
substitute for a further increase. in
income tax. Motor vehicle duties in
Northern Ireland are, however, entirely
within the control of this House.
I had, therefore, to consider whether I
should propose an increase in duty
Minister's Financial Statement 1524
The Budget-
16 MAY 1939
similar to that proposed in Great Britain,
bearing in mind that for some years our
motor vehicle duties, both on private cars
and on commercial vehicles were kept in
excess of the British rates in order to
meet the liabilities of our Road Fund.
Gradually, as the financial position of the
Fund improved, we. have been able to
remove, except in one small item, of
which the Committee are aware, the last
remaining differences in motor taxation
between the two areas.
It is evident that at the present time
the Road Fund as such does not require
an increase in revenue in order to meet
its liabilities, but this is not the purpose
for which the increase in duties in Great
Britain has been made. It is to meet
defence expenditure, and I have come to
the conclusion that Northern Ireland
must equally contribute her increased
share.
Mr. BEATTIE: Step by step.
Mr. ANDREWS: Accordingly, I propose that, as from the 1st January next,
the duties
on private motor-cars and
motor-cycles shall be raised to the same
level as is proposed in the British Budget,
that is to say, that the duty on private
motor vehicles will be 25s
horse power,
per
with somewhat smaller increases in the
duties on motor-cycles. I do not propose, however, to increase the existing
duties on commercial or agricultural
vehicles or duty of £2 on a private car
used for drawing a trailer. I anticipate
that the additional yield from these
duties will provide a sum of £200,000 in
a full year and £100,000 this year, and
this yield will enable a corresponding
increase to be made. in the amount available for Imperial contribution.
Hon. Members may be aware that in
Great Britain the Road Fund is not now
fed directly by the Consolidated Fund
out of the yield of motor vehicle duties as
it is in Northern Ireland. The duties
are retained, like other taxes, in the
Exchequer, and a sum is voted each year
in the. Estimates sufficient to defray the
estimated expenses of the Road Fund for
the year in question. In Great Britain,
therefore, the whole of the proposed
increase will accrue to the Exchequer.
In Northern Ireland, under existing
legislation, the Exchequer merely retains
25 per cent. of the yield of the duties on
private cars and cycles, the remainder of
the duties on motor vehicles being transferred to the Road Fund. In order that
the full benefit of the increase in these
duties may be made available for
Imperial needs it would mathematically
be necessary to raise the amount of the
private vehicle duties to be retained in
the Exchequer from 25 per cent. to 55
per cent. I realise, however, that the
effect of the increased duties may be to
diminish the number of vehicles or reduce.
the average horse power. Allowing,
therefore, for these factors, I propose
that the. Exchequer shall, from the 1st
January next, retain 50 per cent. instead
of 55 per cent. of the duties on private
cars and motor-cycles. I estimate,
therefore, that the. receipts of the Road
Fund itself should not be affected by this
change.
Another increase in taxation proposed
by the British Chancellor, which does
not affect our Reserved Revenue, is the
increase in the duty on estates exceeding
£50,000 by 10 per cent. Although the
number of such estates in Northern
Ireland is comparatively small-I am
sorry to say-I propose that a similar
increase shall be made in Northern
Ireland, with effect from the date of the
Budget Resolution. I anticipate that
this increase will yield a sum of £10,000
in a full year and £5,000 this year.
I propose also to include in the Finance
Bill which will give effect to this
Resolution a clause designed to stop a
possible loophole for evasion of estate.
duty. A similar clause was included in
the United Kingdom Finance Act of last
year, and as the detailed explanation is
very technical, I propose to defer it until
hon. Members have the Bill in their
hands.
Similarly, I propose to include a
clause also taken from the United
Kingdom Finance Act of last year, dealing with a possible method of evading
stamp duty on the part of companies,
and a clause giving exemption from stamp
duty in the case of some statutory
appointments under the Royal Sign
Manual.
Hon. Members already know that substantial expenditure on civil defence and
air raid precautions is anticipated both
here and in Great Britain during the
current year.
In Great Britain, on the
Estimates already presented, over 80 per
cent. of the expenses being incurred on
Minister's Financial Statement 1526
The Budget-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
these services is to be met from borrowing. I would also remind the Committee
that under the Government of Ireland
Act, defence matters are left to be dealt
with by the British Government.
During the last few months our Government has been in consultation with
the British Government to see what expenditure on these services is required for
the protection of the civil population of
Northern Ireland, and how these services
here are to be administered and paid for.
Hon. Members know that my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs, is
responsible for air raid precautions here.
A provisional arrangement has been
reached and it is hoped it will be embodied in the British Civil Defence Bill,
the effect of which would be that the
corresponding services will continue to be
administered by our Government, but
that, in view of the exceptional nature
of the service, the British Government
will assist our Governmental expenditure
by means of a grant in aid. On the
assumption, therefore, that the British
House of Commons will approve of this
provisional arrangement I am providing
on the revenue side of the account a sum
of £300,000 representing the estimated
receipt in the current financial year from
an Imperial grant in aid of our expenditure on these services.
These taxation changes and the anticipated Imperial grant in aid of civil
defence expenditure, together amounting
to £405,000, will therefore increase the
amount available for Imperial contribution and surplus from £531,000 to a
sum of £936,000.
Against this figure I am charging a
further sum of £200,000 which would
otherwise go to increase our Imperial
contribution. It is with the agreement
of the Chancellor of the Exchequer that
our contribution is reduced by this
amount in the current year, in order to
enable me to make a start against the
losses which the Exchequer, I regret to
say, is bound to incur by reason of our
gurantees to the borrowings of the Road
Transport Board.
I am also glad to say that the Chancellor has most kindly expressed his
agreement to corresponding provisionnot necessarily of the same amountbeing made each year over an extended
period. I must, however, tell the House
very clearly and definitely that this
arrangement, both as regards the current
year and as regards the future, is subject
to the condition that we satisfy the
British Treasury that our new transport
scheme will be established on such a basis
as to ensure a sound and economic result.
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am sure that this
arrangement will be welcomed, as if the
conditions are complied with, I am hopeful that it will prevent a special tax
being imposed to meet transport losses.
I therefore deduct this figure of
£200,000 from the available credit
margin to which I have already referred,
leaving a balance of £736,000, of which
£700,000 is the provisional Imperial contribution for this year and £36,000 is
available for surplus and any unforeseen
Supplementary Estimates.
There is one matter which from time to
time has been raised with my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
and myself by local authorities, namely
their desire that a larger State grant
should be given towards mental treatment. This matter was investigated
very thoroughly by the Leslie Committee
and recommendations were made with a
view to certain other grants being
abolished in connection with services
with which it was considered the State
was not so directly responsible, and the
savings applied to increasing the mental
treatment grant. I have been informed,
however, that the local authorities object
to their being abolished, and therefore I
have had to consider the matter
afresh, and from a new angle.
I admit that as the cost of the maintenance of our mental hospitals has substantially increased in recent years our
local authorities have a claim for an
increased grant, and I therefore propose
to increase the present grant of £37,079
a year to £60,000 a year. As, however,
the rates necessary to maintain the
mental hospitals on the existing financial
basis have already been struck for the
present year, this concession will only
begin to operate from the 1st April nest,
and therefore my Budget for the present
year will not be affected. The proposal
will require legislation in the autumn,
and I am asking my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Home Affairs, to consult
with the local authorities in the mean-
Minister's Financial Statement 1528
The Budget-
16 MAY 1939
time with a view to the redistribution of
the combined grant on a just basis between the various institutions.
I also desire to take this opportunity
to announce that the Government proposes to ask Parliament to approve of a
Supplementary Estimate at an early
date for a sum of £10,000, being an ex
gratia grant on the part of the Government towards the victims of the Tourist
Trophy race in Newtownards in the year
1936 and to their dependants. I regret
that the promoters of this race, having
had their freedom from legal liability
settled in the court, have declined to
make any contribution. The Government, therefore, without accepting legal
responsibility, feels that the victims
should not be left without assistance.
The amounts in each case will
measured on the basis of the compensation that the jury at the trial assessed
as a just settlement on the grounds of
equity in the case of Mrs. Hannah
Warden, which formed the subject of the
test case. This item of expenditure has
been included in the provision for Supplementary Estimate to which I have
already referred.
be
I have now reached the end of my
Budget Statement, but may I, Sir, add
that in my opinion the foundations of
our financial structure were well and
truly laid. They have stood, with a few
modifications, the test of time and are
safe and sound to-day.
I am confident that it will be realised
that the increases in taxation, both reserved and transferred, are necessary for
the safety of the Realm, and that they
will, therefore, be willingly and cheerfully
borne as in duty bound by us all as
citizens of the United Kingdom.
One thought has been in my mind today. During the past few months the
Ministry of Finance has had many difficult and important problems with which
to deal. I desire to take advantage of
this opportunity to thank the Financial
Secretary and all my staff for the valuable assistance and loyal support which
they have at all times freely given to
me. I beg to move.

Mr. BEATTIE: The custom of this
House has, in my opinion, been violated
by these Resolutions being presented
before any hon. Member has had an
opportunity of replying to the Chancellor
of the Exchequer. I do not know by
whom you are guided, but from the day
I entered this House until now no such
Resolution has intervened between the
statement by the Chancellor of the
Exchequer and the reply by those on this
side of the Committee.
The CHAIRMAN: There must always
be a Question before the House and
therefore these Resolutions must be proposed.
I
Mr. BEATTIE: I have made my protest and will leave it at that. It is an
innovation in the Budget debate.
never remember it being done before.
Last year I spoke after the Minister, and
I
did likewise in preceding years.
Nevertheless, if you are creating a precedent I will have to examine it before
I can state my objections to it.
I want to congratulate the right hon.
Gentleman, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, on his statement here to-day.
I should like to ask him at what school
he learned his bookkeeping, because it is
a masterpiece. He certainly did not
learn it at any school in Northern Ireland. He has made the position of
Northern Ireland look so bright and
rosy that anyone listening would believe.
we
were swimming in luxury at the
present moment. The reverse is, however, the case. He has actually shown
a balance in his Budget. I am not surprised at that because he was given a
great lead by those who occupied the
position before him. On no occasion has
Northern Ireland ever shown a deficit on
the Budget; there is always a balance.
It is time we came down to plain bookkeeping and got a plain statement from
the Chancellor in respect to the position.
which Northern Ireland stands in to-day
as compared with Great Britain and the
areas attached to it.
We are told that industrial activity
has not been moving as fast as the Government would like. Might I ask what
the Government has done to make industrial activity move faster? They have
given a loan of £72,000, while they
promise loans to the extent of £87,000.
They have done nothing to warrant the
confidence of this House or the confidence
of the people outside it. They are
actually moving on equal lines with
Great Britain in so far as the commodities necessary for consumption are concerned, while the sur-tax is hitting the
wealthy as stated by the Chancellor.
There will soon be no sur-tax payers in
this part of the world. That is not due
to any fault of Members of the Opposition, but it is due to the Government
who, after failing to get Conscription
like Great Britain, are now going to take
the financial resources of the people of
Northern Ireland and place them at the
disposal of Great Britain. That is the
transfer which is now being made.
The whole resources of Northern
Ireland are going to be taken to help
Mr. Chamberlain to build up the defence
forces of the country. I say we can only
contribute as much as we can afford.
The contribution we are being asked to
make under this Budget Statement is
more than we can afford. We want to
be plain speakers in this House. To give
with the one hand and take away with
the other is not, in my opinion, good
bookkeeping. We are talking about
what we are going to give to Great
Britain in the form of an Imperial contribution, while on the other hand we
talk about what the parity arrangement
in regard to the Unemployment Agreement is going to bring into this area due
to the improvement in the unemployment
situation in Great Britain as compared
with Northern Ireland.
We are also told that 80 per cent.
of the expenditure on rearmament is
going to be raised by loans, and that
a large percentage of the rearmament
work is being placed in the North of
Ireland. I challenge that statement.
Two ships for His Majesty's Navy, as
stated by the Chancellor, have been
placed in the shipyards of Northern
Ireland. One depot ship has been
placed up to the moment from the last
naval list. That depot ship is only a
workshop for the smallest craft in the
Navy, the submarines. We are also told
that shipbuilding is going to be assisted
by cargo steamers. Has any provision been
made for the North of Ireland establishments to be part and parcel of the scheme
which Great Britain is adopting at the
present moment, the rebuilding of the

merchant service? Has Northern Ireland
got her name on the list? Will that law
apply to Northern Ireland, and will
money in support of it come here?

I made a few remarks on the Second

pointed out that under the English Bill
no divorce is granted under any circumstances for a period of three years, but
that has been dropped in our Bill. There
are four grounds on which a divorce may

the English Bill does not include two of
them, because a divorce on the ground of
desertion cannot be granted for three
years, and a divorce on the ground of
insanity cannot be granted for at least
five years.
That leaves two grounds still
unaffected, and the effect of the Clause
in this Bill is that a divorce may be
granted on either of those grounds in a
week or two or a month or two after the
marriage has taken place. I suggest that
a Clause similar to that in the English
Act might be introduced in this Bill so as
to keep in step with Great Britain in
this respect.
On thinking the matter over I do not

There still remains the case of cruelty,

May I point out that the first years
of marriage are very difficult. The unmarried members of this Committee,
including the Attorney-General, do not
understand anything about that, but I
could give any Member who wants it a
great deal of information in private.
There are a great many misunderstandings and stupidities possible, and it is a
marvel that so many marriages are
successful as they are in the light of
the amount of ignorance that obtains in
regard to the difficulties of matrimonial
life. If this Clause is left in as it is it
is possible that in an appreciable number
of cases young people who are not hitting
it off perfectly well all the time might
consider divorce, and if they do so in
the first year or two of their married life
every tiff will be magnified, and every
difficulty will be exaggerated until
eventually they will insist on a divorce,
and be able possibly to put their case in
such a way that a divorce will be granted,
possibly to their own great regret in the
coming years when they have had more
experience of life.
That is one circumstance that justifies
a modification of this particular Clause,
in addition to the fact that it is the
English law. There are other factors I
might mention, but I do not want to
elaborate the point at any length. If a
case is peculiarly hard, if the cruelty is
peculiarly hard, and if it is impossible
for a person to live with his or her
partner, there is always the possibility of
a judicial separation, with the possibility
of a divorce at the end of three years.
Some Members of the Committee might
be inclined to object to this Amendment
by using the argument that if you do not
allow divorce on this ground within a
period of three years, desperate people
will see that there are other grounds provided. That, of course, has been the
charge made against the divorce law in
England for the last fifty years or more,
but I do not think that objection has
very much weight in it in the light of the
passing of this Act as a whole. These
people know it is possible to get a divorce
in three years, with the possibility of a
separation in the meantime, and I do not
think the person who would provide other
grounds for divorce is worthy of consideration.
I suggest that this matter should be
taken into consideration, and that this
particular part of the Clause be somewhat modified so as to prevent misunderstanding, and to obviate the possibility
of young people getting it into their
heads that they can have a trial run, a
short honeymoon, and a speedy separation on the ground of cruelty. The
definition of the word cruelty is not

On the other hand,
I do think that the possibility of misunderstanding it has a tendency to

With regard to the merits of the

When one speaks of divorce on the
grounds of cruelty, one, of course, has
to bear in mind the conception of
cruelty as it has been interpreted in the
courts for the past 150 years. Since
the year 1790 it has been recognised by
the courts that for the purpose of
divorce cruelty has a very clear meaning. It does not mean any small or
slight thing, anything that might be the
natural product of what the hon. Member for the University called one of the
tiffs or difficulties of early married life.
In order that cruelty should be a ground
of divorce, it has always been recognised
by the courts that the cruelty must be
grave and weighty.
Judges have avoided attempting to
frame a hard and fast definition, and
it has always been laid down by the
Judges in all the courts, up to and
including the House of Lords, that
cruelty in this sense really means serious
conduct. conduct which involves such
danger to life or limb or health, or an

as
apprehension of such danger to life or
