what is thought of by the courts
cruelty, and what they have always
regarded as cruelty-and it is a ground
from which the Judges have always
refused to be driven-is that cruelty in
order to form a ground of divorce must
be substantial, something creating
danger or apprehension of danger to
life or limb or health which would
really make it impossible for the
marriage to continue as a real marriage,
and would make the marriage, if it continued, a marriage in which one of the
parties would be chronically living in a

If one approaches the question from
that point of view, one will see that we
are not dealing with divorce for very
small reasons, and it is not sought by
the Government in this Bill to provide
for divorce for small reasons. In order
that divorce may be had for cruelty, it
will have to be substantial cruelty.
One can very well foresee instances of

It seems a hard thing that she should

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
Clause comes from the recent English
It is new in English legislation,
but the idea of the Clause is not new.
It is a provision which. was recommended by the very valuable majority
report of the Royal Commission which
sat under Lord Gorell, the Commission
which brought in its historic report in
the year 1912. The Commission dealt
with the matter very fully and recommended that divorce on the grounds of
incurable insanity should be allowed.
When the matter was before Paliament
in the 1937 Bill it was a question which
aroused the gravest and most serious
discussion and consideration. When it
received that consideration at the hands
of both Houses it was passed into law by
a very substantial majority. Therefore.
Matrimonial Causes Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
it is a matter which has not been introduced lightly or without thought.
The hon. and learned Member has
based his argument on the point that
marriage is a contract and that one cannot say a person has been guilty of a
breach of contract and should be
divorced simply because that person,
through no fault of his own, has been
inflicted with insanity and is the inmate
of a mental home. That was considered
by the Gorell Commission, and it was
pointed out that that is based on a misconception; it is based on the narrow
view that marriage is a contract.
Marriage is not simply a contract, it is
much more than a contract, it is a
relationship voluntarily entered into by
a man and a woman for certain wellknown purposes. It is a wrong conception of divorce to treat it as something in the nature of a penalty for a
breach of contract. An action for
divorce brought by a wife against a
husband or by a husband against a wife
is not an action in which to make
rewards or punishments, punishment
because wrong has been done. It is not
an action of that kind at all.
It is an
action brought by a person seeking
relief from an intolerable situation, and
it is that sort of situation which is, unhappily, created by incurable insanity.
The hon. and learned Member for the
University has spoken of insanity and
compared it with other illnesses. He said
if we pass a provision like this we may
have people asking for divorce on the
grounds of other illnesses.
On the very
slightest thought it will occur to one that
insanity is on a different plane from any
other illness. The insanity dealt with in
the Bill involves a person being taken
away from his home and confined in some
sort of institution. His ordinary political
and civil rights are taken away from him,
many of his financial resources are taken
away from him, and when a person is
taken away like that and put in a mental
home and is found to be incurably insane
it is quite obvious that between a person
like that and his spouse there can no longer
exist any of the natural relationships of
married life. In other words, a girl who
is married to a man who is taken away
and confined for many years in a mental
home is deprived of all the privileges and
rights of married life, and she will never
get them back again. There is a
complete severance, and anything in the
nature of family life is broken up for ever.
In a case like that we consider it is
proper there should be an opportunity of
taking proceedings for divorce, and that
divorce should be granted. A person
who is tied to an unfortunate who is
locked up in a lunatic asylum for many
years is really tied to something in the
nature of compulsory celibacy, and the
position is really, for all practical purposes of married life, as if he or she were
married to some dead person. That is a
very difficult situation.
I can quite recognise instances such as
those the hon. and learned Member referred to, where through a sense of loyalty
to the person who is put away the last
thought in their mind would be that of
divorce. There are many people like
that, people for whom we have the highest
regard. This Act, however, does not
compel a person to divorce a partner; it
merely gives an opportunity of coming
before the courts. Take the case of a
young woman married to a man who, unfortunately, becomes insane at an early
age, and she may be left with two or
three small children. She has to go out
to work to earn her bread. He is confined in the asylum. She meets an
honourable man whom she would like as
a husband and her own husband is to all
intents and purposes dead. Is it not
terrible that she should be denied a happy
life? Take the case of a young man whose
wife is incurable and confined in a menta!
home. He has to find a housekeeper to
look after his home. Does it not seem a
difficult thing that he should be compelled
to be tied to a person who can never be
a real wife and who may not recognise his
existence?
There are many hard cases of that kind.
One can well recognise the case where
through loyalty and affection a person
would not think of making use of a provison such as this, but there are a great
number of cases where it would be in the
interests not only of the individuals but
of the community that the parties should
be able to go to the courts and get relief
from an intolerable situation. I suggest
to the Committee that this Clause recommended by the Gorell Commission and
adopted by big majorities in the British
Houses of Parliament during the passing
of the 1937 Act should be adopted in our
Parliament, too.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I beg
to move in sub-clause (2) to leave out
"and the trial before a judge of assize.”
This is a small matter and will make no
material change in practice of the law.
Under existing legislation issues
divorce matters could be sent down to a
court before a judge of assize. Since the
courts here were set up under the 1920
Act I do not think there has been a single
instance in which that provision has ever
been availed of. The ordinary procedure
is to have the issue tried in Belfast before
a judge and jury. It is conceived to be
better to have matters of divorce and
nullity regarded as of great seriousness,
and that they should be tried where you
have all the opportunity of time and care
and so forth in the High Courts here.
The idea is that cases under the Act should
be normally tried here and should not be
kept under a provision sending them
down to the assizes.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand
part of the Bill.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Budget Resolution
Mr. SPEAKER: For the convenience
of Members perhaps I should explain
that it is customary on the Report stage
to have the general discussion of the
Budget on the first Resolution only, and
then for the other Resolutions to be formally passed by the House without
debate. The general discussion is on the
first Resolution.
Question proposed: "That the House do
agree with the Committee in the said
Resolution."
Mr. AGNEW: After listening with
great patience to the Budget proposals
so ably put forward by the Minister of
Finance I felt that for the workers of
Northern Ireland there was very little
hope for the future. We realise that
the prosperity of Northern Ireland depends on industry and also on the effects
of the international situation. But can
we not devise any effective plan by our
own efforts to endeavour to control the
fluctuations which affect many of our
citizens? I would like to know has an
honest attempt been made to deal with
our industrial problems affecting the
welfare of the majority of our citizens.
I am afraid that the economic stability
of Northern Ireland is very doubtful,
because from the industrial standpoint
we cannot see that it is going to guarantee any security to those employed. We
also realise the effects of the war situation, and I do heartily agree that war
settles nothing. Nevertheless, we are
preparing for war. If the same efforts
were made in the promotion of peace it
would be much better for all, because
there is a grave danger lurking at the
back of rearmament and that is the
serious danger of its effects on our social
status.
We cannot spend on one hand
for a destructive policy and at the same
time maintain our social services. There
is serious danger in that respect.
There was one very significant statement made by the Minister of Finance.
He said the test of prosperity in any
State was, how did the masses live? That
is a very significant statement, and I
would ask the Northern Government to
realise and ask themselves the question,
how do the masses live in Northern
Ireland? Are they living with any
degree of security for the future? My
opinion is they are merely existing from
day to day with a certain amount of
insecurity and no guarantee for the
future whatsoever. It is a duty which
the Government must perform. They
must give serious consideration to the
welfare of the masses, because, as we
know, the position is still very serious.
and uncertain. They are industrially
insecure, and I am certain that the Government realise that. If we look at the
strength of our industrial situation, I
will only quote from personal knowledge
in my own constituency and in the
Armagh area. In the Keady district at
one time we had a flourishing linen industry and to-day we find in Darkley,
Annvale and Dundrum the factories and
mills for the production of linen closed.
I would like to ask the Government if
they have given serious consideration to
the state of affairs in that particular
area on the same basis as they evidently
gave consideration to the city of
Belfast. That is a matter that cannot
be evaded. There we find hundreds of
workers willing to work and yet the industry is closed. It is a matter the
Government must face up to.
take Armagh City, we find the spinning
mill and factory lying dormant and the
workers once engaged there are
deavouring to find work elsewhere. The
unfortunate thing is that they are
leaving Armagh.
If we
en-
Can the Government devise no plans
for keeping the workers at home and
giving them the employment they crave
for. We must face up to the realities of
the situation and realise that industrial
stability does not exist in the areas concerned, the areas I am most concerned
with. We must realise that these
workers in the linen industry to-day are
found around the labour exchanges. The
only industry I can see prosperous is the
labour exchanges, where men and women,
boys and girls, in thousands assemble to
receive the amounts to which they are
entitled and which give them a degree of
security. Their claim for work is
apparently ignored. We have been told
that the Trade Agreement with the
United States is going to bring prosperity to the linen industry. I have been
listening to that for a considerable time,
but still there is no prosperity. I would
like to see that promise fulfilled, and
action taken whereby that Trade Agreement would become operative throughout Northern Ireland.

Budget Resolution
If we take the building and allied
trades, there, again, is serious unemployment, and I cannot visualise any
reduction of that unemployment by any
schemes that will be promoted even as
far as housing is concerned. The only
way to solve the unemployment problem
in the building and allied trades is for
the State to take complete control of the
housing needs of the people, otherwise the
local authorities will ignore any demand
made upon them under present circumstances.
At all times we hear the cry for more
rearmament work. That may be for the
good of Belfast, but will rearmament
work bring any
any prosperity to the
provincial areas outside Belfast? (Hon.
Members: Yes.) Will they receive no
consideration whatever? According to
what we see Belfast seems to be the only
place worthy of recognition, and the
other areas are absolutely ignored. It is
not for the want of skilled workers in
these areas. There are ample workers
throughout County Armagh to deal with
any work that may come forward. Can
we not stimulate our old industries without relying absolutely upon rearmaments? It is evident that as time goes
on rearmament will come to a stand
still, and then we will be faced with the
grim realities of the situation.
industries will be already dead.
are we going to do to replace those engaged in rearmament work? We will
find ourselves faced with a serious unemployment problem greater than it is
to-day. Therefore, as I say, we should.
endeavour to stimulate old industries and
revive new ones which will be of a productive nature instead of concentrating
solely on the building up of armaments
for destruction.
Our old
What
When we, realise the burden placed on
the business people, the shopkeepers of
Northern Ireland, by the introduction of
the revaluation scheme, we must face
up to the fact that it is a serious burden
on the business element. Some provision
should be made to reduce that burden.
Much has been said about the London
Office. In my opinion it is very expensive and futile. I would like to know
what Northern Ireland has achieved by
the opening of this office. What new
industries or what increases in trade in
any respect have been secured by the
setting up of that Department? I have
always considered it a very unwise policy
to set up that office, because it was a
means of spending money and placing
one, in charge who in my opinion had no
knowledge of industry or the commercial
life of this part of the country.
Agriculture is recognised as our main
industry. We must give some consideration to the small farming community,
otherwise they will become non-existent.
It does not matter what scheme of assistance is promoted for the farming class,
the small farmers are not in a fit position
to accept it, simply because their little.
holdings and financial standing will not
allow it. I would like to see the small
farmers, who comprise an enormous part
of agriculture life in the Province, receiving consideration. Many of our small
farmers to-day are, unable to pay their
land annuities. I hope the time is not
far distant when the Government will
give serious consideration to the matter
of reducing the land annuities.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. AGNEW: Otherwise the small
farming community will have passed out.
As regards those employed on the land,
let us hope that the charter for better
wages will soon be in force. The farmers
themselves know that the workers are not
paid a sufficient wage. We have been
told that agriculture cannot pay. We
must realise that the larger farmers have
received many advantages and assistance..
Has that assistance been handed down
to those who till the land? Have they
reaped the reward of all the subsidies that
are given?
As to the question of social services,
this is a matter about which I must be
very candid. I feel that our social
services are not in keeping with those
in Great Britain, more particularly in
regard to what is known as public assistance.. I have repeatedly mentioned the
fact in this House that we here are not
following step by step with the British
Government in dealing with the question
of public assistance. We have what is
known as the Exceptional Distress Order.
It is not compulsory. The onus lies on
the local authorities concerned, the
boards of guardians, and I am sorry to
say, with few exceptions, these boards are
not willing to give assistance to the ablebodied unemployed. That applies in my

As to the Transport Board, I see there

present time it means a reduction of
wages for those employed. I would like
that matter gone into in order to safeguard the interests of the workers. We
must maintain the system of transport
on a basis to meet the requirements of
the people. There are areas to-day where
there is no transport whatever. If I
wish to go to Crossmaglen I cannot get
a bus; I must travel round by Newry
in order to get there. Therefore, those
interested in the transport section should
see that facilities are provided in certain
areas so that people will be able to travel
without making a roundabout journey.
There is one issue which the Government have not faced up to. They have
not recognised that this is a distressed
area. There is no use in hiding the
fact any longer. We may call Northern Ireland by whatever name we
wish, such as paradise, but we must
face up to the grim reality that it is a
distressed area. The hon. Member for
South Down (Mr. Brown) said yesterday that to call Northern Ireland a
distressed area would hurt the tourist
traffic. That may be so, but do we
realise the hurt there is to humanity?
We cannot say that industry is strong
or that the welfare of the people is
secure. Why we hide that fact and do
not call this a distressed area is beyond
me.
The British Government were not
afraid to classify certain parts
of
Great Britain as distressed areas, and
the result has been that areas so classed
have received splendid assistance from
the Government by the setting up of
new industries. Why are we afraid to
appoint a commissioner on the same
basis as in Great Britain, The evidence is there. Real poverty is there
and the hardships of the people prevail.
We must, no matter how dignified we
may be, give serious consideration to
the question of Northern Ireland as a
distressed area. I apply that descrip-

tion to my particular area.
call it anything but a distressed area.
We are told that the financial
structure of Northern Ireland is well
and truly laid. It may be well and
truly laid in the case of the privileged
class, but is it so far as the working
class are concerned? Can the Government say the working class financially
are safe? They are not safe, because

that is no real indication of the wellbeing of the masses. That is the real

of Northern Ireland. If they had

Now we come to the new implications

No section of the community will feel

The Government should place the

for the people. They may be wrong, as

predicted, including that awful word

because we have the advantage of the

naturally become, more and more prudent

ever

Joint Exchequer Board. Consequently,

stituency of South Armagh in a way

to discover, the amount of money spent

classes in Ulster. It is a very large sum.
What is spent on the social services
by my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Labour, amounts to 6 millions a
year. When we calculate all the various
services administered by his Department
it amounts to £6,000,000, and when we
add to that the employers' contribution
to the Unemployment Fund it amounts
to £6,500,000. That money is distributed among the working classes under
one heading or another. It is a very
large sum in this area, when you consider that only a few years ago the sum
so spent was practically negligible.
is now running to £6,500,000. And if

classes.

Oral Answers to Questions.
THE £2 AN ACRE TILLAGE
GRANT.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he will make
representations to the Imperial authorities to have the restrictions regarding
the grant of £2 per acre for the ploughing up of permanent grass-land modified
in the case of Northern Ireland, in view
of the fact that the proportion of such
land in Northern Ireland that has been
untilled for at least seven years is
infinitely smaller than across
Channel.
the
AGRICUL-
The MINISTER OF
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The purpose
of the subsidy is to bring under the
plough land which has been under grass
for more than seven years, so that in the
event of an outbreak of war there will
be an increased area of land immediately
available for the production of crops. It
is not the intention that the subsidy
should be paid in respect of land which
has recently been under the plough and
which may be ploughed up again in the
course of the ordinary farm rotation. I
am confident that farmers in Northern
Ireland appreciate the purpose of the
scheme and will be prepared to improve
their old pasture land, so as to be ready
to increase their production of crops in
the event of the need arising.
Mr. BROWN: Will the right hon.
Gentleman consider the advisability of
making representations to the Imperial
authorities to have the farmers here put
on the same basis as farmers in
Saskatchewan, where the gallon petrol
tax is waived to enable them to make
this thing a success?
LEAFLET ON GROWING
TOMATOES.
2. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if it is
a fact that his Ministry does not issue a
leaflet on the growing of tomatoes;
whether a leaflet which is printed and
published by the Ministry of Agriculture
in Eire is being issued from his Ministry on this subject.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Ministry
has not, so far, issued a formal printed
leaflet on tomato growing, but this subject has been a matter of continuous
propaganda and advice from both the
agricultural and horticultural staffs of my
Ministry and County Committees of
Agriculture.
As a result of inquiries which have
been received the question of issuing a
printed leaflet on tomato growing,
having regard to the special conditions
in Northern Ireland, has for some time
been under consideration, and I may tell
the hon. Member that such a leaflet will
be issued in the course of next week.
In the meantime, inquiries have been
directed to publications on the subject
issued by other agricultural departments.
Mr. BAILEY: Might I ask the
Minister if there was not a leaflet distributed in this House by the Minister
of Agriculture in Eire?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: That is quite
correct. The hon. Member will understand that the contents of most of these
leaflets are collected from information
received from countries all
over the
world. This leaflet was particularly
instructive and therefore the Department
issued it at that time.

as

TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Warnock):
I have received a copy of the petition
referred to in the question. According
to the minutes of the Rural District
Council, the petition was forwarded
to the Armagh County Council
the rating authority. I have no

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): There is a very old saying,
not literally true, of course, that he gives
twice who gives quickly. In the course
of my Budget remarks I stated that I
intended to introduce a Supplementary
Estimate which would provide for er
gratia payments to the victims and to
their dependants of the accident which
occurred on the occasion of the Tourist
Trophy Race in 1936 in Newtownards.
The circumstances in which this
tragic accident occurred are familiar
to us all. As a result of it eight
persons were killed, two permanently incapacitated, and nine received injuries of varying degrees of
severity. As the result of legal proceedings in the Supreme Court in a test case
it was decided that the promoters of the
race were not legally liable.
In the circumstances the Government
feels that the unfortunate victims should
not be left without assistance, and,
accordingly, without accepting any legal
responsibility I agreed to make certain
ex
gratia payments, subject to the
approval of Parliament.
The sum of £8,200 is provided in this
Estimate for individual grants, which
number eighteen, varying from £2,000
to £10, and have been fixed after discussion with the solicitors concerned in
the court proceedings and taking into
consideration the report of a firm of
assessors accustomed to deal with third
party motor insurance cases.
In addition, the sum of £300 is to be
paid direct to the Newtownards District

Hospital, to which the injured were
admitted and where several were detained

in the courts. The defendants have met
their own costs, amounting to about
double this amount.
I feel sure that these proposals meet
with the approval of the House. I beg
to move.

Margarine Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: This is
short Bill dealing with the markings
which may be applied to margarine
when sold by retail. In Northern Ireland the law as it stands at present
Margarine Bill-
Agricultural Wages Bill
18 MAY 1939
requires that margarine, when sold by
retail, shall be placed in a wrapper
bearing the word "Margarine," but no
additional words are permitted on the
wrapper.
Application was made last year to the
authorities
appropriate
by British
margarine manufacturers for an Order
in Council under the Merchandise
Marks Act, 1926, requiring all
margarine imported into the United
Kingdom to be marked with an indication of origin, that is to say the name
of the country in which it was manufactured. The application was referred
to the Standing Committee constituted
by the Merchandise Marks Act, which
recommended that the application
should be acceded to and that the Order
in Council should become operative as
from the 1st November, 1939. The
report of the Committee has been under
consideration by the three United Kingdom Departments concerned, and the
Government of Northern Ireland has
been asked to promote the legislation
necessary to enable the proposed Order
to be made effective in Northern
Ireland.
As I have indicated, the law at
present does not permit of an indication.
of origin to be shown on margarine, and
the effect of the Bill before the House
is simply to remove that restriction. I
may say that the law in Great Britain
has recently been amended so as to effect
this removal, and it is desirable that
the law in Northern Ireland should be
brought into line with that in Great
Britain.
manu-
Although margarine is not
factured in Northern Ireland it is most
desirable that the Government of Northern Ireland should co-operate with the
United Kingdom authorities in the
operation of the Merchandise Marks
Acts. These Acts are of great value to
Northern Ireland since under them Northern Ireland goods are treated on the
British market in the same way as goods.
produced or manufactured in England,
Scotland or Wales. They are not
regarded as imported or required to
be marked in any way. There are also,
of course, obvious administrative reasons
which require the law relating to the
importation of goods to be as far as
possible the same here as in Great
Britain. If, for example, goods which
would be required to be marked on
importation into Great Britain could be
imported into Northern Ireland unmarked, such goods might be imported
into Northern Ireland in the first
instance and then, since there is no
customs barrier between Northern Ireland and Great Britain, sent to Great
Britain without their being detected. I
beg to move.

Agricultural Wages Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): Members of the
House are generally aware of the
measures which have been taken by the
Government to assist the farming community during recent years. This assistance has been not alone in the form of
legislation designed to improve the conditions of marketing agricultural produce SO as to enable produce from
Northern Ireland to command a higher
price on the wholesale markets, but also
by means of direct subsidies to the industry. All these measures have been
designed to maintain the position of
agriculture in Northern Ireland, and
there has been a very substantial increase
in the value of the gross output of the
industry during recent years from
£10,380,000 in 1932-33 to over
£16,500,000 in 1937-8.
This increase in the production of
agricultural produce is due to the cooperation of two sets of persons, the
farmer on the one hand and the farm
labourer on the other, and I am confident
that Members will agree that everything
possible should be done to secure that
the position of the farm labourer in
Northern Ireland is improved as much
as possible, and that conditions of work
on the farm should be made increasingly
attractive so as to prevent the drift of
labourers from the land which has, unfortunately, been going on for so many
years. Fundamentally, of course, the
improvement in the conditions of the
agricultural labourer must depend upon
an improvement in the conditions of the
1617 Agricultural Wages Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Sir Basil Brooke]
farmer and the industry generally.
That it is my ambition to achieve, and
I know that farmers do recognise the
efforts which have been made by the
Government to bring improved conditions to the agricultural industry.
A mere catalogue of the measures
which have been adopted is sufficient to
indicate the real value of Government
assistance during recent years. Imports
of agricultural produce have been controlled, both by tariffs and by quantitative regulation of imports; improved
methods of sale of various classes of farm
produce have been introduced under
marketing schemes; direct subsidies are
at present being given by the Government in respect of cattle, milk and
cereal production, and the supply of
fertilisers at cheap rates. The value of
these subsidies amounted to £592,000 in
respect of the last financial year, and
with the increase in the oats and barley
subsidy which is taking place this year,
that amount will probably be very substantially increased in the current year.
There has been the complete derating
of agricultural land at a cost of almost
one million pounds per annum to the
Exchequer, and there has also been the
provision of grants for the improvement
of agricultural holdings under which
£41,000 has been expended during the
past financial year.
All these schemes must have had some
considerable effect in improving the
position of the farmer. Still further
efforts may be necessary in the future,
but the Government may at least take
credit for the very considerable assistance
which is already being provided to the
industry. I am sure that every Member will agree that the agricultural
labourer should benefit in any improvement in agricultural conditions which
occurs, and the machinery for ensuring
that the position of the agricultural
labourer will be safeguarded is provided
by the Measure which I am submitting
for the approval of the House to-day.
Northern Ireland is a community of
small farmers, and on a very large
number of our farms the work is mainly
performed by the farmer himself and his
own family. So much is this the case
that it is often overlooked that there are
a very substantial number of agricultural
labourers employed in Northern Ireland.
The number is approximately 30,000,
and I hope that under this Bill their
position as partners in the agricultural
industry will be established on a firmer
basis than has, perhaps, been the case
in the past.
It must be remembered that the agricultural labourer working on the
scattered farms of Northern Ireland,
very often working alone as the only
paid employee on a farm, or with only
two or three colleagues, must, of
necessity, be in a somewhat isolated
position. He has not the opportunities
for collective action and collective
bargaining which is possessed by the
factory worker who is employed in large
numbers in one of our industrial
establishments. The farm labourer has
to make his own bargain with his employer, the possibility of direct collective bargaining is less than under
factory conditions, and this fact of his
isolation may mean that he is frequently
in a much weaker position to bargain
with his employer than is the case in
other industries.
For this reason the desirability of
establishing statutory machinery for the
regulation of agricultural wages has been
recognised in other countries. An Agricultural Wages Act has been in operation
in England and Wales since 1924, whilst
similar legislation was recently introduced in Eire in 1936 and in Scotland
in 1937. Since 1937 indeed, Northern
Ireland has been the only part of the
British Isles in which an Agricultural
Wages Board has not functioned. I was,
however, anxious that the position of
both farmers and labourers in regard to
the establishment of an Agricultural
Wages Board should be carefully investigated before legislation corresponding to
that already in force in Great Britain
was introduced here.
I
Consequently, about a
year ago
appointed a Departmental Committee to
inquire into the whole position of conditions of employment and wages of
agricultural workers in Northern Ireland.
That Committee included four representatives of the Ulster Farmers' Union.
four representatives of the Transport and
General Workers' Union, and four
Members of Parliament, two drawn from
the Labour Party and two from the
Unionist Party. The Committee presented a
unanimous report, and the
1619 Agricultural Wages Bill-

18 MAY 1939
Second Reading
Measure which is now before the House
has been drafted on the basis of the
report and carries out its recommendations.
Clause 1 provides for the establishment
of a single Agricultral Wages Board to
operate for the whole of Northern
Ireland. The Board will consist of 15
members, of whom six will be representatives of employers in agriculture, and
six representative of workers in agricul-
There will, in addition, be three
independent members appointed by me.
It will be the duty of the Board to fix
minimum rates of wages for workers employed in agriculture. In carrying out
this duty the Board is required by subsection 7 of Clause 2 to have regard to
the economic position of agriculture in
each area for which a minimum rate is
proposed, and also, as far as practical,
secure for able-bodied men such wages as
in the opinion of the Board are adequate
to promote efficiency and to enable a
man in an ordinary case to maintain himself and his family in accordance with
such standard of comfort as may be
reasonable in relation to his occupation.
Before actually fixing wages the Board
is required by sub-section 9 of Clause 2
to give notice of its proposals, and provision is made for objections to the proposed rates of wages being lodged with
the Board, and such objections must
then be considered by the Board before
the proposed wages is finally fixed.
Clause 4 deals with the question of
holidays for agricultural workers, and
provides that each agricultural worker
shall be entitled to six days' holiday with
pay in the year. I am glad to say that
this recommendation was made unanimously by the Departmental Committee
to which I have referred. The enforcement of the wages fixed by the Board
will be the responsibility of my Ministry,
and the provisions for enforcement are
set out in Clause 5 of the Bill.
The House will also be interested in
the provisions of Clause 9, under which
it is provided that the Minister of Agriculture shall make an annual report to
Parliament regarding the proceedings
under the Act, so that Members of the
House will be kept fully informed with
regard to the action taken by the Agricultural Wages Board under the powers
entrusted to it.
I beg to move, "That the Bill be now
read a Second time."

There is at least no visible return from
a job of that kind. The conditions are
very different from what they are in
industry. A farmer may engage four
or five extra hands to deal with the
harvest; he may have to keep those
men
a month, quite conceivably two
months, in order eventually to get the
harvest in. It will be seen, therefore,
that farmers are faced with very serious
difficulties.
I am sure the House was struck with
the expression of the desire for an
understanding as between labourers and
farmers. That understanding has been
exemplified in the report which hon.
Members have had in their hands for
some time. On the Committee that
presented that report there were representatives of labourers and farmers, and
hon. Members will recall that it was
recommended in that Report that in
fixing the wages the economic position.
of the industry should be borne in mind.
That shows that the agricultural
labourer appreciates the difficulties that
his employer very often finds himself in,
and I feel perfectly certain that the
great bulk of farmers in this country
have an appreciation of the difficulties
of the labourers whom they employ. If
that spirit goes on, and is not spoiled,
then you will have a solution of a difficult problem, and I hope you will have
established-what everybody wants-a
true partnership between employer and
employee.

Oral Answer to Question.
COAL IMPORTS COMMITTEE.
Mr. DOWLING asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state if it is
a fact that Northern Ireland is not
represented on any Coal Imports Committee; whether he is aware that limitations
are placed on the import of coal which
adversely affect users of considerable
quantities coming into Northern Ireland; and whether he will take steps to
have a Coal Imports Committee established in Northern Ireland to deal with
all matters of outstanding importance to
consumers.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): So far as I am aware the
only committee of the nature referred
to by the hon. Member is a trade organisation known as the Northern Ireland
Coal Importers' Association.
As the hon. Member will be aware,
the policy governing the marketing of
coal has been the subject of legislation
in the Imperial Parliament and is under
the general control of the Ministry of
Mines, with which Department my
Ministry keeps in close touch. So far as
any limitation of quantities is concerned,
I understand that there has been
difficulty recently in obtaining adequate
supplies of high grade domestic coal, but
I am assured that ample supplies are
now available and that, moreover, the
difficulties which arose were due to a
shortage at the pit head and not to any
limitations on distribution.
As regards any question of price
limitation, I would refer the hon. Member
to the statement by the Prime Minister
in this House on 26th April, 1938, as
to the fixing of definite f.o.b. prices of
coal destined for Northern Ireland, an
arrangement which is still operative.
If, however, the hon. Member will be
good enough to let me have further information as to the difficulties he has in
mind, I shall be glad to have the matter
fully investigated.

The Amendment which stands in my
name is partly a re-draft of the existing
provisions of lines 1-22 of page 6 of the
Bill. The Amendment in the first
instance relates to the provision under
which the small producer is exempted
from the need to make contracts and
may benefit under all the provisions of
the Bill if he registers an agreement
with the Ministry to supply pigs to the
curer of his choice. Originally it was
intended that this provision should be
limited to producers who sold not more
than 20 pigs in any year. In response
to representations which I had received
on this matter, I am prepared to raise
this figure to 30 pigs in the year.
The
producer who avails himself of the provisions of this Clause will be prohibited from selling any pigs otherwise
than to the curer with whom he has
entered into registered agreements until
the number of pigs to be supplied under
those agreements have been delivered.
There will, however, be no penalty for
short delivery of pigs under the agreement unless the producer has sold pigs
to some other person.
Originally the Clause enabled the producer to enter into only one agreement.
It has, however, been represented to
me that many producers may wish to
make one agreement with a roll and
ham curer for the sale of dead pigs, and
another agreement with a Wiltshire
curer for the sale of live pigs. The
Amendment, which stands in my name,
will enable this to be done, provided
that the
aggregate number of pigs
delivered under agreements is not more
than 30 pigs in a year.
There is a further provision to the
Amendment to which I should call
special attention. Power is being given
to the Ministry to refuse to register contracts or agreements for the delivery of
pigs if as a consequence of the delivery
of pigs under these contracts or agreements the quota allotted to any curer
for the production of bacon will be
exceeded. It is clearly desirable that
such a provision should exist, otherwise
it is possible that a curer would accept
contracts or agreements for a delivery
of pigs in excess of his quota for the
production of bacon and if this occurred
harm would be done, both to the producers who had made contracts with that
curer and also to other curers who might
be left short of adequate supplies of pigs
to fulfil their quotas.
The final sub-section of the Amendment is designed to prevent an excessive
multiplicity of contracts or agreements
being submitted for registration due to
various members of a family living on
the same farm making contracts or
agreements. It will be apparent to hon.
Members that the intentions of the Bill
with regard to registered agreements
should be evaded if a farmer, his wife,
and each of his children, all living on
the same farm, entered into registered
agreements for the supply of 30 pigs a
years to a curer. In this way the number
of pigs sold under registered agreements
from a single farm might exceed 30 and
the whole intention of this provision
that it should be confined to a small pig
producer would be evaded.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I beg to move,
that the following sub-clause be inserted:-
"(6) The Pig Industry Council shall
have power to determine that producers
in any area specified by the said Council
shall not enter into direct contracts for
the sale of live pigs except with such
curer or curers as may be determined by
the said Council.”
One of the most important things to be
safeguarded under the new contract
system is the equitable distribution of
pigs between different curers, and also
the elimination of unnecessary transport
of pigs. In the case of dead pigs, which
are normally brought to a market or to
a curer's premises by producers in their
own carts, this question does not arise to
any great extent. In the case of the sale
of live pigs, however, these pigs can
obviously be carried considerable distances before being delivered to a curer,
and it may be found desirable to attempt
to divide Northern Ireland into a number of zones, within each of which producers will supply their pigs to curers in
their neighbourhood. Such an arrangement would have the advantage
of
eliminating unnecessary transport and
would also have the advantage of bringing producers and curers into closer
contact, so that friendly consultation
may take place with regard to such
questions as grading of their pigs and the
production of the proper type of pig for
each factory.
This sub-section will give the Pig
Industry Council, upon which both
curers and producers are represented, the
power to secure as far as possible a satisfactory arrangement for the delivery of

Schemes Under the Drainage Acts.
Mr. MAGINESS: I beg to move,
"That this House, deplores the fact that
at the present time the application of
schemes under the Drainage Acts has
almost ceased, and that the county
councils are generally no longer willing
to prepare. to carry out such schemes, and
consequently is of opinion that in the
circumstances the Drainage Advisory
Committee should be requested by the
Government to investigate the problem
and make recommendations."
I should almost apologise for bringing
before hon. Members a matter that is
neither exciting nor controversial, but
the parlous state. of land drainage in
Northern Ireland at the present time
must be my only excuse. The history of
land drainage to which I wish to refer
very shortly was dealt with by the late
Mr. Pollock in introducing the. 1925 Act,
and there he referred to attempts which
had been made in land drainage going
back to the year 1748. The 1925 Act
which was passed by this Parliament
dealt mainly with two problems.
first problem, with which this Motion is
not directly concerned, was the problem
of those large basins of water and
rivers which flow into and through those
basins like Lough Neagh, Lough Erne,
and rivers such as the. Bann.
The
But the second part of the 1925 Act,
to quote the words of Mr. Pollock, was
"Concerned with the cleaning and
scouring of existing water-courses, the
removal of disused weirs and other
obstructions in the beds of streams so
as to insure that the general drainage
system of agricultural land may, under
conditions of excessive rainfall, be petmitted freely to discharge into the
rivers which carry the waters into the
central reservoirs."
And to that may be added the cleansing and removal of obstructions in these
Schemes Under Drainage Acts 1684
Notice of Motion-
23 MAY 1939
rivers which flow into the sea. For
instance, in County Down rivers like
the Lagan and the Quoile. It is clear
that there must be some organisation to
perform this work. The individual
farmer can do very little to deal with the
river that runs through or borders his
land. He may clean up that part of his
land. He may make it perfect. He may
build a rampart and make provision to
prevent his land from flooding, but if
his neighbours above or below do not
carry out the same sort of work all his
efforts are entirely in vain.
I know one, case where a man built a
rampart some feet high in front of his
land along the River Lagan to save his
land from flooding. Unfortunately the
other farmers whose land bordered that
river did not follow suit-perhaps I
should say fortunately-whatever was the
cause the water came in behind the
rampart and flooded his land, and the
result was when the water subsided the
rampart kept the water on his land
longer than on the land of his neighbours.
In former days there were a number
of different boards constituted to deal
with this problem, and in addition to
that there were landlords. I do not hold
any brief for the landlord class, but it
does seem that here and there, at any
rate, they did exercise a useful function
in helping in this question of land
drainage. Where the land which they
had let to tenant occupiers stretched over
a fair-sized bit of the country through
which a river ran, the landlord had an
organisation and probably the capital to
deal with such a state of affairs. But
fortunately, by a series of enactments, as
beneficial as they were belated, the
incubus of landlordism was swept away
from this country, and after our Land
Act of 1925 we had the whole of the
agricultural land of Northern Ireland
populated by owner occupiers. They had
neither the organisation nor the capital,
nor indeed the power, to do anything
except very minor works in connection
with the drains which ran through their
own land.
The Act of 1925, so ably introduced by
the late Mr. Pollock, was a very great
step in the right direction. This comprehensive scheme of land drainage enactments had been advocated by Irish
Members at Westminster, both North
and South, for many years, and it was
left to this Parliament in the year 1925
to put forward an enactment which did
tackle the matter courageously and
sympathetically. Leaving aside the
question of the central reservoirs and the
major rivers, the county councils were,
by that
that enactment, constituted the
drainage authorities and their work was
divided into two parts. The first gave
them power to control works by the
occupiers of the land, that is, to keep
certain drains and water-courses in
proper condition. But also they themselves as drainage authorities had to
formulate and execute a scheme for land
drainage, and it is with the latter function that this Motion properly deals
to-day.
A river like the Lagan might run
through an area comprising a number of
lands. The land on each side might be
properly drained, and those drains and
ditches be kept in order, but unless the
bed of the river was sufficiently deep, or
the flow of the river sufficiently strong,
in times of excessive rainfall the water
in the rivers rose to such an extent that
those drains leading from the field into
the river could not get rid of their water.
The water remained in the drain and
sometimes flowed back over a very considerable distance. I know of
where it flowed back a distance of a mile
to two miles. In cases where the water
in the river did actually overflow its
banks the very fact of the river being
SO full caused the drains and watercourses to flood the fields either directly
by means of the water overflowing or indirectly, so that the fields became waterlogged.
cases
It was to deal with cases of that sort
that the county council had to formulate
and execute a considerable number of
schemes. And there was a tremendous
lot of trouble encountered by the county
councils in their formulation, and
especially in their execution. I thinkthe Minister of Finance will correct me
if I am wrong-the main idea was that
the persons whose lands were flooded and
whose lands would be improved by these
schemes should, in the long run, pay for
those schemes. Of course the Government gave a grant, a labour grant, and
in certain cases there was a county-atlarge charge put on, but in the main the
idea was that the person whose land was
improved should pay for it-not of course
HOUSE OF COMMONS Schemes Under Drainage Acts 1686
Notice of Motion-
[Mr. Maginess]
in one lump sum, but by sums spread
over a considerable number of years.
Now the county councils encountered
very great difficulty, not in the execution
of these schemes, but in getting from the
owners of the land payment for the works
which had been executed.
The
One example might be cited.
county council would go to considerable
expense in having a river surveyed
properly, levels taken, and an estimate
made of the approximate cost. That
might be in some cases a matter of some
hundreds of pounds, and when the survey
had been made and the cost approximated
you would find the cost of the scheme
would be so big that the farmers whose
lands would be affected by the scheme
could not reasonably be expected to pay.
That was in the opinion of the county
council so much money wasted. Then
again, you might have, through no fault
of anybody's, a scheme which at the outset was calculated to cost so much, but
which during the progress of the work
was found to be costing so much more.
That is not a matter of how good the
survey was or how competent were the
engineers to execute the work. In that
case the farmers who were, perhaps,
willing to pay a matter of 10s an acre,
might be furnished with a bill for 20s
or 25s. Then again, you have had the
county council basing their calculations
partly upon voluntary labour. That was,
the farmers, or owners of land through
which the rivers ran, promised to contribute a great deal of voluntary labour,
but at the end of the work it was disputed
whether this voluntary labour had been
contributed or not. In many cases it
was found that the labour had not been
contributed, and in cases the cost of the
scheme was a great deal more than was
contemplated by the county council.
The county council found there was
endless bother and endless disputes, and
in many cases it finished up by adding
a burden on the general body of ratepayers. I do not wish to blame the
county councils at all. I think their
attitude from the 1925 Act up to the
present time is perfectly understandable.
Nor do I blame the Government or any
one of the Ministers. That is, perhaps,
why I apologised at the outset of this
Motion, because it is peculiar, for it
seeks to blame nobody. It merely hopes
that in future the present system will
be bettered. The county councils having
had all this bother and all this trouble
have now, as a general rule, put their
foot down and said, "We are going to
do nothing more. There are going to be
no more schemes formulated by us. We
are going to put no further scheme into
operation."
We
The Government cannot force the
county councils to formulate or execute
these works. The county councils say, as
they are entitled to say, "We are going to
do nothing more," and if the law remains
as at present nothing more can be done.
The state of the country as regards flooding will gradually become worse..
here are unfortunately subject to an excessive rainfall and this work of land
drainage not only needs to be executed,
but maintained. If the county councils
maintain their present attitude—again I
say I do not want to blame them-there
are going to be no more schemes of land
drainage and the country will gradually
be getting worse and worse and become
more waterlogged in the neighbourhood
of these rivers. That being the case, it
seemed to me it was necessary to bring
it before the attention of hon. Members
so that something would be done.
It seems clear that where you have
only three bodies-the Government, the
county councils and individual farmers
-and if anything is to be done in the
future you must exclude the individual
farmers, who have not the organisation
or capital to back them-you are left
with either the county councils or the
Government. I am only putting forward
a suggestion. It is that we must do one
of two things. We must have an Act
which would have the effect of encouraging the county councils to formulate and
execute these schemes, or the Government must take over the drainage
authority from the county councils and
formulate and execute these schemes
themselves. I do not put forward either
of these suggestions as a correct solution
of this problem. All I wish to do at the
present time is to present the problem
and ask for its consideration so that a
solution may be found, and found
quickly as possible.
as
It is hardly necessary to remind hon.
Members of the benefit of these land
drainage schemes. Most of the money
Schemes Under Drainage Acts 1688
Notice of Motion-
23 MAY 1939
emspent on them is spent on wages, and
consequently it gives SO much
ployment. It is money spent on persons
who will spend it in the country, so that
money that is voted by county councils
or by the Government for these schemes
is money that will circulate and go
through the country. It will also give a
large amount of employment in the
country. When you consider the number of unemployed who are, unhappily,
in the country at present, any schemes
or any enactment which would have the
advantage and effect of lessening that
unemployment must commend itself sympathetically to all Members. Then
again, although the different sums which
are spent on these schemes may in the
aggregate seem very large, one must
always remember that they are there out
of the Unemployment Relief Fund.
You have the advantage that so much
agricultural land is saved from flooding.
It is, unfortunately, generally the best
agricultural land that is beside these
rivers.
I know one particular case where in
the last twenty years a man who owned
a farm of 100 acres had 50 acres
rendered entirely useless in seven years
out of the twenty. He had no crops
whatever. In another seven years the
land was partially used, and during the
remaining years, which happened to be
dry, he could make use of them. A man
who owns a farm like that has to pay
land annuities whether the land is flooded
or not. Land in flooded areas is not
only no asset, but a regular burden.
When one considers that Northern
Ireland is a small area and that every
acre of good land available is an asset
to the community I think there will be
no difficulty in convincing hon. Members
that if this flooded land can be saved it
will be of inestimable advantage not only
to the occupier and owner of the land, but
to the country at large. As I have
said, I do not put forward a solution of this problem. I have given
my suggestion that either the county
councils must be satisfied with some
further enactment which will encourage
them to go forward with these schemes,
or else the Government must take it over
themselves, but at the present time when
the county councils maintain their
present attitude, as I am sure they will
do, it means that there will be no more
land drainage in Northern Ireland.
That, I think, is not a matter which
can be accepted with toleration by hon.
Members. The work is necessary. We
have the labour here. That labour is
going to waste just as flooded flelds are
going to waste. It is only a matter of
organisation. It would not only save
lands from being flooded and release them
for the purposes of agriculture, but it
would also be giving work to those people
who desire work so much.

a

be too high and they

course, I know it can be argued that the

MINISTER

The Londonderry County Committee

interviewed the two candidates and, as a

that they would be prepared to approve of

THE DEFENCE BILL.
3. Major SINCLAIR asked the Prime
Minister whether it is a fact, as reported
in the Press, that the Government proposes to postpone the introduction of the
new Defence Bill until the autumn; and,
if so, whether the Government considers
air raid precautions and the defence of
the civil population of little importance;
or whether it considers that the international situation is such as to warrant
postponement of the measure for several
months without undue risk.
The PRIME MINISTER: The answer
to the first part of the question is in
the affirmative, and to the remainder in
the negative.
I propose to make a statement, as soon
as I am in full possession of the terms
of the Bill at present before the Parliament at Westminster, of this Government's intentions in regard to Civil
Defence.

following passage complained of in the

extract from the draft report of the Joint
Select Committee on Road and Rail
Transport constitutes a breach of the
privileges of the House:
"They have had the position summarised to them in these words-The
transport experiment will cost the Government more than £4,000,000, of

the size and resources of Northern
Ireland a most serious embarrassment

grave consequences to the community.”

Agricultural Wages (Regulation) Bill.

[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Constitution of Agricultural Wages Board).
(1) For the purposes of this Act
there shall be established, as soon as
may be after the passing of this Act,
a body to be called the Agricultural
Wages Board for Northern Ireland
(in this Act referred to as "the
Board"), which shall consist of the
following persons:
Three members appointed by the
Minister of Agriculture, of whom
such one as the said Minister may
designate shall be the chairman
of the Board;
Six members being representatives of
employers in agriculture and
appointed by the Ulster Farmers'
Union and other prescribed
organisations (if any) in such
manner, and according to such
method of distribution as between
the several organisations as the
said Minister may from time to
time determine;
Six members being representatives of
workers in agriculture and
appointed by the Amalgamated
Transport and General Workers'
Union and other prescribed
organisations (if any) in
in such
manner, and according to such
method of distribution as between
the several organisations as the
said Minister may from time to
time determine.

CLAUSE 2 (Duties and powers of
Board with respect to minimum rates of
wages), ordered to stand part of the
Bill.
CLAUSE 3 (Complaints as to
inadequate payment for piece work
where no minimum piece rate has been
fixed.)
Any worker employed in agriculture on piece work for which no
minimum piece rate has been fixed
or any person authorised by such a
worker, may complain to the Board
that the piece rate of wages paid to
the worker for that work is such a
rate as would yield in the circumstances of the case to an ordinary.
worker a less amount of wages than
the minimum rate for time work
applicable in the case of that worker;
and the Board may on any such complaint, after giving to the employer
an
opportunity of making such
representations as he thinks desirable,
direct that the employer shall pay to
the worker such additional sum by
way of wages, for any piece work done
*
by the worker at that piece rate at
any time within fourteen days before
the date of complaint or at any time
after the date of complaint and before
the decision of the Board thereon, as
in their opinion represents the
difference between the amount which
would have been paid if the work had
been done by an ordinary worker at
the minimum rate for time work and
the amount actually received by the
worker by whom or on whose behalf
the complaint is made.

CLAUSE 4 (Holidays and holiday remuneration).
(1) Workers employed in agriculture for time work shall be entitled
to be allowed holidays of such duration as follows, namely, either-
(a) six days in each period of twelve.
months; or
(b) one day in respect of each period
of continuous employment of two
months' duration;
Provided that any such holidays shall
be taken in accordance with such
previous arrangements as may have
been made between the employer and
the worker.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

and it shows that the Minister of Agriculture has a full comprehension of the
result of the Measure. You will observe

Government. I could not do better than
repeat it again-leave. out "Workers"
and insert "A worker." Leave workers
out of work and retain a worker. The
farmer who has two or three workers is
to leave them out and keep one. That
is usually what follows every Act of
Parliament brought forward by this
Government for the last eighteen years,

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I beg to move,
in sub-clause (1) after the word "shall"
(shall be entitled) to insert the words, "in

Hon. Members will appreciate that the
intention of the Bill is that a worker who
is in continuous employment with the
same employer for a period of at least
two months' duration shall become entitled to receive a day's holiday with pay
from that employer in respect of each
period of continuous employment for
two months. It would clearly raise considerable administrative difficulties if
broken employment with different employers were to qualify for holidays with
remuneration. A worker might have
been employed for a month with one employer and then transferred to the second
employer. Difficulties would obviously
arise if the second employer had to give

employer. I do not think that any Member would suggest that such a state of

clear beyond doubt that to qualify for

employed continuously with the same
employer.

any one year there may be broken days.
There might be what you would call a

to try to find a word more in keeping

used to deprive persons of their legal

is an attempt-one of the attempts here

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I beg to move
in sub-clause (5) to leave out from
"years" ("of the said years') to end of
paragraph (b) and insert "contracts are
executed which would but for the provisions of this sub-section provide, when

then the quantity of pigs to be delivered

and each of the said contracts shall have

As at present drafted, the Bill provides that if the maximum number of
pigs in respect of which assistance is
guaranteed is exceeded, then certain of
the contracts which were last received for
registration shall be declared void until
the quantity of pigs is reduced so that
the guaranteed limit is not exceeded. It
has been represented that such a provision may operate unduly harshly on
certain producers who have been late in
submitting their contracts and that, since
it is the intention that a final date shall
be prescribed for the receipt of contracts.
or agreements, it is only fair that every
producer who has entered into contracts
or agreements before the closing date
should be treated alike. Accordingly, I
am moving this Amendment, which will
provide that in any case where, contracts
or agreements received up to a due date
provide for the delivery of a number of
pigs in excess of the guaranteed maximum, then the number of pigs to be
delivered under each of those contracts
or agreements shall be scaled down proportionately. I feel that the House will
agree that this proposal is a more acceptable one than the original provision in
the Bill, and I beg to move accordingly.

Finance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews) This Bill is intended to give
legislative effect to the taxation changes
that I announced in my Budget Speech.
Clause 1 provides for the increase in
motor vehicle duty from 15s per horse-
School-Leaving Age Bill- 1762
Finance Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
power on private cars to 25s per horsepower, together with somewhat smaller
increases on motor cycles. The new
rates are set out in the Schedule to the
Bill. I should like to emphasise again
that these increases do not apply either
to commercial or agricultural vehicles,
the tax on which will remain the same
as at present.
I propose to take this opportunity to
deal with two matters which have
received prominence in the Press since
my Budget Statement. First, that the
tax will cripple the motor industry. I
sincerely hope it will not. I don't think
it will do so.
In this connection I would like to
point out that until some years ago the
horse-power tax was 20s, but I did not
see any sign that the maintenance of
the tax at this figure checked the continual increase in the number of private
motor cars on the road. It was in fact
because of the flourishing state of the
industry that I was able to reduce the
tax without affecting the yield. I cannot, therefore, think that the increase
to 25s, that is, only 5s beyond the figure
at which it was maintained for many
years, can seriously affect the trade.
Hon. Members from their own
experience must be aware that the
annual tax forms a small proportion of
the expenditure which they incur on
insurance, petrol, and other running
expenses such as maintenance
depreciation.
and
The second point which is being made
is that as the estimated increased yield
from motor taxation in a full year,
namely £200,000, just happens to be the
same as the amount to be obtained under
the provisional agreement which has
been made for writing off losses on our
Transport Board guarantees, therefore
motorists are being made to pay for the
Transport Board's losses. This statement will not bear investigation, for
there is no connection between the
two. I secured the agreement of the
Chancellor to the necessary provision
being charged against the Imperial Contribution five weeks before he introduced
his Budget, and I obviously had no
knowledge at the time that he had any
intention of increasing motor taxation
in Great Britain, or that it would fall
to my lot to increase it here. My sole
object in increasing this tax is for
defence purposes as is the case with all
the other increases.
Further, I wish to say definitely that
we cannot, in my opinion, claim equal
citizenship within the United Kingdom,
and all the great advantages of that
position and not be prepared to pay
equal rates of taxation. This is so
obviously true that I am surprised that
I should feel it necessary to state it
to-day.

amount of the duty payable out of the
estates of persons dying on or after the
16th of this month, being the day
following the date of the Budget Resolution. I beg to move, "That the Bill be
now read a Second Time."

Education (School-Leaving Age) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Mr. Robb): The purpose of this
Measure is to postpone for one year the
raising of the school-leaving age as proposed in the Education Act of 1938.
The postponement is necessary because
it has become clear that the arrangement
which must be made to accommodate in
the schools children affected by the Act
cannot be satisfactorily completed in this
school year.
Hon. Members are aware that while
Education Committees in Great Britain
have had three years' notice of the coming
into effect of a similar Measure, the
Northern Ireland Act received the Royal
Assent as recently as November last.
The time thus available to Education
Committees and other school managers
1763 School-Leaving Age Bill-

30 MAY 1939
Second Reading
in Northern Ireland to prepare for the
reception of a new age group of pupils
was short, but we believed that it was
sufficient provided all who would be
responsible for working the Act could
concentrate their energies upon such
preparation.
It has come about, however, that the
attention of the Ministry of Education
and of the Belfast Education Committtee, two most important bodies, has
been directed by the Government, as a
matter of urgency, to preparing a
scheme for the evacuation, care and
education of Belfast children in the
event of the necessity arising.
The Executive Council of the Association of Northern Ireland Education
Committees and individual committees,
among them the Belfast and Londonderry Committees, have, on the grounds
of unpreparedness, requested the Government to postpone the carrying into
operation of the Act.
I would like to give the House some
idea of the difficulty of the problem that
faces the Belfast Committee. There is
no room to spare in the Belfast College
of Technology, and 46 of the 118 Belfast
schools giving instruction
to
senior
pupils are full. Included in these 46
schools are most of the large new senior
schools, which would be the schools best
able to provide suitable instruction for
children between the ages of 14 and 15.
Of the remaining 72 schools, 51 have no
proper facilities, particularly with
respect to practical instruction,
pupils of this age.
for
It was with reluctance that the
Government decided that the Measure
before the House should be introduced
but they are convinced that unless the
postponement it proposes is effected the
1938 Act will be likely for the reasons
I have given to lead to congestion and
confusion so that standards of education
will be lowered and the regularity of
school attendance adversely affected.
I am confident that hon. Members will
agree that it is of the greatest importance
that the raising of the school-leaving
age should come into effect under
favourable conditions and that all those
whose duty it will be to form those conditions shall be satisfied that they have
had proper opportunity to prepare for
their full collaboration in making it an
immediate and successful advance in our
educational system. For these reasons
the Bill has been introduced, and I
commend it to the House.
Mr. BEATTIE: I cannot accept the
statement of the Minister of Education.
I am pleased that he has come here from
the Upper House, and I would like to
see him here permanently once more.
The inadequate time at the disposal of
the various local authorities can be no
excuse for the lack of accommodation
for those pupils who would attend school
during the additional year. My chief
concern is for those children who will be
deprived of the right during the coming
year to attend school for that additional
year. The children who are thus being
sacrificed should have the first consideration. The Government should not have
adopted a policy of surrender to the local
authorities who were in the main opposed
to extending the school-leaving age. I
have for years advocated extending the
school age to sixteen. Others have
advocated extending it for a longer
period. We have now got to postpone
this Bill, which was going to be a blessing to working class children in the
North of Ireland because of the failure
of the local authorities, which had neither
heart nor eye for this Measure, to provide the necessary accommodation in
time. Now we have got to wait another
year until the accommodation is ample
for the extra pupils. At the end of a
year I presume that something else will
have arisen and we will again be asked
to postpone the Bill until finally it
becomes a dead letter.
I feel very disappointed at the attitude of the Government in acceding to
the request of the local authorities.
There is a certain argument in favour
of the postponement of the Measure
from the point of view of the Roman
Catholic schools. They have to provide
at least 50 per cent. of the cost of
erection, and they have a big difficulty
to contend with in making arrangements
for the additional number that would
attend in the extra year. But the
regional education committees have no
excuse at all. They have a very big
purse to dive into in order to provide the
accommodation that will be required.

several members of the Butter and Cream

Members of this House, but that he has
gone outside of this House. to select a
member to represent the Opposition.
That is an injustice on the top of an

and cream industry, a representative of

plete outsider
represent Labour
interests in the Butter and Cream Board.

I want to assure the hon. Gentleman

to recognise the value of the Public

Mr. BEATTIE: You do not, because

better. We have large sums allocated

the progress of a certain Department in

Then, again, I understand there has

using motor-bicycles. A bicycle accommodates one man and yet we use largepower cars which accommodate two men.
I think that is over service. This service on the highways can be done as

There is another point I want to make.
A suggestion was made about it, but no
notice was taken of it. The police have
been decorated with a class of tunic which
is somewhere about 150 years old. When
I was in the Army I had a similar tunic,
but I had also a summer tunic. The
Police Force have only one tunic for winter
and summer. It is a high stiff-collared
tunic. I ask Members of this House to
fit one of these tunics on themselves and
do street or point duty or any other
class of duty during the kind of weather
we have had these last two or three days,
and they will find that it is very
injurious to health and injurious also to
the skin. It creates in the neck the very
dirty looking things known as blackheads.
These are caused by the sweat of the
person and the dye from the tunic. I
suggest that there should be an improvement in the uniform of the police.
In summer time there should be a serge
jacket with the lapel collar turned down,
so as to give freedom to the neck and
ventilation to the, body, so much required
in
these hot summer days, which
I hope we will have a lot of this
summer. That question, although raised

has been brought to my notice that the

my attention that the

HOUSE OF COMMONS

in the city of Toronto the compulsory
pasteurisation of milk has been in force
since 1915.

This Bill discloses the fact that about
£900,000 is to be set apart in the course
of the year to defray the charges of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
addition, a sum of £166,000 is to be set
apart to defray the charges of the Special
Constabulary. At the present time it
is a harvest home for the Special Constabulary. It means that all told a sum
of about £1,100,000 is needed for the
policing of this petty area in which crime.
is almost negligible, and in which the
cost of administration is bloated beyond
comparison. Two and a quarter millions
are to be set aside for educational services.
The only comment I make on that is
that for every £93 of public money that
is expended on the provision and equipment of the denominational schools of the
majority of the population, only £7 of
public money is provided for corresponding purposes of the denominational
schools of the minority in this area. That
statement of fact and figures bears its
own comment.
The Bill also makes clear one other
fact; that the cost of public services of
the Six Counties has risen to twelve and
a half million pounds, costing £10 per
head of every man, woman and child
in the Six Counties every year. That is
almost as much as the entire cost of the
British administration of all Ireland
before 1921, and it is two million pounds
more than the cost of the Six Counties
two years ago.
It indicates, I think, the
deadness of public spirit in this area that
in a matter of the very short space of
two years there can be a jump in public
expenditure amounting to two million
pounds, and it is passed by as if it was
of no account whatever. A storm over
the Pigs Marketing Board would create
far more excitement.
One explanation may be
be that we
have in this Parliament no really effective
Opposition. We have nothing in the way
of an effective Opposition to check the
Government's rampaging and riotous
living.
Mr. GRANT: Order more gas masks.
Mr. CAMPBELL: The Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Labour cannot forget his old days. I should have
thought that now that he was quietly
enmeshed in the toils of subordinate
office he could maintain a certain amount
of discretion, but the old Adam will break
out. We find that here at Stormont we
have really the only Parliament in the
world in which Opposition of an effective
character finds no place. The Prime Minister called for a Protestant Parliament.
He ambitioned a sectarian Opposition to
confront a sectarian Government. Let
him whistle down the wind until that
Opposition materialises. A legislative
body where an Opposition cannot exist
bears within itself the seeds of dissolution and decay.
I come now to the Ministry of Home

much of the energy and much of the
imagination of the Constabulary are expended in raids on Catholic homes, carried out under the Special Powers Act.
Those raids are almost always futile, and
are always provocative, alarming and
terrorising, especially when conducted in
the dead hours of the night. As a rule
nothing incriminating is found, but
humble people are frightened. Needless
to say these invasions of the sanctity of
the home do not go beyond the houses of

I am not an extremist in my methods.
I have attended this Parliament as I
thought right, as a matter of duty, and
in the interests of my own people. It is

back benches. I also wish to refer to the
fact that since Christmas last, a matter of
almost six months, 32 or 33 men have
been interned in Belfast Jail under orders
made by the Minister of Home. Affairs
under the Special Powers Act. Those
men have not been charged with any
offence; they have not been brought to
trial. Elsewhere they would be deemed
innocent. The presumption in the case
of a man who is not convicted of an
offence is that he is innocent of that
offence. Of course, we know that habeas
corpus is suspended in the Six Counties.
I do not think it is suspended in any
other part of the British Commonwealth.
no
The Government would have
hesitation in bringing these men to trial,
many people say, if they had a particle
of evidence against them. They have not
been brought to trial, because there is no
proof against them, and, therefore, they
are languishing in jail. Some of those
men, for all that is known, may be
the victims of false information
maliciously given against them. by
enemies; they have no security against
that; the public have no security against
that. The ukase of the Minister of
Home Affairs is the first and last word

the courts; the courts of justice are
closed to them; the Minister supersedes
all that. It is a state of affairs without
parallel in any civilised community.
It will be said by the. Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, that those men can appeal against
