the very Ministry which has interned
them. The Appeal Tribunal, as I understand it, is constituted of members and
officials of that Ministry. Is that not
most remarkable and anomalous
machinery? In recent months Catholic
ladies of high character have been made
to realise what an atrocious offence it is
to wear what is called an Easter lily.
Peaceful meetings to be addressed by
Members of Parliament of this House
and of Westminster as a protest against
a British Act of Parliament in an area
legislated for and administered by the
British Parliament have been suppressed
by the local Executive.
The Government discrimination against
Catholics in the matter of public employment has become intensified, if that is
possible. In four out of the Six
Counties Catholic Clerks of the Crown,
appointed in pre-partition days, have
been superseded by gentlemen not of their
persuasion. I do not criticise those gentlemen; I do not say they are not fitted
for their offices, but I do draw attention
to the gradual change in the aspect
of affairs in that particular domain.
The Permanent Secretaryship of the.
Ministry of Education has gone the same
way. In fact, it may be said with perfect truth, that no Catholic in the Six
Counties is now allowed to hold a key
post in any Department.
I see, that the Minister of Labour is
in his seat. I am informed that no
Catholics are employed as inspectors and
investigators of claimants' means under
Part II of the Unemployment Insurance
Act. I am told that perhaps two or three
Catholic medical men are employed as
referees or examiners under the National
Health Insurance and Blind Persons
Acts. The religious test is the definite
policy of all public boards controlled by
the Prime Minister's friends. The
gerrymandering of local government
areas, with the resultant paralysing of
Nationalist electoral majorities, enforced
by the Government through legislation
and administration, has as an aim and an
attainment the exclusion of Catholics
from public employment. The cue has
been, "Destroy their nests." It is a
traditional policy.
The Ministry of Home Affairs have
made huge grants to public authorities

initiated a system of recruiting unskilled

lessening of employment of Catholics in
its various departments and undertakings
until such now amounts to less than 7 per

The discrimination by local authorities derives force and momentum from
the discrimination enforced by the
central authority as the mainspring of
its administration. Out of some fifty
district inspectors of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, some five profess the
religion of the minority. Out of each
draft of 65 recruits for the Royal Ulster
Constabulary in a year only five on the
average are Catholics. Queen Victoria
at one time wrote to her Prime Minister,
Mr. Gladstone, that Orange proclivities
were a disqualification for all Irish responsibilities. Under the régime now
unhappily here, such proclivities are the
only avenue of approach to official
honours and emoluments. Times have
changed with a vengeance in the Six
Counties. High English notabilities are
crying off from official visits to the Six
Counties. Visits of British Home Secretaries and others are loudly heralded in
advance only to be cancelled. Those
people are showing signs of disinclination
to make contact with the Stormont junta.
There is no need to wonder at the cooling
off. Irish opinion is too strong for this
outside and officious interference.
Just now Jews everywhere are expressing the bitterest feelings over the British
plan of an independent Palestine State
in which Arabs will outnumber the Jews
by two to one, and declaring that the
British Government are going the way
of turning a peaceful and orderly Zionism
into a merciless conflict, in which the
Arabs will have everything to gain by
success and nothing to lose by failure.
They are saying it is a betrayal of Jewish
hopes and rights and a putting of the
Jews in a permanent minority. The remarkable thing is that the parallel is very
close here, because a British Act of
Parliament handed over one-third of the
people of the Six Counties to the domination of a small faction acting for twothirds without guarantee for the rights or
aspirations of the minority.

I am speaking about the early stages

What happened with regard to the
police? We set up a Committee, a very
powerful Committee of the House, at
that time to guide us as to what would
be fair in regard to the constitution of
the Police Force. The report of that
Committee is there for anyone to read.
After considerable thought and consideration the deliberate decision of that
Committee, as contained in the Report,
was that two-thirds of the Force should
be Protestants and one-third Roman
Catholics. I thought that was very fair
because it corresponded to the division.
of the population within the Ulster
area. We immediately began to recruit
men and took members of the old Royal
Irish Constabulary into consideration as
well as others who desired to join the
new Force.
What occurred? We were immediately faced with a boycott of the
Force. The Roman Catholics were
warned, by a higher authority I presume, that on no account were they to
join the new Royal Ulster Constabulary.
Seeing that one-third of the Force could
not be filled by the co-religionists of the
hon. and learned Member, were we to be
satisfied with only 2,000 police for the
whole of Ulster or were we to recruit the
3,000 recommended by the Committee

from those who desired to join? Of

2,000. We were going upon the
experience gained by the police authorities prior to the Act of 1920, and it was
thought by competent judges that about
3,000 was the correct number for us to
enroll. Whose fault was it?
How is this Government to be blamed
for a state of affairs like that? Surely
the hon. and learned Member, who
practices in our Courts and is one of the
senior King's Counsel in Ulster, can see
for himself exactly where the blame lies?
It does not lie with us. If 1,000 Roman
Catholics had come forward at that time
to join the Force the same as the
Protestants to safeguard the peace of
our common country the question would
never have arisen. When such strong
pressure was brought to bear on men
to boycott the Police Force, I am not
prepared to stand here and apologise to
anyone for the action taken at that time.
That uneven number is, I presume,
perpetuated to-day? I do not know, I
could not tell without making inquiries
what the proportion of Roman Catholics
to Protestants in our Force is. It

influence which
was brought to bear
upon men not to join the Force, and
I will leave it to the hon. and learned

Another point I should refer to is the
question of local authorities. These
authorities are elected throughout Northern Ireland a democratic basis.
Appointments are made on the qualifications of the candidates, and I cannot see
how this House can influence the County
Councils or the Urban or Rural District
Councils or any of the other democractically elected bodies as to what
officials they should employ. Those are
matters for those bodies so long as the
local government is carried on in the
same way as it has been for many years.
I will, therefore, leave that point
because I am sure the hon. and learned
Member will recognise that in a democractic country no one can interfere with
those democratically elected as we are
ourselves.
Looking back upon the past 13 years--
it is now very nearly 18 years since all
the powers of Government were
entrusted to our hands-I have no feelings of regret for any steps taken by my
colleagues and myself in connection with
the various services necessary for us to
carry on.

Mr. MAGINESS: I beg to move, in
the Schedule to this Bill of the various
licences and rebates to omit the words,
"If used for drawing a trailer, an
additional sum of £2," which is charged
in respect of trailers in this country.
When presenting his Budget the Minister of Finance spoke about the necessity
of equal sacrifice with Great Britain
and we all were most sympathetic to him.
I think myself people in this House, and
certainly on this side of the House, were
agreed that Northern Ireland and Great
Britain should share equally in the sacrifices they are making in a common cause.
If this country had to be prepared for
any eventuality it is clear the money
must be found for that, and I think the
people of Northern Ireland were prepared to do their part in finding that
money. Hence, although many of the
Members here who represent agricultural
constituencies greatly regretted and disliked the increased tax on horse-power,
we did not feel justified in opposing that
increase of 10s because we sympathised
with the difficult position of the Minister
of Finance. We knew the money had
to be raised and we accordingly were
prepared to support him in most of the
proposals which he put forward.
But while we are prepared and,
indeed, cheerful and willing to bear
equal sacrifices in having the country
prepared for eventualities, we did not see
why we should be called upon to bear
more than equal sacrifices. We agreed
that sacrifice should be equal, but in this
particular matter the sacrifices are not
equal. We are paying 25s per horsepower with the people in England just
as last year, and the year before we
paid 15s. But we are called upon-at
least some of the inhabitants of Northern
Ireland are called upon-to pay an
additional tax of £2. Many of the
farmers run vehicles of a considerable
age to and from the markets and fairs,
perhaps not worth more than £20, while
they pay £16 or £17 in tax. Why
should they pay the additional tax of £2
which farmers in England are not called
upon to pay. I have asked myself the
reason for this £2 and I cannot find the
answer to it.
Originally we were told that the
damage done. to the roads by these
trailers was such that it was necessary to
have a tax put on,
tax put on, and consequently
this £2 tax was imposed to help the Road
Fund. But the money raised by the
licensing of motor vehicles is out of proportion to the amount spent on the roads.
It can no longer be put forward that the
money raised by taxing motor vehicles
is used for the upkeep of the roads. We
are far and away beyond that stage.
The roads have. been improved so much
that less and less money need be spent
on them. Consequently the money now
raised by taxation of motor vehicles is
simply part of the General Fund. This
£2 tax affects farmers who travel to fairs
and markets. I am not concerned with
the gigantic trailers which carry tons of
produce, but with the farmer who goes
about his business with a small, light
trailer attached to his ordinary car. They
can do little damage to the roads.
Naturally if a farmer is paying 25s per
horse power in taxation he feels, I think
we ought to feel, that he spends as much
as he should, certainly as much as he can
afford.
or
I am not going into the reason
suggesting any reason why this extra
£2 tax is placed on Northern Ireland
farmers, but I do say that there is a tax
being placed on the farmers at the
present time which the farmers in no
other part of the British Isles are asked
to pay.
If this basis of equality of
sacrifice holds good in one direction it
should hold good in another.
If we
agree the tax per horse power should go
up from 15s to 25s in order that we may
share equal sacrifice others are making
across the water, then we should not be
asked to pay an additional £2 per trailer

It is one

I am thinking of the general good of

classes in the community. I realise

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): Hon. Members know how
anxious I am at all times to meet their
wishes, but I regret that I am unable to
do so on this occasion. I have learned
how popular it is to reduce taxation and
how unpopular it is to levy it. Still,
that is a consideration which I cannot
allow to influence me unduly. I must
look at matters of this kind on their
merits, and I do feel that this is a very
reasonable tax. It is very small in
amount, only £2, and I cannot help but
feel that anybody who looks at this
matter from a reasonable point of view
will come to the conclusion that as
trailers do to some extent wear the roads
it is not reasonable to feel that they
ought to contribute something towards.
the upkeep of those roads.
I would point out in that connection
that although portion of the money.
'
collected in connection with motor
duties is retained in the Exchequer, the
great proportion of it is used for the
upkeep of our roads. I do not think
that this can be cited as an example for
parallel legislation with Great Britain
because the conditions are not the same
in both areas. The number of roads in
our area in relation to the population is
excessive as compared with the position
in Great Britain.
Then again, as the hon. Member for
Pottinger has said, the fact that a
trailer, very often without a proper
coupling arrangement, is attached to a
motor car itself indicated the liability
to accident. I myself a few months ago
saw an accident, not a very serious one,
I am glad to say, caused by a trailer.
One motor would have without doubt
passed the other motor, but the trailer
having lengthened the point of danger
received the blow from the other motor
car. That accident would not have
taken place if the trailer had not been
there.
I would like to point out to hon.
Members that although I am always in
favour of following Great Britain except
on an occasion such as this, I feel there
is a justification for a departure in this
instance, and although I do not wish to
adopt the role of a prophet I would not
be surprised if some day the British
Chancellor of the Exchequer would
follow my example in this connection.
I do feel there will be a great deal of
justification for taking that course.
May I point out to my hon. Friends
that although I felt called upon to raise
the taxation on private motor cars I did
not at the same time raise the taxation
on the trailers? Taxation on the trailer
remains the same, and, as I have
mentioned, it is only £2. I would.
therefore, appeal to my hon. Friends
that as on many occasions I have met
their wishes on this occasion they should
meet mine and not press this to a
division.

Oral Answers to Questions.
SCRAP IRON FOR GERMANY.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state what
was the quantity of scrap iron, etc.,
shipped from the Port of Belfast to
Germany:-(a) during the year 1938,
(b) the first four months of the present
year.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have had inquiries
made of the Belfast. Harbour Commissioners and understand that during the
year 1938, 4,074 tons of scrap iron were
shipped direct from the Port of Belfast
to German ports. There do not appear
to have been any direct shipments since
1st January, 1939. No information is
obtainable as to any quantities of scrap
iron which may have been exported to
Germany via ports in Great Britain.

4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received a
resolution from the Lurgan Board of
Guardians urging that the vaccination
laws in Northern Ireland should be
amended so as to bring them into line
with the laws at present in force in
England; whether the vast majority of
the other Boards of Guardians in Northern Ireland have expressed similar views
by resolution or otherwise; and whether
it is the intention of the Ministry to
have such widely expressed views given
effect to.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Warnock): On
behalf of my right hon. Friend, in
reply to the first part of this question,
I have received the resolution referred to
by the hon. Member. With regard to
the second part of the question, it is not
a fact that the vast majority of Boards
of Guardians have expressed similar
views to those contained in this resolution. I am not, therefore, aware of any
general desire for the amendment of the
law, and I do not therefore propose to
take the action suggested by the hon.
Member.

In spite of this I am fully alive to the

necessary precautions to meet this danger.
At the same time, it must be obvious to
all of us that there is a varying degree
of vulnerability in Northern Ireland,
and according to expert advice the main
danger zones are:-
(1) Belfast, and its approaches, by
which I mean roughly a triangle which
would include the area Larne,
Lisburn, and Donaghadee;
(2) The County Borough of Londonderry;
and in the Government's view the precautions to be taken in these areas must
be of a much fuller character than in
the remaining parts of Northern Ireland.
I must emphasise, however, at this
stage, lest it should be thought that my
words mean that no air-raid precautions
are to be taken throughout the less
vulnerable part of Northern Ireland, that
this is not the Government's intention.
Rather do we urge local authorities over
Northern Ireland to carry out their
statutory functions under the Northern
Ireland Air-Raid Precautions Act of
last year, and to submit schemes which
should ensure, at any rate, the speedy
distribution of respirators in time of war,
the establishment of a number of First-
Aid Posts, and the provision of the
necessary training in air-raid precautions.
by way of lecture and otherwise.
It
must be obvious to hon. Members that
very considerable movements of population will take place in time of war, and
it would be indefensible to withhold
from any of our citizens that knowledge
of how they should act during a
threatened or an actual air raid, because, if allowed to remain ignorant on
these matters they might endanger not
only their own lives but the lives of
those amongst whom they are temporarily
resident or working. I am glad to be
able to announce that since the Act of
last year was passed a number of local
authorities have submitted
schemes
which, with a few reservations on certain
matters, the Ministry of Home Affairs
has approved, and the Ministry has now
before it an advance copy of the general
outlines of the Belfast County Borough
scheme which contains evidence of very
considerable activity, and shows that the
Council realises its responsibilities.
As in Great Britain power will be
taken in the Bill to enable the Government to ensure that local authorities shall
carry out their statutory duties in respect
of the preparation of A.R.P. schemes. I
do not anticipate for one moment, knowing the long record of splendid service of
local authorities, that such a provision will
ever have to be utilised, but no Government can divest itself of the ultimate
responsibility of ensuring the safety of
the people in the area under its control.
Here I should like to mention for the
information of hon. Members that the
Government has had under review the
fire-fighting service in Northern Ireland,
especially in the more vulnerable areas,
and in order to be able to deal effectively
with the results of any incendiary bombing that may occur, 187 fire engines of
varying types have been ordered by the
Government-some have already arrived,
and an early delivery of the remainder
has been promised. These machines will
be manned by members of the Auxiliary
Fire Services, in which a very considerable number of volunteers have already
been enrolled and are under training, but
for which still further recruits are
required, particularly in Belfast.
I shall deal now with the main provisions which it is proposed to include in
our Civil Defence Bill. First, the shelter
provisions which may be divided into
public shelters, shelters for factories and
commercial buildings, employing more
than 50 persons, and, lastly, domestic
shelters.
In so far as public shelters are concerned, it is proposed to enable local
authorities to select buildings which would
be suitable for use as public shelters, or
other air-raid precautions purposes. The
authorities may then enter the buildings
and may adapt them and execute such
works as may be necessary to reinforce
them and make them safe. The occupiers
are not displaced during peace time, at
any rate, but they will be temporarily
inconvenienced during the period of
adaptation, and the adaptation may
render the premises less convenient.
Ample safeguards will be provided for
any person having any estate or interest
in the premises selected by the local
authorities, and, of course, the occupiers
will be entitled to receive compensation
in respect of any damage they may sustain by reason of interference with their
premises. This provision of public shelters
Statement by Prime Minister 1550
Civil Defence-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
will be limited to the more vulnerable
areas, and the local authorities will be
allowed to count their expenses for grant
in accordance with the provisions of the
Northern Ireland Air Raid Precautions
Act, 1938.
Coming now to shelters for factories
and commercial buildings, I must inform
the House that the position in Great
Britain is that in those more vulnerable
areas designated by the Government it is
made compulsory for the owner of any
factory or commercial building employing
more than 50 persons to provide air-raid
shelters sufficient for the needs of the
employees. Having given the most careful consideration to all the aspects of the
matter, the Government does not feel that
in Northern Ireland it is necessary to
impose any general compulsory system,
but rather that power shall be given to
the Government, acting on such information and expert advice as it may receive from time to time, to specify certain
areas and buildings in which measures
of protection must be taken. The use of
these compulsory powers would, of
course, be confined to areas which are
adjudged to be most vulnerable to air
attack, and, in so far as factory premises
or commercial buildings are concerned,
would, as in Great Britain, be limited to
those which employ more than 50 people.
Provided the shelters are in accordance
with the approved designs to be embodied
in a Shelter Code, which will shortly be
issued, grants-in-aid at the rate of 5s 6d
in the pound of approved expenditure on
these works will be made by the Government. I am gratified to learn that plans
have already been submitted by certain
concerns in Northern Ireland for the purpose of providing shelter for their
employees, and I would urge that when
areas or buildings are specified the work
should be put in hands at once, for there
is no reason to delay the provision of
shelters until the Bill comes before
Parliament in view of the undertaking I
have given that the provisions as to money
grants will have retrospective effect.

The PRIME MINISTER: Moreover, I should make it clear that,
within any area which
may be
specified, it is the Government's
intention that the grants shall be paid
for shelters provided by employers even
in cases where there will be no compulsion
on them to make such provision. To this
there will be certain exceptions, which
will be enumerated in the Bill.
A provision will be included making it
compulsory for every person who employs
more than 20 people in any factory premises or commercial building to ensure
that his employees are trained as respects
the routine to be followed in the event
of an air attack, and that a suitable
proportion of those employees are trained
and equipped to give first aid treatment,
to deal with the effects of gas, and to
fight fire.
I come next to the provision of shelters
by the Government. The questions of
the need for the provision of such shelters,
for a limited area in Northern Ireland,
and of the type of shelter best suited to
local conditions, are receiving the careful
consideration of experts on behalf of the
Government, and I am not yet in a
position to make a definite statement on
the matter.
If, on the advice of these experts who
are at present devoting their time to this
thorny subject, the Government decides
to issue domestic shelters, then it will be
the duty of the local authority to give
the persons to whom they are supplied
advice as to the position in which they
should be erected, and where the local
authority is asked to do so, it may
help in erecting them.
The continued functioning of public
utility undertakings in time of war is of
major importance. General provisions

as
Very great importance is attached to
the obscuration of lights in Northern
Ireland in time of war, as this matter
affects not only our own safety but that
of parts of Great Britain, because, for
example, lights in Northern Ireland
would assist an enemy 'plane to fix its
position in relation to certain parts of
Great Britain. There is no doubt that
during war Northern Ireland would have
to carry out a complete and efficient
arrangement for the obscuration of
lights, and it is for this reason that I
welcome the experimental black-outs
which have already been carried out with
such conspicuous success in the Bangor
and Larne areas.
The provisions which the Government
will introduce relating to this matter are
aimed at securing that in factory and
public utility undertakings appropriate
steps shall be taken now to ensure that
if and when an emergency arises the
premises can be blacked-out without delay. No grant is made to factories or
public utility undertakings in connection
with this blacking-out, except in cases
where any process carried on involves
the emission of flames or glare not
capable of being screened by means
which would suffice in the case of
ordinary lighting of a building, and in
the latter case a grant of one-half the
approved expenses can be made. Provision will also be included to safeguard
local authorities who may, contrary to
Statutes requiring them to provide
lighting, have to extinguish or dim
lighting in highways or public places for
the purpose of exercising air-raid precautions, or testing devices for enabling
the movement of traffic to continue in
unlighted streets. Camouflage may also
be required for the purpose of making
certain premises less readily recognisable
by aircraft, but a notice will be served
by the Government in each specific case
and a grant-in-aid at the rate of 50 per
cent. of the approved expenses may be
made.
I now turn to the important question
of the training of volunteers for nursing
duties in an emergency. I should like
to explain that in England and Wales
the arrangements for the training of
nursing auxiliaries have been entrusted
to a Central Emergency Committee
specially appointed by the Minister of
Health, and the Committee have deputed.
their functions throughout the country to
local emergency organisations which are
under the charge of the medical officer
of health in each county or county
borough. Similar arrangements have
been made in Scotland. It has been
decided, however, that in Northern Ireland it would be more practicable to concentrate in the Ministry of Home Affairs
the work which is being done in England
and Wales by the Central Committee and
to ask the Ulster Joint Committee of the
Order of St. John and the British Red
Cross Society to assist scheme-making
authorities in making training arrangements in each locality. The Ulster
Joint Committee have expressed their
Statement by Prime Minister 1854
Civil Defence-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
willingness to co-operate in this way, and
the Government has now prepared a
definite scheme for the formation of a
Civil Nursing Reserve, whose object it
will be--
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order.
Mr. NIXON: Finish the statement tomorrow.
The following is the remainder of the
Prime Minister's statement :
(1) to supplement the nursing staffs of
hospitals;
(2) to provide suitably trained staff for
first-aid posts set up by local
authorities; and
(3) to supplement the district nursing
staff in those districts which will
be used as reception areas under
the Government evacuation scheme.
Power will be taken in our Bill to cover
the cost of the training in advance of
persons who express their willingness to
offer their services as nurses in time of
war. If this nursing reserve is to be
trained efficiently and without delay, it
will be essential to have the full cooperation of local authorities. I have no
reason to doubt that local authorities will,
as they have always done in difficult
times, play their part fully in order to
ensure an efficient scheme. Arrangements
are now in course of preparation by the
Government to secure that, in the event
of war, facilities will be available for the
treatment of casualties and also for the
storage and preservation of medical
stores, beds, blankets, drugs, etc.
I come now to the question of evacuation. In Great Britain responsibility for
evacuation of the civilian population has
been placed, to a very large extent, upon
local authorities, but as the problem here
resolves itself, in the Government's view,
into the preparation of a scheme for the
evacuation of some 70,000 children, and,
in addition, elderly infirm people and
cripples from one area only, it was decided
that the preparation of the scheme should.
be the responsibility of the Government
itself, with, of course, the co-operation of
the local authorities. It may never become necessary to put this evacuation
scheme into force, but it is our duty to
ensure that, should this course prove desirable, a workable scheme is ready to
effect the evacuation of those to whom I
have referred in a smooth and efficient
manner and without delay. Very considerable progress has already been made
with this work, and many thousands of
voluntary offers to house children have
been received by the Government. The
problem is, however, a very big one when
one bears in mind that the questions of
transport, food, health, and continued
education becomes more and more important as the duration of a war extends. I
consider it inevitable that the Government must ask for compulsory powers of
billeting, and I cannot doubt that in asking for these powers for this humanitarian
purpose it will have the unqualified support of every Member of the House.
The last specific matter to which I need
refer is the proposed inclusion in our Bill
of provision for payment of compensation
to those who sustain personal injury in
time of peace while carrying out civil
defence duties for which they have volunteered. This is, of course, a very necessary provision, and one which I know will
appeal to all hon. Members.
Finally, may I ask for full support in
furthering our civil defence plans of all
Members of this House, of local authorities, and of every member of the general
public, for there is not one of us that
cannot help in some way. We still want
volunteers for all aspects of our air-raid
precautions, and I would urge all those
who can, to come forward now and
volunteer for this very important work,
rather than that they should take too
complacent a view, with the result that if
an emergency arises they will not be able
to render the assistance they themselves
would desire, either to their own families
or their fellow citizens.

of the necessary precautions held up
because of that,, and therefore it will be
made retrospective. That will not

Members to freely criticise the Bill when
it comes before the House. That disposes
quite clearly of that point.

remain at home and have it appear that
there was no Irish contingent at all able
to join with those in Great Britain? We
sent a contingent for two reasons-first,
to show our intense loyalty, and,
secondly, to pay a slight tribute of
respect to their Majesties on their return from their successful tour in
Canada and the United States. I think
we took the right step in deciding to
send a contingent to represent Ulster on
that important occasion, for the two
reasons I have mentioned, and for many
others. The occasion allowed our representatives to see whether there was anything more we could do to improve the
situation over here, while they also had
the advantage of conversing with those
who are engaged in similar A.R.P. work
in other parts of the United Kingdom.
I would like to point out that the
whole system of A.R.P. can only be a
complete success-and with anything less
I should not be satisfied-if everybody
in this country will do his and her part.
The machinery is all there. The text
book for National Service is in the hands
of everybody, detailing the various
channels through which their individual
activities can be utilised. They are told
exactly what they can do, and there are
willing workers prepared to go anywhere
in order to teach the more technical subjects.
So far I am satisfied with the personnel
already offered. It may be that in a short
time I hope the shortest possible-I will
be able to report to the House that every
one of these voluntary organisations is
completed in personnel. But we have to
struggle the Government has to struggle
-against a considerable number of difficulties. These difficulties are only before
us to be overcome.

Now I will switch on to the police. I
am not going to attack the police. I never
attack them. The police have been
attacked by their authorities in a way
calculated to destroy the moral of the
police. I have given notice to the Parliamentary Secretary. A short time ago
there was a row up the Crumlin Road,
a revolver was lost, and the prisoner got
away. The next day he was arrested,
brought before the court, and convicted.
I know there was no very deep political
move behind it. It was a row got up
on the spur of the moment. Well, what
happened? Someone went down to headquarters, and made a complaint that the
police exceeded their duty, and there were
anything from five to seven good men
and their families transferred-I cannot
say whether it is five or seven-and their
homes broken up.
Then someone else went down and said
that this had demoralised the police. The
authorities saw it from a new angle, and
instead of admitting that they transferred the men for what they did they
pretended that they transferred them for
what they did not do. In other words
they made it out that they transferred
them for letting the prisoner go and not
making a regular smash and slaughter in
the locality. It was a case of Mr. Facingboth-ways trying to please both sides.
But one thing they did do. They
punished five or seven good men and their
families, and demoralised the whole force,
for the police now do not know where
they are. What was written on the files
transferring them was that they showed
lack of moral courage. In other words,
they were moral cowards. That is what
was written on the file. That meant they
were pretending that the police should
have killed and shot and slaughtered all
round them. Now, what are the police
to do?
In May 1937 there was a sergeant in
that locality who used his firearms with
fatal effect, and the law as laid down at
the inquest and confirmed by the Crown
and the learned judge, because the
Crown prosecuted to the last letter, is
this: It was only in cases of treason or
treason-felony that an officer was entitled
to shoot, and then only if the offender
could not be otherwise apprehended.
Desertion or absenting without leave
was neither treason nor felony. That
was the law as laid down by the City
Coroner and afterwards confirmed by the
Crown, and the police with that in their
minds during this scuffle did not use
their firearms. They did not shoot anyone, because that was the law laid down.
It is most regrettable where life is lost,

around to see people wearing Irish linen,
but they have to go to New York to
see it. The Government should set a
headline here and now by telling us that
in future they will equip the Royal
Ulster Constabulary with light summer
uniforms of Irish linen. I support and
back up every suggestion made in this
House that will contribute towards the
prosperity of the linen industry.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
if the Irish linen for the uniforms of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary will be
made from Russian flax or of linen made
from flax grown in Northern Ireland.
Mr. BROWN: I am all in favour of
linen produced in Northern Ireland from
home-grown flax. We are sending four
millions out of Northern Ireland every
year for foreign flax, and all this Government can do is devote £150,000 for three
years to find some ways and means of
preventing that money going out of the
country.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: The question of imports is a matter for the
British Parliament. We have nothing
to do with that.
Mr. BROWN: I want to see the
Royal Ulster Constabulary supplied with
a light uniform made of Irish linen from
flax grown here. That will contribute
greatly to the comfort of the force and
to the prosperity of the industry.

BANGOR-DONAGHADEE ROAD
ACCIDENT.
2. Major HALL-THOMPSON asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
is aware
that a motor-car killed a
pedestrian on the Bangor-Donaghadee
Road near Donaghadee on the 8th
instant; whether the accident was chiefly
due to the fact that there is no footpath
provided on this road, and whether he
will make representations to the Local
Authority drawing attention to the
necessity for a footpath.
SECRETARY
The FINANCIAL
(Lieut-Colonel Gordon): I have been
asked to take this question on behalf of
my right hon. Friend.
I understand that the accident to
which the hon. Member refers occurred
at a place where there is no footpath on
either side of the road, but the road,
although narrow, is straight with a clear
view and in good condition, and it is,
therefore, open to question how far the
absence of a footpath was a contributory
cause of the accident.
I have, however, been informed that
cidents have previously occurred at the
same place, and I shall, therefore, ask
the Donaghadee Urban District Council
to consider carefully what action can be
taken to make the place safe for road
users.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: Arising
out of the reply, might I ask the hon.
and gallant Gentleman if it is a fact that
schemes such as these, if approved, would
receive a grant to the extent of 85 per
cent. from the Ministry of Labour?
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Any improvements which the Urban District
Council may undertake, if they come
under the Regulations, will, I am sure,
be most sympathetically considered by
the Ministry of Home Affairs.

THE WAR WITH GERMANY.
The PRIME MINISTER:
refer to the Motion that stands in my
name I would particularly like to associate
myself with the words which fell from
Mr. Speaker's lips to-day with regard to
our old Friend the late Member for Bann
Side.
I feel very much, indeed, the loss
from a personal point of view, as well as
from a Parliamentary one. The name of
Young in Ulster is renowned and the loss
of another member of the family is a
serious matter for us at this time. I
know well the work that the late Mr.
Young's father and brothers have all done
for the community, and the late right
hon. Member lived up to the highest
traditions of an Ulster gentleman.
I rise to-day in a difficult state of affairs
so far as we here are concerned. I would
have called the House together earlier,
with your permission, had I thought that
any good service would be rendered either
to Members or to the community; but as
will be realised the situation up to a few
days ago did not, in my opinion, justify
calling the House together, because I felt
that it would not be long before some
decision was taken one way or the other
which would clear the air so far as being
able to address hon. Members is concerned.
We are met now after most exhaustive
endeavours on the part of Mr. Chamberlain to secure peace throughout the world.
He admits it himself, I am sure with a
very sad heart, that all he did on behalf
of the country failed, and, therefore, we
here to-day are in a state of war, and we
are prepared with the rest of the United
Kingdom and Empire to face all the responsibilities that that imposed upon
Ulster people. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
There is no slackening in our loyalty.
There is no falling off in our determination to place the whole of our resources
at the command of the Government in
Britain. They have established now a
War Cabinet, and I have already communicated with those of them whom I
know best to say privately and, I am sure,
publicly now as well, that anything we
can do here to facilitate them in the terrible times that lie ahead they have only
1903 The War with Germany

4 SEPTEMBER 1939
The War with Germany
just got to let us know and we will do it.
In that I feel I have the backing of the
whole House. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
We are met also with no mean record
behind us of what has been done by the
Ulster people. During the past month
the response to the call for volunteers has
amounted to 45,000, while the actual enlistments in the ordinary forces of the
Crown have more than doubled, although
hitherto Ulster has stood at the very top
so far as enlistment for the Army is concerned. That again is a matter of great
satisfaction, but much more requires to
be done. I am sure the crisis during the
past few days will have nerved many of our
youth to rally to the colours where they
know that not only are they defending
their own homes, but the Empire, and
where they must know that their own
people and women folk must be guarded
as far as possible from dread bombing or
any other machinery of war.
Whilst I am on this subject I would
like specially to stress what we as a
Government owe to the local Press for
helping us most generously with regard
to recruiting for national defence and for
A.R.P. purposes. I really shudder to
think what would have happened had they
not come along voluntarily and without
any pressure on the part of the Government done everything possible in order to
help the people to understand the situation
and, at the same time, point out where
the path of duty lay. I wish to pay that
high tribute to our local Press.
There is another matter-and the
earlier I deal with it the better-and
that is to ask the people to be careful
to discriminate between the orders issued
practically all day and every day by the
B.B.C. The B.B.C. have felt it necessary to curtail our own local station
here, but we do get from two stations,
the Scottish Regional especially, the
fullest information that is handed to
them by the various Government departments. The only trouble in the minds of
some people must be whether all these
orders affect us in Ulster. We have
specially approached the various departments in London, and asked them to be
kind enough to descriminate very carefully in issuing any Orders between the
words "United Kingdom," which naturally cover Northern Ireland, and “Great
Britain," which refers merely to citizens.
on the other side of the Channel.
It is,
of course, like many of the Acts of Parliament which are. passed, difficult for the
ordinary man in the street to realise
what comes from London in the way of
instructions or orders and what comes
from Stormont with regard to instructions and orders, but that will be clarified
in a few days. Each department of the
Government here will from this on deal
with the specific matters which are entrusted in their care. I refer, of course,
to the multiplication of orders in regard
to food distribution, oil, and all those
matters which affect the daily life of the
people. Each department headed by my
right hon. Friends here will be always
ready and always on the spot to reply
to any inquiries and to explain what is
applicable to the. Ulster area.
of
I might illustrate what I mean by
what happened when the instructions
came through with regard to the closing
down of theatres, cinemas and buildings
which hold very large numbers of people
-with the exception, of course,
churches. That power is applicable over
the whole United Kingdom. My colleagues and I, however, had decided the
day before that so far as this area was
concerned we did not think it necessary
to close those places for the present at
all events. There is a great differentiation
naturally between the enormous crowds
that attend famous football matches in
London-where thousands and tens of
thousands attend, where if a bomb were
dropped the casualties would be enormous
-and the comparatively small gatherings
here in regard to any form of sport. We.
felt that the citizens should have sufficient liberty to go about and take part
in open-air amusements as much
possible. If the necessity does arise at
a later date, of course, stringent regulations should have to be enforced here
also.
as
Before I refer to one or two particular
matters I would like to state-and I am
sure it will be received with great satisfaction by the whole public-that on-I
was going to say on the verge of war,
but standing here with actual war declared, as regards our normal finances I
can assure the House that these are in a
thoroughly sound condition. I am glad
to say that arrangements have been
made by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, with the Treasury
The War with Germany
The War with Germany
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
that the British Exchequer would help
our exchequer funds to meet the exceptional expenditure of war time, even
should it be necessary for this House to
pass parallel legislation with that of
Great Britain. Adjustments will be
made from time to time from the British
Government's Vote of Credit. Therefore,
this House and the people of Northern
Ireland can rest assured that any
reasonable expenditure to meet wartime contingencies is already provided
for. The Minister of Finance proposes
to introduce forthwith a Bill to increase
the amount available in the Civil Contingencies Fund from the existing
statutory figure of £100,000 to the figure
of £400,000.
Now, I would like to touch upon
evacuation. I am sure we were filled
with admiration to read in the Press
and hear over the B.B.C. of the
marvellous accomplishment in England
in regard to the removal of school
children from London and other congested areas throughout the country to
their temporary new homes.
It appears
I
from all reports that that was carried
out without any untoward incident, and
I am hopeful that if and when the time
comes we here have to take a similar
step it will be done with the same
celerity and willingness on the part of
the population. Might I especially
appeal to the reception committees.
know that the preparations for the
evacuation of school children in the city
of Belfast are fast nearing completion,
and I am sure that just as across the
Channel the work of the volunteers,
those kindly persons who will conduct
the children to their new homes and see
them safely installed, will be carried out
efficiently.
A point that may possibly be raised
to-day is the want of equipment in certain
parts of the country and also with regard
to special requirements. We have felt all
along that we should give way, and give
way gracefully, to those parts of the
United Kingdom in greater danger than
ourselves. The consequence has been
that the supply of certain requisites has
not yet reached us in this area. The Government so far as it is concerned is up
to date in the perfection of all its plans
with the exception of having to wait the
arrival from the other side of certain
articles which I need not enumerate here
in the House. But I do not think it will
be very long before we are supplied with
what we consider absolute necessities. It
must be understood that we ourselves have
voluntarily said, "Take care of the most
vulnerable parts; look after them first;
we are somewhat removed from the danger
zone, if I may use that expression; we
will hold on and do what we can until
you are able to supply us with the necessary equipment.'
The next point to which I would particularly call attention has to do with the
farming community. In the agricultural
districts of Ulster in normal times the
products exceed very largely the local
requirements; but the moment we come
into the scheme of food rationing we
must be prepared to undertake exactly
the same rationing here as in other parts
of the United Kingdom. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do not want people
to say that we are self-contained; that we
have far more food here than would
necessitate such a rigid scheme as food
rationing might impose. I do not want
them to look upon it in that light.
want the people to take a full view of the
United Kingdom as a whole-England,
Wales, Scotland and ourselves all in one.
Whatever produce we can send across the
Channel makes it somewhat easier on the
whole of the citizens rather than upon a
favoured few. I am sure I will not
appeal in vain to the farming community
to do all in their power to produce more
crops and in that way lessen the British
difficulties which are so very onerous.
I
Then I must touch upon another matter.
The Government have for some time past
been visualising trouble not only from the
common enemy, Germany, and her allies,
but have also been most carefully thinking out plans with regard to the specific
dangers in our own area. Orders have
been given for the "B" Special Constabulary to be immediately placed upon
the basis they were on before they returned
to the drill category, that is to say, patrol
category. I would like to explain to the
"B" Special Constabulary three of the
reasons which moved the Government to
withdraw them temporarily from the
category of patrol men. We discovered
that a certain amount of exaggeration
was being made out of the
fact that our "B" Specials so well
patrolled the roads that visitors here on

their annual holiday were getting the

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Since

our midst we took into our care last night

Hear, hear.)
I would like, to make a statement with
regard to our proposals. We must ensure
that we are in complete control, that we
are masters of our own house, and not
here at the permission of anybody else.
We are not here for the citizens to have
their lives and property endangered by
a lot of cowardly assassins, men who never
hesitate to do what they can to destroy
the State Especially at this moment,
when the. Empire is at war and when
every assistance is wanted, nothing should
be done to put sand in the wheels of our
defence here at home.
There is then the point, who are these
men? I can describe them in a sentence.
They are the King's enemies. That is
the way to describe men who carry on as
they did some few hours ago when they
dragged the uniform off one of our
volunteers going to the front. Are such
men not the King's enemies? Can any
punishment be too great for them? (Hon.
Members: No.) I say not, and the
Government are determined that whatever precautions are necessary will be
taken, and that whatever severity can be
dealt out to men of that class this Government is quite powerful enough, thank
God, to mete out. It is determined to
see that there will be nothing of that
kind to disturb the public peace. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I do not often speak like this. This
is, as far as I am concerned, my third
experience of a great war. I have seen
both sides of the picture. I have seen
the fighting side, and I have also seen
the home side. It is difficult for
people at home to realise what war means
abroad. Knowing, as I do, how the men
abroad day and night look to the home
people to keep steadfast and not to
allow anything to be given away during
their absence, not only do I feel strongly
in issuing the solemn warning to the
wrongdoers who may crop up in Ulster,
but I feel it is necessary to assure those
who are boldly going out under the flag
of Britain that they will not be neglected
or disgraced in their absence. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
There have been many emergency
measures passed in the Imperial Parliament, some of them applying to us here
in Ulster and others referring only to
Great Britain. This House will have to
pass certain emergency measures as
rapidly as possible. Hon. Members will
have before them the Bill with which we
propose to deal to-day, and I want just
to foreshadow what the Government
propose to do. If we get the Second
Reading of this very important measure
of defence taken to-day, I think we will
be able to complete all its stages tomorrow. Then we propose to take other
Bills, keeping the House sitting up to
Thursday. After that, I give my solemn.
pledge on behalf of the Government that
the House will be called together from
time to time as the necessity arises.
If this House were the only medium
for conveying to hon. Members and the
public outside vital information I would
not hesitate to sit day and night, but as
the British Government have arranged
so carefully with the B.B.C. to let everyone know the latest information as far
as it is desirable, of course the necessity
for meeting here does not arise, especially
as so many of us are very busy at important duties. I know that a very
large number of my hon. Friends, both
behind me and on the benches opposite,

HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Warnock) :
Before I begin to outline the proposals
of this Bill, a Bill to make further provision for Civil Defence, I must express
regret that it was not possible to circulate
a copy of it earlier. We are compelled
by the march of events to introduce it
earlier than we had anticipated, and the
Bill, as circulated, is incomplete in one
particular. Hon. Members will have
noticed that there are in the draft Bill
as circulated no proposals regarding
domestic shelters-shelters for private
houses. I will, later on, outline what
the Government proposals are, and they
will be submitted for consideration by
the House by way of amendment on the
Committee. Stage.
As members are aware, we derive many
of our powers to legislate on defence
matters from the British Civil Defence
Act, which came. on the Statute Book
in the middle of July, 1939, and it was
not possible, therefore, to introduce our
Bill earlier. But, although we were unable to introduce our Bill, advantage has
been taken of the Parliamentary recess
forward so much of the measures
to press
as could be undertaken without legislative sanction. The Air Raid Precautions organisation has been constantly
under review; the fire-fighting appliances
of the city of Belfast have been increased
enormously; plans for evacuation of
children and mothers, of which I will
have something to say later on, have been
virtually completed; measures for the
treatment of air-raid casualties have been
considered, and I think will be found
reasonably adequate. The training of
nursing personnel has been pushed ahead,
and the foundations of shelter policy have
been laid by the publication of the code
of instructions on the approved standard
and by the publication of designs and
plans for domestic shelters.
This present Bill follows the British
measure very closely. I am not one of
the people who believe in always following
British legislation, but in this case there.
is good reason. First of all a great deal
of thought went into the British measure.
Secondly, we are bound very largely
financially to Great Britain, and it is
right and proper that our grant shall be
on the same. scale as in Great Britain,
and, thirdly, I think I can properly say
that the provisions of the Bill which apply
to the south-east of England and the
industrial Midlands would probably be
more than adequate in the case of Northern Ireland, which is less vulnerable than
these, areas.

suitable for a public air-raid shelter to

any area so defined-a compulsory areathe obligation is placed upon the occupier

As I have said, the provisions in regard to domestic shelters have not been
included in the draft Bill circulated. As
you know after a good deal of consideration the British Government decided to

issue to persons whose incomes did not
exceed £250 a year a type of steel shelter
which is known as the Anderson shelter.
We do not intend to supply the Anderson
shelter here. There are three reasons
why we have come to that decision. In
the first place we are not sure that they
would be available in considerable quantities at the present time and deliveries
might be slow. Another and perhaps
more potent reason is that the Anderson
shelter depends for its maximum efficiency
on being sunk into the ground to an extent of about three feet and the excavated
earth piled round about. Any person
who knows the conditions in Belfast will
realise that in a great many districts that
is quite impracticable and the shelter
would, in many cases, especially in winter
time, be simply a receptacle for water.
and, in addition, could not be occupied.
The third reason which induced us to
exclude the Anderson shelter was that its
dimensions are inconvenient, having regard to the size of the average area of
Belfast kitchen houses. We have, rightly
or wrongly, for good or ill, decided
against the Anderson shelter.
We did consider with technical experts
a series of alternatives, and ultimately
we decided to supply a brick and concrete
structure. It will comply with the recog
nised standards of production. It will
be available much more. rapidly, almost
immediately. It will be constructed of
materials available locally. It will be
constructed by local labour. It will be
available in seven or eight different sizes
and types, and the type whose dimensions
suit the yard can be chosen. As I said.
in Great Britain the shelters were provided free to any person whose income
was under £250 a year.
We are not
going to apply that test. What we do

absolutely free to every householder who

of which does not exceed £13. That
means, in other words, occupants of
houses which let at about 11s per week.
That figure is not a final figure at all. It
is a matter which the Ministry will be
prepared to consider later on. At the
moment the issue of these shelters to

house will occupy some little time, and

which are most likely to be subject t

if he thinks I could be of any useful

It will not mean any additional expenditure. It would be a committee of advice

Again we are told that we are not to

The Parliamentary Secretary
did not mention what sort of structure

up shelters of the Anderson type in the
Division I have the honour to represent,
but if I was putting shelters in the street
I would build them thirty feet below street
level, where we would have a chance of
escaping. They would at least be underground. I was told that the London
County Council could not agree on a
scheme of underground shelters. I have
examined that school of thought, but the
London area has underground shelters in
the tunnel system. At the present time
they are being made gas-proof, and they
are certainly bomb-proof.
Mr. WARNOCK: You are referring
to the underground railways?

Mr. WARNOCK: It has been officially

The Government said you cannot do

have to do the same. The Government

Under this Bill I see many opportunities

WAT
1945 Financial Provisions (Money)— HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Lt.-
Col. Gordon): The purpose of this Resolution, as was stated yesterday, is to
raise the amount available in the Civil
Contingencies Fund from the present
figure of £100,000 to a figure of £400,000.
The Civil Contingencies Fund is a fund
entrusted to the Ministry of Finance for
the purpose of meeting expenditure in
anticipation of a Vote of Parliament in
connection with services which cannot
await the passing of a supplementary
estimate. It is desirable, as a precautionary measure, to ask Parliament to
place at the disposal of the Ministry of
Finance this increased sum in view,
firstly of the uncertainty of what we may
have to spend under war conditions on
what I may call our domestic services
as distinct from expenditure on
services in our area, which are the responsibility of the Imperial authorities; and,
secondly, the possibility of our Government finding it necessary to finance in
the first instance expenditure which is
later recoverable under arrangements
made. with the Treasury. Nothing in
the nature of a final charge on the fund
is involved, seeing that Parliamentary
approval will in due course be sought, as
in the past, to repay before the end of
the financial year any sums which may
have been charged temporarily to the
Civil Contingencies Fund. I beg to move.
war
Mr. BEATTIE: I object to the wording of this Resolution, in so far as we
are limited to £400,000. If that is going
to be the limit of the protection under
civil contingencies that might arise in
Northern Ireland to the people of Northern Ireland-
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: No, no.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Civil Contingencies Fund would be to meet
expenditure on matters arising perhaps
out of the conflict now taking place over
Europe. I do not think the Financial
Secretary can deny that.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Might I
intervene to save discussion? I would
like at once to remove any impression
which might exist in the hon. Member's
mind that this £400,000 will meet what
may be planned. It is merely increasing
the amount which may be carried in
what I would call a suspense account. As
the House votes money, so it is repaid
into this fund by Estimates. As
amounts are sanctioned by Parliament,
so the amount will be increased and then
we may spend £400,000 again. It is
only a suspense account. There is no
limit whatever. As long as this fund
is repaid you can come back and spend
more. It is not limited; it is in the
nature of a suspense account.
Mr. BEATTIE: I thank you for the
explanation, but still a suspense account
means, I understand, money that is
voted by Parliament for civil contingencies, so that we can draw on that
account without coming to Parliament
for its sanction. We are not living in
normal times at the moment, and I
perhaps would go further than the
Financial Secretary would ask the House
to go.
That is the reason I objected to
his opening remarks. I would give an
unlimited amount into the custodianship
of the Minister of Finance, so that if
emergency does arise finance can be
immediately provided. He would have
it in his power to go up to the extent
of half a million or a million if
nceessary. Those are wider powers I am
prepared to give the Minister of Finance
than the Financial Secretary is asking
for.
We never know the moment you may
be called upon
to provide enormous
amounts of money for the protection of
our people, and the emergency wil
certainly call for quick decisions.
I feel that this fund should be
increased not from £100,000 to
£400,000, but I would
go up, if
necessary, to £1,000,000. I think now
the hon. and gallant Gentleman sees the
point I am placing before the Committee.
It is so that he will not have to wait
till Parliament is summoned back again
to get the amount necessary to carry on
the work of the protection of the people.
Mr. HENDERSON: I do not think
there is any doubt about it, as the hon.
Member has pointed out. If it is necessary to have another £400,000 the
Government will get it. They are only
making preparation now. I think the
statement made by the hon. Member will
pacify the House. If it is necessary to

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The various
grants and expenses to which the approval
of the Committee is sought are very fully
and clearly set out in the Resolution. I
would like, however, to point out that the
grants which the Government are proposing to make are generally the same
as those authorised by the British Civil
Defence Act, with one exception.
Great Britain the grant of 5s 6d in the
£ to employers towards providing airraid shelters for their employees is confined to those whose premises are situated
within specified areas where protection is
compulsory. In Northern Ireland it has
been decided to offer the same grant to
employers in the voluntary area of Belfast
and the approaches to it although there
will be no obligation on these employers
to provide shelters if they do not wish to
do so.
It is quite impossible to give any estimate of the burden which this Resolution
will place upon the Exchequer, but all
expenditure incurred under this Bill,
with the exception of that incurred by

wise advice, but I think that side of the

Ballykinlar has brought Newcastle and
Dundrum into the danger zone. The
people of that district who are living in
houses of £13 valuation are entitled to a
free distribution of air-raid shelters.
That is what I am asking for, and I
think that is a reasonable request to

All the people who are living in areas

of shelters. I think that is a reasonable

CLAUSE 21 (Training of employees).
(1) This section applies to every person who employs more than twenty
persons in any factory premises or in
any commercial building.
(2) It shall be the duty of every
person to whom this section applies,
not later than one month from the
date on which this section first applies
to him, to make a report in writing,
in the case of factory premises, to the
Ministry and, in the case of a commercial building, to the local authority,
stating what measures he has taken or
is taking or proposing to take to secure
that all the persons employed by him
in the premises or building are trained
as respects the routine to be followed
in the event of an air-raid and that a
suitable proportion of those persons
are trained and equipped to give firstaid treatment, to deal with the effects
of gas and to fight fires.
(3) The Ministry may, in the case
of factory premises, and the local
authority may, in the case of a commercial building, serve on an employer to whom this section applies a
notice in writing requiring him to take
such measures in relation to the aforesaid matters as may be specified in the
notice, and it shall thereupon be the
duty of the employer, subject to the
next following sub-section, to comply
with the requirements of the notice.
(4) Any person upon whom a notice
is served as aforesaid may, within
fourteen days after receipt of the
notice, appeal to the Ministry, and the
Ministry may on any such appeal
cancel or vary the notice, and the
decision of the Ministry shall be final.

NEW CLAUSE (Erection of shelters
provided by the Ministry).
(1) Where the occupier of any premises has been provided on behalf of
the Ministry with materials for an
air-raid shelter to be erected on the
premises, the local authority shall give.
him advice as to the position in which
the shelter should be erected:
Provided that, where the materials
are sold to the occupier, the local
authority shall not be under any duty
to give such advice until requested by
the occupier.
(2) Any occupier to whom advice
has been given as aforesaid may erect
the shelter in accordance therewith,
and may for that purpose break up the
surface of any land in his occupation
whether paved or not, but shall take
due care not to damage any drains,
sewers, pipes, cables or other works;
and the right conferred by this subsection on any occupier may be exercised notwithstanding any agreement
or restrictive covenant to the contrary,
and notwithstanding any limitation on
his interest in the premises, and he
shall not be liable to pay damages in
respect of any act which is reasonably
necessary for the due exercise of the
right conferred on him, or, if he has
exercised due care, for any damage
done by him to drains, sewers, pipes,
cables or other works.
(3) The local authority shall in
giving any advice under this section
exercise such care as is reasonable in
1981 Civil Defence Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
the circumstances of the case, but unless they fail to exercise such care, they
shall not be under any liability in respect of any damage caused by or in
consequence of the erection of a shelter
in accordance with advice given by
them.
(4) Where any such materials for an
air-raid shelter have been provided on
behalf of the Ministry without charge
then, unless the occupier of the premises refuses his consent, it shall be
the duty of the local authority themselves to erect the shelter, and the provisions of sub-section (2) of this section
shall apply in relation to the local
authority as they apply in relation to
an occupier erecting a shelter in accordance with advice given by the local
authority:
Provided that, in such cases as may
be prescribed, the occupier of the premises shall repay to the local authority
the cost of erecting the shelter and
such cost may be recovered summarily
as a civil debt by the authority from
the occupier of the premises.
(5) For the purposes of this Part of
this Act, references to the erection of
an air-raid shelter include references to
the affixing of the shelter to, or the
embedding of the shelter in, any part
of the premises and the carrying out of
any other works necessary for the
proper erection of the shelter.
(6) Public utility undertakers who
carry on a gas, water or electricity
undertaking shall not, unless they
have been guilty of negligence, be
liable to pay damages for or in respect
of any loss of life or injury or damage
to persons or property resulting from
damage done by any occupier to any
pipe, cable, or other work in the exercise of the powers conferred by subsection (2) of this section:
Provided that nothing in this subsection shall be in derogation of any
provision of the Workmen's Compensation Acts (Northern Ireland), 1927
and 1931.

Mr. WARNOCK: Yesterday when I
introduced this measure I indicated that
provisions with regard to domestic
shelters would be submitted to the House
by way of amendment to-day. The new
Clauses, or most of them on the Order
Paper, relate to these shelters. I think
everyone will agree that this question has
been debated at considerable length, and
I will not do more than occupy the time
of the House for two minutes. The
general provision is that free shelters
will be provided in Belfast to begin with
for all householders with a poor-law
valuation of £13 or less. That covers
65,000 houses. We propose to begin
immediately with the erection of these
in the most vulnerable areas. It will
take some time to complete them. From
time to time we will extend the area in
which we will operate, and if the people
of the city want them they shall have
them and have them free. I hope when
hon. Members look at the designs that
they will approve. A good deal of work
has been put into the design, and I hope
it will prove satisfactory.
In addition to the provision in regard
to shelters there is a provision-I do not
know that it is very important-for
strengthening basements. We have very
few basements. There is a proposal for
affixing appliances for strengthening
basements. That covers the new Clauses
down to Clause 6. Then there is a provision for the restriction of the removal
of shelters and appliances, and there is
provision for the execution of works by
the owner of a dwelling-house. In many
cases it may be limited by the document
of tenancy, and power is given to make
the necessary alterations. There is provision that the Ministry may make such
regulations as are necessary to carry
these works into effect. I shall be happy
to answer any questions if any are
raised.
In addition to that there are four sub
clauses for additional recruitment for the
Royal Ulster Constabulary. As Members
are aware under the 1922 Act it is not
possible to recruit a person over the age
of 35 years. It
It may be necessary-it
has already been necessary in connection with certain work to take on some
additional people, one or two retired

NEW CLAUSE (Restriction of removal of shelters and appliances).
(1) Any materials for an air-raid
shelter or appliances for strengthening
a basement provided free of charge on
behalf of the Ministry and with the
consent of the recipients shall not be
removed from the premises for which
they were provided without the consent in writing of the local authority.
(2) Any air-raid shelter erected or
appliances affixed by the local authority
under the preceding provisions of this
Part of this Act shall not be removed
from its position without the consent
in writing of the local authority.
(3) The consent of the local authority
under this section may be given absolutely or subject to conditions.
(4) Any person who removes any
shelter, materials or appliances in
contravention of this section, or contravenes any condition subject to which
the consent of the local authority was
given to the removal thereof, shall be
liable on summary conviction to a fine
not exceeding twenty pounds.
Provided that no person shall be
convicted under this sub-section if he
proves that he did not know and had
no reasonable grounds for suspecting
that the materials or appliances were
provided on behalf of the Ministry free
of charge, or, as the case may be, that
the shelter was erected or the
appliances were affixed by the local
authority.

The first is the Glebe Loan Act. That
Act was passed in 1870 after the disestablishment of the Irish Church, and
the purpose of the Act was to enable

By the
Amending Act 49 and 50 Victoria-the
Act of 1886-it was provided that the
original Act might be continued by the
Expiring Laws Continuance Act every
year, and accordingly it has been
put in the Schedule of the Expiring Laws Continuance Act every
year.
It is still in operation, but I
understand that the last operation under
the Act was more than ten years ago,
and I should not be at all surprised to
see this Act disappearing from the Schedule very shortly.
The second Act is the Harbours, Docks,
and Piers (Temporary Increase of
Charges) Act, 1920. Up to that time.
the charges and rates which might be

undertaking should not be. carried on at
a loss. It was deliberately framed in the
form of a temporary Act, so that the

matter from time to time, and it has
been continued from year to year.

will be made.

Mr. HENDERSON: There is a matter
which, in my opinion, is of vital importance at the present time, and I would
like the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Home Affairs to go into it.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates) rose.
Mr. HENDERSON: I did not see the
right hon. Gentleman.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps the
hon. Member would give me some details
of what he complains about.
Mr. HENDERSON: This question I
am raising concerns ex-service men in
Northern Ireland, and especially in
Belfast. As the right hon. Gentleman
knows, a child on entering school is
required to have a birth certificate for
which sixpence is charged. There are
hundreds of ex-service men who were unemployed until the outbreak of war and
practically nothing was going into the
home. In order to qualify for the Army
allowance a man, if he has four children,
must pay 3s 7d for each certificate of
birth, a total of 14s 4d. I have a case
in point where a mother had to pay
14s 4d, and the husband before joining
up had been unemployed for four or five
years. That is a great hardship. The
Government in cases where ex-service men
of all creeds and classes joined up should
wipe that out and see that these people
are not charged more for the certificates
than they previously paid when the
children were entering school. These
men should be given some encouragement. Two ex-service men, a Catholic
and a Protestant, have sent me letters
complaining of this. Dozens of others
have asked to get the charges stopped.
The only way to get them stopped is to
give instructions to the poor-law institutions to have this evil removed forthwith.
When these men are going to sacrifice
their lives their wives should not be

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Henderson]
asked to pay this exorbitant sum. Where
does the 3s 7d go to? I think the
Minister should also go into that question.
The officials have not much trouble in
writing out a duplicate birth certificate.
It is only justice I am asking for. I
believe the Minister will see that the
right and proper thing is done on behalf
of these men whose wives are struggling
along until the Army allowance is
received. Any such money paid should
be refunded.
There is another matter that affects
the well-being of the poor and rich alike.
The rich can pay for the commodities
they want, but the poor cannot. During
the past few days there has been an
exorbitant rise in the price of foodstuffs. In some cases sugar has been
raised to 8d. No one will stand for that.
I hope the Government will take immediate steps to see that there is no profiteering at the expense of the people of
this country, whether rich or poor.
Bacon has gone up from 1s 3d to 1s 8d
per lb., and, as I say, there are cases
where sugar has been raised to 8d. There
is no necessity for that. There should
be a store of sugar within the British
Empire, and there is no excuse for such
a huge increase in commodities. The
people responsible for such tactics when
the Empire is engaged in such a titanic
struggle should be immediately clapped
in jail. If I had anything to do with
the Government I would put them in
jail. It is the only way this thing can
be stopped. I am satisfied that the
Minister of Commerce will see that it is
stopped immediately. On last Saturday
afternoon my Own little girl had
occasion to go to a shop to purchase tea
and sugar. My wife always purchases
the tea and sugar in a certain shop and
the grocery goods in another shop.
Before the little girl could get the tea
and sugar she had to buy other commodities. I hope that sort of thing will
be stopped. I trust that no profiteering
of this nature will take place in the
future. Having drawn the Government's
attention to the matter, I hope they will
take immediate steps to have it stamped
out and see that the people are protected.
Mr. BYRNE: I support the hon.
Member in what he says. I have a letter
from one of my constituents stating that
she had to pay 14s 4d for certificates.
Seeing that these men are going out to

cannot afford to pay. I am a member

on the dole and some are getting

of profiteering. It is a crime for any

If the Northern Ireland farmer buys

for our people at the lowest possible cost.
If this great programme of tillage is
going on it will go on-we should take

Northern Ireland and Great Britain can
get food at the lowest price.
