The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): I fully appreciate the very
helpful way in which hon. Members on
both sides of the House have put forward
their views in connection with the important matters which they have raised. In
the first place I should like to say definitely and distinctly that the Government
will do everything humanly possible to
stop profiteering. That is a definite
pledge on behalf of the Government and
it will be given effect to in every way it
is possible to give effect to it.
With regard to the birth certificates I
admit that the charge made in connection
with the cases the hon. Member has referred to appears to me to be unreasonably high. My department is already in
touch with the War Office in connection
with the matter and I hope it may be
possible to have the charge reduced. I
am advised it will require special legislation to do so, and if legislation is required I will endeavour to make it
retrospective to cover such recent cases
as those to which hon. Members opposite
have referred.
Mr. BYRNE: Will those who have
paid the amount get it returned to them?
Mr. ANDREWS: That is what I mean
by saying I hope to be able to make it
retrospective. The hon. Member for
Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) raised the question of the training of teachers. As the
hon. Member knows we are, unfortunately, at war, and economies will have to
be made wherever possible. The Training College has been taken over, as possibly the hon. Member is aware-I am
referring to Stranmillis-and if we were
to continue to train teachers we should
have to take a new building and adapt
it for the purpose. This would
mean considerable expense. The hon.
Member knows that at the present time
there is a surplus of teachers. That
being so we would not be justified, in my
opinion and in the
the opinion of my
colleagues. in training teachers at
present.
Again, there are various ways in
which the matter can be dealt with.
There are teachers who are on the point
of retirement and, if necessary, some of
these teachers will be asked to give their
services for a longer period. As we are
at war I am quite sure they will be quite
willing to do so. I want to assure the
hon. Member that the Government are
quite determined that education shall not
be prejudiced by the course which we
feel it necessary to adopt. There are
various way in which any shortage that
may occur can be made good. I am sure
the hon. Member will appreciate that
after all sacrifices will be expected from
almost everyone. It is a pity that
certain of the pupils who have done one
year may not be able to complete their
course as soon as they had hoped, but
the Government will, no doubt, be able
to arrange that the year which they have
served will count towards the period of
their training, and, therefore, they will
not be prejudiced in that way. In
other words, we will provide, in carrying
out these economies, that as far as
possible unreasonable hardship will not
be imposed upon anyone.

con-
I am informed that there is no shortage
of feeding stuffs whatever in the country,
but that in certain cases prices were
raised just after war was declared, and
that in order to cope with the rather
critical position that arose it was decided
that the price which retailers could
charge should not exceed the price.
which was charged in the previous week.
Very many farmers have telephoned and
written to the Ministry that they could
not get feeding stuffs unless they paid a
higher price, and they have been instructed-I think the House should know
this that if they are required to pay an
exorbitant price they should pay the
amount demanded, get a receipt from
the retailer who supplied the feeding
stuffs, showing the quantity they
obtained, and send it to the Ministry.
If the retailer or supplier of feeding
stuffs has exceeded the price laid down
he will be prosecuted.
I am sure the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Minford) realises that when a
catastrophe such as war breaks out
things cannot run as smoothly as before.
I am hoping, however, that within a very
few weeks all matters in regard to feeding stuffs and the control of sales will be
working smoothly, and that his anxiety
will be allayed. I appreciate that at the
present time there is anxiety and so far as
the Ministry is concerned it will do all
it can to remove the difficulties which are
bound to arise at a time such as this.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 19th September, 1939.
The House-which stood adjourned
from Thursday, 7th September-met at
Three of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER in
the Chair.
Paper Presented.
Ministry of Commerce :
Minute assigning Powers and Duties
to Departmental Officers. (By Act.)
Oral Answer to Question.
WAR RISK INSURANCE.
Mr. BROWN (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Commerce if the
compulsory war risk insurance scheme for
stocks held by traders of £1,000 and
over provides for different rates of
premiums for different regions, and if his
Department has made any representations or proposes to make any representations to the Board of Trade with a view
to the provision of a lower rate of
premium for Northern Ireland than that
applying in more vulnerable areas in
Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I would draw the hon.
Member's attention to Section 9, subsection 3, of the War Risks Insurance
Act, which provides that "different rates
of premiums may be prescribed in relation to different descriptions of goods and
according to the place at which, and the
circumstances in which, the goods
insured are situated."
Questions relating to the incidence of
the rates of premium in respect of the
compulsory insurance of goods are under
active discussion with the Board of Trade
at the moment. The hon. Member will
appreciate, however, that there are a
number of considerations other than the
one mentioned by him which fall to be
taken into account in dealing with this
matter.
Agricultural (Emergency Provisions)
Bill.
The PRIME MINISTER: In introducing the Motion which stands in my
name on the Paper, it is necessary for me
to make a statement to the House on one
or two matters of vital importance. It
goes without saying that we here, equally
with Great Britain, will be forced to take
various measures on the financial side to
concentrate the whole national effort on
winning the war, and in this matter we
propose, as far as we can, to take parallel
steps with Great Britain. It will be
necessary to cut to a minimum all urnecessary capital expenditure, and my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, has already given an assurance to
the Imperial Chancellor of the Exchequer
that we will introduce whatever economes
it may be thought desirable to impose,
so as to set capital free for war purposes.

Steps have been taken to ration the

force for the regulation of prices. I am

Commerce in operating a controlled
system, the

With regard to petrol, rationing will
come into force on 23rd inst. I am informed that most people have already
received the basic ration appropriate to
the vehicles which they use, and in many
cases supplementary rations have been
approved and issued by the Petroleum
Department. Special consideration is
being given in the case of doctors and
others engaged in essential services, and
in all such cases the maximum additional
ration is being granted. It must be
realised, however, that the granting of
an additional ration in any particular
instance must be limited to cases where
it is clearly proved that the granting of
an additional ration is essential in the
national interest.
Every effort is being made to deal as
generously with the commercial user, and
the Petroleum Department is in constant
consultation with the representatives of
traders using commercial transport with
a view to devising schemes of planned
delivery in order to ensure the most
efficient use of the available transport as
well as to conserve petrol supplies. I
hope the public will realise that petrol
is one of the most important articles used
in connection with the war and that,
where they can, they will conserve their
own consumption. I know that our
people will, in the national interest,
accept the sacrifice involved.

Mr. SPEAKER: Before proceeding
further with this debate I should say the
constitutional question raised in a modified form by the hon. Member for Pottinger should be clear in our minds. The
Government at Westminster passed a
Defence of the Realm Act, which applies
to Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
By virtue of that Act they issue Orders
in Council, giving definite instructions as
to what is to be done in Great Britain
and Northern Ireland from the point of
view of the defence of the realm. One
of those Orders, for instance, is the
Blacking-out Order. Another Order is
the Compulsory Tillage Order. The

Agriculture (Emergency Provisions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
be
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It will
obvious to hon. Members that this is a
War Measure. Its sole purpose is to
enable the Ministry to conduct the tillage
campaign as far as possible on the same
principles as will be operating in Great
Britain. As the House is probably aware
the Secretary of State for the Home
Office has delegated his powers under the
Defence Regulations in so far as they
relate to agriculture and agricultural
land, and that, therefore, my Ministry
now possesses through the Secretary of
State the same powers in respect of
Northern Ireland as are possessed by the
Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries in
respect of England and Wales.
Agriculture Bill--
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
•
Mr. BEATTIE: Do you mind telling
us what those powers are?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The
powers
are under certain Sections of the Defence
Regulations, and I should imagine that
copies are available in the Library. The
powers are given to the Minister of Agriculture, who has no power to delegate
them beyond himself.
In England and Wales the Minister.
has proceeded by appointing his own War
Agricultural Committee in each county
composed of people selected by himself
and has appointed the staff of these committees.
I propose
in Northern Ireland to
utilise the services of the existing county
agricultural committees, and I think the
advantages of doing so in Northern Ireland are so obvious that there is no need
to detail them.
It will, however, be essential that the
existing county agricultural staffs should
be transferred to the Ministry. The
reason is simple. The Ministry has no
power in connection with the tillage campaign to delegate the powers conferred
upon it under the Defence Regulations,
1939, and, therefore, unless the staff become officers of the Ministry they cannot
be utilised in connection with the food
production campaign.
Moreover, in operations of this kind
there must be a concentration of energy
which involves direction from a single
centre just as in an army you must have
unity of command to obtain the best results.
I want to emphasise particularly that
the interests of the transferred staffs are
fully protected. The position and prospects of no officer can be worsened and
might even be improved. Pension and
other rights will be fully preserved. When
the emergency period is over the transferred officers will return to their
counties with their emergency service in
the Ministry counting for pension purposes, and I hope every officer will
go
back with an enhanced reputation and
a feeling that he has gladly answered the
call and done his bit.
This Bill also enables the Ministry to
appropriate the proceeds of the 1d rate
levied for agricultural purposes by the
county councils. As the House is
probably aware, approximately 75 per cent.
of the income of county agricultural committees is provided by the Ministry, and
their income from whatever source can
only be spent on schemes and for purposes
approved by the Ministry.
Ministry. As the
county agricultural staff will for the
period of the emergency be members of
the Ministry's staff paid by the Ministry,
and, as the amount levied by the rates
only pays a fraction of the cost, it is
obvious that the proceeds must come into
the Exchequer as an appropriation-in-aid
for the period of the emergency.

Now as to county committees, needless
to say we appreciate fully the need for
their continued activity to the fullest extent consistent with the policy of staff
concentration already indicated.
example, a very large proportion of the

I need not, of course, emphasise that
the county agricultural committees will
have much more important duties to perform under the food production campaign
and I know I can count upon their wholehearted co-operation and assistance-and
I shall need it-in the heavy task that
now devolves upon my Ministry. I may
say that I myself hope at the earliest
possible dates to meet each committee and
discuss the programme we have in view so
that local conditions and views may be
taken into account.
It is essential that we should get ahead
as rapidly as possible with the increased
tillage, campaign. This Bill is an essential
part of the machinery, and if we are to
succeed in our efforts I must get the
machinery established with the least
possible delay.
So much for the Bill itself. Before I
sit down, however, I would like to make
a special appeal to all people living in
this area, irrespective of their politics or
anything else. The position to-day is too
serious for us to consider matters which
perhaps in the past we used to discuss
with some heat, because there can be no
surer fact than that if we do not succeed
Agriculture Bill-
Second Reading
19 SEPTEMBER 1939
in winning this war the liberties of the
British people will be lost and a Nazi
Europe will be established.
What, then, is the position? We can
supply men-voluntarily-and we are
doing so. We can loyally co-operate in
all rationing schemes, whether of food or
fuel, as they appear.
But more.
As a
predominantly agricultural country we
can, and must, play our part to the very
uttermost of our resources in the production of more and still more food. It
is just as important that we at home.
should maintain our food front intact and
in perfect working order as it is that our
gallant fighting men should keep their
front-line trenches unbroken.
During the last war food prices rose
beyond all reasonable limits. This cannot,
and must not, occur again. The farmers'
interests must be protected, but so must
those. of the industrial worker and the
town dweller. Only by teamwork can we
succeed. Mention of the town dweller
reminds me that the House may be interested to know that only last week I
received a deputation of business men
who, without any prompting from my
Ministry or anyone else, are preparing
to band themselves into a voluntary
organisation so that they, their employees.
and their vehicles may be available, on
even the shortest notice, to go out and
help where needed with the essential work
of harvesting the nation's food. I am
confident that the House will agree that
the efforts of these gentlemen are worthy
of the highest praise. To me personally
this display of really practical patriotism
was most heartening, and those gentlemen
have set to the community a splendid
example of the teamwork to which I have
already referred as being so vital at the
moment.
As far as the farmers are concerned,
I am convinced that the majority of them
are both willing and anxious to do all
in their power to help, and that it will
be unnecessary for me to use the very
wide powers delegated to me by the
Secretary of State. Those powers will be
there, but, knowing Ulstermen as I do,
I am sure that the necessity to resort to
them will only be of rare occurrence.
I am afraid, however, that the even
tenor of our farmers' habits and some
of their established customs and methods
may have to be changed in certain.
respects. We also must remember-and
remember constantly, and even sympathetically, that we are certain to encounter
difficulties, disappointments, and possibly
even breakdowns-but with mutual confidence and co-operation I am firmly
convinced that we can surmount all these.
I would ask our farmers, if things
do not seem just as they would wish
them or if they do not seem to be run
just as they were in the last war-to
picture war as I have seen it myself-war
with its streams of refugees, its terrible
bombardments, its devastated areas and
as
to remember that we are fighting the
power which is forcing this horror on
country after country, and that any discomforts we may undergo here are
nothing compared to the horrors that
many people are suffering at the present
moment. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I have seen these things, and I have no
words to describe the impression that is
still with me twenty-five years later.
For my Ministry and myself I can give
my farmer friends the assurance that we
shall do everything we can to make easy
the changes and smooth over the difficulties, so that we all may go forward
together confident that each one is doing
his best to play a worthy part in the
battle for freedom and decency. I beg
to move.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This Bill can, at
the present time, properly be regarded
as a war measure, but it is not entirely
one of that nature, for it will, I hope,
continue to operate with benefit to Northern Ireland when peace is with us
again.
I think we must all recognise that for
many years it will be necessary to
maintain considerable military forces in
all countries, including Northern Ireland.
As hon. Members in this House are
aware, in the past the principal military
establishments that were maintained in
Ireland were almost all in the area that
is now outside Northern Ireland, and I
am confident that the House will agree
crease
It is common knowledge that the
British Government's rearmament plans
have already involved a considerable inthe personnel of military
establishments here. Some of these
establishments, no doubt, must be regarded as purely war-time provisions, but
others are quite evidently of a more
permanent character, being, in fact, part
of the ordinary peace-time arrangements
of the Department in question; and it is
in connection with these that I present
this Bill. Certain of these depots will
provide permanent employment for a
very large number of civilian employees,
and in certain cases it has been found
impossible to obtain housing accommodation for such persons in the neighbourhood.
The Government consider it is important that every facility should be
afforded to the military authorities, and
that, therefore, the local authorities in
Northern Ireland should be in a position
to provide the necessary houses, as loca!
authorities in England are. I should
like to remind the House that this is
purely a permissive Bill. The local
authorities to whom it is proposed to grant
the additional powers conferred by the
Bill are the urban and rural sanitary
authorities. The former have at present
power to provide houses only for persons
whose wages fall below a certain limit.
whereas rural sanitary authorities are at
present authorised only to provide houses
for persons coming within the statutory
definition of "agricultural labourer."
Generally speaking, this accommodation
would be required for civilian employees
only, but it might be desirable in some
cases to provide houses for married
members of the Forces of the Crown, and
the Bill has been drafted so as not to
exclude provision of this kind being
made.
Housing Bill-
Second Reading
19 SEPTEMBER 1939
The persons for whom houses are required are in a position to pay economic
rents, and it is not, therefore, anticipated
that any loss could accrue to the local
authorities. There would be, however,
a certain element of risk. For example,
it might at some later date be decided
to close down a depot, or possibly the
personnel of the depot might
might be
materially reduced. The likelihood of
such events taking place would of course
be factors that the local authority would
have to take into account before deciding upon embarking on building operations under the Act, and the Bill provides
that if a local authority feel in any
particular circumstances that this risk is
one that they should not take entirely
upon their shoulders, then it will be open
to the Government to share it with them,
as provided in the Bill.
I may say, however, that local authorities in England have already provided a
very large number of houses in connection
with those Crown force establishments
without any such support from the
Government, and I anticipate that, where
the need arises, local authorities will be
prepared to take similar action here.
Where they decide that the circumstances
justify them carrying any risk there may
be, then they are given a very free hand
indeed in carrying out their scheme; but,
on the other hand, if the Government is
asked to share the risk with them, then
it is only right that a very much closer
supervision should be exercised on behalf
of the Government.
I think I should tell the House that
this problem has, in fact, arisen in connection with a particular depot in a particular rural district. The House will, I
am sure, understand the reasons why I
do not refer to the particular district.
But I can give the assurance to the House
that the Bill has been drafted in the
closest co-operation with the local
authority of that area. I think that is
the only case where the need is acute.
But I have been informed by the military
authorities that there is likely to be need
in a very short time for providing similar
accommodation not alone for the civilian
people employed in the barracks, but for
the married men there. I beg to move.

Education (Evacuated Children) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): I need
only say a few words about this Bill.
An Act is already on the Statute Book
dealing with the evacuation of school
children from Belfast. Their safety in
a possible emergency having been provided for by the Ministry of Home
Affairs it is obvious that the next step
is to provide for their education if and
when evacuation takes place. The
measure of which I am about to move
the Second Reading has this object in
view.
At the outset of my remarks let me
make it absolutely clear that like the
previous evacuation measure this is only
precautionary. It is only in order to
meet a situation which might arise. We
all hope that it may never be needed. I
make these remarks because I know that
the word evacuation has an alarming effect
and seems to give rise to wild rumours of
immediate emergencies. There is no
reason at present to anticipate that any
sudden emergency will arise. There is
no question of using the powers which we
ask Parliament to confer until it does,
but we must have our organisation prepared in order to ensure that the educational side of our national life does not
suffer.
If and when the children from Belfast
are sent for safety to the country districts
their education must be continued. Under
these circumstances it becomes the duty
of the education authority of the reception area to make suitable provision for
the elementary education of the children
transferred to that area. They will do so
as far as practicable in consultation with
the evacuating education authority. It
is necessary as regards elementary education to extend the existing powers and
duties of the education authorities of the
receiving areas SO as to cover these
children. They must have power to
recover any legitimate additional expenditure which they may have incurred on
educational services for the evacuees.
It is necessary also to arrange for the
assignment of a suitable number of
teachers from Belfast to the schools where
their services are most required. A
teacher thus assigned to another school
will serve under the orders of the education authority or the voluntary manager
as the case may be of the school to which
he is sent, but he will nevertheless still be
regarded as in the employment of the
authorities of the evacuating schools, who,
in certain circumstances, may fill the
vacancy arising through the retirement
or death of that teacher.
In order, however, to make the fullest
use of the available teaching power the
Bill provides that in the filling of
vacancies in schools in an evacuating area
or in a receiving school, the services of
redundant assigned teachers are first to
be availed of, unless the Ministry is satisfied that there are good reasons why this
should not be done.
A few other matters also come within
the scope of the Bill which includes also
provision for the making by the Ministry
of any regulations necessary to give full
effect to it. I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

constituency I am interested in
Belfast getting a fair deal regarding
the financial burden they will be called
upon to bear. I do not see any other
Belfast representative. on this side of the
House. That is the Belfast ratepayers'
point of view, and I have given it serious
consideration. I believe it warrants the
serious consideration of the Cabinet.
The next point I want to raise is this.
Ministers are very fond of reminding me
about the step-by-step policy with
England. If evacuation does take place
we have a large percentage of teachers
in Belfast who will have to be assigned
to the respective areas where the evacuees
are received. That means disturbance.
It means that these teachers will be compelled to remove from their homes to
homes or lodgings in the country. That
will entail additional expense to the.
teachers, and it will mean that 'their
income is reduced. They must continue
to maintain their homes in the city and
at the same time they will have to pay
for their board and lodgings in the area
to which they are assigned.
In England the Government has conceded free billets to the teachers. I do
not agree that free billeting is the proper
arrangement to make. It has long been
accepted that people, even in civilian life,
should not suffer owing to disturbance
due to war conditions, and during the
last war subsistence allowances were given
in such cases. I ask that every teacher
who is transferred to a country district
should receive. 5s a day subsistence allowance, or that there should be allocated
to each teacher 35s a week for board
and lodging. That is a reasonable
request. Owing to the emergency,
England has not yet made that concession,
but they at least give free billeting to
the teachers. In the interests of the
continuity of education these two points
should be further considered by the
Cabinet of Northern Ireland. I want to
see that everything will run smoothly.
when the word "go" is given. We may
never require this. I hope we will not. It
may never operate, but if we are to make
the machine run perfectly and smoothly
the subsistence allowance to teachers

Mr. BEATTIE: Might I suggest to the

The PRIME MINISTER: In the first

Great Britain, where a local education

approved expenditure.

not been such a transfer. Why should
there be any such difference in the position in Northern Ireland?
Mr. GORDON: One hon. Member was
interested in the courts, while the other
was interested in the right of appeal. I
will explain the position. First of all,
in reply to the hon. and learned Member
for Iveagh, let me say that the conditions which apply in Great Britain will
apply here so far as the courts are concerned. Many years ago power was
given to the insurance officers to grant
benefit and also to refuse benefit on
application being made. The officer
examined the applicant's form to see
whether or not he had the requisite
number of stamps, whether he was
available for work, and he then decided
whether or not the applicant was
entitled to benefit. A change was
made and the insurance officer was
given power to allow benefit, but not to
disallow it. The result was that all
straightforward claims of which he
had no suspicion were granted by the
insurance officer. If the officer was
suspicious as to whether the employment
was bona fide he referred the claim to the
court of referees. He could determine
whether a man was capable of work or
available for work, but he had to refer
such cases to the court of referees because
it was so laid down by law. The insurance officer could have decided cases
where employment was lost by misconduct or where a person had left his
employment voluntarily, but the law laid
it down that such cases had to be referred
to the court of referees. The insurance
officer could also have determined cases
where a claimant had refused work, but
the law said that such cases must be
referred to the court of referees.
We
It is quite probable that a man might
have to wait a fortnight before his case
was heard because it would be too expensive to bring one person before a court on
the day following his application.
waited until we had a number of claims.
and, as I said, it would probably be a
fortnight before they were decided.
Under the complex conditions at the
moment we have decided to shorten the
whole procedure and, consequently, we
are going to proceed under this Bill. We
Sittings of the House 2136
Adjournment
20 SEPTEMBER 1939
[Mr. Gordon]
have not done so as yet, but we are going
to give power to our insurance officers to
determine cases formerly dealt with by a
court.
Supposing a man comes forward and
claims benefit, and we think his employment was not bona fide-the hon.
Member for Pottinger knows what I mean
by that, for he mentioned it during the
course of the discussion-our officer will
at once determine whether it is bona fide.
or not. If a man feels aggrieved he can
then apply to the court of referees and
have his case examined by them. Under
the new conditions it will be necessary for
us to simplify procedure so as to act with
expedition because we do not know what
a day or a week may bring forth in connection with the war. We must be
determined to act at once, but let me
impress upon the House that whatever we
do it will not be harmful to any applicant
applying for benefit.
Question put, and agreed to.

the House shall meet on Wednesday, 27th September, and shall
transact its business as if it had
been duly adjourned to that date.
and at its rising shall adjourn until

CENSORSHIP OF LETTERS IN
FREE STATE.
1. Mr GAMBLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if it
is a fact that letters coming from Belgium
to Sion Mills in Co. Tyrone are being
censored by Free State Authorities, and
if so will he make representations to the.
proper authority to have this arrangement altered.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
My attention has been drawn to two
instances where letters from overseas to
addresses in Northern Ireland have been
subjected to censorship while in transit
through Eire. I immediately took up
this matter with the Imperial authorities
and am now awaiting the result of their
enquiries.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask if the
Minister would urge upon the Government the necessity of making representation to the British authorities for the
appointment of a censor in Northern
Ireland to work in harmony with the
British Ministry of Information?
CLOSING OF TRAINING COLLEGES.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she can state when it
is proposed to reopen the Training College
for teachers, and whether the candidates
who have already qualified for admission
to these institutions will be called up for
training when the colleges resume:
whether the Ministry will supply those
candidates who failed to reach the educational standard required for admission
to training with particulars of the marks
awarded to them in the different subjects
of examination, so that they may be
enabled to qualify for other employment:
and whether she can state what action the
Ministry proposes to take to safeguard the
interests of students in training who have
completed a portion of their courses and
are now debarred owing to the closing of
the Training Colleges from qualifying as
trained teachers within the period originally specified.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): As the
hon. Member is aware, there are thre
colleges in which students are trained for
service as public elementary teachers in
schools recognised by the Ministry.
Stranmillis Training College premises
having been taken over by the military
authorities, the Ministry is under the
necessity of providing alternative accommodation. This will involve some delay
but it is hoped to begin the work of the
session at an early date.
Work at St. Mary's College, Belfast.
has already begun and it is understood
that St. Mary's, Strawberry Hill.
London, will reopen on 30th September.
With regard to the second part of th
question, the final tests for women apply-

ing for admission to Stranmillis have just
been held and the successful candidates
will shortly be called for training. Women
students who recently qualified for admission to St. Mary's College, Belfast, have
already been summoned to training.
As regards men, it is not proposed to
admit any men students to either Stranmillis Training College or Strawberry Hill
Training College as a result of the. King's
Scholarship examination held earlier this
year, but those men students who completed their first year of training in June,
1939, are being permitted to return to
their College this year in order to complete their normal course of training.
All candidates at the King's Scholarship examination held this year-whether

of the students in attendance, during the

Mr. BEATTIE: I think the second

TILLAGE OF GOLF COURSES.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether golf courses in whole
or part, and other extensive sports
grounds, come under the terms of the
compulsory tillage order, and, if so, on
whom the responsibility will rest for
having the terms of the order carried out.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The intention is that
occupiers of golf courses or other extensive sports grounds where the land is
suitable. for cultivation should contribute
their due quota to the increased tillage
area demanded by the emergency. Each
such case would be considered on its
merits, bearing in mind always the paramount importance of increased food production. The Tillage Order provides that
responsibility for complying with its provisions rests, in all instances, on the
occupier of the land concerned.
Mr. BROWN: I thank the Minister
for his satisfactory reply.
Mr. BEATTIE: Does the Minister
mean that a percentage of the football
grounds in the city of Belfast should be
tilled. If so, is recreation not as important as tillage of grounds of that
description?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think football grounds would come under the provision exempting areas under ten acres
from tillage. Football grounds are not
ten acres in extent, so they will be all
right.
STORMONT ESTATE.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether the Government will
consider the taking of steps to have the
three hundred odd acres of land comprised
in the Stormont Estate surrounding the
Houses of Parliament ploughed up for
suitable crops in connection with the
increased
in
tillage effort Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): The hon. Member will be glad
to hear that my Ministry took action on
the 1st September and consulted the
Ministry of Agriculture as to the best use
that can be made of the Stormont Estate
for food production during the period of
the war. As the hon. Member is probably
aware, certain portions of the estate are
already used by the Ministry of Agriculture for plant-breeding purposes, egglaying competitions, and for grazing
animals in connection with experiments
which are at present being carried on.
In regard to the remainder of the
estate, it has been decided, in consultation

with the Ministry of Agriculture, to

PRICES OF FOODSTUFFS.
5. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can state the
respective charges to consumers to-day of
the following foodstuffs:-tea, sugar,
bread, milk, butter, eggs, bacon, ham,
meal, rice, lentils, tapioca, jams, beef,
and canned fruit, as compared with the
charges at the. outbreak of the war;
whether a maximum limit of charge is in
force in respect of any of these articles;
whether it is a fact that vendors here and
there are exacting prices for some articles
in excess of the prices charged by others;
and whether anything has been done or
will be done. by his Ministry or other
competent authority to secure to consumers uniformity and equality of prices
of necessary foodstuffs during the war.
Mr. BARBOUR: I regret that I have
not available the information which
would enable me to draw a comparison on
the lines suggested by the hon. Member
between the prices charged for certain
foodstuffs at the outbreak of war and the
prices ruling to-day. The hon. Member
may rest assured, however, that any complaint regarding excessive charges for
foodstuffs will be carefully investigated by
the Food Control Committees appointed
by the local authorities throughout the
Province. The Ministry of Food, as the
hon. Member will be aware, is throughout
the United Kingdom the Department
responsible for the control of the prices
of foodstuffs.
I understand that Orders in Council
have already been issued establishing the
wholesale prices of a wide range of commodities, and that the Ministry of Food
is gradually extending his control to the
retail prices of the most important foodstuffs.
The prices prescribed by the Minister
of Food, both wholesale and retail, are
published in Schedules to the relevant
Orders in Council. As the hon. Member
will be aware, they are subject to variation from time to time, but both the
original prices scheduled and subsequent
variations are receiving wide publicity in
the public Press.
With the hon. Member's permission
I will circulate with the Official
Report a list of the wholesale and retail
prices so far prescribed, as in force on
Tuesday, 26th September.

to the House on the 19th September that
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Commerce, proposes to introduce, shortly
certain proposals designed to combat

matter will be very carefully borne in
mind. I may state that it is proposed-
APPOINTMENTS FOR TEACHERS.
7. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state what steps
the Government propose to take to provide employment for candidates who have
qualified for admission to Courses of
training as elementary teachers, and are
now prevented, owing to the closing of
the Training Colleges, from entering on
these courses; and whether he will consider the advisability of reserving a proportion of appointments in the Government service for such candidates during
the period that will elapse until the
colleges reopen.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply to this
question. I regret that the Government is unable to make special arrangements for the employment of those
candidates who have qualified for
admission to courses of training as elementary teachers. My hon. Friend will
appreciate that the Government is still
bound by its undertaking to give a preference to ex-service men in connection
with temporary work.
Major HALL THOMPSON: May I
say it would give great satisfaction to
many were these people to qualify to
become ex-service men?

PRICES FOR PIGS.
(by
Major HALL THOMPSON
Private Notice) asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether the Pigs
(Provisional Prices) Order, 1939, made
on the 3rd September, 1939, by the
Board of Trade under the Emergency
Powers Regulations, fixing prices for
pigs sold for slaughter, applied to pigs
sold to curers in Northern Ireland, and,
if not, what steps are being or have
been taken to have similar prices prescribed for Northern Ireland.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Order
made by the Board of Trade on 3rd
September, 1939, was not intended to
apply to Northern Ireland. The position is that my Ministry, after consultation with the Pig Industry Council,
requested the Ministry of Food to have
an Order made prescribing for Northern
Ireland prices based on those contained
in the Order made on 3rd September,
1939. An Order has, in fact, now been
made and has been operative in Northern
Ireland as from 27th September, 1939.
ISSUE OF TRAVELLING PERMITS.
Mr. CLARK (by Private Notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention has been drawn to the complaints made of delay and inconvenience
caused by the present system of issuing
travel permits for journeys between
Northern Ireland and Great Britain.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, sir.
I have taken a note of the complaints.
which have been made, and in particular
the proceedings in another place on the
26th instant. Hon. Members will, I am
sure, bear with me if I deal with this
matter at some length.
I should explain that the permit system
as a whole was introduced by the Imperial
Government under powers granted by the
Defence (Emergency Powers) Act, and
my Ministry's responsibility on the
matter is confined to the machinery for
issuing the necessary permits to people.
who wish to leave Northern Ireland for
Great Britain.
We are at war, and it should hardly be
necessary to point out to hon. Members
that in the first place it is essential to
restrict unnecessary cross-channel traffic
to a minimum; and that in the second
place the history of recent events, both
in Great Britain and in this country,
render it all the more necessary in wartime to ensure that the character of
persons who are permitted to travel has
been fully investigated. This Government
is in duty bound in this, as in all other
matters, to lend its loyal co-operation to
the Imperial Government in the carrying
out of such measures as seem to it to be
necessary for the successful prosecution of
the war.
No reasonable person can expect that in
normal cases the necessary investigations
can be carried out without some delay
and inconvenience to travellers. Inconvenience and delay there must be, if the
scheme is to be effective, but every effort
has been made, and will continue to be
made, to reduce hardship to a minimum,
and I resent very much the allegations of
incompetence which have been made in
another place on the basis of a hypothetical case which never occurred, and
for which there was absolutely no
justification.
In fact, no single concrete case has yet
been brought to my notice whereby any
avoidable hardship has been caused by
the action or inaction-of the police
authorities in administering the travel
permit scheme; and, indeed, on the
contrary I am aware of many cases in
which, by the co-operation of all concerned, permits have actually been made.
available for travel on the evening of the
day on which application was made.
As regards people in Great Britain who
wish to travel to Northern Ireland, I
know that there has been a considerable
amount of congestion at the Passport
and Permit Offices with resulting delay to
applicants for Travel Permits. In such
cases as have been brought to my notice
every effort has been made to assist the
Imperial authorities with a view to the
reduction of such delay and inconvenience
to a minimum, but the matter is entirely
within the control of the Imperial Home
Office.
What is the, real burden of the complaint which has been made? It is that
in the instructions to the public they are
warned that there may be a delay of
ten days between the making of their
application and the issue. of a permit
Where inquiries have to be made, and
statements checked, delay is inevitable,
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
28 SEPTEMBER 1939
and it is only right that the public should
be warned accordingly. In the vast
majority of cases where applicants are
well known nothing like ten days' delay
does in fact occur. Of a number of travel
permits issued on the 26th instant, for
instance, the applications were dated as
follows:-three dated the 23rd; nine
dated the 25th; one dated the 26th; and
six others bearing application dates from
the 16th to the 19th instant-all these
six were, however, for people who had
stated that they did not wish to travel
before the 29th instant. I am quite satisfied that there is no real justification for
complaint on the part of any single
member of the community who is prepared
to co-operate loyally in these and other
necessary restrictions which war unfortunately compels us to impose. Little
short of 6,000 travel permits have been
issued in the relatively short period
during which the scheme has been in
operation, and so far from the officers
responsible being guilty of "gross incompetence," as has been suggested in
another place, I consider that they have
handled a very difficult situation with tact
and efficiency.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman take into consideration the
question of issuing permits as was done
during the last war? Is the Minister
aware that during the last war permits
were issued for a period of three, six, or
twelve months? I had a permit for the
duration of the war. Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that there are a number of persons in Northern Ireland who

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Housing (Emergency Powers) Bill
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This Bill, which is
similar in terms to one recently passed
by the Imperial Government, enables
local authorities to repair buildings which
may be required for housing purposes, and
which may have been damaged by enemy
action.
I should like to state briefly to the
House, the necessity for the Bill and the
immediate objects which the Bill seeks
to achieve. Hon. Members will, I
know, agree that if extensive damage
should be caused to house. property by
air raids or other enemy action, more
especially in what may be called workingclass areas where there is no alternative
accommodation available, it would be
essential, under these circumstances, that
steps should be taken immediately to
repair buildings which have been
rendered unfit for habitation.
If work of this nature is to be carried
out it may be that the person having
control of the property is either unable
Housing Bill-
Second Reading
10 OCTOBER 1939
or unwilling to go to the expense of
making the premises fit for habitation.
In order to get over this difficulty the
Bill empowers local authorities in such
circumstances to carry out the essential
works. The local authority, before
taking any action to repair property so
damaged must give at least 14 days'
notice to the person having control of the
property, and take into consideration any
representation that may be made by such
person. It may be necessary, however,
in some cases to conduct what might be
called emergency repairs in order to safeguard the health of the occupants of
those houses. It may be, for example,
that sewers might be damaged and hon.
Members will appreciate how necessary it
would be for that work to be undertaken
at once. Provision has been made in the
Bill for the carrying out of the repairs
coming within this category without due
notice being given where the local
authorities consider that the work should
be done at once.. I think the hon. Members will agree that such provision is
absolutely essential in the circumstances
suggested.
The only other aspect of the Bill to
which I would draw the attention of the
House is the method to be adopted to
finance the cost of the repairs which will,
in the first instance, fall on the local
authorities, but such cost will become recoverable against the owner by the local
authority.
Clause 3 of the Bill provides that loans
will be made available to local authorities
by my department on such terms and
conditions as may be approved of by my
right hon. Friend the Minister
of
Finance. The local authorities will not
be asked to repay the loan or any interest
thereon until the end of the war, nor will
the local authority be entited to recover
from the owner of the property any expense that may be incurred in carrying
out the repairs until the end of the present emergency. I think that is all that
is necessary in dealing with this matter.
I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

The PRIME MINISTER: I wish to
thank the hon. Member for giving way.
I propose in future, if it will suit the
convenience of the House, to make a
statement from time to time on the
Adjournment instead of answering questions put before the beginning of
business, which rather cripples any discussion that may be required afterwards.
I would like to state that the Government propose to carry on the Session
just in the ordinary way-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and in order that it
may last for as long a period as possible.
we have decided to meet only on the
Tuesday and Wednesday of each week
after this week. We require the three
days this week to conclude the business
we have on hand. After that we propose to have sittings only on Tuesdays
and Wednesdays. Further, if it is the
desire of the House, as the days become
shorter, to meet at an earlier hour than
three o'clock, the Government will be
quite content to meet the wishes of
the House in every possible way. My
right hon. Friend, the Chief Whip, wil
ascertain the feelings of all sides of the
House in order to come to an understanding that will be satisfactory. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I would like to announce also the
regrettable absence of the Minister of
Commerce owing to illness. I am sure
the whole House sympathises with him.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance has very kindly added to his
other very onerous work the duties of the
Minister of Commerce during his absence.
which I hope will not be prolonged.
I think it will interest the House if I
give the very latest information regarding our contribution to the war in reference to man power. Through the
courtesy which we always receive from
the general officer commanding, Major-
General Pollok, I am enabled to give the
following information. Recruiting for
the three services is progressing very
favourably. Recruiting centres have
been established in Belfast (two of them).
in Omagh, Londonderry and Enniskillen
and another will be opened shortly at
Portadown.
The regular units during
September obtained the full numbers
required. The Third Anti-Aircraft
Brigade, of the regiments of
which is commanded by the hon
and gallant Member for Mid Antrim
(Lieut.-Colonel Patrick), is recruiting
very strongly, and it is hoped will be up
to full strength within another month.
More tradesmen, he informs me, are stil
one
The European War

The European War
required. The North Irish Horse has
obtained three non-commissioned officers
and when these are trained it is hoped
that the counties of Tyrone, Fermanagh
and Armagh will supply all the men required for this unit.
The 102nd A.A. Brigade, which is
under the command of the Clerk of the
Parliament, Lieut.-Colonel Chichester, is
recruiting men between 29 and 50 years
of age for home defence-anti-aircraft,
signallers, Royal Army Medical Corps,
Royal Army Service Corps and Royal
Army Ordnance Corps-and recruits are
coming in as fast as they can be dealt
with.
I think it should be only right to comment on how satisfactory this report from
our general officer commanding is to all
of us. It reminds me of the old spirit of
the Ulster Division when recruiting took
place for that arm of the service, the
result of which was to the honour and
glory of Ulster. I should like to refer to
those who are joining or have already
joined the colours. These include a
number of our own Members of Parliament, a very large number of civil
servants and members of the Press
Gallery. You are all aware of the gallantry of the young man who sat in the
Gallery so long listening to our debates.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We all
know he was almost the first if not the
very first casualty, but, fortunately,
not a serious one, and we express our
grateful thanks and tender our congratulations to his parents that he has been
spared to carry on. We all hope to see
him home once more taking notes of our
debates. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
One word about those fine young fellows
of our Province who are joining or have
already joined the various units which go
to make up the great British Army. I
felt quite sure at the start when things
began to look serious for the United
Kingdom and the Empire that there
would be no holding back on the part of
those who have the old spirit of Ulster.
I think that has been fully justified, and
day by day, almost hour by hour, our
gallant young men are going out to
serve their King and country. The
same feeling animates their parents,
brothers, sisters and relatives generally
and we trust they may be sustained
during the absence of those who have
gone forward so valiantly to do their
duty. We are all filled with pride at
what is being done to help the Mother
Country, and we are not done yet. I am
certain that those whose duty lies at home
will all pull their weight and do what they
can to make it easy to win the war. It
will be won, but it will be won much
easier if we all pull together. Let each
and all give help, especially those who
are in high positions, and co-operate
willingly and heartily with the Government.
One of the vital contributions which
Ulster can make for war purposes is
tillage. The national efforts which our
farmers will be called upon to make are
important. The duties they perform are
carried on day by day during their lifetime and may appear somewhat mundane
and something they take in their stride.
It may be that they do not realise and
cannot have brought home to them the.
importance of doing everything they can
to produce more and more of those commodities that are required to carry us
through this struggle. The Minister of
Agriculture proposes to bring into cultivation an additional 250,000 acres and
he is confident he will be able to do that
with the growing trust in the Ministry
and the undoubted feeling that there will
be wise guidance. I know he has invited
and received the heartiest co-operation of
the agricultural committees of
counties, and if they all pull together
the object aimed at will be accomplished.
This extra ploughing is most essential
and every assistance will be given where
new land has to be broken up.
Minister's motto, I think, is "Plough to
victory," and if he can help in any one
way throughout the struggle that lies
ahead by giving advice, the people have
only to call on him or on those civil
servants who are so able in their particular spheres of action.

My col-
With regard to equipment, of which
one hears criticism now and again, the
facts are as follow: The personal
equipment for the A.R.P. workers continues to arrive and is distributed at
once. I asked before that there should
be a little give and take with regard to
certain articles necessary for A.R.P.
purposes, because this Government had
not received the supply to which it was
entitled, but since then the position has
very much improved. For instance, the
fire-fighting appliances are coming forward better and Belfast is approaching
its standard position, while other
vulnerable points have also been supplied;
in other words, when those necessary
supplies come into our hands there is no
avoidable delay in having an immediate
distribution made. So if there is still
something outstanding those who are
looking forward to further equipment
will understand that we will not delay a
moment in the distribution.
I may say that almost all essential
medical stores, stretchers, et cetera, have
been distributed in Belfast and several
towns in the vulnerable area. Fresh
supplies are arriving and being distributed daily.
Now, with regard to national registration, I would like to say one word. I
mentioned to the House on the last
occasion that the food rationing forms
would be issued as quickly as possible
and used for the compilation of the
National Register. Identity cards will be
issued as soon as possible. Heavy work
is involved, and some people may receive
their cards before others. I may say
that the moment notice is given that
such and such a thing will be done there
is sometimes impatience if it cannot be
acted upon just on the instant, but these
very extensive arrangements in connection with the distribution of food, and
so on, require a tremendous amount of
clerical work at the beginning.
When we start we may seem to some
to be rather slow, but as soon as the
machinery gets to work everything will
go, I hope, as smoothly as on the other
side. I would warn those who may be
impatient that some will get their identity
cards before others. With such a distribution throughout the whole of our
area it will be impossible that each householder should receive his cards on the
same day or possibly even in the same
week, but there need be no nervousnes
on that account. Everything will follow
along smoothly, I hope, once we start.
Of course, announcements will be made
in the Press in the ordinary way in orde
to give full notice when the distribution
will be made. Meanwhile, there is no
necessity for any inquiries as to the work.
because it will be carried out as expeditiously as is humanly possible.

ment. The hearty and generous manner

enrolment forms which have

nection with National Service committees

I come next to rationing schemes.
There have been some doubts here and
there as to the necessity for any form of
rationing in our area. People ask why
should meat be rationed when we have
a surplus. There is great danger in
ignorance on a subject of this kind as
it may lead to irresolution and indifference on the part of our people. A
want of determination and intelligent
co-operation with the Government in this
connection is undoubtedly a difficult and
rather delicate matter. We must share
and share alike with our fellow citizens
across the water, otherwise we might find
ourselves looked upon as people who are
not pulling their full weight, which is

I want now to refer to the black-out,
which is enforced under the Defence of
the Realm Regulations. I have been in
consultation with people who come from
London, Liverpool, Manchester, and
France, and I am going to say this about
our black-out our black-out is more
drastic than that of France. Northern
Ireland, for some reason that I cannot
understand, has gone to the extreme so
far as the black-out is concerned. I say
that this matter calls for the immediate
attention of the Government. The Prime
Minister, in his capacity as head of the
Civil Defence Department, has instructed
the police to take certain action. The
first action they took was to get all the
windows of the Belfast tramcars painted
blue. A more ridiculous and outrageous
proposition never was put into operation.
The citizens have tolerated this with
patience.
Why were Belfast Corporation compelled to do this? Because some police
officer said he would accept no other
method of black-out. This is, the Commissioner of Police. In London, Liverpool and Manchester no such conditions
exist. In Paris, I understand, no such
conditions exist. I say we have got to
have an easing-off of the extreme
measures which have been put into operation in connection with the black-out.
Remember, when I say that, I do not

I say nothing of the sort. I am one
hundred per cent. for all the protection

enemy aircraft from which the black-out
is to protect us. People are being
challenged nightly by air-raid wardens

There is going to be a Bill about prices.
When the Government were asked about
profiteering this was taking place. The

I will give an illustration of what is going

to certain
builders to erect houses which could be

was to be 7s 9d per week, but
they are now asking the tenants
to pay 11s per week. I claim that that
rent for a house with a valuation of £11
is too high. It really amounts to ls for

a fair deal to people. who take these
houses.
The Minister rendered a great social

allow any landlord to interfere with it.

I have here. a list of houses in.
the city of Belfast compiled by a

of Newry Urban District

Emergency Budget-
Committee
11 OCTOBER 1939
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 11th October, 1939.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
BILL PRESENTED.
Essential Buildings and Plant (Repair of
War Damage) Bill,
"to provide for the repair of buildings.
used for purposes essential to the welfare of the civil population and the reinstatement of the plant of undertakings
carried on for such purposes where the
buildings or plant are damaged by war.'
Presented by the Minister of Commerce,
supported by the Minister of Finance.
To be read a Second time to-morrow, and
to be printed. (Bill 37.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Ways and Means.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Emergency Budget.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): For years the citizens of the
British Empire have been hoping that
reasonableness and justice would prevail
over brutality and aggression, and that
peace
would be maintained. Mr.
Chamberlain and his colleagues have
striven incessantly to save Europe from
the awful catastrophe of another terrible
war. When, however, the German Army
invaded Poland in spite of warnings
often repeated and clearly given, all hope
of appeasement was gone, and since the
3rd September our Empire has been at
war. No one can tell whether it will be
of short or long duration. Before
victory is obtained, however, over the
forces of disruption and evil I fear it will
mean sacrifice, sorrow and suffering impossible to express in words.
One of the many tasks before the
country is to provide money to carry on
the war. Thousands of millions of
pounds will be required, and it is in this
direction as well as in all other war
activities that the people of Ulster desire
fully to play their part. Many gallant
men will join the Forces of the Crown.
Others will be required to carry on
administrative duties and those businesses
in particular that will be necessary to
produce munitions and the other essentials
of war, and which will be required to
maintain our export trade, which is
recognised to be vital from a financial
point of view. Again, others will be
engaged on tilling and increasing the
fertility of the soil to the greatest extent
possible, so that our necessary food supply
may be secured. To-day it is to the
financial side that we have to direct our
attention.
This is my first war-time Budget, and
I trust it will also be my last under such
distressing circumstances. We all hope
that an honourable peace may be possible
before it is too late to prevent an appalling loss of life and world-wide destruction. During the past few weeks I have,
of course, been in close consultation with
the British Treasury. A special and very
satisfactory agreement has been made on
a number of finanical matters to meet
war conditions, which I will explain to
the Committee later. I propose, however, first of all to give hon. Members
a short review of our balance sheet for
the current year as it now stands.
Hon. Members will be interested to
know how the increases in taxation in the
British Chancellor's Emergency Budget
affect our revenue. I do not propose to
give details of these increases, as they
must be known and felt by us all. The
increases, however, in income tax and
surtax and the excess profits tax are estimated to give us a further £820,000 this
year.
The increases in customs and
excise duties that is to say, the duties
on wine, beer and spirits, sugar and
tobacco are estimated to produce a
further £420,000 this year. This will
increase our reserved revenue by a sum
of £1,240,000 over my Budget Estimate.
I will now refer to our transferred
revenue, such as estate duty, stamp duty,
motor vehicles duty and entertainments
duty, all of which is levied and collected
by this Government-these are all items
of revenue which will be, unfortunately,
adversely affected by the war. I estimate
that estate duty at the existing rates will
produce £60,000 less than the estimate;
stamp duty £20,000 less; entertainments
Emergency Budget-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
duty £5,000 less; and in the case of
motor vehicles duty I am budgeting for a
fall of £310,000. In all, I estimate that
these transferred taxes will yield £375,000
less than I budgeted for, owing to the
changes brought about by the war.
Owing to the gradual improvement in
the employment situation which, I am
happy to say, took place during this year
before the war broke out, and to the
further opportunities of useful work of
many kinds which are now open to our
workers as a consequence of the war, the
relative employment position in Northern
Ireland compared with Great Britain will
be better than was anticipated at the
beginning of the year. Consequently,
the sum which our Exchequer will receive
during the year from Great Britain in
respect of unemployment under the Reinsurance Agreement is anticipated to be
£600,000 less than I expected. For
reasons to which I will refer later, the
British Treasury have agreed that if the
reinsurance receipt, now estimated at
£1,175,000, is not reached this year, a
special grant will be made from the
Imperial Vote of Credit to our Exchequer
to make up the difference. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) This Treasury
guarantee is given, of course, on the
understanding that unemployment legislation and administration in Northern
Ireland is maintained similar to that in
Great Britain. Other items of revenue
are in general unchanged since my last
Budget. In all, the total revenue is expected to reach a sum of £17,098,000.
I now turn to the expenditure side of
the account. In my previous Budget this
year I estimated an expenditure on Consolidated Fund Services of £1,073,000
and Supply Services £12,350,000, with a
provision of £200,000 for Supplementary
Estimates. On the other hand, a sum of
£300,000 as previously arranged was included on the revenue side to take into
account the first instalment of the 80 per
cent. grant from Great Britain in aid of
our Exchequer expenditure on civil defence. The total net expenditure on
these Services was, therefore, estimated
to be £13,323,000.
It is, of course, apparent that in some
cases expenditure will be considerably.
less than the estimate and in others that
a result of the war substantial inas
creases may be anticipated; in particular,
blocks of staff will fall to be transferred
from peace-time to war-time activities.
Apart from this, new war-time services,
which are wholly Imperial in character,
will require to be carried out by our departments either under agency arrangements or under delegation of authority
from Imperial departments. To quote
only a few cases, I would refer to petrol
rationing, food control, and the intensive
cultivation of land. No financial complication arises in the case of such services as
the expenditure on staff and allied
charges will be separately costed and recovered in full from the Imperial
Ministries concerned, and the moneys
actually disbursed will be similarly
obtained; it follows that the expenditure,
apart from staff costs, will not be reflected
in our accounts.
The question of the expansion for war
purposes of our normal services involving
a substantial excess expenditure does not
present the same simple problem, but I
am glad to be able to inform the House
that under the arrangements which have
been made, such excess expenditure will
not finally remain upon our Exchequer.
In order to calculate the amount to be
reimbursed to the Northern Ireland Exchequer on this account it was necessary
to assume a standard of peace-time expenditure as proper to be met in the usual
way, and the excess above such a level
of our actual expenditure will be made
good from the Imperial Vote of Credit.
This peace-time expenditure level has
been agreed after very careful consideration at a sum of £12,300,000, a figure
which covers both Supply and Consolidated Fund Services, and any approved
expenditure over and above what I may
call this peace-time datum line will be
recouped to us on the understanding that,
in general, similar economies to those
which are being and will be made in
ordinary peace-time services in Great
Britain will also be carried out in Northern Ireland, thereby enabling our claims.
on the British Exchequer to be reduced
to the same extent. On the same principle
-as I have already stated-we shall be
recouped for any amount by which the receipts under the Reinsurance Agreement
fall below the revised estimate of
£1,175,000. Provided, therefore, we go
in step in economies with Great Britainand I have given this understanding-the
2199 Emergency Budget-

11 OCTOBER 1939
Committee
British Treasury will put us in funds to
meet all excess expenditure due to the
war. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Arising out of the special war-time
adjustments I have outlined, the British
Government have agreed that instead of
the receipt of £300,000 which I provided for in my first Budget in recoupment of 80 per cent. of our Exchequer
expenditure on civil defence, they will
cover our civil defence expenditure as
part of the broad settlement governing
excess expenditure, and this arrangement
makes it unnecessary to operate upon the
£750,000 grant in aid, of which the
£300,000 was to have been a first instalment. The effect of this change will undoubtedly be that from now on our
Exchequer civil defence cost will be met
in full by the British Exchequer. This
arrangement is, of course, on the underlocal
standing that
authorities and
private individuals continue to bear their
due proportion of this expenditure.
I would like at this stage to record
my appreciation of the consideration
shown by my right hon. Friend, the
British Chancellor of the Exchequer, in
agreeing to these arrangements, which I
gratefully describe as essentially just and
generous to Northern Ireland. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I now turn to a proposal which I wish
to put before the Committee. In his
Emergency Budget the Chancellor of the
Exchequer raised the percentage rate. of
the estate duty on estates between
£10,000 and £50,000 by 10 per cent.,
and substituted an increase of 20 per
cent. for the increase of 10 per cent. in
the rate of duty on estates above £50,000
provided for in this year's Finance Act.
I propose that the same increase should
apply as from to-day in Northern
Ireland. This increase is expected to
provide £15,000 to £20,000 this year,
and in a full year, in all probability,
substantially more. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
I also propose to introduce three, very
technical clauses dealing with the evasion
of estate duty, which have already been
embodied in Imperial legislation and
have not so far been followed in Northern
Ireland. I am sure hon. Members will
agree that, as far as possible, our legislation on this subject should continue on
similar lines to that in Great Britain.
Hon. Members and Ulster people
generally will be gratified to know that I
expect our Imperial Contribution for this
first year of the war will reach, due to
the changes I have outlined, the sum of
£2,000,000, leaving a provisional surplus
of £29,000. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Our credit stands high. Our financial
system is sound, but it would not be
proof against extravagances or waste.
It is for me, with the assistance of my
colleagues, which is being freely given, to
see that only necessary expenditure is
incurred, and that our resources are conserved as far as possible in order to be
devoted towards winning the war, which
is not of our Empire's making.
In these days the statement is frequently made in quarters that should
know better that in the fight for liberty
and justice Ireland is standing neutral.
That charge, I regret to say, can be
truly brought against the Free State,
now called Eire, but it is grossly untrue
and unjust as regards Ulster, and if
proof of this were necessary it is to be
found in the facts and figures which I
have disclosed to-day. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

Trade Boards Bill-
Second Reading
11 OCTOBER 1939
Trade Boards Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): We propose in this Bill to
make two changes which I think are very
necessary, and which at the same time
will bring the, law dealing with trade
boards into conformity with the law in
Great Britain. These proposals in no
way interfere with conditions of employment or wages paid in the trade board
industry, neither do they prevent the
setting up of trade. boards, but make it
easier to bring such machinery into
action.
The outlook of the community in
regard to social matters has developed
considerably during the past twenty
years, and as a result many Acts have
been passed
passed to meet the new
and
changing conditions. When trade boards
were first introduced it was the intention
to regulate wages in those trades where
wages were unduly low, and during all
the years that trade boards have been in
operation they have done much to assist
the smooth working of industry and to
create more harmonious relations between
employers and workpeople in the industries concerned. Too often men are
inclined to resort to a trial of strength
under jungle conditions, which leads
nowhere and which ultimately creates
bitterness and ill-feeling in the industry.
I have found through my long and
intimate association with the. Ministry of
Labour that it is at a round table conference, where each section of the
industry has an opportunity to express
its views freely, that agreement can most
easily be found and good relations cultivated and fostered.
We propose in this Bill to take power
in respect of the constitution of trade
boards to appoint, where it is considered
necessary and desirable, three independent members instead of one as at
present. With the increasing complexity
of industrial conditions and industrial
legislation, such as holidays with pay, we
feel that a single appointed member has
added responsibility, and we desire to
strengthen the board by the appointment
of two additional members to any board
as we think fit.
There are small boards where it might
not be necessary, but the larger boards,
where complicated and controversial
matters are more apparent, might call
for extra support in arriving at a
decision. The present chairman is a man
of great patience and resource, and
during all the years he has acted as chairman he has given the utmost satisfaction
-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and I
trust that for many years to come. we
will have his invaluable assistance.
Mr. BEATTIE: Who is this superman?
Mr. GORDON: Mr. Reid.
Mr. JOHNSTON: He is all right.
Mr. BEATTIE: When you hear an
employer saying he is a decent chap
Mr. SPEAKER: We cannot carry on

with or experience of perhaps that

connection with these boards.
The second change we propose to make
is that of substituting Special Order
procedure for Provisional Order procedure. I should explain to the House
that before a trade board is established
the Minister must first of all ascertain

are complied with. He must then inform the interests concerned, both employers and workpeople, of his intention.
to apply the Act to that trade, and give

any objections or representations which
they may desire to make and to which
he must give careful consideration. It is

I am sure that hon. Members will agree

The necessity for this amended legislation has been borne in upon me for
some time, and I feel that I owe it to

I commend this Bill to the House. I

Housing (Emergency Powers) [Money].
Considered in Committee under
Standing Order No. 65.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to authorise the
payment out of moneys provided by
Parliament of any sums required by the
Ministry of Home Affairs for the purpose
of making loans to local authorities under
any Act of the present Session to empower local authorities to make fit for
housing purposes buildings damaged by
war and for purposes connected therewith." (Governor's Recommendation
signified.-The Minister of Labour).
Housing Bill
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
SECRETARY
The FINANCIAL
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): This Resolution provides that any loan made to a
local authority under the provisions of
the Housing (Emergency Powers) Bill to
enable buildings damaged as the result of
enemy action to be repaired, shall be
obtained from moneys voted by Parliament. In view, however, of the fact
that the local authority cannot charge
interest or recover any portion of their
expenditure during the period of hostilities, it is not proposed that the local
authority shall be required to repay the
loan to the Exchequer, or to make
interest payments in respect thereof, until
the war is ended. In making the money
available from voted sources instead of
from the Government Loans Fund this
House is following the procedure adopted.
in Great Britain.
It is impossible to estimate the amount
of the charge, if any, which may arise
out of the passing of this Resolution, but
expenditure for war purposes of this kind,
incurred in the issue of loans under the
Bill, will be caught up under the broad
settlement governing excess expenditure
reached with the Treasury, to which my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, has referred this afternoon in
his Budget speech. Any sums issued
will be reimbursed to the Northern Ireland
Exchequer, and the sum ultimately
received in repayment of the loan, or as
interest on it, will be paid into the
Exchequer. I beg to move.

ditions in the matter of pay, etc., as

EX-CIVIL SERVANTS RECALLED.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the total
number of ex-civil servants whose
appointments had formerly been determined through superannuation, marriage,
or voluntary retirement, and who have
been recalled to service under the present
emergency; whether he can state the
names of these officers and the ranks
severally held by them since their reappointment; whether it is a fact that
married women in certain instances are
being recalled to Government service as
shorthand-typists when there are large
numbers of persons fully qualified for
this duty both within the service and
outside it, the latter being unemployed.
Mr. ANDREWS: The total number
of ex-civil servants who have been recalled to service in the present emergency
is only 10, of whom 9 are still in post;
their names and the ranks held by them
since their reappointment are contained
in the statement which I propose to
circulate in the Official Report.
Such re-employment is in accord with
the practice which has been introduced,
with Treasury authority, in the Departments of the Imperial Civil Service, and
it has been considered necessary and most
desirable as a war-time measure to take
advantage of the assistance of these experienced officers to meet a situation
which has arisen partly from the withdrawal of a number of civil servants who
have joined the Crown Forces and partly
on account of the expansion of departmental activities due to the War.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
whether the Minister intends to circulate
the names of the positions of the married
women who have been recalled or is the
number included in the ten.
Mr. ANDREWS: Yes.
Mr. BEATTIE: The total number is
ten?
Mr. ANDREWS: Yes.
