TRAINING OF MEN STUDENTS.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether it is a fact that first
year men students have been called up
for training in the English Training
Colleges in the session of 1939-40, and,
if so, will a similar course be followed
in connection with men students who
have passed the 1939 King's Scholarship
examination in Northern Ireland.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): The
answer to the first part of the question
is in the affirmative. In reply to the
second part I can only say that the
decision of the Government, to discontinue for the duration of the war the
training of men students who have not
already had a first-year course, was taken
after careful consideration and in view
of the urgent need for economy in public
expenditure. The Government is not
prepared to alter that decision.
MOTOR CARRYING RESTRICTIONS
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the Government
intend, in view of the National
Emergency, to remove motor carrying restrictions as has been done in Great
Britain, and thereby continue their step
by step policy.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It is not the intention of the Government to ask Parliament to remove the restrictions on the
carrying of goods for hire which were imposed by the Road and Railway Transport Act of 1935, because there is no
apparent reason why such a step should
be taken.
Every effort possible must be made to
ensure that petrol and oil are not being
used except for services which are
essential to the life of the community,
and it is therefore to the public interest
that public transport, rail and road,
should be used to the fullest possible
extent, and that except in exceptional
circumstances the supplies of fuel which
have been granted to owners of vehicles
should not be used for relatively longdistance journeys.
Where it is desirable in the public
interest that vehicle owners should be
allowed to carry goods for hire the Act
already provides machinery for doing so,
which is by way of arrangement with the
Transport Board.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
reply, why does the Government propose
to put the people of Northern Ireland in
a
worse position as regards transport
than the people of Great Britain? Do
not the same reasons apply in Great
Britain as apply here, and, that being
so, why do not we follow the lead of the
Imperial Parliament in this respect?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The condition
of affairs in Great Britain and that in
Northern Ireland are entirely different.
In Northern Ireland the Road Transport
Board have control completely over the
roads. In England it is slightly different
where licences are issued to groups of
owners using vehicles for the conveyance
of goods.

EARLY CLOSING OF SHOPS.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the. Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can inform the
House when it is proposed to introduce
legislation for the earlier closing during
the war of all staff-employing shops in
Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If, as appears
from the hon. Member's question, he has
in mind any idea that the Government
propose to discriminate in this matter
between shops which employ staffs and
shops which do not, I can assure him
that the Government has no intention
of introducing any such legislation.
The question as to what, if any,
emergency restrictions should be imposed
upon shops on account of conditions
arising from the war is at present receiving consideration, but I am unable
to inform the hon. Member as yet what
the decision of the Government on the
matter is likely to be.
There are a great many conflicting
points of view to be taken into account
before taking action in a matter which
so vitally affects the interests and livelihood of so many members of the general
public and the trading community.

Cranfield, Kilkeel, Co. Down, and other
lighthouses in Northern Ireland; and
whether he will make representation to
the appropriate quarters to have the
lighting of same modified
possible.
as far as
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): The hon. Member will appreciate that vessels at sea require guidance
from lighthouses, and the scope of that
guidance is a matter which falls within
the jurisdiction of the Imperial Parliament. I am aware, however, that the

DISPENSARY MEDICAL OFFICERS
ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
the
8. Mr. STEVENSON asked
Minister of Home Affairs whether he will
take steps to ensure that medical officers
(whether dispensary medical officers or
part-time medical officers in local
authority hospitals), who go on active
service, will receive a proportion of their
salary during their absence; and whether
their position in respect to pension rights
and age of retirement will be safeguarded.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Provision has
been made by the Local Government
Staffs (War Service) Act, 1939, for local
authorities to make up any difference between service and civil pay to any employee who joins the Services, and to safeguard their pension and other rights.
These privileges will extend to medical
officers. A similar Bill has been introduced by me here, and the Second Reading of the Measure will be taken shortly.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: May I
ask if the Minister will use his influence
with the British Medical Council to see
that medical practitioners who joined up
just prior to mobilisation get the same
generous treatment as is extended to
those who have joined since mobilisation?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes.

allowed to relieving officers and subofficers
sanitary

Next I come to a very important thing.
the increase of our Imperial contribution.
All Members of the House and people
outside the House know how it has been
possible to increase the Imperial contribution. At the moment we are in the
position of having increased taxation

That is the surplus amount of taxation
which the right hon. Gentleman is going
to hand over to the Chancellor of Great
Britain, but the right hon. Gentleman
has responsibilities at home. He must
remember that that additional taxation
amounting to £1,240,000 has reduced the
purchasing power of the people. It has
reduced their standard of life.
Owing to the imposition of that amount
the cost of living has increased by 20%
to 25%. I would advise the right hon.
Gentleman to be very careful in his state-

He
ments about handing money away.
cannot afford to hand over £2,000,000 to
the Chancellor without making the people
at home suffer, and suffer to a greater
extent than the people of Great Britain.
The British people will not suffer through
the lack of finance. The increase of 25%
will create demands from the professional
and other classes. The working classes
will ask where their purchasing power has
gone to, and all we can say is that the

£1,240,000, plus £760,000, making a

The cost of living is soaring because
the Government has failed to grapple
with the situation and to deal with the
profiteering which has taken place in
regard to foodstuffs, clothing, and every
other essential for the wellbeing of the.
people. Now there are going to be applications for improved wages conditions
from every unit in Northern Ireland
owing to the increased cost of living.
Once you allow profiteering to go to the
extent it has gone you have to accept the
responsibility of adding to the purchasing
power of the people in order to keep
normal industry moving. The right
hon. Gentleman wants to keep the normal
industry of Northern Ireland moving
and at the same time help towards the
fulfilment of Britain's obligations in the
successful prosecution of the war.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is not Britain
alone.
Mr. BEATTIE: To help the democracies of the world to keep the position
they now occupy. That is more suitable
to me. I do not want to go too far, but
there is no use in making these elaborate
statements about your financial loyalty
and your practical help and your lip
sympathy. I believe in carrying the
thing out, and the first duty of everyone
is to look to the interest of those whom
we are at the moment controlling. That
is my first claim on the right hon.
Gentleman. I claim the people of
Northern Ireland are entitled to all
increase of wages and salaries of at least
25 per cent. to meet the increased cost
of living. That claim will be made all
round, from the labourer to the highest
professional class, and it has to be conceded.
We are going to have a reduction in
many things that we get revenue from.
Owing to the petrol rationing there is
going to be a reduction in the amount
got from motor taxation upon which we
depended greatly for our local revenue.
We are now going to follow step by step
in regard to estate duty taxation. I do
do not mind that so much, because I and
the people I represent spend our estate
as we live. When we die there is
generally nothing left but debt, and I
do not think you can derive much tax
from debt. The additional estate duty
tax which is being applied will not, I
think, have very much effect in Northern Ireland, because the taxable capacity
of Northern Ireland is very small compared with the taxable capacity of Great
Britain. When you look at the huge
sums produced by taxation in Great
Britain the amount realised from taxes
in Northern Ireland is as a drop in the
ocean. In the building up of the British
Budget we are a very small entity, and I
want to assure the right hon. Gentleman
that if he thinks he is not reducing the
purchasing power of the workers by
handing over £2,000,000 to the British
Exchequer he is making a great mistake.
The time will come when We shall
make our demand, but we will allow a
reasonable time to elapse before we make
it. I hope that hint will be received in
the spirit in which it is given, but a
sliding cost-of-living scale must be introduced for the period of the war.
I am not too young to remember the
aftermath of the last war, particularly
as it affected the Unemployment Insurance Fund. We had built up a reserve
of many millions for the benefit of those
who had contributed to that fund, but
for a period after the war that fund was
used not alone for those who had built
it up, but as a sort of after-war service
for all members of His Majesty's Forces
who had served during the war. I did
not complain at that time, but I did
complain when the distribution of the
remaining amount was made on the
establishment of this Parliament. Then
the allocation of the fund left us in the
unhappy position of having a debt of
over £2,000,000 to meet in the new fund
transferred to Northern Ireland. I do

as much

We still have 40,000 unemployed in
Northern Ireland, and I appeal to the
right hon. Gentleman to re-consider that
Imperial contribution of £2,000,000,
because money is of no importance at
the moment. What we want is man
power and material for the successful
prosecution of the war, but money is all
important at home. We must keep
industry going and we must keep the
people in a state of physical fitness, and
that can only be done by means of
money. Therefore, I hope a sliding costof-living scale will be introduced for the
benefit of all workers, whether in
industry or in Government, police, or
other services, and that it will be secured
by Act of Parliament.
Mr. NIXON: We are now considering a supplementary Budget to assist,
broadly speaking, in prosecuting the war
to a successful conclusion. I am prepared
to support that Budget and to bear my
share of any sacrifice that may be
necessary for that purpose. It does not
matter what it is, even if it is half my
income, provided it is made all round to
bring the war to a successful conclusion
and to down Hitler for all time, for there
will be no peace in the world until that
is achieved. At the same time that will
not be done by squandering money. I
have confidence in both the Minister of
Finance and the Parliamentary Secretary
so far as the control of expenditure is
concerned. If I had not I would not say
it. You might spend millions and
millions and get no military benefit
whatever-often the reverse.
Is the money that is being voted spent
to the best advantage in Northern Ireland? In this case there is a vote for
the Imperial Government, and I have no
hesitation in saying that they are wasting money wholesale over there. They
always do, unfortunately. Are we spending what is retained here to the best
advantage? People might be working,
writing their name, and yet doing
nothing useful. I have in my mind at
the moment the Food Control Offices. I
am not going to criticise them, because
I know they are very busy in those offices.
Hampton House is dealing with petrol
supplies, and I know they are very busy
there, working until 10 o'clock at night.
What I want to know is, what is the
crowd doing in Stormont Castle? If
they were dealing with food or petrol or
any other service we could understand
it, but does anyone know what they are
doing? They may be working all right:
they may be copying and writing, but
where there is a lot of writing there is
never efficiency.
I want to know from the Minister
what practical work they are doing!
They did not give out gas masks. They
were given out by volunteers. They were
doing nothing about the building of these
shelters that are being erected all over
the city. We may have our own opinion
about the utility of these shelters, but
they are being put there for a good
purpose. They have nothing to do with
food or petrol. They may be exercising
a sort of superior control, but that
amounts to nothing. I am told the
place is full of them. It must be when
it was necessary to put the Castle at their
disposal.

When we visualise how this money will
be scattered in the holocaust of war, we
should be very careful to consider the peace
aspect. Peace, after all, has its glories

in the increased cost of living, and how

I do not see any provision in this Budget
statement which would enable workers to
look forward to the future with any

the picture is painted there are defects,
and the sooner we get a clear explanation of the facts the better as regards the
social well-being and security of the
working classes.
It is all very well to provide millions
for a front hundreds of miles away, but
I should like to ask the Minister of
Finance a very blunt question does he
give the same consideration to the home
front? Has he made any provision for
it? The home front is as important as
any other front. There would be less
destruction there, and that is what I
am most concerned with. I look for the
reconstruction and the building up of
this country on a basis of peace and
security. With the heavy burdens that

There is a point I want to make particularly in reference to the speech of the

generally are living in poverty and unable

The hon. Member for South Armagh

we all
regret have to be made. In England

savings should be made here.

estate inside a few years?
The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Black): This question relates to the first
Resolution which has been passed by the
House and not to the Resolution we are
dealing with now. The answer to that
is, estate duty is leviable at these rates
on any estate when death takes place.
If a man dies and leaves his estate to his
son estate duty is payable on the man's
death. If the son dies within ten, five.
three or two years afterwards estate duty
on the value of the son's estate has to be
paid at his death, with this exception that
a reduction of rate is allowed in certain
cases where a short interval occurs between the deaths.

(Bill 38.)
Teachers' Salaries and Superannuation
(War Service) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mrs. PARKER: The title of this Bill
is so fully explanatory of its contents
that very few words are required to
commend it to hon. Members.
Its main principle is the granting of
every facility to those teachers and
officers in the various classes of
recognised schools and training colleges
who may desire to serve in their country's
defence. In such circumstances it is only
right and proper that a grateful country
should try to ensure that they do not
suffer financialy whilst serving-and that
if they are spared to return and resume
their ordinary employment, when they
come to retire their pensions will not be
less because they served in the fighting
forces.
The least we can do is to see that,
whilst so serving, anxiety as to the
financial position of those belonging to
them will not weigh upon their minds
and that they go with the knowledge
that their positions are waiting for them
on their return. Where the teacher or
other officer receives his salary direct
from the authorities of the school-as
distinct from the State-we enable and
in certain cases will assist those
employers to follow a similar course. I
am confident that they will try to deal
as generously—————
Notice taken that ten Members were
not present; House counted, and ten
Members being present
Mrs. PARKER: As I said, I am confident that the authorities will try to deal
as generously as possible with those
members of the staff who "go to the
war."
We propose, further, that if the
teacher or officer whose salary is borne
on the Parliamentary Vote should lose
his life any payment by way of salary
made as contemplated in this Bill should
be continued to the widow or other
dependants for a period up to six months.
In regard to superannuation,
Government proposes to offer generous
terms to all the persons concerned. These
are the broad outlines of the Measure.
I hope it will receive the sympathy
and support of the House. I beg to
move.

desire to bring up the question of having

I made inquiries from a number of

executive officers.

Food control is a matter for the

an Imperial service. The clerks of all
the local authorities have been invited
by the Ministry of Food to undertake
the duties of food executive officers, and
they have the assistance of local committees which are appointed by the loca.
authority and are representative of consumers and traders. Every clerk to the
local authority is the local food executive
officer. The food executive officers are
working voluntarily at present, but the
payment of the staff is made direct from
the Ministry of Food in London. The
money is not voted by this House, but
all the staff are paid direct from the
Ministry of Food in London.

it appears that the Ministry of Food

food executive officers that they were to

SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
Mr. BROWN: The Prime Minister
stated very fairly earlier to-day that if
it was the general desire the time of the
sittings of this House would be changed.
I wish to say that so far as I can
ascertain there is no general desire for
any change in the sittings of the House.
I want to point out that all the resources
of the Empire are being mobilised at the
present time to fight for the continuation
of such a Parliamentary system as ours
and, therefore, we must be careful that
we are not deprived of any of our rights
under that system. I am quite certain
the. Prime Minister would not deliberately
do so, because there is no greater democrat
than the Prime Minister himself. He is
the most accessible of men, but he might
unconsciously deprive Members of this
House of some of their rights.
In the first place it has been suggested
that the House should in future meet at
11-30 a.m. That would deprive country
Members of their valuable right of
getting questions answered in the usual
form, because very few of us could get
to this House at 11-30 in the morning.
It would mean that we would have to
raise these questions on the Motion for
the Adjournment and put both ourselves
and the Ministers concerned to very great
trouble, and with far less satisfactory
results. I would like that to be borne in
mind. It would also interfere with meetings of the Belfast Corporation, which
meets at 11 o'clock.

week, Tuesday and Wednesday, instead

The PRIME MINISTER: With

desires.
The reason that moved certain Members
to suggest Tuesday and Wednesday in
preference to Tuesday and Thursday was
simply that, being in the neighbourhood
of Parliament, they would rather stay the
night and be done the next day and get
home without having to come back.
That desire I can quite understand. I
had also to consider the convenience of
the staff of this House. It is quite
obvious that if everything is opened up
and prepared for the Members coming
here, sitting on Tuesday and then on
Wednesday is very much simpler than
closing down and having to re-open again.
That is the only feeling I had with regard
to the matter. If the hon. Member will

ment I believe that 11-30 would be the

civil
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): Sir Roland Nugent
is an ex-civil servant who served with
distinction in the Diplomatic Service and
the Foreign Office; he was also director of
the Federation of British Industries for a
number of years.
The Foreign Office had arranged to

Sir Roland Nugent is serving without

2267 Employment Control Bill-

Second Reading

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Finance (No. 2) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): This Bill is intended to give
legislative effect to the proposals outlined
in my Budget speech last week. Clause
1 increases the rates of estate duty to the
same extent as they have been increased
in Great Britain. Clauses 2, 3 and 4
deal with evasion of estate duty, and
similar clauses are already embodied in
British legislation. Under the Finance
Act, 1894, an annuity or other interest
which has been purchased or provided by
a deceased, either by himself or in concert
with someone else is subject to duty. This
provision has in the past been not infrequently evaded, and I think the best
way to explain the intentions of Clauses
2 and 3 of this Bill is to give an example
of the type of evasion which they are
designed to prevent.
If, for example, a man makes a gift
of, say, £50,000 to his son more than
three years before his death and the son
lends it back to him at five per cent. interest, and with the £2,500 a year pays
the premiums on a life insurance policy on
his father's life for £50,000, the result is
that this insurance policy is not brought
into the deceased's estate, and duty is
consequently not paid upon it. Clause 2
is designed to prevent this occurring. A
further result is that when the father
dies he is indebted to his son for a sum
of £50,000, and as that is a debt due from
his estate at the time of his death
that sum is deducted from his
estate before duty is charged, so that
in such a case the duty on £100,000 would
be evaded. Clause 3 is designed to prevent this sort of evasion. Clause 4
similarly deals with the payment of duty
on a beneficial interest provided by a
deceased and which passes on his death.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Control of Employment Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The
OF
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY
LABOUR (Mr. Grant): The object of
this Bill, which corresponds to a recent
Act of the Imperial Parliament, is to
prevent the labour supply for urgent
work in war time from being diverted to
less essential occupations by advertising
and "poaching". It, therefore, proposes
to control advertising for, and engaging
workers in, a number of industries. This
seems a serious undertaking; but it is not
so drastic as it sounds. To begin with,
before there is any control at all, the
Ministry must make an order setting out
the classes of employers and workers.
affected. That order must be laid before
'both Houses of Parliament; and either
House can annul it by Resolution.
The worker, too, is amply protected.
He cannot be compelled to take employment with a particular employer, or to
leave employment with which he is
satisfied. If he wants to leave he is free
to do so. If he wishes to accept a job,
the Ministry cannot withhold consent
unless it is able to offer him suitable
alternative employment. If he does not
think that the alternative job is really
suitable he can appeal to the Court of
Referees; if he wins his appeal he will be
entitled to compensation on a basis to be
set out in regulations; and the only fly
2269 Employment Control Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Grant]
in the ointment from his point of view
is that he will not be allowed to draw
compensation and unemployment insurance benefit in respect of the same period.
That is the essence of this Bill. I have
tried to put it as briefly and, at the same
time, as clearly as I can. There are other
clauses in the Bill, all necessary and all
contributing towards the same end, but
I should not be justified in taking up the
time of the House by doing more than
referring to them. Penalties are fixed
for offences; arrangements made through
trade union placing machinery, approved
by the Ministry, are to be outside the
scope of the Bill. I would like to elaborate
that particular point because those of us
who know what trade union arrangements
are will appreciate the fact that there are
arrangements made between employers
and the unions so that if they ask for
men to fill vacancies the unions supply
the men to the different employers. These
placing arrangements will not be interfered with by this Bill. There is the
usual clause providing for Orders and
Regulations being laid before the House.
I can imagine hon. Members looking
with no very friendly eye on Clause 3,
which provides for the appointment of
inspectors. But I can assure them that
this is only a precautionary measure, and
we do not expect that any new appointments will be made. As a matter of fact,
the Minister and I have already had
applications from numbers of people.
looking for positions as inspectors under
this Bill, but we have already our own
staff of inspectors under the Unemployment Insurance and Factory Acts. Owing
to the emergency legislation which has
passed through this House those
inspectors are not as fully occupied in
their ordinary occupations as they would
be in normal times, so that we expect
they will be able to cope with this particular legislation to which I am now
asking the approval of the House.
We have, in the employment exchange
service, machinery for operating the
main provisions of the Bill, so far as the
engagement of workers is concerned; and
where scientific, professional or technical
qualifications are needed we can draw
upon the Central Register for National
Service. By this means, we hope to do
something substantial to secure that
labour wanted for vital national work
is not frittered away in the scramble of
competing advertisers.
Compared with Great Britain, our
problem is, of course, a small one, but
it is as necessary here as it is on the
other side to protect the labour position
of firms engaged on work essential in
war time. In the absence of corresponding legislation in Northern Ireland, there
is the possibility of having the labour
essential for our firms attracted to
employment in Great Britain. At the
same time we should be unable to make
the best use of labour suitable for the
requirements of our firms engaged in war
work.
I stated at the beginning that this Bill
is practically identical with the one in
Great Britain with just one exception. In
the British Bill there is set up a committee representative of employers and
workpeople. They will discuss with the
Ministry the necessary formula for any
trades that require to be protected, and
then an order will be made. We considered this matter very carefully over
here, and came to the conclusion, and I
think rightly so, that it would be unnecessary to set up a committee in Northern
Ireland because the committee in Great
Britain will have already decided what is
a priority occupation. We will only make
our orders on identical lines with those
in Great Britain.
I think I can promise the House that if
there is any trade in Northern Ireland
that would require to be dealt with as a
priority trade which is not so dealt with
in Great Britain the persons concerned,
that is, the employers and the employees.
will be consulted before any order is
made; but, on the other hand, if we set
up a committee and they came to a
different decision to the committee in
Great Britain and said that a certain
trade was not a priority trade we would
be in the very difficult position of having
men in Northern Ireland declared by our
committee not to be in a priority trade
being called upon to go to Great Britain
to take over jobs there. We do not want
any of our essential workers removed from
Northern Ireland to other parts of the
United Kingdom.
This may seem a little involved, but I
believe hon. Members will appreciate the
point I am putting up. The sum and

to the enemy.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF

(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): This Supplementary Estimate for Cabinet Offices
is required-first, to provide for

the
year under the Prime Minister's

sympathy with the cause of the Allies to

CLASS III. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £10 be granted to His Majesty for
the services of the year ending 31st
March, 1940, to defray the Salaries and
Expenses of the Ministry of Home
Affairs."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Warnock): The
Committee, of course, will recognise that
this is purely a token Vote in connection
with the expenses which are incidental to
the petrol rationing scheme under the
Defence of the. Realm Regulations. This
work has been undertaken by an officer
of the Ministry of Home Affairs, and
the sum of £10 asked for is purely a
token Vote.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not the big bad
wolf which the Minister of Finance has
tried to represent that I am. This is one
vote of which I approve. Not only that,
but I can speak very highly of the
services which those connected with the
rationing scheme are rendering. They
have many difficulties to contend with.
I always come out into the open to fight
an enemy, and I will continue to do so,
but I recognise good service when it is
rendered. I wish to compliment the
Department dealing with the rationing of
petrol. While saying that I should like
to make an appeal in regard to rationing.
An enormous amount of unnecessary
work has been thrown on the Department.
As every hon. Member of this House is
aware under this scheme we must keep
within our power a certain storage, and
that must be maintained daily.
Large numbers of people in Northern
Ireland are at the moment using very
high-powered cars. It is up to every
2319 Supplementary Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs 2320
18 OCTOBER 1939
member of the community to help the
commercial side of our life-the people
who have to go into the highways and
byways to carry on their lawful duties.
These people should be given special consideration, but they can only receive it
if the high-powered cars not used for
commercial purposes are curtailed. I
would recommend in this House and also
outside it that, where possible, lowpowered cars should be used. If that is
done a greater mileage will be covered for
the same amount of petrol, and it will
also help those engaged in commercial
pursuits to receive an additional supply
of petrol. I wish to express my appreciation of the great service which is being
rendered to motor users by the petrol
rationing Department.
Question put, and agreed to.

Mr. WARNOCK: This, again, is a

have done on previous occasions, a loan

over a difficult period. It is considered
an essential service as part of the railway
runs in Northern Ireland. I understand
they get some similar accommodation
from the Government of Eire. I beg to
move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not in harmony
on this occasion, as I know the
history of this railway. It may, at the
moment, be of some service in the
national interest, but it only covers a
very small mileage in Northern Ireland.
The greatest percentage of the line is in
Eire. It is only throwing good money
after bad to give them a loan of £2,500
free of interest. For many years a joint
contribution has been made for the upkeep of this railway, and it has never reestablished itself as a paying proposition.
At the present time this railway can be
done without due to the modern form of
transport on the roads. Road transport
in the area in which this railway operates
is all that is required at the present time.
I understood that we had heard the
last of the claims from this railway. It
may be said that a great number of men
are employed on the line, and that the
idea behind the Government giving this
loan is to keep them in employment. I
say quite openly in the House that that
is not the policy I pursue. I do not
believe in advocating class legislation. I
have never done so, and I hope I never
will. A number of men are employed in
the workshops, but there is no earthly
reason why they should not be employed
with the road transport section which is
all that is required for the conveyance of
passengers and goods on the part of the
line which operates in Northern Ireland.
I do not feel justified in saying that I
agree with this loan. There may be
other matters of which I am not aware
which the Government took into consideration when deciding to give this
loan free of interest. I presume it was
due to the emergency conditions. If
that is so I should like to know more
about it before I vote. I wish I could
get the Government to concede a sum of
£2,500 to the 140 applicants who have
been denied outdoor relief by the Commissioners in order that they might be
tided over the difficult period that lies

gentlemen associated with this railway

I may be wrong.
Eire has an obligation to this railway

comprehensive review of the air-raid precautionary services of the Ministry
during the past few months. But having
regard to the present situation, and particularly to the words which the Speaker
uttered at the inauguration of this
sitting, I do not propose to go through
any review of many of the items down
in this Estimate.
The first item is general equipment and
materials, and as the Estimate shows it
is very largely concerned with the purchase and storage of general equipment
such as respirators and other equipment
in connection with the air-raid precautionary service. There has been,
as

are

Civil nursing reserve is a token Vote.
Then the next Vote is evacuation. When
I spoke last in this House on the
question of evacuation I was frankly a
great deal happier about it than I am
to-day. It is a thing which I sincerely
hope will not be put into operation at
all. The reason is not because of any
fear of not getting the children out of
Belfast to their destination, but it is
because since the matter was last before
the House I have been in various parts
of the country looking at the accommodation available for the children, and
the housing conditions in Northern
Ireland are such that in many cases I
fear that we will not be able-not by
reason of any difficulty of organisation
but by reason of the shortage of accommodation to find really good billeting
accommodation for the children if we
have to deal with the seventy thousand
odd which we have on the list. Getting
the children out of Belfast is a mere
matter of mechanical organisation. I
believe the organisation is absolutely
sound. I hope so. But so far as billeting of the children, having regard to

regard to the knowledge I have of the
housing accommodation in many parts of
the country, frankly I am scared of it
and I hope it will never have to take
place.
-

The next thing is the grants to public
utility undertakings, £77,000. That
figure looks big. It is very big. But it
is not really £77,000, because £48,000 is
repayable. It includes grants or loans
or advances to three railway companies,
the London, Midland and Scottish, the
Great Northern, and the Belfast and
County Down. I had better tell
the House the circumstances. Under
the Civil Defence Bill it is the
duty of the Government to secure the
due functioning of the railway systems of
the
country. In Great Britain the
method the Government Department
used was a block grant of £4,000,000 to
the railways which they divided amongst
themselves in proportions that I am not
familiar with. We did not think the
situation is comparable in this country
so far as risk is concerned with that in
Great Britain.
What we did is, we got into communication with the companies and we
found out the normal consumption of
coal, rails, chairs, sleepers, or essential
services. What we have done is that we
have financed the purchase of certain
supplies for each of the three railways
in order to ensure that there shall always
be in reserve a sufficient supply of
material to ensure due functioning. For
instance, I think in the case of the Belfast and County Down Railway we have
financed the supply for some months of
coal and a certain quantity of rails and
sleepers which they appeared to have some
difficulty in getting. Of the provision
for these public utility undertakings of
£77,000, £48,500 is repayable and a great
deal of the rest is for the protection of
vital parts of the railway. We have
made grants in respect of adequate protection of signal cabins.
The provision of shelters is selfexplanatory. The grants are in respect
of shelters for persons employed in
factories and commercial buildings. As
Members know under Civil Defence the
provision of shelters is compulsory in
respect of factories and commercial buildings where shelters have to be made for
the employees. The purchase of material
for the erection of domestic shelters takes
up a vote of £25,000. Those are the
only items I think on which I can
properly comment. I would have liked
to have given a comprehensive survey of
the whole work if possible, but in the
circumstances I think it is not necessary.
I will be happy to give any information.
that is in my power.
Mr. BEATTIE: If I was silent it
would be taken that I agreed that no
criticism should be given on matters of
importance. I am not agreed. It is not
my intention to go into questions such as
we are considering, because if I did I
would have to set out the pros and cons of
my argument and it would be heard on
the wireless within a night or two from
the noted announcer who comes on the
air. I reserve to myself the right when
I feel disposed to open out on any particular matter. I do
not agree to
speeches in Parliament being curtailed.
It is not within anybody's right to curtail them. I could give a full survey of
everything on the Estimate, but if I did
that I might endanger others as well as
myself. Therefore, I am going to
refrain from doing anything of the sort
on this one occasion. If things improve
as they are doing at the moment I do
not think the occasion will ever arise. I
have been looking into the matters
mentioned by the Parliamentary Secretary and they are moving satisfactorily.
They are by no means altogether satisfactory yet, but they are moving in that
direction. If things do not improve as
fast as I like, perhaps I may have to
come here and ask for an explanation.
I am satisfied, however, that the services
given under this heading are progressing
as fast as it is possible to move.

MUNICIPAL PENSIONS.
1. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state when
the promised Bill enabling the Belfast
Corporation to pay pensions to municipal
employees on the wages list will be introduced.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am sorry that I
cannot, at the moment, say whether the
proposed Superannuation Bill will be introduced during the present emergency.
As the hon. Member is aware the time of
Parliament is at present fully occupied
with legislation of a war-time character
and other measures of a less urgent nature
have had to be postponed.
Mr. BYRNE: I would like to say in
reply to the right hon. Gentleman that
this matter has been negotiated for the
last three or four years-
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member for
Falls must put his remarks in the form
of a question. He can ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether he is aware.
Mr. BYRNE: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman to give us some hope that this
Bill will be introduced in the present
session.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have every
sympathy with the object to which the
hon. Gentleman has directed my mind,
but it has not been altogether the fault of
the Government that legislation has not
been introduced prior to this, because in
introducing measures of this kind we try
to bring the local authorities with us. I
can assure the hon. Member that I do not
close the door by any means, but I do not
wish him to press the matter at the
moment. It has not been lost sight of.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the

House an assurance that a general measure
for the superannuation of local government employees will be introduced in this
session of Parliament in view of the
urgency of that measure to apply to old
people hanging on for the purpose of
getting a pension under the scheme.

will be introduce the Bill when the
officials vote for it themselves?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not quite
follow.
Mr. NIXON: I ask the Minister to
introduce the Bill when the officials themselves vote for it.

MEDICAL TREATMENT OF
EVACUATED PERSONS.
3. Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether
any arrangements, and if so what
arrangements, have been made for the
medical treatment of evacuated persons,
should such evacuation become necessary.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Detailed
arrangements have not yet been completed and the hon. Member will
appreciate the difficulty of doing so
before the numbers which may be sent
to each locality can be closely estimated.
For any immediate emergency institutional treatment will be provided in
the hospitals in the same way as if the
evacuated persons requiring it were
actual casualties and this is being taken
into account in the Emergency Hospital
Scheme; domiciliary treatment will in
similar circumstances be provided by the
dispensary and district nursing services
for those who do not require treatment in
hospital. It is not contemplated that
these services should bear this burden
indefinitely and steps are being taken to
supplement them. A considerable number of candidates for the Civil Nursing
Reserve are being specially trained in
district nursing and the best means of
augmenting the medical services is under
investigation and will, I hope, be settled
satisfactorily very soon.
Mr. BROWN: Arising out of the
Minister's reference to medical treatment of these children after they are
evacuated, I would like to ask if the
Minister will give an assurance that these
children will be medically examined
before they are evacuated, So that
children suffering from disease will not
be sent to disease-free homes as has happened across the Channel?

Sir DAWSON BATES: Since the
Commissioners of the Belfast Union were
appointed in March last 2,072 applications for outdoor relief have been
granted and 392 applications have been
refused.

circumstances.

(Sir Basi! Brooke): According to official

being taken to

TREATMENT OF CONTAMINATED
CLOTHING.
9. Major HALL-THOMPSON asked
the Prime Minister what steps have been
taken to provide adequate treatment for
contaminated clothing in cases of gas
attack.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Trials carried out with the co-operation of the British Launderers' Research
Association have established that the
decontamination of clothing and underwear can be carried out by ordinary
laundry processes, subject to certain
precautions, and the Ministry is in touch.
with the local Launderers' Association
inviting their assistance in the matter.
As regards the decontamination of protective clothing and equipment, ordinary
laundry processes and machinery are not
so suitable, and local authorities will
make their own arrangements; suitable
boiling tanks, an adequate supply of hot
water and drying space are the main
requirements.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: I regret
to say I did not hear all the reply. I

in communication with the local

with contaminated clothing?

consideration at the present time by the

you.

the people. However they may be
criticised on other grounds, I do not
think that any criticism of the Government can properly be levelled on the
ground of any penuriousness or stinginess
in
connection with the air-raid precautionary services or civil defence. If
any case in which any deficiency is due
to lack of money is brought to my notice
I shall bring it before the Minister. I
do not think there will be any difficulty
in regard to any of the services from the
financial aspect.
In regard to equipment, it is coming
in much better. There was a time when
equipment could not be got, but it is
coming in much better now. The House
will understand why I am not giving
particulars, but I hope from now on as
far as equipment is concerned there will
be a continuous improvement.
I would like to see all these air-raid
wardens and other people giving
voluntary service treated with great
generosity, but this air-raid precautions
service in this country and in Great
Britain in its essence is a voluntary
service. It has been found in Great
Britain that the extension of the paid
service has tended to destroy the
voluntary service. It is quite obvious to
anybody who reads the papers that
throughout the whole country there is a
tendency now to get back as far as
possible to a voluntary basis. We have
tried in this country to keep it on that,
and I think we have succeeded rather
better than in England. That is not due
in any way to a reluctance to pay the
money, but because we feel that the
service is better as a voluntary service
than as a service in which 15 per cent.
of the people are paid and 85 per cent.
are unpaid.
Mr. BEATTIE: On a point of explanation. I hope the hon. and learned
Gentleman did not understand from my
remarks that I was criticising the Government for not being generous financially. I think I made it quite clear
that they were very generous and that
it was the local authorities who were not
spending the money.
Mr. WARNOCK: In my remarks on
the financial aspect I was replying to the
hon. Member for Falls (Mr. Byrne).
Mr. NIXON: The Parliamentary Secretary said the Government were very
generous in regard to spending in connection with this matter. I know it is
very difficult for the Government to
satisfy all the people, or even half the
people, because if they are over-generous
they are charged with reckless spending.
Sometimes the people who would charge
them with reckless spending would be the
first to charge them with neglecting their
duty by not spending more. I stand for
wise spending. You can spend a lot of
money and have very little.
Take the air-raid shelters that we see
here and there. about the centre of the
city. I would like to know what they
cost. I do not want to state where they
are, but they are certainly not where
the people. are. Were tenders received
for them? And in the event of an air
raid how many people would they accommodate ? I do not want to criticise the
Government because this is a case in
which I could criticise, them if I wanted
no matter what they did. I only want
to criticise where I believe I am doing
some good. Take an air-raid shelter in
the centre of the city holding 50 or 100
people.. If anything happened whoever
was near it and was able to run would
be in it in about half a minute, whilst
those who could not run could not get
into it, but would crowd outside it.
There would be ten outside trying to get
in for every one inside.. If a bomb was
dropped the people outside. would get the
contents.
I do not want to be taken as advocating the putting up of a great many airraid shelters. I do not care. whether that
2347 Supplementary Estimates-

24 OCTOBER 1939
Housing Bill
pleases people or not. I am prepared to
take my chance if a bomb comes, and
there is no shelter within two miles of
where. I live. I am very much afraid
this is money you will never see.
I am
also afraid these shelters are costing 100
per cent. more than they should cost. I
know that if the Government and the
Corporation did not put up something
they would never hear the end of the
criticism.
Many of those gentlemen who have.
been appointed wardens-I do not care
twopence whether this pleases them or not
-away at the back of their heads visualise themselves in permanent jobs. They
get restive and trouble people, including
myself. If you gave a job to everyone
who wants one you would bankrupt the
State in no time. I know at the same
time there are many voluntary workers.
The job was advertised as voluntary from
the start, and anyone who does not want
to take it up on that basis should stop at
home. If he wants a paid job and is of
military age, I know where he could get
one. Some of them are only trying to
work themselves into positions in the
A.R.P. service in order to be in a sort of
funk-hole during the war. Much the
same thing happened during the last war.
There was some sort of body-I only refer
to this to show how money was wastedcalled Home Defence. They were supposed to be protecting the shipyards, but
I was for many months at the shipyards
at night time, and they were only a
nuisance. They interfered with workmen
and halted them when they had no right
to do so. One of them got a swim on my
recommendation.
A great many of these people do more
harm than good. They are only in it so
that they will not have to join up. I
want them to be watched by the Government. I cannot say the Government
could have done a lot more. They could
have squandered more, but I do not
want them to squander because as sure as
we are all here there will be a day of
reckoning for every penny over-spent.
Although I may be a bit out of place I
wish to say that I am well satisfied with
the progress of the war, and I am not a
person who takes an optimistic view without grounds for doing so. We will see
this thing through, but keep your hand
on your purse as tight as you can because
it will be useful yet.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
Teachers' Salaries and Superannuation
(War Service) [Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session To make provision with
respect to the war service of teachers and
of officers and servants in training
colleges and for purposes connected therewith' it is expedient to authorise the
payment out of moneys provided by
Parliament of any increase attributable
to the passing of the said Act of the present Session in the sums so payable under
Section seventy-five of the Education Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923."-(Governor's
recommendation signified-The Minister
of Labour.)
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): The additional
charge on public moneys which may be
expected to accrue as a result of this
Resolution are in respect of:-
(1) The payment of the salaries of
teachers acting as substitutes for those
public elementary teachers who join up
for war service. There will, of course,
be a saving on the salaries of the
absent teachers to the extent that the
teachers' pay which they receive while
away will be abated by the amount of
their military pay. The present calculation of the net additional charge is
£2,000 per annum;
(2) The payment to the various
managing authorities of the incremental portion (or proportion thereof)
of the salaries of secondary, technical
and other classes of teachers, who join
up;
(3) The payment of increments for
war service of teachers who return to
teaching service and of trainees who
take up teaching service after the war.
The total cost to the Exchequer will,
of course, depend upon the numbers of
teachers who join His Majesty's Forces
and the war pay which they receive.
beg to move.

I think it is quite obvious that the
secondary and technical full-time, teacher
is in a completely different category from
the public elementary school teacher
under this Bill. It is true that neither
the secondary nor the technical nor
public elementary school teacher is employed by the State, but the public
elementary school teacher is paid by the

liability of the State, and if the State
were to recognise any other liability, as

the Second Reading and as the hon.
Member for Pottinger has said to-day,

cremental liability-our sole liabilitythat the State proposes to act very

I
Take the case of a teacher who joins
the forces when his salary is £300.
think that case was cited by the hon. and
gallant Member on the last occasion when
he spoke. This £300 is made up of £210
basic salary and £90 increment. If the
teacher were drawing £100 war pay and
the governing body proposed to bring him
up to civil pay they would pay him £200.
Our considered proportion of contribution
towards this would be £60, but under the
Bill we may have power to pay the full
£90 to the governors should their finances
appear to require it. This would leave
the governors with something in hand
towards a substitute teacher. I can give
even a better case showing the generosity
of the Government. Take a teacher who
serves in his school's O.T.C., where he
becomes a captain or a major. His civil
pay is, say, £390-£210 basic and £180
increment. His war pay is £380, so that
the governing body need only pay him
£10. Nevertheless if the circumstances
of the school so requires-and it is to the
circumstances of the schools we are looking the Ministry may pay as much as
£180. It seems to me this would go a
very long way towards providing the
salary of a first-class substitute.
Those are two instances of what I maintain is the generosity which the Ministry
may exercise under this Bill. If the
teacher is unmarried the governors may
not consider it necessary to pay the full
salary, but if we think it advisable for
the good of the school, looking to the
question of finances, we may still pay the
full increment. It is quite true, as I
think the hon. and gallant Member said,
that teachers who join now, unless they
have been in the O.T.C., will be required
to join as privates, but I think we can

On one hand, as I have said, there is a

what class of the community they belong.
to slow starvation.
I submit that it is utterly indefensible.
Nothing is calculated to give greater

dark waters of the North Sea, who are

Guardians.

was a time of peace. The blast of war

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Local Government Staffs (War Service)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The main purpose
of this Bill is to provide that local
authorities may be in a position to ensure that any of their employees undertaking war service shall not be any worse
off on that account. In the first place,
it enables local authorities to pay to, or
on behalf of, any of their employees
undertaking war service the balance of
their civil pay, that is to say, if an employee's remuneration from war service is
less than what he would have received
had he remained in the service of the
local authority, the local authority
may pay the difference to him or on his
behalf to his dependants.
In the second place, it preserves the
superannuation rights of any employees
who were serving in a superannuable
capacity, and provides that the period
of war service of an employee will be
aggregated for superannuation purposes
and reckoned in the same manner as
service in his civil capacity. The Bill
will apply to all persons or bodies of
persons who receive or expend the proceeds of any local rate, but may be
extended by the Ministry to any other
public body.
The Bill does not apply to teachers,
as they have been dealt with in a
separate Bill. I do not think it is
necessary to say anything more. The
Bill is self explanatory. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill
be now read a Second time."

have this Bill passed. That is the first
point, because it is only within recent
hours that I have read in the newspaper
about representations being made for the
provision of financial assistance to those
who have joined up and that resolution
has been turned down. So I would like to
know the number of local authorities who
have asked that this Bill be introduced to
give them an opportunity to make up the
difference in pay between military and
civil. I cannot object to it.

Unemployment Insurance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
are now
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The Bill which we
considering can rightly be described as at
peace-time measure, and the necessity for
it rests on the fact that Great Britain
passed a similar measure in July of this
year. The Bill deals with some important issues as well as a number of minor
matters, which I propose to put before
the House. One of the principal
objects of the Bill is to give effect to
recommendations of the Unemployment
Statutory Committee with regard to
holidays, suspension of work, continuity
and benefit to adult dependants. As the
question of holidays is referred to in
several Clauses of the Bill, I think it
necessary to offer some explanation. The
word "holiday" has not been used in any
previous Unemployment Acts, but
decisions have been given, both here and
in Great Britain, on what is known as
customary or recognised holidays, and
holidays of this kind have always been
decided for unemployment benefit purposes by the umpire. But the spread of
the movement for holidays with pay has
increased the number and variety of
holidays which cannot be classed as
customary or recognised, and this undoubtedly has given rise to complications
and anomalies in their treatment for the
purpose of unemployment insurance.
In the report submitted by the Unemployment Insurance Statutory Committee
their main recommendation was that insured persons on holiday should not be
treated as unemployed, and that power
should be taken by the Minister of
Labour, by regulations, to define holidays
and to make the necessary exception for
persons to whom the holiday comes, not
as a break in employment, but in the
course of unemployment. As an accompaniment to this proposal, the Committee
recommended an extension within which
a fresh waiting period should not be required. These facts will doubtless convince the hon. Members of the necessity
to make perfectly plain the need for
drawing a distinction between holidays
and unemployment. That distinction is
shown in sub-section 1 of Clause 1, where
it states:
"An insured contributor shall not
2391 Unemployment Insurance Bill 25 OCTOBER 1939

Second Reading
be deemed to be unemployed for the
purposes of the principal Act on any
day on which he is on holiday."
The Bill provides that days of holiday
are not to be treated as days of unemployment for unemployment insurance
purposes. At the same time it gives the
Ministry of Labour power to define by
regulations the circumstances in which
insured persons are to be regarded as
being on holiday for the purposes both
of unemployment and of health insurance. It gives a similar power for
dealing with the allied questions of
whether remuneration has been received
in respect of the holiday, and whether
insurance contributions are payable for
the holiday period. Through the operation of these powers it should be possible
to put the insurance position of holidays
on a sound and equitable basis, and so
remove the present difficulties and inequalities which are being experienced in
dealing with benefit claims covering
holiday periods.
In some instances firms have continued
to make payments to their workers while
suspended or unemployed. These payments are a bar to the receipt of unemployment benefit and also raise the question of liability to pay insurance contributions. The present law may create
hardship in cases of this kind, and
Clause 2 provides that if the payments
comply with conditions laid down in
Regulations made by
made by the Ministry,
benefit rights will not be disturbed, or

Two important concessions to insured
persons are contained in Clauses 3 and 4.
At present continuous periods of unemployment separated by a gap of not more
than 10 weeks can be linked up to form
a continuous period of unemployment,
and so avoid the necessity for serving
another waiting period. Under Clause 3
the gap is extended from 10 to 20 weeks.
Days of holiday are also to be regarded
as non-existent in calculating continuous
periods of unemployment, and they cannot be taken into account for continuity.
The second concession is contained in
Clause 4. The classes of adult dependants
for whom dependants' benefit may be.
claimed are extended to include, under
certain conditions, a grown-up daughter
or sister who is living with the claimant
and who is wholly or mainly maintained
by him. This concession is accompanied
by a relaxation in favour of female adult
dependants who provide not more than
one lodger with accommodation, but not
with board. The provision of accommodation of this kind is at present a bar to
the payment of dependants' benefit, and
this bar the Clause proposes to remove.
The Clauses to which I have referred
deal with the more important changes
contemplated by the Bill, but I should
like to make a special reference to Clause
15, under which long hirings in agriculture will cease to attract rebates of agricultural insurance contributions at the
end of twelve months from the date on
which this Bill becomes law. Both
here and in Great Britain it has been
found that the administrative cost of
giving the rebates appreciably exceeds
the amount of the rebates themselves.
Our experience has shown that the £170
paid out in rebates over a year cost £200
in administration, and taking into
account the small amount involved in rebates, I do not think that the continuance of the scheme can be justified.
In addition to the Clauses which I have
already mentioned there is a number of
other Clauses in the Bill which deal with
matters of minor importance. I am sure
the House would not desire me at this
stage to go into each one in detail. It
may be sufficient if I refer briefly to
some of them.
Clause 6 widens the powers of the
Ministry to deal with applications for
supplementary schemes. Clause 7 fixes
the date from which contributions may
be credited for school attendance after
age 14 as the date of the 14th birthday.
Clause 8 empowers local education
authorities to pay travelling expenses to
persons attending authorised courses.
Clause 9 authorises the Ministry to make
payments to juveniles attending courses.
for persons under the age of 18. Clauses
10, 11 and 13 bring unemployment insurance law into line with health insurance
practice. Clause 12 will enable the
Ministry to make with Great Britain, on
a wider basis, a reciprocity agreement
for unemployment insurance. Finally,
Clause 14 enables certain persons, otherwise excepted, to be brought into unemployment insurance.
To sum up, the Bill aims at placing
unemployment insurance in relation to

APPOINTMENT OF ASSISTANT
PRINCIPALS.
The following question stood upon the
Order Paper:
1. Mr BROWN.-To ask the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
number of young men together with their
names and addresses who have been
brought over from Great Britain within
the past three months and given appointments as Assistant Principals in the
Northern Ireland Civil Service, and to
what Ministries they have been assigned;
whether through coming to Ulster these
young men have escaped military conscription; whether they were among those
who sat for an examination held in
London for the administrative grade in
the British Civil Service but were not
successful in securing appointments;
whether there are any young men in
Northern Ireland capable of holding
these appointments; whether he can state
who made these selections and appointments; and whether considering the cost
and inconvenience involved in attending
these examinations in London steps will
be taken to hold similar examinations in
Belfast which shall be open to all candidates in the United Kingdom.
Mr. BROWN: With your permission
I desire that question No. 1 should be
allowed to remain over for the present.
GAS MASKS FOR HILLSBOROUGH.
2. Mr. MAGINESS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
certain persons in the employment of the
Government residence at Hillsborough,
County Down, have been supplied with
gas masks, and upon what date were these
supplied; whether the other residents of
Hillsborough have not yet been supplied
with gas masks, and, if so, upon what
basis has the distinction been made; and
whether he will guarantee that all the inhabitants of Hillsborough will be supplied in the near future, and whether in
future all the residents of a particular
area will be supplied with gas masks at
the same. time without distinction.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The answer to the
first part of the hon. Member's question
is in the affirmative. Respirators to the
number of twenty-seven were issued to
Government House last month. It is necessary for many members of the establishment at Hillsborough to come to the
city on frequent occasions, and it was for
this reason that respirators were issued.
It is not possible at present to say when at
future issue of respirators will be made.
Mr. BROWN: Might I ask the
Minister to give some indication as to
when the provincial areas in general will
receive gas masks as there is considerable
uneasiness?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I see no sign
of it.
RENT RESTRICTION.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the Rent and Mortgage Interest Restrictions Act has been extended to bring into
control all houses in Great Britain up to
£100 valuation to the extent that 98 per
cent. of the housing accommodation, including all new houses which have been
built, are now controlled, and whether
he will extend the Northern Ireland Act
to include all houses, old and new, on a
similar valuation to prevent profiteering
in rents, and give the same protection to
the tenants in Northern Ireland as is extended in Great Britain.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that the Rent Restrictions Acts have been
extended by an Act passed recently by
the Imperial Parliament. The question
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
of introducing similar legislation in this
House is at present receiving consideration, and I hope to announce the Government's intentions at a later date. The
matter is one of extreme difficulty and it
is necessary to have regard to hardships
that may arise on either side.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman is the Government prepared at the earliest possible
date to introduce a similar measure and
especially is it prepared to concentrate
on Section 2 and Section 3 (1) for Northern Ireland as being all important for
the protection of people both in businesses
and in dwelling-houses?.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot at
this stage say any more as to the intentions of the Government, but I have told
the hon. Member I will be able later on
to state what the intentions of the
Government are.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Will the right hon.
Gentleman recognise the principle that
tenants in Northern Ireland are entitled
to equal protection with tenants in Great
Britain the same protection as across the
water?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government has always given the same protection here as other tenants get.
TRANSPORT BOARD'S PURCHASE
OF HORSES.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if the
Transport Board have recently purchased horses and lorries for the carriage
of merchandise in the city of Belfast;
and whether the Board is now in competition with carriers in the city whose
business has not been acquired by the
Board.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
that the Transport Board when taking
over the road transport undertaking of
Messrs. W. W. Kennedy & Company
acquired the portion of the firm's
business which related to the carriage of
merchandise in Belfast, and which was
inseparable from the undertaking which
the Board was obliged to acquire.
Under this arrangement the Board
obtained 17 horses, and is now engaged
in the carrying business in Belfast, but
only to the extent to which Messrs.
Kennedy formerly carried.
PETROL SUPPLIES FOR
FARMERS.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
farmers in South Down, Mourne, and
other parts of Northern Ireland are
unable to obtain sufficient quantities of
petrol to keep their threshers and
tractors going, and that the supplies
they are receiving are being obtained
only after long delay; whether petrol
for such work in Great Britain is exempt
from any rationing restrictions, and if
so whether he can state why a similar
policy is not being carried out in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware that farmers in South Down, or
in any other part of Northern Ireland,
are unable to obtain sufficient quantities
of petrol to keep their threshers and
tractors going, and no complaint has
been made to the petroleum officer or
to my Department which would indicate
that such is the case. The remainder of
the question, therefore, does not arise.
Mr. BROWN: If I give the Minister
the names and addresses of the persons
concerned will he see that they get the
required amounts of petrol?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure if
the hon. Gentleman gives the information to the petroleum officer he will
attend to it. I would remind the House
that this is entirely under the control of
the Board of Trade in England
and beyond providing the staff and
accommodation we have no control over
the matter.

Scheme, the number of these new books
that have been re-lodged at the different

for the week ending 25th October, 1939,
and the number of persons who are still
in employment on the Rationing
Scheme.

EMPLOYMENT OF ALIENS IN
BELFAST.
8. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether it is a fact that aliens
are employed by Messrs. Goorwitch in
their making-up factory in Belfast, and,
if so, under what privilege are these
aliens allowed to be employed; and
whether it is a fact that the Aliens Act
prohibits any aliens taking up employment in Northern Ireland or Great
Britain.
Mr. GORDON: The answer to the
first part of the question is in the
affirmative. As regards the second part
of the question, the employment of
aliens is governed by the provisions of
the Aliens Acts and Order. Under
these provisions, prior to the outbreak
of hostilities, aliens were permitted to
enter employment in Great Britain or
Northern Ireland, subject to the production of a permit in writing issued to
the employer by the Minister of Labour
in Great Britain. The aliens in question, ten in number, were permitted to
enter this employment for the purpose of
assisting in the establishment of a new
industry which has already provided
work for 160 of our own people.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the Provisional
Order issued as to the employment of
aliens is only for the purpose of giving
training for a definite period, and in
view of that fact will he now make a
provision whereby our own workers who
are unemployed can take up this employment in the firm mentioned?
Mr. GORDON: I should like to say
that two of these people engaged in the
work are in a skilled or key position in
the industry, and it is as a result of the
training they are able to give the workpeople engaged that we are able to carry
on that new industry.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister not
aware that some of our own local people,
who are highly efficient for carrying out
this work, are the most important in |
this new industry established by this
firm?
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Gentleman
can rest assured I will not lose sight of
that.
FOOD OFFICE STAFF IN
ENNISKILLEN.
9. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state how the
clerical staff at Enniskillen has been
recruited in the urban and rural districts
for the food rationing scheme; how
many persons were appointed and the
number employed through the medium
of the labour exchange; whether it is a
fact that one ex-head constable, one expostmaster, and one inland revenue
official are employed who are in receipt
of handsome pensions; and whether
these persons were signing at the labour
exchange before being employed.
Mr. GORDON: I am informed that
the entire clerical staff of the food
executive officer for the Enniskillen
urban district was recruited through the
employment exchange, while in the case
of the rural district this method of
recruitment was adopted as far as practicable. The staff originally appointed
for the two offices numbered 13, of
whom nine were recruited through the
employment exchange.
Of the three officers referred to by the
hon. Member as in receipt of pensions,
I am informed that one-the ex-head
constable was registered at the employment exchange, and owing to experience
gained on food control work in the last
war was selected as deputy food
executive officer for the urban district.
The ex-inland revenue official referred
to was appointed food executive officer
for the urban district as the town clerk,
owing to indisposition, was unable to
undertake duties in connection with
food control. This appointment was
made by the Ministry of Food upon the
nomination of the Urban District
Council. The ex-postmaster referred to
is employed as deputy food officer for
the rural district. I have been given to
understand that no other person with
the requisite qualifications was available.
I may add that substantial reductions
have subsequently been made in the
staffs of these two offices.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister
aware that the vice-chairman of the
Rural Council Food Control Commitee,
Mr. Coulter, who is a large farmer, has
his boy of 15 years of age acting as

OLD-AGE PENSIONS.
10. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware of the
growing poverty amongst old-age pensioners in Northern Ireland owing to the
increased cost of living; and whether he
is prepared to increase all pensions on a
cost-of-living scale so as to prevent hardships amongst this class in the Six
Counties.
Mr. GORDON: For reasons of which
the hon. Member and the House are
aware, it would not be advisable to introduce legislation to increase the rate of
pension in advance of corresponding legislation in Great Britain. Cost of living
is no doubt a factor which will be taken
into account when the question of an
increase is under consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman not aware that the cost of
living is due to the war, and is it not
also a fact that any increase in the cost
of the social services during the war
period will be compensated for by Great
Britain? In view of the heavy increased
cost of living to old-age pensioners here
will he concede that amount of increase
to all these pensioners seeing that the
amount will be recouped by the British
Exchequer ?
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's statement that it would not
be wise to legislate on this question in
advance of Great Britain, will the right
hon. Gentleman see that pensioners are
brought up to the same standard as pensioners in Great Britain by getting as
much from another source as will bring
the pension up to £1 a week? Is the
Minister aware that in England although
the pensioner, as the Minister correctly
states, only gets 10s a week, yet he also
gets 10s from outdoor relief or whatever
you like to call it, which brings him up
to £1 a week? Will the Minister bring
the pensioners here in line with those in
Great Britain in accordance with his own
suggestion?
Mr. GORDON: The old-age pensioners
in Northern Ireland are in line with those
in Great Britain as far as Government
pensions are concerned. The hon. Gentleman has raised a question dealing with
another authority. I have no power to
deal with a national matter.

SLAUGHTER OF PIGS.
11. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether it is in the interests of farmers that pigs should be
slaughtered at the weight of 1 cwt. when
they are capable of being fed economically
to greater weights; whether he is aware
that the curers are getting too many pigs
of this weight owing to the increased
fixed price given for them; whether the
curers are offering bonuses to pig producers to induce them to feed their pigs
up to 2 cwt. before slaughter, and
whether this practice would stop if the
price was raised to the English level for
all pigs.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The present prices for
pigs in Northern Ireland fixed by order
of the Minister of Food show a difference
of 4-5s per cwt. between the price of carcases under 170 lb. dead weight and over
that figure but under 200 lb. This difference is similar to that which has always
prevailed in Northern Ireland between
Wiltshire pigs and roll and ham pigs. In
fact the price differential has been as
much as 6s per cwt. in the past. I am
not aware of the payment of bonuses such
as the hon. Member suggests, but I am
satisfied that the existing differences in
prices are necessary in order to maintain
a balance between the Wiltshire bacon
trade and the roll and ham bacon trade
in Northern Ireland.
It is not desirable at the present time
that farmers should be encouraged to
market pigs at heavy weights as would
be the case if the same prices were paid
for all carcases up to 200 lb. dead weight
as suggested.
It is not a fact that curers are getting
too many pigs of light weight.

PIG AND CATTLE RATIONS.
Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware of the
fact that those merchants in provincial
towns and rural districts who have

installed mechanical mixers for the
purpose of supplying their customers
with pig and cattle rations have been
refused any share of the available meals,
and that the mixing and providing of
suitable rations for pigs and cattle has
been, and is being, confined entirely to
the millers; whether he is aware of the
fact that the price arranged for the pig
mixture has been based on a wrong idea
of costs and that any merchant who
would be provided with the same
material for this mixture would be able
to put this on the market at a price at
least one pound per ton less than the
present fixed price.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I greatly
regret that there is at present a definite
necessity to conserve supplies of imported
feeding stuffs to the greatest extent possible. For this reason my Ministry has
asked all provender millers to discontinue for the present the sale of straight
feeding stuffs and to sell only certain
emergency rations. There has
quently been a temporary interruption in
the release of straight meals and feeding
stuffs to country merchants, but, much as
I regret it, I am satisfied as to the necessity for this action at this juncture.
conse-

the hon. Member's question, the prices
prescribed in the Feeding Stuffs (Maximum Prices) Order made, by the Minister
of Food and applicable to the whole of
the United Kingdom are maximum ones
and not fixed prices, as he mistakenly
suggests. There is nothing to prevent
any merchant in Northern Ireland selling the feeding stuffs specified in the
Order at less than the maximum prices
prescribed therein.
