jobs in an indirect way should be compelled to go through the Labour Exchange before they are regarded as
qualified to take up that work. It is
not too late to do that.
I made inquiries as to what happened
in Great Britain, and I found that a
very high percentage of the labour required was obtained through the Labour
Exchange. A small percentage of key
men was recruited indirectly, under the
Chief Executive of food, who could not
obtain that class of labour through the
Exchange. You know the position in
Northern Ireland. We have singers,
acrobats, comedians, people of every
description who never were in industry,
and who never knew what a Labour
Exchange really was, in jobs that should
have been filled through the Exchange.
That applies to people domiciled in Belfast, Londonderry, Fermanagh, indeed
throughout Northern Ireland. The
majority of these people are of independent means; they do not need to
work. Are they going to sit in comfort
at the expense of the hundreds signing
at the Labour Exchange?
I say that that state of affairs should
not exist. I hope the Government will
see that it is not allowed to continue, and
will call upon the Minister responsible
in London to reorganise the staff of the
Food Councils that now exist in Northern
Ireland. I believe that representations
of that kind will receive sympathetic
consideration. Investigations made in
Scotland are receiving sympathetic consideration, and I believe an application from Northern Ireland will be
given the same consideration.

Mr. MAGINESS: The question I had
put down on the Order Paper to-day and
which was not reached related to
matter which is troubling a great many
people in Northern Ireland at the
present time. The Minister of Agriculture has called upon the farmers of
Northern Ireland to plough some 250,000
additional acres. That is a tremendous
undertaking, but one on which the farmers
of Northern Ireland are most anxious
to engage. They know, as everybody
knows, that food production at home is
essential. They know that every ton of
food produced at home is worth one or
two tons produced from abroad, and consequently it is essential that the land
should be ploughed and the seed sown.
But as
the Minister of Agriculture
knows, with the possible exception of
last year, less and less land in Northern
Ireland was being put under plough.
The farmers were for the most part
devoting their attention to the livestock
industry with the result that when they
are called upon to make an additional
effort they have not got the wherewithal
to make it.
I do not wish to raise the point to
embarrass the Minister in any way. I
merely wish to raise it to see if I cannot
help both the Ministry and the farmers
in this matter. Two hundred and fifty
thousand acres are required to be
ploughed. There was a scheme put up
by the Minister by which a number of
tractors would be imported into this

I have made inquiries as to how many

90 tractors brought into this country

evident, I think, that with this relatively
small number of tractors there can be
nothing like the number of acres put
under plough which the Minister
requires. Draft horses in the country
are scarce compared with what they used
to be, and consequently it is essential if
this acreage is to be put under plough

not only the tractors but the implements.
which go with the tractors-ploughs
cultivators and so on.

the
Regarding the Cattle Order,
Minister in reply to me spoke of Northern Ireland sharing the same war-time
limitations and restrictions as rule across
the Channel. None of us can quarrel
with that, but if we share the same wartime restrictions and limitations we should
at the same time share some of the
prosperity that the war has brought to
industry across the Channel. We are not
doing that. The Government here should
say to the Imperial Government that we
are prepared to play our part not only
in regard to the 7s 6d income-tax and in
various other ways but industrially as
well.
Our great firms are prepared to play
their part more than they are allowed
to at the present time, and I suggest
it is the duty of the Government to tell
the British authorities that we are prepared to play our part industrially if
they would give us a chance of doing so.
It is very strange to me that we have not
a single munition factory in Northern
Ireland. I have never got a satisfactory
answer to my questions as to why that is
so. Surely in the matter of these motor
tractors we have enough engineers to
assemble them in Northern Ireland.
What is to prevent them from sending
these parts here and expediting their
delivery in the manner very properly
suggested by the Member for Iveagh?
Now, in regard to what the Minister
has said about war-time restrictions and
limitations in Northern Ireland and
across the Channel, there is one matter
in which the Government instead of
keeping step by step have gone one step
ahead. In the announcement made some
time ago that golf clubs would be compelled to comply with the terms of the
Compulsory Tillage Order, they went a
step ahead of England because there is
no such compulsion there. It should be
remembered that the golf clubs in Northern Ireland have admitted members of
the fighting forces as honorary members.
They play a certain part in maintaining
the moral both of the civilian population
and of the fighting forces.
In view of those facts and also of the
fact that a great deal of the land of these
golf courses is not arable land and would
not produce crops in any great degree,
that the many thousands of pounds spent
in improvements would be absolutely lost,
and that thousands would have to be
spent after the war to restore the courses
so that golf could be played, the Minister
should make it clear that the position in
Northern Ireland will be the same as
that in Great Britain, namely, that it
will be optional for these clubs to till

Minister will be able to give an assurance

in

responsibility and independent jurisdiction vested in them, or is the ultimate

to give some assistance to hon. Members
in these matters which are of real and
pressing importance at the present time.
Mr. SPEAKER: The question that
the hon. and learned Member for
Central has quite rightly raised is a
difficult one, namely, how far this House
can discuss matters which are really
within the province of the Imperial
Parliament but in respect of which our
Ministries are asked to act as agents, to
a certain extent, for the Imperial Parliament. The hon. and learned Member
for Iveagh referred specifically to the
question of tillage. With regard to that
matter it is perfectly clear that it is
entirely in the hands of the Ministry of
Agriculture. As regards the other
matters-food control and so on, they are
definitely Imperial and should be raised
as questions. That is the exact and
technical position. In SO far as a
Minister is able to arrange the
Ministerial details I think this House has
a right to question him on those points,
but not to debate them. There is an
essential difference in that.
What I propose to do is to consider
this matter very carefully and give a
considered ruling. It will be a written
ruling which I shall very carefully consider, and I hope that will give the
House some guidance as to how to
proceed in these difficult matters.

Mr. MINFORD: I rise to support the

Tillage in Northern Ireland

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I will deal,
first of all, with the question raised by
the Member for South Down regarding
the ploughing up of golf courses.
agree with his contention. We have gone
into this matter to see whether it is of
any value to plough up golf courses, and
there are so many difficulties in the way
-shallow drains and removing bunkersthat it would not be worth while applying the Order to golf courses. I should
like to say that the golfing society and all
golf clubs have shown the greatest anxiety
to do everything they can to help us.
When we went into the matter it was
found to be impracticable and would be
a waste of time and labour.
I will now deal with the other question which is a most important one and
which has been receiving the attention
of myself and my Ministry's officials
ever since war broke out. The question
has been raised by the hon. and
gallant Member for Iveagh, whom I
congratulate on his new position. What
he says is perfectly true. The farmers
in this country are prepared and willing
to do their share and more than their
share in regard to producing food, but
unless they can get proper equipment for
that work obviously they cannot carry
it out. The position is this.
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries on
the other side is in charge of the
distribution of tractors, and
so far
The
Northern Ireland has not succeeded in
getting the number of tractors that are
required and that we should have. We
have actually got some ninety tractors
and ploughs. I could get another sixty
tractors without ploughs, but that obviously
is a mere flea-bite seeing that we are
looking for 1,400 tractors in order to
plough the 250,000 acres in Northern
Ireland.
It is only right to state that if we
cannot get ploughs, difficulties will be
placed in the way and we cannot expect
the farmers in Northern Ireland to carry
out the Tillage Order. If this happens
I shall amend the Order at any stage so
that they will not be compelled by law
to do what is expected. My Ministry
have most carefully set out the methods
by which we intend to do the work, and
also the machinery required. If we
cannot get the machinery the farmers can
rest assured that the Order will be
amended in such a way that they will
not be compelled to do an impossibility.
Mr. BROWN: Could we not assemble
the tractors here?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: That is a
business matter which may come up in
the future. I would be very glad if
such a thing could be done. The hon.
and gallant Member for Iveagh raised
the question of the Ford-Ferguson
tractor. I happen to own one myself,
and it is a very suitable tractor for the
small fields in this country. I am given
to understand that there are a sufficient
number available in America and that it
would be possible to get them were it
not for the pound and dollar position.
Each purchase made in America has an
effect on the £ at the present moment,
and the Government at Westminster are
naturally watching the position very
carefully.
I should like to inform the House that
I took steps recently which may overcome
this very difficult problem. The hon.
and gallant Member was also correct in
saying that the Ford-Ferguson tractorit is now being made at Messrs. Ford's
in America—is considerably cheaper than
the Fordson which was made at
Dagenham. It is also in every way more
suitable for the small fields here. I
want the House to know that the anxiety
which they feel is shared by myself to a
very marked degree, and that every effort
will be made by myself and my Ministry
to see that the proper implements are
supplied so that the farmers will have
straw with which to make bricks.
The hon. Member for Falls (Mr.
Byrne) raised the question of the small
farmers. An arrangement which we have
in mind at present-it is now beginning
to work-is that certain farmers will
buy these tractors on what I might call
the hire-purchase system. When they
get them they will, during the period
of the emergency, be compelled to plough
100 acres either of their own or another
farmer's land. If they do not do so the
Ministry has power to remove the
Adjournment-
Purchase of Tractors
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
ploughs. The hon. Member need have
no fears in regard to the small farmers
because there will be plenty of tractors
available to do the work if I get what I
want. In addition to that scheme we
intend to have a few travelling circuses
in each county to fill in the gaps where
there are not sufficient ploughs to do the
work. Therefore, the small farmer will
be looked after, and the hon. Member
need have no fear in that respect.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Minford) raised the question of the
dairy farmer. That is a more difficult
point. I will explain it in this way.
Each farmer will have a tillage order
served upon him to plough ten per cent.
over and above the acreage he ploughed
in 1939. He must have one fifth of his
arable area under the plough, but in no
case need he have more than 50 per cent.
of his holding under the plough. That
is the first consideration. The question
in regard to the dairy farmer is a very
long one, but I will try to make my
reply as short as possible. The argument
has been put forward that the whole of
the acreage of the dairy farmer is being
grazed, and that if he is compelled to
plough the ground he will have to reduce
the number of his cattle. The dairy
farmer should remember that probably
we may be about 25 per cent. short of
animal rations next year and, therefore,
unless he is prepared to grow his own
stuff there will be that shortage of
rations. I think the best solution of the
problem-I am not saying it is the
actual solution-of rations is for the
dairy farmer, if he lives near Belfast,
to comply with the Tillage Order by
hiring a sufficient acreage on some
other farm. He could keep his own
grazing which he required immediately
and hire land for tillage in another place.
That could be arranged quite easily.
The general organisation which we
intend to set up in the Ministry will include an organising officer in each county
and area, and then if a farmer wishes to
appeal against the Tillage Order he will
be visited by an officer and the matter
can be discussed.

PIG INDUSTRY COUNCIL.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
date of the last meeting of the Pig
Industry Council; whether this Council
is still in being, and if so, what are its
present functions since the price of pigs
is now fixed by the Minister of Food;
whether the chairman, Sir Dudley
McCorkell, is drawing his salary and
travelling expenses or other allowance,
and whether he will state the gross
amount of salary, expenses, and other
allowances of all kinds drawn by Sir
Dudley McCorkell since the Pig Industry
Council was created up to the present
date.
a
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The last meeting of
the Pig Industry Council took place on
September 20th.
is
The Council
statutory body established under the
provisions of the Agricultural Marketing
(Pig Industry) (Northern Ireland) Act,
1934. Apart from fixing prices for pigs,
a function which it will not in future
exercise, its duties include advising and
reporting to my Ministry on the granting of bacon curers' licences and on the
production, marketing and grading of
pigs and bacon, the development of agricultural education and research connected
with the production of pigs and bacon,
and such other matters as may be
referred to the Council by my Department.
The total amout of salary and travelling
expenses drawn by the chairman since
the Council was established have been-
Salary, £1,066 13s 4d; expenses, £33
15s 9d. There have been 54 meetings of
the Council proper during this period in
addition to 14 special or committee
meetings.
I may add that I am satisfied that this
remuneration has been fully warranted,
and I would remind the hon. Member
that it covers not simply attendance at
meetings of the Council but a considerable volume of other work in connection
with the business of this body.
Mr. NIXON: Would it not be better

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Agricultural Returns Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It
interest the House to know that agricultural statistics in Ireland have a long
history behind them. They were first
brought in during the time of the famine
in 1847, when, naturally, the food
question was one of very great importance, and it is rather interesting
that we now, very nearly a century later,
should be discussing this question of
statistical returns when the question of
the food supply is of equal importance.
Since 1847 there has only been a break
of three years in the collection of
statistics in agricultural matters and that
was during the period of the last war.
During the whole of this period the
agricultural community and every farmer
has come, to expect the visit from the
police or other officers who enumerate
and gather together the necessary
statistics.
I would like at this time to say how
much I and my Ministry appreciate the
willingness with which all farmers have
given that information, which, of course.
is invaluable. The information has
been treated as a matter of confidence
and our attitude, has been upheld in our
courts of law. Under war conditions
however the position is slightly different.
In view of the Tillage Order which has
been made it will be necessary to have
certain information to use in the event
of that order not being carried out. The
first Clause of the Bill deals with the
making of returns which will in future
be placed upon a statutory basis, as
has been the case in Great Britain since
1925. These returns will continue to be
treated in confidence in exactly the same
degree as they have been treated in the
past.
Under Clause 2, however, it is provided that during the present emergency
2467 Agricultural Returns Bill-

1 NOVEMBER 1939
Second Reading
the returns may be used at the discretion of the Ministry in connection
with the increase or maintenance of
production of food by means of agriculture, and particularly so as to facilitate
the proper distribution of agricultural
machinery, implements, seeds and fertilisers and feeding stuffs. I am confident
the House will recognise the need for
information regarding every detail of our
agricultural production being available
at the present time. Accordingly, I
commend the Measure to the approval of
the House. I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. ELLIOTT: In connection with
agricultural returns, I should like to
have heard from the Minister the
necessity for this Bill. First of all, I
would like to know if this is a war emergency Bill. If it is a Bill that is going
to do anything to help us win the war
I will be all out for it, but I think unless
the Minister can show us that there is
really some necessity for it we ought not
to have any further legislation dealing
with agricultural returns, or make it any
more impossible for farmers to carry on
at the present time. We have already
furnished returns to the Ministry. We
have the census returns, and in addition
we have very often other returns to make
out. They are supposed to be sent in in
confidence to the Ministry, but unfortunately these confidential returns are
not always confidential. That is by the
way. I cannot see for the life of me how
any farmer is going to carry on if this
Bill is put on the Statute Book. I do
not see how he can keep all the returns
suggested in this Bill.
At the present time we have under the
Ministry of Agriculture a great number
of statisticians who are dealing with
agricultural returns. If we are going to
have more agricultural returns I would
like to know from the Minister are we
going to have an increased number of
statisticians and officials in the Ministry
to deal with these returns. If you refer
to the Bill you will see Clause 1 sets out
that returns must be furnished to the
Ministry in relation to (a) the utilisation
of the land, and (b) the acreage of the
several crops on the land and the acreage
of the land used for grazing and for
other prescribed purposes. Every farmer
will require to make out a proper return.
He will require an ordnance survey map
of his farm to be able to furnish minutely
his returns to the Ministry. On the
other hand, if the farmer furnishes returns
which are not correct the Ministry may
come down on him for furnishing false
returns. I do not blame them for that,
but I think it is absurd that these returns which are made from time to time
should be thrown into the wastepaper
basket in the end. They are very irksome and troublesome to the agricultural
community at the present time to make
out. Then we are asked to furnish the
numbers of live stock and poultry on the
land. As everyone knows if a farmer has
a pig farm he may have 20 pigs more
to-morrow than he has to-day. If I
furnish my returns to-day and show the
number of pigs on the farm and the
inspector comes round in two or three
days he may find 20 or 30 more. I have
to convince him that the pigs arrived at
the farm the day after the returns were
sent in. If I do not convince him I can
be indicted, because I did not make out
a proper return. It is the same with
poultry.
I cannot for the life of me see that all
these returns and queries are necessary
at the present time. If the Minister
states that it is for the purpose of helping
to win the war I will withdraw my opposition to the Bill. I want to know is the
Bill introduced only to win the war. Is
it going to be a war measure, which will
be brought to an end when the war is
over? Then we have to furnish returns
of the numbers of persons working on the
land. We have had these returns furnished to the Ministry. I have the police.
sergeant coming to me periodically asking
for these returns. He inquires whether
they are men or maid servants, men or
boys, the wages being paid and the hours
of working, and on top of that we are
going to have further returns to make
out. It would take any farmer who is
engaged in mixed farming to have a
statistician and bookkeeper doing nothing
else but making out returns. Then we
have to furnish "the nature and extent
of the agricultural produce obtained from
the land during such past period as may
be prescribed." It does not set out what
is wanted. We have no idea what is
going to be prescribed. I for one think
this is uncalled for and it would be better

so that in the event of a prosecution the
farmer can be convicted out of his own
mouth on evidence that the Act compelled
him to give. The Minister of Agriculture
attempted the same thing in another Bill
in this House, and I am glad to say that
the Senate turned it down. That is the
principle that the learned Attorney-
General wants introduced in this Bill
against, I say it advisedly, the most lawabiding section of the community, a
section of the community that on the
authority of the Minister of Agriculture
has for a generation voluntarily given
any information that was required.
The Attorney-General said that if I
had been prosecuting under the old tillage
orders I would have expected to have
evidence like this by which I could compel
the accused to give information to convict
himself. Not at all, I would not have
been allowed to do that, and I can tell
you that unless our judges are prevented
by Act of Parliament they are just as
good now as they were then. I should
like to see myself going into court and
putting evidence before a judge that the
accused was compelled to give. I would
not be long in the court; I would not be
long in the force, and I would not be a
pensioner now. But the Attorney-
General wants that principle put into an
Act of Parliament. That is the gist and
the substance and the point of his speech,
and it is absolutely contrary to and cuts
across British law.
What are you to do when you charge
a man with an offence?
The man is
cautioned that he is not bound to say
anything, but that anything he does say
will be taken down in writing and may
be used in evidence against him. The
Attorney-General wants to get out of all
that. This is the thin end of the wedge.
The Attorney-General wants to put a
form into the hands of the farmers and
to compel them to fill up that form and
to sign it. Then if there is any question
of a prosecution you can go in and lay
down that evidence before the court and
that is to be conclusive. I am surprised
that any man with a legal mind-for
you generally get fair play from men
with legal minds-should come in here
and make any such suggestion or proposal. I could understand it if you were
dealing with a secret organisation or
2485 Agricultural Returns Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Nixon]
something that was trying to create
trouble in the State, but the farming
community, I say again, is the most
law-abiding section of the community,
and that statement cannot be contradicted.
I was working amongst the farmers
for years and years and the biggest
crime they ever committed was keeping
a dog without a licence or some trivial
thing like that. But here you want to
make criminals of them, and the Attorney-
General uses his position and persuasive
powers in that direction. We know what
will happen to the Bill in this House,
but we do not know what will happen
to it in the Senate. I had the privilege
of sitting on a Committee with Members
of the Senate, and I must pay a great
tribute to them, particularly to those who
might be called the aristocracy. That is
where, so far as I can see, you get true
liberty in Northern Ireland. That is my
experience, and I must bear testimony
to it.
I would ask hon. Members-they are
quite competent to think for themselves
not to be carried away by the Attorney-
General. Do not give a vote to compel a
farmer to do what the greatest criminal
in the land is not compelled to do. No
man is compelled to open his mouth if a
charge is to be preferred against him, but
the Attorney-General wishes that the
farmers should have to do so. The
Attorney-General, the Minister of Agriculture, or the Minister of Finance, did
not tell us how a similar order to the
Tillage Order was enforced during the
last war. It was enforced without any
difficulty. There is a great incentive to
farmers to give information. Do they
not get a certain subsidy for their tillage.

Essential Buildings and Plant (Repair of
War Damage) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time.'
is
Mr. ANDREWS: Hon. Members will
no doubt have observed that this Bill
bears a close resemblance to the Housing
Bill introduced by my right hon. Friend
the Minister of Home Affairs and read
a Second time in this House on Tuesday,
10th October. That Bill provided for
the repair of dwelling-houses rendered
unfit for habitation through war damage:
this Bill seeks to make similar provision
for the repair of other classes of buildthe maintenance
ings
of which
essential to the welfare of the community
as a whole, and for the repair or replacement of essential plant in like circumstances. As to whether a lan is to be
made will be, in the first place, for the
appropriate Ministry to decide, subject
to the approval of the Ministry of
Finance. The appropriate Ministry, in
each case, will be the Ministry concerned
with the purposes for which the building
is used or the undertaking is carried on.
Loans will be made available under the
Bill irrespective of whether the buildings
concerned are owned by local authorities
or privately, but in the latter event loans
will only be available if the owner is
willing, but unable without financial
assistance, to have the necessary work
carried out.
A loan to a private owner may, in the
first instance, be made by the local
authority of the district where the property is situated, and that authority may,
in turn, obtain a loan for an equivalent
amount from the appropriate Ministry.
For buildings to come within the scope of
the measure they must have been rendered
wholly or partly incapable of use for their
normal purpose through war damage, and
this normal purpose must be one regarded
as essential to the welfare of the civil
population. The buildings must, moreover, be capable of being repaired at a
reasonable cost, and repair must be
essential owing to the scarcity of other
buildings suited to a like purpose. Loans
for the reinstatement of essential plant
will be made available under similar conditions.
Broadly speaking, the Bill seeks to
ensure that essential buildings and plant
will not remain out of action as the result
of war damage, and the community be so
deprived of the uses which such buildings
or plant represent. The necessary loans
will be secured by a mortgage or debenture or floating charge according to the
circumstances of the case.
I feel that this measure is not a very
controversial one, and I hope it will
meet with the approval of hon. Members
on both sides of the House. I beg to
move.
Question, "That the Bill be now read
a Second time," put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for Tuesday next.

A.R.P. AT STORMONT CASTLE.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether it is a fact that the
only part of Stormont Castle occupied by
the officials on Air-Raid Precautions
and Civil Defence is the servants'
quarters on the top flat; whether he can
give any reasons why the lower accommodation in the castle is not being made
use of, and whether it is a fact that the
British Government is paying for the
full accommodation of Stormont Castle.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): It is a fact that the top floor
of Stormont Castle is now being utilised
for staff purposes; also a considerable
portion of the ground floor is in the
occupation of the Cabinet Secretariat.
The question of utilising the remainder
of the castle to the best advantage is
being carefully considered.
In reply to the last part of the
question, I would refer the hon. Member
to my Budget statement on 11th October
last, in which it was made clear that
approved excess expenditure on transferred services above a certain figure
would be recouped by the British
Government.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
portion of the castle was at the disposal
of the Cabinet Secretariat and the remainder at the disposal of the Prime
Minister. Now that the Prime Minister
is residing at the seaside will the right
hon. Gentleman see that the officials of
A.R.P. are housed in a decent respectable way, and allocate the other portion
of the castle which is more suitable for
staffing purposes to those people who are
compelled to occupy little garrets at the
present moment?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have already said
that the matter is being arranged, and
I am pleased to add that the staff will
be comfortably provided for.
Mr. BEATTIE: I accept the right
hon. Gentleman's assurance if he carries
out the transfer from the top garrets to
respectable rooms in the building at the
earliest possible date.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am not prepared
to give any guarantee at the moment as
to what arrangement will be made,
beyond saying that such arrangements
will be carried out as will be acceptable
to the staff.
Mr. BEATTIE: Thank you.

em-
Mr. GORDON: I have been asked by
the noble Lord, the Prime Minister, to
reply to this question.
Careful consideration has been given
to the question of setting up a body
similar to the British Advisory Council,
but it is felt that such a Council would
tend to overlap and duplicate the work
of existing committees which cover a
wide range of activities.
Connected with my own Ministry there
are 19 local employment committees and
9 unemployment assistance committees.
representing employers and workers and
other interests, and the number may be
increased by the establishment of committees contemplated in the Control of
Employment Bill, which was recently
passed by this House.
It will be realised that these committees are representative of employers
and workers. Furthermore, as the hon.
Member is aware, every interest in our
compact community has ready and direct.
access to Parliament, and we are prolonging our Session to facilitate Members in bringing forward any matter
which they desire to be considered
urgently.
In the opinion of the Government.
these existing channels of communication enable all sections of our people to
find rapid and adequate expression for
their views.
UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG DEEP
SEA WORKERS.
11. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware that the
dislocation of traffic due to the war has
resulted in acute unemployment among
deep sea dockers, and a surplus of employment across the Channel; and
whether he is prepared to make arrangements for the interchangeability of
labour, and thus save the unemployment
funds from the severe drain which is put
upon them by such serious unemployment amongst these deep sea dockers.
Mr. GORDON: Employment for deep
sea dockers both here and in Great
Britain has been affected by war conditions, and there is at present no demand
in Great Britain for the services of
Northern Ireland dockers who are unemployed.
As the hon. Member is aware, arrangements have already been made in Great
Britain to meet any temporary shortage
of dock workers at a particular port by
the transfer of workers from neighbouring ports; but should a demand arise for
the services of Northern Ireland dockers
my Department will be glad to facilitate the transfer of dockers who desire
to take up employment in Great Britain.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The price the

in the

Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to raise a
matter and I want to be as careful as
I can in regard to it. Last week I
referred to the provision of materials for
the A.R.P. wardens in the city of Belfast.
Since then I have been taking a deep
interest in the matter and tried to see
how far it was possible to accommodate
this voluntary labour. I went round
several of the posts. I want to tell the
Parliamentary Secretary that I am sadly
disappointed to think that the Belfast
Corporation have refused to receive representations at the A.R.P. station in
Academy Street. I am also disappointed
to learn that men who are out all night
in order to give the greatest possible
assistance to the citizens should be refused
the materials necessary for carrying out
their duties.
I feel that this matter must be dealt
with by this House. If the Belfast
Corporation are made a grant of money
for the carrying out of certain work in
connection with protection from attack
from the air they cannot hold up that
necessary work. I have a very serious
complaint to make regarding my own
district, which is a danger zone. I ask
any Member of the House to come with
me round this area. If he does so he will
be shocked and horrified at the conditions
some of the men and women are working
under. It is very trying to them to carry
out their duties. I am satisfied the
Corporation have the money and all the
assistance they require from this House,
and so I would like the Parliamentary
Secretary to make inquiries in order to
find why the work is not being carried
out by the Corporation.
A few days ago a notice was placed on the
door of the premises in Academy Street
stating, "No visitors allowed." What did
that mean? It meant you could not make
any representations to that department in
regard to any complaint you wished to
lodge in connection with air-raid protection. I feel this matter has to be more
extensively ventilated in this House than
it has been up to the present. If the
area I represent is not going to get
more consideration than it has got in the
past I will ask the Parliamentary Secretary to take a note of what I say and see
that that area has at least the materials
necessary to enable the voluntary workers
to carry out their duties.

actual position in regard to equipment in

has been and will be no reluctance on

we have not withheld money for any

service that can be called essential, and
I am not aware of any criticism made by

Mr. BEATTIE: Might I ask the
Parliamentary Secretary whether he will
make inquiries as to what the Belfast
Corporation are doing with all this
equipment the Government has supplied
to them, and will he see that the Belfast
Corporation does not neglect the workers

--at least those in the danger zone.
Mr. BYRNE: I have had many complaints from those who are giving voluntary service in connection with A.R.P.
They say that after working all day they
go out at night and travel about the
streets looking for lights, and they
receive no remuneration whatever. From
what I have been told they will not
continue to do this work unless they are
remunerated in some way. I have heard
them say they do not even get a cup of
tea. I would ask the Parliamentary
Secretary to give these people some consideration or they will not continue to
carry out these duties. Yesterday I
heard a man say he could not continue to
carry on this service and attend to his
work. I know these people will not go
on carrying out these duties unless their
services are acknowledged.
Mr. WARNOCK (by leave of the
House): If the hon. Member thinks
there is any lack of appreciation on the
part of the Government or the Belfast
Corporation in estimating the services
given by voluntary workers under A.R.P.
I can assure him he is greatly mistaken.
It is, I think, one of the finest features
of this service that it is purely voluntary.
I believe it will be a success because of its
voluntary character. As I stated when
this question was raised before, I believe
the introduction of payment for this
service would ruin the whole A.R.P.
scheme. I believe it will be a success in
so far as it is voluntary, and in that
I think the members of the Belfast
Corporation are entirely at one with the
Government. We discussed this matter at
considerable length with the Lord Mayor,
the Town Clerk, and officials of the
Ministry, and we came to the conclusion
that this matter is better left on an unpaid basis as far as possible.
In England, when the crisis arose in
September, the A.R.P. service was, to a
considerable extent, put on a paid basis,
but it was found that twenty per cent.
of the people were paid, and that caused
the greatest discontent amongst the other
eighty per cent. The burden of paying
for this service in this country would
amount to several hundred thousand
pounds a year in Belfast alone. I believe
that if we commence to pay those engaged
in A.R.P. work we will destroy the
service. I am convinced we will continue
to get the service from the people of
Belfast on a voluntary basis. I acknowledge with gratitude the services which
they have given, and I am sure I am
speaking on behalf of the whole Government on this matter when I say that
these services are very highly appreciated
indeed.

LOANS FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE
PURPOSES.
Mr. THOMPSON (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Finance whether
his attention has been called to the introduction by the Chancellor of the
Exchequer in the House of Commons
yesterday of a National Loans Bill, and
whether any steps are contemplated here
in order to assist in raising money for
National Defence purposes.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): This Government is, of
course, prepared to fully co-operate with
the British Chancellor in every possible
way to assist in raising funds for
National Defence purposes, and, as a
first step, it has been decided to set up
a representative Committee to be called
the Ulster Savings Committee for
National Defence purposes. His Grace
the Governor has graciously consented to
be patron, and the Lord Chief Justice
has very kindly agreed to act as chairman. The initial meeting of this Committee will be held to-morrow, when the
whole position will be explored. There
is already in existence in Great Britain
the National Savings Committee, which
has carried on actively since its establishment during the last war, and this
central committee operates through the
medium of the local committees which
function throughout the country.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask is the
right hon. Gentleman prepared to inform
the House of the names of the members
of this Committee that he has appointed
for National Loans?
Mr. ANDREWS: No. I have already
told the hon. Member that it will be
fully representative.
Mr. BEATTIE: I ask you are you
prepared to give the names of those
already appointed? Are they political
parasites of your own party?
Mr. ANDREWS: You will find that
out to-morrow. It is not my intention
to disclose the names to-day.
Responsibility for Emergency Matters.
Mr. CAMPBELL: On a point of
order. May I renew my request to you
of yesterday week for a ruling as to
whether matters relating to Government
control of food, petrol, tillage, et cetera,
can be raised in the present emergency
by question or debate in this House, and
whether Ministers have any responsibility
to this House in these matters, and if they
have the extent of such responsibility?
Mr. SPEAKER: In reply to the hon.
and learned Member for the Central
Division of the County Borough of
Belfast, I have carefully looked into the
question as to
to the procedure to be
followed by this Parliament in dealing
with questions arising out of the present
War Emergency legislation, and now I
give my considered ruling:
It is clear that the Emergency Powers
(Defence) Act, 1939, makes provision for
the defence of the Realm, and in so doing
Northern Ireland.
applies to
The
Defence Regulations are made under that
Act and any Regulation, whether or not
it applies to Northern Ireland, must be
laid before the Imperial Parliament as
soon as may be after it is made, and
either House of that Parliament can by
resolution annul a Regulation within the
next twenty-eight sitting days after the
Regulation is laid before it. For these
Regulations, therefore, the primary and
the ultimate responsibility rests with the
Imperial authorities who are directly responsible to the Imperial Parliament.
In the House of Commons of that
Parliament there are members who
are returned to represent constituencies
in Northern Ireland, and, generally
speaking, it is through them that
Northern Ireland questions on Imperial
2515 Appropriation Bill-

8 NOVEMBER 1939
Third Reading
and reserved matters should be brought
before the House or the Imperial
authorities, as the case may require.
It is obvious that it would be out of
order to criticise in debate the policy of
the Imperial Government, but in my
judgment it would be in order—
(a) to put down questions asking for
information from Ministers who
are the heads of Northern Ireland
Departments acting as agents of
Imperial Departments,
(b) to put down substantive motions
asking the Government of Northern
Ireland to make representations to
the Imperial Government on any
particular matter arising out of
orders and regulations made under
the Defence of the Realm Act or
other War Emergency legislation
passed by the Imperial Parliament.

Liability for War Damage (Miscellaneous
Provisions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): This is another
of those measures necessitated by the
present emergency, which, I am sure,
hon. Members will regard as entirely noncontentious in character. It deals with
goods that are the subject of what is
called a bailment. Bailment has been
defined by a distinguished authority as
"a delivery of goods, on a condition expressed or implied, that they shall be
2525 Buildings (War Damage) Bill HOUSE OF COMMONS
Agricultural Returns Bill- 2526
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
restored by the bailee to the bailor as
soon as the purpose for which they were
bailed shall be answered." The circumstances in which goods may be the subject
of a bailment are very varied. They may,
for example, merely be deposited with a
friend to keep, or lent to him for use, or
let out on hire. They may be left in the
custody of a warehouseman or entrusted
to a carrier to convey a distance, or to an
agent to sell. The common underlying
principle, however, is that the property
in such goods can belong to one party
only, even though the goods may be in
the possession of another; in other words,
possession without ownership, such as
goods on approval for sale or return.
The aim of the Bill is to relieve the
bailee of liability for goods in his possession which suffer loss or damage as a
result of war. Should any of the
clauses not be clear to hon. Members I
shall be glad to give any information
required during the Committee stage. I
should perhaps add that this Bill is based
on a corresponding enactment passed by
the Imperial Parliament, which gave
statutory effect to the recommendations of
the Committee on Liability for War
Damage, which reported on this problem
early in September last. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for Tuesday next.

SCHOOL-LEAVING AGE.
2. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she is aware that
great hardship is being caused to many
parents owing to the fact that children
who have attained the school-leaving age
of 14 are not allowed to leave school until
the end of the term and whether she will
take steps to see that children are
permitted to leave school when they are
14 years of age in all cases when they
have obtained or are promised employment.
Mrs. PARKER: Whilst parents may
occasionally suffer some inconvenience, I
am not aware that there is any general
hardship in the matter referred to.
The Education Acts give power to the
education authority to make by-laws for
prescribing two or more dates in each
year as the dates for terminating compulsory school attendance and a child is
deemed to attain the age of fourteen on
the prescribed date next succeeding the
fourteenth anniversary of his birth. The
selection of the dates is a matter for the
education authority and the Ministry has
no power to interfere. There is nothing
in the Education Acts to empower either
the Ministry or the education authority
to grant exemption from school attendance before the prescribed date is reached
on the ground that the child has obtained
or is promised employment.
Mr. THOMPSON: If I give the Parliamentary Secretary the name of a
widow mother whose child became 14
years of age on 2nd October last and who
had already got a position and had to
give it up on account of the ruling of
the authority will she look into the
matter?

that great hardship is often inflicted
upon parents-people who have very
little income-when they have succeeded
in
getting appointments for their
children, and because they cannot leave
school for two or three months those
positions are lost? Great hardship is
inflicted upon parents.

authority and the Ministry has
has no
power to interfere. I think that answers
all three hon. Gentlemen who have
spoken. I am aware, as I said, that
some inconvenience is necessarily caused

£2 PER ACRE SUBSIDY.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if
in the case of conacre or other lettings of
land the £2 per acre subsidy for ploughing up of grass land will be payable to
the owner of such land or to the person
taking it for the season.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I would refer
the hon. Member to the provisions of Subsection (1) of Section 29 of the Agricultural Development Act, 1939.
The ploughing grant is payable to the
person at whose expense the land has
been ploughed up and brought into a
state of cleanliness and fertility for the
sowing of an approved crop.
In the case of land let in conacre the
person renting it will normally be entitled
to claim for the grant if that person
performs all the necessary cultivation,
including ploughing. In some instances,
however, the owner has had the grass land
ploughed up at his expense prior to
letting it to another person who has
carried out the subsequent cultivations.
In these cases it is provided that the grant
shall be divided amongst the persons concerned in such proportions as the Minister
of Agriculture and Fisheries may direct.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister
consider increasing the amount in the
case of persons who will have to work on
Sundays in ploughing up the land in
accordance with a recent pronouncement?
HIRING LAND FOR TILLAGE.
5. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether if a dairy farmer
follows the advice given by the Minister
in the House on Tuesday, 31st October,
of hiring land for tillage from a neighbour, will the ploughing of the land so
hired be taken into consideration in
assessing the liability under the Order of
the neighbour from whom the land was
taken and the area which he has to
plough.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I can best
explain the position, perhaps, by giving
the hon. Member a hypothetical example.
If the neighbour has in all 50 acres of
arable land and lets 10 acres to the
dairy farmer for cultivation the neighbour is still liable under the Tillage
Order to cultivate one-fifth of his total
arable area of 50 acres. He will not
satisfy the Order by tilling one-fifth of
the remaining 40 acres. The letting of
a portion of his land does not relieve
the owner of that land of obligations
under the Order.

PASTEURISATION OF POOLED
MILK.
10. Rev. Professor CORKEY asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether in
the event of milk coming into Belfast for
liquid consumption being pooled he will
consider the expediency of having all
such milk pasteurised so as to prevent the
possibility of widespread epidemics being
caused by milk-borne germs.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The question of pooling the supply of
liquid milk available for the Belfast
market is not under consideration. I see
no reason why the sale of liquid milk in
accordance with the present high
standards of quality laid down under the
Milk and Milk Products Acts should not
continue. The latter part of the hon.
Member's question does not, therefore,
arise.
Mr. NIXON: Is the Minister aware
that many children will not under any
circumstances drink pasteurised milk?
Rev. Professor CORKEY: Is the
Minister aware that undulating fever has
been wiped out in many cities by the
process of pasteurised milk.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think the
milk is so clean in Northern Ireland that
it does not require pasteurisation.

correct. The question of what affords
adequate sustenance for an individual
will, of course, depend upon the particular circumstances of each case-for
example, the age and occupation of the
person in question-and each case is dealt
with in the light of particular information presented to the guardians, and in
these circumstances no useful purpose
would be served by taking the action
suggested.
I would remind the hon. and learned
Member that the Ministry is precluded
by statute from interfering in individual
cases for the purpose of ordering relief.
In other words, the question of the
amount of relief to be given is one for
the board of guardians.
As regards the last part of the question, so far from cuts averaging 25 per
cent. having been made in outdoor relief,
the amounts have been increased
generally by approximately 10 per cent.
on account of the estimated increase in
the cost of living. Reductions have been
made for various reasons in a few cases,
and the Commissioners of the Belfast
Union would be prepared to justify their
action in these cases if the names are
furnished.

Mr.
13. Mr. CAMPBELL (for
Beattie) asked the Minister of Labour
whether he can state if it is
a fact
that twelve labourers signing at the

Islands, Scotland, at the rate of 1s 2d
per hour, and whether, owing to these
men, who have wives and families, refusing to take this work on the conditions offered, they have been disallowed
for six weeks benefit; whether it is a
fact that owing to inclement weather in
this area it is impossible to get full time
employment as no guarantee is given for
a full week's work; and whether he is
prepared to reverse the decision of the

compensation to their wives and families
at home.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I understand that the hon.
Member's question refers to the Strabane
Employment Exchange.
Vacancies in the Orkney Islands were
circulated by the Ministry of Labour
and National Service in Great Britain
for a number of men accustomed to pickand-shovel work. The wages were 1s 2d
an hour for a 66-hour week, the working hours to be reduced to 48 when
enough men had been obtained. Board
and lodging were provided for an
inclusive weekly charge of 21s 6d. Outside work at this time of the year in every
district is liable to interruption from
weather conditions.
The vacancies were offered in the usual
way to suitable men on the register of
the Strabane Exchange, and 77 men
accepted the employment. In addition,
35 volunteers who had heard of the
vacancies asked to be submitted for the
work. On the other hand, 43 benefit
claimants, of whom 26 were married men
and 17 single men, refused the offer.
Their claims were. disallowed by the
insurance officer, and 25 of the men have
since appealed to the court of referees.
As the decision on their claims rests
entirely with the statutory authorities,
it would not be possible for me to interfere in any way with the decisions reached
by those authorities.
My Department is not in a position
to pay special weekly allowances to
married men who are transferred through
the Northern Ireland Employment
Exchanges to work in Great Britain.
Mr. NIXON: Is the. Minister aware
that suitable men in Belfast wanted to
go on this job and were not allowed to
go by the Ministry of Labour? If the
Minister wants the names of the men I
can give them. They live in my constituency.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Execution of Trusts (Emergency
Provisions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
object of this Bill is to empower trustees
and personal representatives and other
persons holding fiduciary positions to delegate the duties of their trusts while they
are on war service. As hon. Members are
aware, it is a broad, general principle of
our law that persons who undertake such
duties as those of trustees or executors
must perform the duties of the office themselves. They must perform the duties
personally; they cannot delegate them to
others. Of course, that principle is a
most admirable and salutary principle in
time of peace, but if it was to be adhered
to strictly in time of war it would be
quite impossible to conduct the due
administration of estates, the due
winding up of estates, and the due
administration of trusts.
In regard to any trust, whether it is
an elaborate or complicated one or is a
small one, duties have to be performed
from time to time which, according to our
existing law, can only be performed by
the trustee or personal representative
personally. Accounts have to be passed,
Execution of Trusts Bill-
14 NOVEMBER 1939
Second Reading
leases have to be made. If a lease has to
be executed by a trustee it has to be
executed by the trustee personally. He
cannot appoint anyone to execute it for
him. In the same way sales and purchases of investments have to be made
from time to time, and when a trustee is
the person concerned he must sign the
transfer document or deed himself.
And so when a considerable portion of
the population is abroad on war service
it obviously becomes necessary that those
of them who occupy the position of
executor or trustee should be enabled to
appoint someone to execute the special
duties for them while they are out of the
country and cannot easily be reached.
The object of this Bill is to enable
such persons as are executors and
trustees while engaged on war service to
appoint someone to carry out their duties
for them.
Hon. Members will be aware that at
an early stage in the last war it was found
necessary to have legislation of this type
passed. A couple of Acts were passed,
I think, during the first year of the last
war on quite the same lines as this Bill
at present before the House. They were
found to be of value, and to have worked
well and to be satisfactory. This Bill is
really on the lines of the two Acts passed
in 1914 and 1915. Of course, during the
last war Acts passed by the United
Kingdom legislature applied equally to
Ireland and to England. Now, of course,
we can legislate for our own Province,
and the English legislation does not apply
to us. The English legislation was passed
into law about a month ago, and this Bill
is substantially on the same lines as the
English Act with the necessary modifications for Northern Ireland.
I do not think hon. Members will wish
me to go through the Bill in detail. It
is essentially technical in its provisions.
The operative provision is really contained
in the first clause of the Bill which enables
trustees, personal representatives, and
tenants for life while they are out of the
country and cannot get back owing to the
war to execute power of attorney appointing some other person to carry out their
duties for them. The following clauses
are really consequential and ancillary to
the provisions made in the first clause to
enable the purposes of the Bill to be
carried out.
It
As I say, this is a technical Bill.
might be called a lawyers' Bill, but if
any Member wishes an explanation as to
any particular provision I shall be very
happy to endeavour to give it to him,
but I think I would be unnecessarily
taking up the time of the House by going
one by one through the separate clauses.
I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. NIXON: I have read through
the Bill and it is undoubtedly necessary.
It is one of the emergency Bills brought
in here that are necessary. As the
Attorney-General has stated, there were
similar Bills passed during the last
war and they were found necessary.
It would be much to the good if the
Government would confine itself to necessary emergency legislation like this Bill,
which we can all support.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.

Mr. CAMPBELL: Before the House
rises this afternoon I wish to direct
attention to a question of administration
on which I feel very keenly indeed.
That is with regard to the reply given by
the Minister of Home Affairs earlier
to-day concerning the question of outdoor relief in rural areas. Some little
time ago I dealt with the question of
outdoor relief in the city of Belfast, and
my remarks this afternoon will apply
almost exclusively to this matter, as it
concerns most of the rural areas in
Northern Ireland.
We are now at the beginning of what
is going to be an exceptionally severe
winter, a winter that may bring very
acute and grievous sorrow to many homes
in this Province, a winter that will
certainly bring distress to the large
majority of homes in this Province, and
a winter that will make demands on the
lives, limbs, and money resources of our
people. The fact that this war is proceeding throughout this winter will mean.
sacrifices from every hearth in Northern
Ireland. It certainly calls and will call
for economy as rigid as it can be
practised, both public and
and private
economy. But the least defensible form
of economy that should be practised in
time of war is economy, either public or
private, at the expense of the very poorest
class.
I do not want to draw any picture in
regard to what their lives are the daily
struggle with its cold and hunger. It is
a struggle of the very keenest kind. At
the same time, although a war is on,
there are a large number of people here.
and elsewhere in these islands who are
living in luxury, and these people hardly
know what outdoor relief means. It is
a mystery to think that it is a thing
that never meets their gaze, or comes
within their ken. This relief at the
most is a very poor pittance, but, poor
and small as it is, it helps to keep
together the body and soul of people
who are driven to the starvation level.
It is a question of life, and death for
them.
""
Here, according to the information I

if not the majority, of local authorities,
that outdoor relief is doled out with a

the expression
meagre hand," but I
think I am speaking within the bounds.
of moderation when I say it is doled out
with a most frugal hand, and being so
doled out it falls very hard on large
numbers of the respectable poor. In the
case of others I am told that outdoor
relief is being reduced.

same thing? What is wrong? We have
a Government, we have full control, and
yet the figures presented here to-day
show that the boards of guardians, even
with their 10 per cent. increase on the
sum of 5s per week, are
not very
generous.
It is terrible to think that charitable
bodies should be burdened with the care
of those who unfortunately are poor. It
is not the duty of charitable institutions,
which serve a very useful purpose, to do
so. They carry on a job which has been
neglected by the Government. The
Government have sat watching, but yet
have never interfered in regard to the
treatment of those in receipt of outdoor
relief. Surely the Government are
anxious to see a generous amount given
to those in need. If the poor-law
authorities in Great Britain are given
full power to provide a decent standard
of living, why should the Northern
Government not seek and find information as to the treatment meted out to the
recipients of outdoor relief in this area?
I have often spoken on this matter in
this House and in my own constituency.
The conditions that prevail and the
amounts paid under the Newry Board of
Guardians should be a matter for serious
investigation. We cannot minimise the
fact that poverty prevails. It may be
said that local authorities have the right
to deal with these matters in their own
way. We feel that the poor-law authorities are not dealing justly with these
unfortunate people. If a person is poor
why should he be deprived of sufficient
means to give him food, clothing and
shelter? There is one thing the Northern
Government could not guarantee under
existing conditions-they could not do so
even before the war-that the working
classes, particularly those affected by
unemployment, are guaranteed food,
clothing and shelter.
We should realise that the local
authorities in Great Britain set an
example for us to follow. If they spend
large sums for the. relief of poverty it
is only right that the Northern Government should do likewise. We are told
that the war is being carried on for the
cause of freedom. If that be so, then
the removal of poverty and its disabilities
is as big a job for the Northern Government. If the Government leave those.
affected by unemployment at the mercy
of the poor-law authorities all I can say
is that serious hardships and poverty will
prevail. Surely the Northern Government will not allow that state of affairs
to continue.
Mr. MINFORD: I rise to take part

When he came out of hospital he was

of guardians, and they gave. him the
magnificent sum of 10s.
I want to impress upon the Minister
of Home Affairs that he should make a
searching investigation into this case of
a man, in the year 1939, when the cost
of living is high, being doled out 10s a
week to maintain himself and his wife
and five children, and to pay a house
rent of 4s 6d a week, leaving him 5s 6d
a week to eke out an existence. I am

guardians, because it
it has been the

an old-age

Northern

I will give one case as an illustration.
A man and his wife had a shop of the

They were not able to pay their way.
They got a small shop on the Woodstock
Road, and I helped them to get it.
would say it is as cheap a shop with

-I am not sure about it myself and I

Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard
to the questions raised in the House this
afternoon may I say at the outset that
I have the greatest possible sympathy for
these poor people who are unable to find
work and who have as a result to go on
the rates. That sympathy, may I say,
has been shown in the most practical way
by this Government since it was formed
some 20 years ago. One has only to turn
to the various Acts passed in regard to
relieving unemployment which I need
hardly mention now, and to the extension
of the poor-law relief system. Hon. Members are well aware that in the earlier
stages of our Parliament workhouses
were quite common in Northern Ireland
and the principle of outdoor relief was
non-existent. Outdoor relief only existed
for the old and infirm. Able-bodied
persons were compelled to go into the
house. Our object has been with these
various Acts to encourage employment,
and to give outdoor relief so as to avoid
the stigma, which I think is an unfair
stigma, of any person having to go into
the body of the house. That policy the
Northern Government has carried on.
It is all very well to talk. It has been
said that money is the root of all evil,
but I do say in regard to relieving unemployment that the absence of money is
one of the biggest evils we have to face.
It is very easy for hon. Members to get
up and say provide more money, let
the Government take over the entire
question of destitution and cut out the
boards of guardians. Well I would be
very slow in a country like this to
advocate the removal and extinction of
the boards of guardians, because after all
somebody has got to pay the cost of
destitution. Is it to be the taxpayer or
the ratepayer? I venture to say that the
local authorities, boards of guardians,
who know the needs of the locality, are
in a very much better position to
investigate the various cases that come
before them than a body of civil servants,
no matter how good they may be, set
up at Stormont.
have
I am glad to see that the hon. and
learned Member has been good enough to
admit to-day that the Belfast Commissioners, who take the place for the
time being of the guardians,
increased the allowances to the ablebodied people who seek relief. In his
question the hon. and learned Member
stated that the commissioners had
reduced the allowance by 25 per cent.
I would remind him that instead of
reducing it by 25 per cent. they have
increased it by 10 per cent. May I just
give one or two figures to show the scale
which the boards of guardians act on as
a general principle. In some cases they
give more and in other cases less, but
this is the general average. Take the
case of a man and woman with four
children; they get relief to the extent of
33s a week. A married man and his wife
get 22s a week. The scale ranges up to
something like 40s a week.
These are facts. The House must
realise that there is bound to be a certain
amount of fraud in life. There are
claimants coming up again and again to
the Commissioners in Belfast-and the
same thing applies to other towns-who
have not done any work or attempted to
do any work for five or six years. They
do not show the slightest inclination to
work. There must be a limit to this.
After all somebody has got to pay. The
ratepayers have to a certain extent to be
considered. It is perfectly true that in
Unemployment Relief Schemes 2572
Adjournment-

the country areas the scale is perhaps
less than in Belfast, but taking it on an

week. That is not what I would call a
generous amount or even an adequate

Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I do not
justify it. After all the Government
under the present law cannot directly
interfere with the scale of relief meted

of guardians was that the auditor would

Member for Woodvale mentioned the

class.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I will only
deal with it as far as my Ministry is concerned. It does not mean because a man
has a shop which produces nothing for

guardians for outdoor relief.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I hope he will

Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like
the House to realise somebody must take

increase of taxation and rates, and yet

practically suggest that the Government
should maintain on an extravagant scale
all people who cannot find work. We are
a democratic country. Are we going to
turn ourselves into a dictator country or

are not satisfied with the relief given
they can turn their representatives out
and get somebody else. It is suggested
that boards of guardians should be wiped
out and everything with regard to
distress and relief centred at Stormont.
That is not a thing I would advocate
at all.

public.

Wednesday, 15th November, 1939.

Agricultural Wages (Regulation) Bill.
Order for consideration of Senate's
amendments read.
CLAUSE 4 (Holidays and holiday
remuneration):
Senate amendment:
At end of the Clause add the following
sub-section :-
(7) For the purposes of this section
periods of employment with the same.
employer separated by intervals not exceeding in the aggregate eight days in
any period of two months during which
the worker has not been employed by
any other employer shall be deemed to
be continuous employment.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): This new sub-clause
was inserted in another place to meet representations made during the consideration of the Bill in Committee in this
House by, I think, the hon. Member for
Pottinger. The hon. Member suggested
that a farmer might evade his liability to
give a worker one day's holiday with pay
in each period of two months by discharging that worker for one day before the
end of his two months' continuous employment and then re-engaging him. This
amendment is designed to secure the hon.
Member's object as far as is reasonably
possible. It provides that isolated days
of unemployment during any two months'
period shall not debar the worker concerned from receiving one day's holiday
with pay from his employer provided
that these intervals of unemployment do
not aggregate eight days in two months,
and that during all those days the worker
has not been employed by any other
employer. I beg to move, "That this
House do agree with the Senate in the
said amendment."
Amendment agreed to.

Gas Undertakings Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews) This is a short and simple
Bill, of a non-controversial nature, designed to remove two anomalies in the
law affecting gas undertakings. The first
provision of the Bill allows officers of a
gas company constituted under a special
Act of Parliament to be appointed to the
board of directors, and thus brings Northern Ireland into line with practice in
Great Britain. Secondly, the Bill clarifies
the procedure to be followed by local
authorities making application for
statutory powers with regard to the
supply of gas.
It is desirable that its passage should
be expedited in order to facilitate the
internal administrative arrangements of
an important public utility undertaking.
One of the directors of the company is
now serving with the colours, while two
are unable to act owing to illness; and
the powers proposed under the Bill will
enable the manager to be appointed to
the board of the undertaking. I beg to
move.
Question put and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.

PETROL PROSECUTION IN
CO. TYRONE.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
the name, address, and the Electoral
Division for which he sits, of the
Member of the Tyrone County Council
who was prosecuted for the storing of
petrol without a licence, as stated by the
Minister in the House on Tuesday, 7th
instant.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The name of the
member of the licensing authority in
County Tyrone to whom I referred on
the 7th instant, in answering the hon.
Member, is Mr. Adam Dickie,
Dickie, of
Market Square, Dungannon. The
licensing authority concerned is, however,
the Dungannon Urban District Council
(of which Mr. Dickie was a member until
recently) and not the County Council.
apologise to the House for describing the
gentleman as a member of the County
Council rather than of the Urban District
Council.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is the right hon.
Gentleman not aware of the fact that
Mr. Adam Dickie is not a member of
the Dungannon Urban Council?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
said in my answer that he was until recently a member of it-from 1926 to
May 1939, and during that time he was,
of course, responsible along with others
for issuing licences.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is the right hon.
Gentleman now satisfied that no member
of the Tyrone County Council had petrol
stored in any place without a licence?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would point
out that the character of the County
Council has not been depreciated in any
way.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is the right hon.
Gentleman prepared to withdraw the
stigma which he tried to place on the
Tyrone County Council in his answer on
a previous day?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly.
The only difference is that the hon.
Member has transferred the indignity
from the County Council to the Urban
Council.
Mr. ELLIOTT: The Member referred
to is not a member of the Urban Council,
and it is not fair to withdraw the
stigma from the County Council and
place it on the Urban Council.
ACCIDENTS DUE TO BLACK-OUT.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can give the
House the figures showing the numbers
of fatal and other accidents in Northern Ireland due to the "black-out"
regulations.
Sir DAWSON BATES: During the
month of September, 1939, 167 road
accidents occurred; 22 persons were
killed and 185 were injured. During
September, 1938, there were 151
accidents; 7 persons were killed and 157
were injured.
Of the 22 fatal accidents in September
of this year, 8 occurred during the hours
of darkness; 6 of these were attributable
to the "black-out," while in the case of
the remaining two the "black-out" was
in part responsible.
During the month of October, 1939,
151 road accidents occurred; 13 persons
were killed and 169 were injured. During
the same month in 1938 there were 158
accidents; 10 persons were killed and
183 were injured.
Of the 13 fatal accidents last month,
9 occurred during darkness; 6 of these
might be attributed to the "black-out"
regulations, but carelessness was also in
evidence in each case.
Information is not yet available as to
the number of the non-fatal accidents
that can be attributed to the "blackout."
Mr. BROWN: Do I gather that there
is an increase in the figures for October
over those of September?

SUNDAY WORK AND UNEMPLOY-
MENT BENEFIT.
6. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Labour whether unemployment benefit
will be disallowed to a farm labourer who
refuses to work on Sunday and who has
been notified by the Employment Exchange for that work on the application
of a farmer, as it would be disallowed if
he refused to work in similar circumstances on a week-day.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I presume the hon. Member has
in mind workers other than those employed on a seven-day basis.
If a vacancy involving a greater amount
of employment on Sunday than has
hitherto been the normal practice of the
farming industry is offered through the
Employment Exchange to a worker signing the Register, and he considers that
the employment is unsuitable, the matter
at his request would be referred to a
court of referees in order that an impartial decision on his claim might be
obtained. This undoubtedly safeguards
the interest of that class of worker.
SABBATH OBSERVANCE IN RURAL
DISTRICTS.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Prime
Minister whether it is the considered
policy of the Government that farmers
and farm labourers throughout Ulster
ought at once to abandon their traditional
practice of Sabbath observance, and work
the whole seven days of the week.
The PRIME MINISTER: The answer
is in the negative.
SUBSIDY ON 1938 CROP.
8. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether it is a fact that
the Imperial Government has paid the
farmers the full subsidy on the 1938 crop
while the farmers of Northern Ireland
have only been paid fifty per cent.; and
whether the Minister can state the reason
for this delay in Northern Ireland and
give the date when the balance will be
paid.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries have paid the first
and second instalments of the subsidy on
the oats and barley crops harvested in
1938, to which I presume the hon. Member's question refers. Growers in Northern Ireland have been paid the first instalment of this subsidy, and, in regard
to the delay in paying the second instalment, I would refer the hon. Member to
the answer given to the question raised
by the hon. Member for Woodvale on the
25th October last. I may add, however,
that the work entailed in the payment of
the second instalment is being pushed
ahead with all possible speed, and that
these payments will be completed by the
end of the present month.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
CONTROL OF MEAT AND
LIVESTOCK.
9. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can give the

scheme for the control of livestock and
meat in Northern Ireland.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Perhaps the
hon. Member will repeat his question in
a week's time.
Mr. BROWN: Is the Minister aware
that the House is not sitting in a week's
time?

Time Act."

is not brought forward in any spirit of

heretofore we have supported, and will

I start with the Prime Minister's own

was along these lines:-
This Council is strongly of the
opinion that the regulations in regard
to the "black-out" are being enforced
far too stringently in districts like
Warrenpoint which are situated so remotely from vulnerable areas.
While admitting that complete darkness may be essential in areas which
geographically lend themselves to
aerial attack, the Council consider that
a modified scheme should and could be
introduced for many areas such as their
own urban district. When such
vulnerable cities as Paris and Liverpool can enjoy a measure of street
lighting there appears little reason for
the extreme measures which are being
enforced in this district and the
Council urgently requests the Govern
ment to reconsider the instructices
issued in this respect.

At the meeting of the Holywood Urban

We have had two deaths in Holywood

coincide roughly with the lighting-up
period. The original order was that the
black-out period began at sunset and
ended at sunrise. Those representations
were made for a relaxation throughout
•
the whole of the United Kingdom, and I
certainly would not have the sanction of
the Cabinet to make representations to
the Home Office in Great Britain for a
differentiation as between Great Britain
and Northern Ireland. No such representation was made.
Mr. BROWN: But you made representations.
Mr. WARNOCK: The representation
that was made to the Lord Privy Seal
and the Home Office by the Ministry was
that it might be desirable throughout
the entire country, that is the whole of
the United Kingdom, to have an extra
half-hour at either end. That commended
itself to the Imperial authorities and was
done. But when I look at the Order
Paper I find that the hon. Member to-day
wants a differentiation between Great
Britain and Northern Ireland. It is now
perfectly clear that there is no generalised
lighting throughout Great Britain, and
when the hon. Member wants an example
he has to go to the Orkney Islands.
Mr. BROWN: In Great Britain.
Mr. WARNOCK: There is no city
in Great Britain in which there is
generalised lighting. Experiments were
made in Liverpool, as the Prime Minister
read from the answer of the Lord Privy
Seal to the House-there was another
question a little later on to which the
same answer was given-stating that that
system of lighting was not found suitable.
The Lord Privy Seal was not able
at present to hold out any hope
of a special system of street lighting. If any such modification was
introduced here it would mean a
differentiation between this country and
Great Britain. I see he wants to go
hand in hand with Great Britain so far
as petrol is concerned, but in regard to
restrictions we are not to go hand in
hand. I do not think this Government
would agree to adopt that attitude, nor
do I believe it is an attitude that would
be approved by the great majority of the
people of this country. The views expressed by the hon. Members for Antrim
and North Derry were more in accord
with the feelings of the people of this
country than the views expressed by the
hon. Member for South Down.
