Mr. BYRNE: There is a subject of
which I have given notice to the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs. I refer to pensions for
workers in the Belfast Corporation. I
have taken a deep interest in this matter
for the past number of years. Sometime
ago an arrangement
arrived
between representatives of municipal
workers and the Belfast Corporation in
regard to a pension scheme. The Government, I understand, is not in a position
to carry through a measure. As I have
taken a great interest in this subject I
am going to make one or two suggestions.
I should impress upon the Government
the necessity, pending the introduction
of their proposed Bill relating to pensions
of employees in local authorities, of introducing and passing through as quickly as
possible a one-clause measure which would
enable the Corporation to retire upon
superannuation their employees
65 years of age.
over
At the present time in Belfast there is
a considerable number of these old men
whom the Corporation are retaining in
their service in the hope that they will
obtain a pension when the necessary
measure is passed. At the same time,
owing to the reduction of work in many
of the departments, staffs are being
reduced. It is very desirable that no one
who has been specially trained in A.R.P.
work should have to leave the service on
account of shortness of work, as his
A.R.P. training would be lost. It would
be much more sensible if the old men
could be dispensed with on pension and
the men trained in A.R.P. retained so
that they would, in an emergency, be in
a position to act as volunteers. The
matter is very pressing and of great
practical importance from the point of
view of the defence of the citizens in the
event of an air raid.
I would appeal to the Government to
pass a measure empowering the Belfast
Corporation to pay pensions to men who
have been in their employment 30, 40 or
50 years, and who are hanging on until
a pension scheme is put into operation.
We all know how sad it would be for a
man who has served for forty years in
the Belfast Corporation to be turned out
a month or two before a pensions scheme
came into operation. I would like to
read the following letter I received from
one of the men I refer to:-
-
Would you bring it up in Parliament about the Corporation pensions.
I am over 70 years old, and have been
working over 30 years. I thought I
would have got my pension five or six
years ago, but it is as far back as ever
with the war. I am not telling my
name for fear I get the sack. Will
you please do your best for us. I cannot leave my work. My old woman
is dependent on me.
These are cases I am meeting from
day to day. I have been a long time
in the Belfast Corporation, and I know
that some of these old men have died
when they should have been retired with
pensions. I feel very strongly in this
matter. Salaried officials of the Belfast
Corporation with salaries up to £2,000
a year receive a pension on retirement
without any trouble, and they do not
contribute one halfpenny towards it.
These poor working men are prepared to
pay a contribution towards their pension,
and it is considered by those who have
gone into the matter that after some
years the scheme will pay for itself.
Therefore, I think the Government
should have no hesitation in empowering the Belfast Corporation to put the
scheme into operation.
It is not impossible for the Government to pass a one-clause measure, and
I make this last appeal to the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs to give this matter very
serious consideration. In April last provision was made by the Finance Committee of the Belfast Corporation for
paying these pensions. In the interval
of nine months the Corporation has not
received the necessary power to put the
scheme into operation, and I appeal to
the Government to give the Corporation
that power.

1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can give the
House the result of his representations
to the Minister of Food respecting proposed modifications in the administration
in Northern Ireland of the scheme for
the control of meat and livestock.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): As I think the hon.
Member is aware, the principles of this
scheme when it comes into operation will
apply throughout the United Kingdom.
Discussions are in progress, and I think
the hon. Member may rest assured that
when the scheme comes into operation in
Northern Ireland he will find that it will
fulfil its functions with the least possible
inconvenience to those concerned.

Gentleman aware of the fact that certain

be deprived of this position, and can he
give the House an assurance that the

their former positions when the war

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I cannot give
au assurance, but as far as possible they
are trying to employ as many of these
men as possible.

period is past will these men who have

COMPULSORY INSURANCE
AGAINST WAR RISKS.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can give the House
the result of his representations to the
Board of Trade regarding the compulsory
insurance against war risks of manufacturers' and traders' stocks of £1,000
or over, and whether he has been able
to secure a lower rate for Northern
Ireland in view of the degree of vulnerability being less here than in Great
Britain.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
5 DECEMBER 1939
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour) (who was received with
cheers): I am glad to be able to inform
the hon. Member that the Imperial
Government have now agreed that where
goods are covered by a policy of insurance under Part II. of the War Risks
Insurance Act, 1939 (which deals with
commodity insurance), they will be
deemed to be covered even when in
transit between a port in Great Britain
and a port in Northern Ireland. This
important concession means in effect that
if goods covered by a policy under Part
II. of this Act are lost at sea by enemy
action the trader will be indemnified
without being required to have paid a
marine war risk premium.
The hon. Member will also be aware
that the Board of Trade has again been
able to lighten the burden of commodity
insurance generally, by a reduction of 50
per cent. in the rate of premiums
originally announced.
Both these concessions operate as from
December 3rd, 1939.
Mr. BROWN: May I be allowed to
thank the Minister for the reply and to
say how delighted every Member of this
House is to see him back again to deliver
his reply and to be basking once more in
the sunshine of his charm and old-world
courtesy.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
PETROL FOR LORRIES IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received a
statement issued by the Northern Ireland
Private Motor Lorry Owners' Association
contending that the basic ration of petrol
for lorries in Northern Ireland is considerably less than the English basic
ration, and calling for a step by step
policy with Great Britain; and whether
he will make inquiries from the
Petroleum Officer regarding the matter
and acquaint the House of the result.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have received the
statement referred to by the hon.
Member. As I have already stated in
this House, petrol rationing is a matter
for the Board of Trade, and the
Petroleum Officer acts under instructions
given by that Department.
I have, however, made inquiries and
understand that while, owing to differing
conditions, the basis under which petrol
for lorries is rationed in Northern Ireland differs from that which obtains in
Great Britain, the arrangements in force
here are such as would operate not less
favourably than those in Great Britain.
I further understand that the Board of
Trade are at present reviewing this
question in the light of experience
already gained.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Minister
how he reconciles his statement regarding
this Government having no responsibility
in this matter with the fact that across
the ration books the words are printed,
"This book is the property of the Government of Northern Ireland."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer is
perfectly simple. At the time the Act
was brought into force the authorities in
England, owing to the difficulties they
had, had overlooked the question of
Northern Ireland. We took the question
in hands ourselves. I hope the hon.
Member will take my assurance that the
responsibility rests entirely with the
Board of Trade.
Mr. BROWN: I am perfectly satisfied
with the Minister's explanation.

he say how many men from Strabane
eventually took employment in this remote area, and whether the men who did
go there will be paid for the hours during
which they were willing to work, but were

Mr. GORDON: I would like to thank

regarding the matter.
Mr. GORDON: It would be exceedingly difficult for me to answer that, but
I would like to say that when vacancies
are notified from Great Britain to our
exchanges, we are always anxious to give
an opportunity to men who have limited
opportunities here. If they refuse to
accept the employment, and the courts
determine what just cause is, there is no

Mr. CAMPBELL: Did the court, in
one case in Co. Fermanagh-Enniskillen
-recognise the refusal in the circumstances as justifiable?
Mr. GORDON: It is not for me to
suggest what the decision of the court is.
In some circumstances the court examines
the cases to find out whether the man

conditions are, and if they feel there is

the court states so. As far as these cases

at a good wage, infinitely better than the
wages offered to labourers of a similar

were asked to leave.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I ask leave of the

Mr. GAMBLE: I would like to ask

considered?

WAR-TIME EXPENDITURE.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether it is proposed to set up
in Northern Ireland as in Great Britain,
a Select Committee of the House on wartime expenditure.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
ANDREWS): The answer to my hon.
Friend is in the negative.
The hon. Member will appreciate that all
additional expenditure to be incurred in
this area arising out of war conditions
will, in the main, be incurred by Northern
Ireland departments acting as agents of
Imperial departments, and that such
expenditure will, therefore, automatically
come under review by the Select Committee proposed to be set up by the
Imperial Parliament. I would refer my
hon. Friend in this connection to Mr.
Speaker's ruling on the subject of the
responsibility of this House in relation to
agency expenditure of this kind.
In regard to expenditure which is the
direct responsibility of this Parliament,
I am satisfied that an effective check is
being exercised by my colleagues and by
myself, and furthermore, this House
scrutinises very fully the Estimates which
are presented to it, whereas in the
Imperial Parliament this is only possible
to a much more limited extent. In
addition there is, of course, the check on
expenditure by the Public Accounts
Committee.
Mr. BROWN: While not disputing
what the Minister has said, I would like
to ask him whether he is in a position to
inform the House-he probably may not
be-if any of the Northern Ireland
representatives at Westminster are or will
be included on this Select Committee?
Mr. ANDREWS: I cannot answer
that question. I have no knowledge as
to who will be on the committee.

The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Black): With regard to the question put
by the hon. Member for South Down, if
there are two occupiers they are together
regarded as the occupier and they are
both liable to make the return, but if

return has been made and the duty under
the Act has been complied with.
Regarding the question put by the
hon. Member for Woodvale, I think he
is dealing with the word "implied".
According to the Amendment,"
'Occupier' includes any person who,
by virtue of any contract, or by virtue
of any agreement, whether express or
implied, is, on the prescribed day,
entitled to use, for his own benefit, any
land as agricultural land.
You can understand a man going in
either as tenant or as a person taking a
conacre letting. He would come under
the expressed agreement made with the
owner of the land, but there
be some
may
cases where no expressed agreement has
been made. For instance, a man may be
allowed to go into occupation, or remain
in occupation, of land without a definite
agreement. Such a case might be that of
a man who is the tenant of a piece of
land dying. No administration is taken
out, and some relative goes in and
remains on the land maybe for a year or
two years.
It would be considered in
that case that he was there under an
implied agreement with the landlord, and
this definition is inserted to cover cases
of that nature where there is no expressed
tenancy agreement.
Amendment agreed to.

Castlederg Labourers Benefit 2632
Adjournment-
5 DECEMBER 1939
L
Mr. CAMPBELL: Before this House
rises this afternoon I would like to draw
the attention of the Minister of Labour-
I am sorry he is not here at the moment,
but the Parliamentary Secretary is
present to this question of the migration
of labourers from a very remote part of
County Tyrone to a very remote area of
these islands. That very remote area is
not designated, and I cannot indicate it
with any precision. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary knows where that very
remote area is. It is not in Siberia, and
it is not in China. It may be anywhere
on the face of the map, but I asked the
Parliamentary Secretary if he can say
how many seas the Tyrone labourer
would have to cross to reach this remote
area, and he did not answer. I asked
him how many hundreds of miles he
would have to travel to reach this remote
area, and again he gave me no answer.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Grant): There is a good
service from Germany.
Mr. CAMPBELL: The Parliamentary
Secretary knows the position exactly.
Across the water they may know with far
greater precision than we in this House
know the area that is indicated, but the
reason I mention the matter is this.
Though these men are in a sense under
compulsion to leave a remote part of
County Tyrone, I cannot find that there
is any precedent at all for any compulsion of any kind being exercised on an
English, Scotch, or a
a Welsh labourer
to leave a remote part of England,
Wales, or Scotland and come to a remote
part of Northern Ireland. It seems to be
all the one way that any compulsion of
this kind is now being exercised for the
first time with regard to our labourers,
and they the very poorest class of
labourers in our area.
The Minister said this afternoon that
17 claimants had been disallowed benefit
because they had declined to accept
employment in this remote area. More
than half of those-nine-are married
men. If they went to this area they
would have two homes to maintain.
They would have their home in their own
part of this country, and they would
have a home or lodgings in this remote
district. They would thus have two
homes to maintain, and I do think it is
unreasonable to exercise any form of
coercion or compulsion in a matter of
this kind upon people of this class; to
force them to leave their homes and their
wives and children to travel to districts
which are completely strange to them, to
live in surroundings completely strange
to them, and to live under Arctic conditions of weather which are totally strange
to them. To force men to do all this
under compulsion is not reasonable.
The right hon. Gentleman has made
reference to the wage. He says the wage
offered in this area is infinitely better
than the wage they can hope to earn in
the Strabane district of County Tyrone.
What is the wage? It is 77s a week.
That is the gross wage. You must take
off that 21s 6d, which is the figure fixed
for their board and lodging. That leaves
55s 6d a week, and out of this has to
come the cost of maintaining their home
in County Tyrone. All told, 27 men have
left Belfast to to this area.
go
Some
number, it may be very few, have gone
from other parts, but the total number
that has gone from Northern Ireland is
very, very small.
I want to ask the Minister this,
because I am not clear about it. In the
case of men who go to this remote area
and are willing to work at a rate of 1s 2d
per hour, but who are prevented by the
exceptional severity of the winter
weather from working continuously
during the week, will they be paid for
the hours when they were ready and
willing to work but were prevented from
doing so owing to the severity of the
weather. It may be that they will get
no remuneration whatever for those
hours during which they were willing to
work but were prevented by the conditions prevailing in these high latitudes.
If that is so the wages would not be 55s
a week net, but might be a great deal
less than 55s a week, because anyone who
is familiar with the climate prevailing in
this particular part of the country knows
that the weather conditions there in the
winter months are exceptionally severe.
I know the Minister of Labour is not
hard-hearted by any means. I know he
feels he is acting under a sense of duty in
this matter. It may be said with some
plausibility that if the wages are higher
than in this country why do not the men
jump at this offer, but you must have
regard to all the conditions. I do think
Castlederg Labourers Benefit 2634
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
it is not reasonable to exercise any form
of compulsion on labourers in Northern
Ireland to drive them out of our territory
into conditions which may be totally alien
to them. There is a great country with
millions of people quite contiguous to this
remote area, and is it possible that
recruits for work in this remote area cannot be found there instead of going to the
County of Tyrone and the borders of
Donegal. These men have to travel sixty
miles to Belfast even and cross the sea
again, and if the Minister thinks it is
reasonable to exercise that form of
coercion or compulsion on them I would
not care to accept that view.
I do feel that in this matter there is
not reciprocity with the British labour
exchanges. I have never heard of a case
in which a British labour exchange has
compelled a labourer in a remote part of
England or Scotland to take up employment in Northern Ireland. If there is
such a case I am sure the Minister would
have heard of it, and I think it is not
right on our side to bring any form of
compulsion on applicants who are a
helpless and defenceless class of our
community.
Mr. BROWN: I want to refer to the
unemployment figures issued this morning by the Ministry of Labour for
Northern Ireland. They show that there
were 5,743 more people unemployed in
Northern Ireland in the month of
November than in the previous month,
according to the Ministry of Labour. In
view of those figures I suggest it is the
duty of this House to discuss ways and
means of stopping this increase in our
unemployment figures. Owing to the
conditions that exist to-day the number
of unemployed should have shown a very
big drop, but, unfortunately, it has
shown this increase.
On Saturday night I read in the
"Belfast Telegraph " an announcement
that committees had been set up throughout Great Britain to consider the
mobilisation of the industrial resources of
the country. The "Belfast Telegraph "
called special attention to the fact that
there was no mention whatever
of
Northern Ireland. Under a huge black
heading it announced "Belfast not
mentioned." I want to know why Belfast
was not mentioned. Are we playing our
part in this country or are we not? Are
we to be allowed to play our part
industrially as well as otherwise? These
committees cover thirteen areas, for which
commissioners have been appointed. I
suggest that we should have some information as to why Northern Ireland
was not included.
A short time ago there was a meeting
in London of representatives of the
Dominions, of the Colonies, and of India
to consider the mobilisation of the
industrial resources of the Empire. I am
not aware of any invitation having been
sent to the Prime Minister of Northern
Ireland. Is it possible to find out why
Northern Ireland was not included in
that meeting of the representatives of the
Dominions, of the Colonies, and of India?
Every part of the Empire was represented
with the exception of Northern Ireland.
I think we are entitled to have some
information on this subject. When flax
prices were being considered recently the
Northern Ireland Minister of Agriculture
was not even consulted by the British
Minister of Supply. Northern Ireland
does not seem to have received any consideration in this matter.
I wish to call attention to a speech
delivered by Lord Addison.
He points out that the best use is
not yet being made of the hundreds
of small firms capable of contributing
to the war effort. In the last war there
were munition factories everywhere.
Small firms undertook big jobs, and
did them well. It is true that modern
methods have enormously increased the
speed of production of guns and shells
and aeroplane parts, but while the
plant and labour of a large number of
small firms remain unemployed, we
ought not to be satisfied.
The Minister of Agriculture, in reply
to a question put by me to-day, has not
given any definite information as to what
is to be done with regard to the procuring
of parts for agricultural tractors and
having them assembled in Northern
Ireland. Are we not to be allowed to
assemble these parts for agricultural
tractors? We have hundreds of firms
whose employees have been thrown on the
road because of petrol rationing and food
restrictions. These various firms could
speedily and effectively assemble these
tractor parts. I suggest that a deter-
Castlederg Labourers Benefit 2636
Adjournment-
5 DECEMBER 1939
mined effort should be made to have the
Smaller industries of the Six Counties
given an opportunity to play their part
in this present emergency.
Mr. AGNEW: I am interested in this
question of sending labour to Great
Britain. There is one question that
should be answered-was all local labour
used up in that country before any labour
was asked for from Northern Ireland?
When we consider the season of the year,
with the short days and short hours, we
can easily visualise the number of hours
per day which any man can work. There
would inevitably be broken time, particularly as far as non-skilled labour is
concerned, and that is bound to create
serious hardship, as the man, if he is
married, has two homes to keep. He has
got to pay 21s 6d in that particular area,
and he has to forward a sum of money
to maintain his wife and family. If he
has a bad week, with broken time, what
is the result?
are
I am certain that in Great Britain there
is an ample supply of labour available
before tapping the resources of Northern
Ireland. The amount paid per hour is
not very creditable-1s 2d. There are
unskilled workers in the city of Belfast
earning more, and yet these men
asked to leave Northern Ireland to go to
a place which is not too healthy as far
as weather conditions are concerned, and
are expected to exist there and to provide
the means of livelihood for those dependent upon them on 1s 2d an hour, I
admit that a court of referees is a
statutory body, but at the same time the
position created by this compulsionbecause it is nothing else should be
carefully considered.
A man who seeks employment in a
certain place designated by a particular
Government department, is in duty
bound to face up to the realities of the
situation in order to see how he is going
to fare. The result is, if the court of
referees states he has refused suitable
employment or is not available for work,
he is disallowed benefit for six weeks.
Where is he to go during that period of
six weeks? The Government of Northern
Ireland have made no provision for that
state of affairs. Before any such schemes
are attempted, and before men are sent
to any part of Great Britain, due consideration should be given to the conditions that prevail in the particular area
concerned, and especially to find out in
advance if any local labour, as we may
term it, is available.
It would not be fair to local labour if
men from Northern Ireland were sent
anywhere that the Department desires
without due consideration of the conditions. I would ask the Minister of
Labour to go into this question, because
it is a serious one, and there are possibilities that in the near future such work
will be offered again. We want a
different set of conditions. We want
conditions that will guarantee a decent
standard of living to the worker who has
to go to Great Britain and at the same
time has to provide for his dependents
living at home in Northern Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: I am very sorry to have
to tell the House that the position will
be very much worse before it is better.
The last day I was here the Government
were attacked for not allowing people to
take up work in Great Britain, and now
they are attacked for compelling them to
go. I am not going to dwell on that
aspect of the question, but, at all events,

Let me make it plain to the House that

When it is found in a district in Great
Britain that there is not sufficient local
labour the jobs are circulated in the
"Clearing House Gazette " through the
exchanges in Great Britain and Northern
Ireland. Then we see whether the conditions of employment are good, and
whether it would be right and just and
reasonable to ask men here to accept that
employment. When we are satisfied that
it is reasonable to ask them to take the
employment we make an offer of work,
and if they refuse to accept it we are compelled by Act of Parliament to submit
their case to a court of referees.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 6th December, 1939.
The House met at Twelve of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the. Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
PRICES FOR CROPS AND
LIVESTOCK.
Mr. BROWN asked the Prime Minister
whether he has forwarded to the Imperial
authorities the memorandum presented to
him and the Minister of Agriculture, by
the Ulster Farmers' Union asking the
British Government to assure farmers an
economic price for crops raised under the
Tillage Order during the next three
years; to take over the 1939 potato crop
in order to recoup growers their financial
losses due to the stopping of exports to
foreign countries; to appoint the Ulster
Ministry of Agriculture, with certain
outside assistance, to administer the flax
scheme, and at the same time announce
prices for the 1940 crop on a scale to be.
approved by representatives of growers;
and to guarantee a price for fat cattle and
sheep; and whether he has received any
reply to same, and, if so, what was the
nature of the reply.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have discussed the problems referred to with the
Imperial Ministers concerned, but am
not in a position to make any announcement in advance of anticipated statements
by the responsible. Departments. I can
assure the hon. Member that most careful
consideration is being given to the representations put forward by this Government and our Members at Westminster,
working in co-operation. Farmers should
with complete confidence proceed with the
task of putting every possible acre of land
under plough.
Mr. BROWN: While thanking the
Prime Minister for his reply to my question, part of which deals with livestock,
may I ask if he or the Minister of
Agriculture can give. us any information
as to the alarming shortage of feeding
stuffs for such livestock, reported in last
night's "Belfast Telegraph," the new
editor and assistant editor of which, Mr.
R. M. Sayers and Mr. Thomas M'Mullan,
we all most heartily congratulate, on their
well-merited promotion?
The PRIME MINISTER: I may say
that the conversation covered cattle as
well, and the answer I have given here
applies to livestock as well as feeding
stuffs; that is to say, in time we will be
able to give the House information as to
what is going to be done.
Mr. BROWN: Once again I thank the
Prime Minister for his satisfactory
assurance on this point. Perhaps you
would permit me to put this point in a
spirit of helpfulness: Will the Government explore the possibilities of taking
over the surplus and unsaleable stocks of
potatoes in Northern Ireland and erecting silos at various centres for their
storage, in a cooked condition, to augment
depleted supplies of ordinary feeding
stuffs?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I do not think at the
moment there is any great necessity for
that, because potatoes are being sold for
feeding stuffs by farmers in the various
localities. Actually, in point of fact,
there is no difficulty at the moment in a
man who wishes to sell potatoes selling
them, perhaps not at a satisfactory
price, but at a better price than a few
weeks ago.
Mr. BROWN: A hopeless price.

report that the House has this day
attended in the Senate, when the
Proclamation proroguing this present
Session of Parliament was read by the
Speaker of the Senate as follows: :-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
shall, in His Majesty's name, summon,
prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of
Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the
nineteenth day of December, one thousand
nine hundred and thirty-nine:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, Knight of the
Most Noble Order of the Garter, Knight
of the Most Illustrious Order of Saint
Patrick, Governor of Northern Ireland,
by this Proclamation do publish and
declare His Majesty's pleasure that the
said Parliament be, as from the reading
of this Proclamation in the Parliament of
Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday,
the nineteenth day of December, one
thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine.
AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the
said nineteenth day of December, one
thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine,
assemble and be holden at Stormont for
the despatch of divers urgent and
important affairs, and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to
give their attendance accordingly.
Given this sixth day of December, one
thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine.
(Signed by his own hand),
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
